title: Spanish A1
description: Latin American Spanish from your first word to CEFR level A1, the level of the Instituto Cervantes DELE A1 exam. Grammar lessons cover sounds, spelling and written accents, greetings, ser and estar, numbers, gender, articles and adjective agreement, the present tense with its stem changes and irregular verbs, hay, gustar, ir a + infinitive for plans, reflexive verbs for daily routines, telling the time and giving dates, commands for directions, and a first look at the past with the preterite and the present perfect. About 700 everyday words, with Mexican usage as the standard and Spain's words noted, are learned through typed vocabulary reviews with pronunciation, conjugation drills practise the present, the preterite, the perfect and the imperative, and a reading list points to graded readers and free material you can use on your own.
author: Erudior

lessons.title: Sounds, letters and written accents
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Spanish is easy to read aloud: each letter has one sound (or two, by a simple rule), and the
accent marks show which part of a word to stress. With the sounds in this lesson you can read
any Spanish word, and usually write a word you hear.

You'll learn the alphabet as it's said in Mexico, the five vowels, the consonants that differ
from English, the stress rule and the written accent, along with the first words everyone needs:
greetings, *por favor* (please), *gracias* (thank you), and how to ask someone to repeat or
spell something. Read every example out loud.

## The alphabet

Spanish has 27 letters: the 26 of English plus *ñ*. Older books also list *ch* and *ll* as
letters; since 2010 the Spanish language academies count them as pairs of letters, but you still
need their sounds. You need the letter names to spell your name.

| Letter | Name | Letter | Name | Letter | Name |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| A | a | J | jota | R | erre |
| B | be (*be grande*) | K | ka | S | ese |
| C | ce | L | ele | T | te |
| D | de | M | eme | U | u |
| E | e | N | ene | V | ve (*ve chica*) |
| F | efe | Ñ | eñe | W | doble u |
| G | ge | O | o | X | equis |
| H | hache | P | pe | Y | ye (*i griega*) |
| I | i | Q | cu | Z | zeta |

B and V are pronounced exactly the same in Spanish (more on that below), so their names would
sound the same too. In Mexico people tell them apart as *be grande* ("big b") and *ve chica*
("little v"); you'll also hear *be larga* and *ve corta*. Spain says *uve* for V and *uve doble*
for W. The academies recommend the name *ye* for Y, but many people still say *i griega*
("Greek i").

## The five vowels

Spanish has five **[[vowel]]** sounds, written *a, e, i, o, u*, and they never change. English
vowels slide and blur ("go" ends in a "w", "day" ends in a "y", and unstressed vowels shrink to
"uh"). Spanish vowels are short, clear and steady.

| Vowel | Sounds like | Example |
|---|---|---|
| *a* | the *a* in "father", but shorter | *hola* (hello), *nada* (nothing) |
| *e* | the *e* in "bet" | *nombre* (name), *de nada* (you're welcome) |
| *i* | the *ee* in "see", short | *sí* (yes), *escribir* (to write) |
| *o* | the *o* in "or", with no "w" at the end | *no*, *adiós* (goodbye) |
| *u* | the *oo* in "food", short | *luego* (later), *muchas* (many) |

The picture shows where each vowel sits in the mouth: *i* and *e* at the front with spread lips,
*o* and *u* at the back with rounded lips, and *a* low in the middle with the mouth open widest.

![A vowel chart shaped like an upside-down triangle. The front of the mouth is on the left, the back on the right; the top is a closed mouth, the bottom an open one. i is front and high with spread lips, e is front and in the middle, a is low and central with the mouth wide open, o is back and in the middle with rounded lips, u is back and high with tightly rounded lips.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

When *i* or *u* stands next to another vowel, the two usually blend into one **[[syllable]]**:
*gracias* is *gra-cias* and *buenos* is *bue-nos*. Each vowel keeps its sound: *bue* is "bweh".

## Consonants that differ from English

Most consonants sound roughly as in English. These are the ones to learn:

| Spelling | Sound | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| *h* | silent | *hola*, *hasta luego* (see you later) |
| *j*, and *g* before *e* or *i* | a breathy "h" from the back of the throat | *jota*, *gente* (people) |
| *g* elsewhere, and *gu* before *e* or *i* | hard g, as in "go" (the *u* is silent) | *gracias*, *guitarra* |
| *gü* | "gw" (the two dots say: pronounce the u) | *pingüino* (penguin) |
| *c* before *e* or *i*, *z*, *s* | all "s" | *cinco* (five), *zeta*, *despacio* (slowly) |
| *c* elsewhere, and *qu* before *e* or *i* | "k" (the *u* in *qu* is silent) | *con permiso*, *¿qué?* |
| *ll* and *y* | the same sound, like English "y" in "yes" | *me llamo* (my name is), *yo* (I) |
| *ñ* | "ny", as in "canyon" | *mañana* (tomorrow), *eñe* |
| *r* (inside or at the end of a word) | a single quick tap, like the "tt" in American "butter" | *pero* (but), *por favor* |
| *rr*, and *r* at the start of a word or after *l, n, s* | a rolled r, several taps | *perro* (dog), *Roberto*, *Enrique* |
| *b* and *v* | the same sound; soft between vowels | *buenos*, *vez* (time) |
| *d* between vowels | soft, like the "th" in "this" | *nada*, *adiós* |
| *ch* | as in "church" | *muchas gracias* |

Pronouncing *c* (before *e, i*), *z* and *s* all as "s" is called **[[seseo]]**; it's the norm in
all of Latin America, while most of Spain says *z* and *ce, ci* like English "th". Pronouncing
*ll* and *y* the same is called **[[yeísmo]]**, the norm almost everywhere. Because of them, you
can't always tell from the sound whether a word has *s*, *c* or *z*, or *ll* or *y*. That's what
*¿Cómo se escribe?* is for.

The letter *x* is usually "ks", as in *taxi*. In a few names it keeps an old sound: the breathy
*j* in *México* and *Oaxaca* ("MEH-hee-ko"), and "s" in *Xochimilco* (in Mexico City).

## Where the stress falls

Nearly every Spanish word of two or more syllables has one stressed syllable, said a little louder and
longer. This is called **[[word stress]]**, and Spanish has a rule for it that works for almost
every word:

1. If a word ends in a vowel, *n* or *s*, stress the second-to-last syllable: *HO-la*,
   *GRA-cias*, *BUE-nos*, *a-pe-LLI-do* (surname), *es-CRI-be* (writes).
2. If it ends in any other consonant, stress the last syllable: *de-le-tre-AR* (to spell),
   *fa-VOR*, *es-pa-ÑOL*.
3. If a word breaks rules 1 and 2, it carries a **[[written accent]]** (´) on the stressed vowel:
   *a-DIÓS* (ends in *s*, but stressed at the end), *per-DÓN* (sorry), *LÁ-piz* (pencil),
   *te-LÉ-fo-no*.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Does a word need a written accent?
  accDescr: First find the syllable you hear stressed. Then look at the last letter of the word. If the word ends in a vowel, n or s, the normal stress is on the second-to-last syllable; if it ends in another consonant, the normal stress is on the last syllable. If the stress you hear is where the rule puts it, write no accent, as in hola and favor. If it is somewhere else, write an accent on the stressed vowel, as in adiós, lápiz and teléfono.
  A["Say the word and find the stressed syllable"] --> B{"Last letter: a vowel, n or s?"}
  B -- "yes" --> C["Normal stress: second-to-last syllable"]
  B -- "no" --> D["Normal stress: last syllable"]
  C --> E{"Is the stress where the rule says?"}
  D --> E
  E -- "yes" --> F["No written accent: hola, nombre, favor"]
  E -- "no" --> G["Write the accent: adiós, perdón, lápiz, teléfono"]
```

The written accent is part of the spelling, and it is used on capital letters too (*Ángela*).
In this app, use the buttons under the answer box; on a phone, press and hold the vowel.

An accent also breaks a vowel blend into two syllables: *día* (day) is *DÍ-a*, two syllables,
not "dya".

## Accents that tell words apart

A few short words are spelled the same except for the accent, which tells you which word it is.
This is called a **[[diacritic accent]]**:

| With accent | Without accent |
|---|---|
| *sí* — yes | *si* — if |
| *tú* — you | *tu* — your |
| *él* — he | *el* — the |

Question words carry an accent too: *¿qué?* (what?), *¿cómo?* (how?).

## ¿ and ¡: marks at the start

Spanish opens a question with ¿ and an exclamation with ¡, so you know from the start how to say
the sentence: *¿Cómo se escribe?* (How is it spelled?), *¡Hola!* The opening mark goes where the
question starts, which isn't always the start of the sentence: *Perdón, ¿puede repetir?* (Sorry,
can you repeat?). When you type answers in this app, you can leave both marks out.

## Greetings and polite words

The greeting depends on the time of day:

![A bar showing the day from 6 a.m. to midnight. Buenos días covers the morning until about 12 noon. Buenas tardes covers the afternoon and early evening until it gets dark, about 7 or 8 p.m. Buenas noches covers the night. A small note says buenas noches is also used to say goodbye at night.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

- *Buenos días* (good morning) until about midday; *buenas tardes* (good afternoon, good
  evening) until it gets dark; *buenas noches* (good evening, good night) after dark, both to
  greet and to say goodbye.
- *Hola* (hello, hi) works any time and is friendly; many people say *Hola, buenos días*.
- Goodbye: *adiós* (goodbye), *hasta luego* (see you later; also just "bye"), *hasta mañana*
  (see you tomorrow).
- *Por favor* (please), *gracias* (thank you), *muchas gracias* (thank you very much), *de nada*
  (you're welcome).
- *Perdón* (sorry) for a small mistake or bump. *Disculpe* (excuse me) to get a stranger's
  attention politely. *Con permiso* (excuse me) to pass someone, leave a room or leave the table;
  in Mexico the answer is often *Propio* or *Adelante* ("go ahead"). The three overlap in
  real life (*perdón* can also get attention, and *disculpe* also apologizes), but these are
  their most typical uses.
- *Sí* (yes) and *no* (no). *No* also means "not": *No, gracias.*

## When you don't understand

These are the most useful phrases of your first months: *¿Puede repetir, por favor?* (Can you repeat, please?), *más despacio* (more slowly), *otra vez*
(again). In Mexico you'll hear *¿Mande?* (Pardon? Yes?) when someone didn't catch what you said, or
to answer when someone calls your name; it's polite and very Mexican.

To ask how a word is written, say *¿Cómo se escribe?* The answer is the letters one by one
(to spell is *deletrear*), with help for letters that sound alike: *con be grande*, *con hache*
(with an h), *con doble ele* (with ll), *con acento* (with an accent).

## Dialogue: at a reception desk in Guadalajara

> Recepcionista: Buenas tardes.
>
> Kate: Buenas tardes. Mi nombre es Kate Hughes.
>
> Recepcionista: ¿Mande? ¿Puede repetir, por favor? Más despacio.
>
> Kate: Sí, perdón. Kate… Hughes.
>
> Recepcionista: ¿Cómo se escribe el apellido?
>
> Kate: Hache, u, ge, hache, e, ese.
>
> Recepcionista: Otra vez, por favor.
>
> Kate: Hache, u, ge, hache, e, ese.
>
> Recepcionista: Gracias. ¿Y el nombre? ¿Con ka?
>
> Kate: Sí, ka, a, te, e.
>
> Recepcionista: Muchas gracias.
>
> Kate: De nada. Con permiso… ¡Hasta luego!

Good afternoon. — Good afternoon. My name is Kate Hughes. — Pardon? Can you repeat, please? More
slowly. — Yes, sorry. Kate… Hughes. — How is the surname spelled? — H, U, G, H, E, S. — Again,
please. — H, U, G, H, E, S. — Thank you. And the first name? With a K? — Yes, K, A, T, E. —
Thank you very much. — You're welcome. Excuse me… See you later!

*Mi nombre es…* means "my name is…" (Lesson 2 teaches the more usual *Me llamo…*). Kate spells
with Spanish letter names: *hache, u, ge*.

## Pronunciation

- *gracias*: "GRAH-syahs", two syllables, with a tapped *r*; *c* before *i* is "s".
- *hasta luego*: the *h* is silent: "AHS-tah LWEH-go".
- *perdón*: stress at the end because of the accent; tap the *r*.
- *disculpe*: "dees-KOOL-peh"; the final *e* is a clear "eh".
- *apellido*: "ah-peh-YEE-doh"; *ll* is a "y" sound.
- *deletrear*: "deh-leh-treh-AR"; every vowel is pronounced, *e* and *a* in separate syllables.

## Common mistakes

- Pronouncing the *h*. *Hola* is "OH-lah"; *hasta* is "AHS-tah".
- Sliding the vowels. *No* is a short, pure "no", not English "noh-w"; *de* is "deh", not "day".
- Shrinking unstressed vowels to "uh". Every vowel in *muchas gracias* keeps its own sound.
- Reading *j* and *ge, gi* as in English. *Jota* starts with a breathy "h", and so does *gente*.
- Forgetting the opening ¿ or ¡ in writing. They're part of correct Spanish.
- Leaving out a written accent: *adios* and *perdon* are misspelled, and *si* (if) is not *sí*
  (yes).
- Spelling with English letter names: *e* is "eh", *i* is "ee", *j* is *jota*.

## Key points

- Five pure vowels, *a, e, i, o, u*, always pronounced the same; the only silent vowel is the *u*
  in *que, qui, gue, gui*.
- *h* is silent; *j* (and *g* before *e, i*) is a breathy "h"; *ll* and *y* sound the same;
  *c* before *e, i*, *z* and *s* are all "s" in Latin America; *b* and *v* sound the same.
- Words ending in a vowel, *n* or *s* stress the second-to-last syllable; others stress the last.
  A written accent marks every exception.
- *sí/si, tú/tu, él/el*: the accent changes the word.
- Questions open with ¿, exclamations with ¡.
- *¿Puede repetir, por favor? Más despacio. ¿Cómo se escribe?* — use them often.

lessons.title: Greetings, introductions and ser
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 1 gave you the sounds and the first polite words. Now you'll have your first real
conversation: say hello, ask someone's name and how they are, say where you're from and where
you live, and ask the same questions back. To do that you need three things: the choice between
the two words for "you", *tú* and *usted*; the first three forms of the verb *ser* (to be); and
a handful of question words.

## Two ways to say "you": tú and usted

Spanish has an informal and a formal word for "you" when you talk to one person:

- *tú* is informal: for friends, family, children, and people your age in relaxed places;
- *usted* is the **[[formal address]]**: for strangers, older people, customers and staff in shops
  and offices, your boss, a doctor, a police officer.

In Latin America, *usted* is the safe choice with anyone you don't know, and switching to *tú*
too early can sound pushy. If someone speaks to you with *tú*, you can usually answer with *tú*.
Young people often use *tú* with each other from the start. Habits vary between countries,
regions and families, so listen to what others use with you.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Choosing tú or usted for one person
  accDescr: To choose a word for you when talking to one person, ask first whether the person is a friend, a family member or a child. If yes, use tú. If not, ask whether the person is about your age in a relaxed setting and already uses tú with you. If yes, use tú. If not, for example a stranger, an older person, someone at work or an official, use usted. When unsure, use usted, which is never rude.
  A["Talking to one person"] --> B{"A friend, family member or child?"}
  B -- "yes" --> T["tú"]
  B -- "no" --> C{"Your age, relaxed setting, and they use tú with you?"}
  C -- "yes" --> T
  C -- "no" --> U["usted: strangers, older people, work, officials"]
  U --> D["Not sure? Use usted. It is never rude."]
```

The verb changes with the choice. *Usted* takes the same verb form as "he" and "she", because
it comes from an old phrase, *vuestra merced* ("your grace"): *¿Cómo está usted?* (How are you, formal?),
*¿Cómo estás?* (How are you, informal?).

## The verb ser (to be)

Spanish verbs are listed in the dictionary in a form ending in *-ar*, *-er* or *-ir*, called
the **[[infinitive]]**: *ser* (to be), *hablar* (to speak). To use a verb, you change its ending to
show who is doing it. This is called **[[conjugation]]**. *Ser* is irregular, so its forms have to be
learned by heart. Here are the singular forms (the plural comes in Lesson 6):

| Person | ser | English |
|---|---|---|
| *yo* | *soy* | I am |
| *tú* | *eres* | you are (informal) |
| *usted* | *es* | you are (formal) |
| *él* (he), *ella* (she) | *es* | he is, she is |

*Yo* (I) is written with a small letter, unlike English "I". *Él* and *ella* are taught fully in
Lesson 4; you need them now only to understand *es*.

Use *ser* to say who someone is and where they're from:

*Soy Ana.* — I'm Ana.
*¿Eres Daniel?* — Are you Daniel?
*Usted es el señor Ruiz, ¿no?* — You're Mr Ruiz, aren't you?

### Ser de: where you're from

*Ser de* + a city or country means "to be from": *Soy de Chicago.* — I'm from Chicago. *¿De dónde
eres?* — Where are you from? (informal). *¿De dónde es usted?* — Where are you from? (formal).
The *de* moves to the front of the question, before *dónde*, because Spanish doesn't leave a
preposition at the end the way English does ("where … from?").

*Soy de Toronto, en Canadá.* — I'm from Toronto, in Canada.
*Ella es de Puebla, una ciudad de México.* — She's from Puebla, a city in Mexico.

### Vivo en: where you live

To say where you live, use the fixed phrase *vivo en* (I live in): *Vivo en Denver.* The question
is *¿Dónde vives?* (Where do you live?, informal) or *¿Dónde vive usted?* (formal). The verb
behind these, *vivir*, is taught in Lesson 7; for now, learn the phrases as they are.

## Names: me llamo, te llamas, se llama

The everyday way to give your name is *Me llamo…*, literally "I call myself…". Learn the three
phrases as they are; how they work is explained in Lesson 16.

| Question | Answer |
|---|---|
| *¿Cómo te llamas?* — What's your name? (informal) | *Me llamo Laura.* — My name is Laura. |
| *¿Cómo se llama usted?* — What's your name? (formal) | *Me llamo Jorge Ramírez.* |
| *¿Cómo se llama?* — What's his/her name? | *Se llama Sofía.* — Her name is Sofía. |

The question word is *cómo* (how), not *qué* (what): Spanish asks "how do you call yourself?".
*Soy Laura* (I'm Laura) is just as correct and very common.

When you meet someone, say *Mucho gusto* (nice to meet you; literally "much pleasure") or
*Encantado* if you're a man and *Encantada* if you're a woman ("delighted"). The answer is the
same phrase, or *Igualmente* (likewise).

## How are you?

| Question | Who to | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| *¿Qué tal?* | anyone, casual | How are things? / How's it going? |
| *¿Cómo estás?* | *tú* | How are you? |
| *¿Cómo está usted?* | *usted* | How are you? |

Answers go from good to bad: *muy bien* (very well), *bien* (well, fine), *más o menos* (so-so;
literally "more or less"), *mal* (not well, badly). Politeness asks you to return the question:
*Bien, gracias, ¿y tú?* or *Bien, gracias, ¿y usted?* Use *también* (also, too) when you agree:
*Yo también.* — Me too.

*Estás* and *está* come from a second verb meaning "to be", *estar*, which is taught in Lesson 9.
For now, *¿Cómo estás?* and *¿Cómo está usted?* are fixed phrases.

## Question words

A **[[question word]]** opens a question that can't be answered with yes or no. Each one has a
written accent and the question opens with ¿:

| Question word | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| *¿quién?* | who? | *¿Quién es?* — Who is it? |
| *¿cómo?* | how? | *¿Cómo te llamas?* |
| *¿dónde?* | where? | *¿Dónde vives?* |
| *¿de dónde?* | where … from? | *¿De dónde eres?* |

## Señor, señora, señorita

*El señor* (Mr, sir, gentleman), *la señora* (Mrs, Ms, madam, lady) and *la señorita* (Miss, young
lady) go before a surname. Talking about someone, use the article: *La señora López es de
Monterrey.* Talking to someone, leave it out: *Buenos días, señora López.* Alone, they're polite
forms of address: *Gracias, señor.* In Mexico *señorita* is used for girls and young women and
is common in shops; *señora* is used for older or married women. Many women don't like being
called *señora* too early, so go by the person's age, and follow what others call her. In writing
they're often shortened to *Sr.*, *Sra.* and *Srta.*

## Filling in a card

The picture shows a student card, the kind of form where you'll see these words: *nombre*,
*apellido* (*apellidos* when there are two), *ciudad* (city) and *país* (country).

![A student ID card from a language school in Mexico. It has four filled-in lines: Nombre Daniel, Apellidos Ruiz Castro, Ciudad Monterrey, País México.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## A kiss or a handshake?

In Mexico and much of Latin America, women greeting women, and men greeting women, often touch
right cheeks with a light kiss sound, even at a first meeting in a social setting. Men usually
shake hands, and friends may add a hug. At work and in formal meetings, a handshake is the norm.
These are general patterns, and they vary by country, region and person; follow the other
person's lead.

## Dialogue: at a party in Monterrey

> Daniel: ¡Hola! ¿Qué tal?
>
> Kate: Hola. Bien, gracias. ¿Y tú?
>
> Daniel: Muy bien. Me llamo Daniel. ¿Cómo te llamas?
>
> Kate: Me llamo Kate. Mucho gusto.
>
> Daniel: Encantado. ¿De dónde eres?
>
> Kate: Soy de Denver, en Estados Unidos. Y tú, ¿eres de Monterrey?
>
> Daniel: Sí, soy de aquí. Pero vivo en la Ciudad de México. ¿Quién es ella?
>
> Kate: Es la señora Ortiz, mi maestra de español. ¡Señora Ortiz! ¿Cómo está usted?
>
> Sra. Ortiz: Más o menos, Kate, gracias. ¿Y usted, joven? ¿Cómo se llama?
>
> Daniel: Me llamo Daniel Ruiz. Mucho gusto, señora.

Hi! How's it going? — Hi. Fine, thanks. And you? — Very well. My name's Daniel. What's your name?
— My name's Kate. Nice to meet you. — Delighted. Where are you from? — I'm from Denver, in the
United States. And you, are you from Monterrey? — Yes, I'm from here. But I live in Mexico City.
Who's she? — She's Mrs Ortiz, my Spanish teacher. Mrs Ortiz! How are you? — So-so, Kate, thanks.
And you, young man? What's your name? — My name's Daniel Ruiz. Nice to meet you, ma'am.

Notice the switch: Kate and Daniel use *tú* with each other, but Kate uses *usted* with her
older teacher, and the teacher uses *usted* with Daniel, whom she doesn't know. New words in passing:
*pero* (but), *aquí* (here), *mi maestra* (my teacher), *joven* (young man).

## Pronunciation

- *usted*: stress on the last syllable, "oos-TEHD", with a very soft final *d*.
- *llamo, llamas*: *ll* is a "y" sound: "YAH-mo".
- *señor, señora*: *ñ* is "ny": "seh-NYOR".
- *ciudad*: "syoo-DAHD"; *ciu* is one syllable.
- *país*: two syllables, "pah-EES"; the accent breaks the vowel pair.
- *encantado*: "en-kahn-TAH-doh"; the *d* between vowels is soft, like "th" in "this".

## Common mistakes

- Using *tú* with everyone. In Latin America, start with *usted* with strangers and older people.
- *¿Qué te llamas?* Wrong: the question word is *cómo*: *¿Cómo te llamas?*
- *¿Dónde eres de?* Spanish puts *de* first: *¿De dónde eres?*
- *Usted eres.* *Usted* takes the *es* form: *usted es*.
- Writing *Yo* with a capital in the middle of a sentence: *Y yo soy de Canadá.*
- Saying *encantado* as a woman. Women say *encantada*.

## Key points

- *tú* (informal) and *usted* (formal) both mean "you" for one person; *usted* uses the *es* form.
- *ser*: *yo soy, tú eres, usted es, él/ella es*. *Ser de* = to be from: *Soy de Denver.*
- *¿Cómo te llamas? / ¿Cómo se llama usted?* — *Me llamo…*
- *Mucho gusto. Encantado / Encantada.*
- *¿Qué tal? ¿Cómo estás? ¿Cómo está usted?* — *muy bien, bien, más o menos, mal*, then *¿y tú? /
  ¿y usted?*
- Question words: *¿quién?, ¿cómo?, ¿dónde?, ¿de dónde?*
- *señor, señora, señorita*: with the article when you talk about someone, without it when you
  talk to them.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Numbers, age and phone numbers
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Numbers come up in almost every conversation: your age, your phone number, a price, a room
number, the time. This lesson teaches the numbers from 0 to 100, how to ask and give your age,
how Mexicans read a phone number, and how to say an e-mail address. With Lesson 2 you'll then be
able to fill in a form or give your details at a counter.

## 0 to 15: learn them by heart

| | | | |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 *cero* | 4 *cuatro* | 8 *ocho* | 12 *doce* |
| 1 *uno* | 5 *cinco* | 9 *nueve* | 13 *trece* |
| 2 *dos* | 6 *seis* | 10 *diez* | 14 *catorce* |
| 3 *tres* | 7 *siete* | 11 *once* | 15 *quince* |

Watch the sounds from Lesson 1: *cinco* and *doce* have the "s" sound of *c* before *e, i*;
*cuatro* is "KWAH-tro"; *seis* rhymes with English "case"; *nueve* is "NWEH-veh"; *diez* is
"dyes". *Once* (11) is "OHN-seh", nothing to do with English "once".

## 16 to 29: one word

From 16 to 19, Spanish says "ten and six", written as one word with *dieci-*: *dieciséis* (16),
*diecisiete* (17), *dieciocho* (18), *diecinueve* (19).

From 21 to 29, *veinte* (20) shrinks to *veinti-*, again in one word: *veintiuno* (21),
*veintidós* (22), *veintitrés* (23), *veinticuatro*, *veinticinco*, *veintiséis* (26),
*veintisiete*, *veintiocho*, *veintinueve*.

Why do *dieciséis, veintidós, veintitrés* and *veintiséis* have an accent? Apply the stress rule
from Lesson 1: they end in *s*, so the stress would normally fall on the second-to-last syllable.
But the stress is on the last one (*vein-ti-DÓS*), so it needs a written accent. *Dos*, *tres* and
*seis* alone are one syllable and need none.

## 30 to 100: tens + y + units

| | | |
|---|---|---|
| 30 *treinta* | 60 *sesenta* | 90 *noventa* |
| 40 *cuarenta* | 70 *setenta* | 100 *cien* |
| 50 *cincuenta* | 80 *ochenta* | |

From 31 to 99, say the ten, then *y* (and), then the unit, as three separate words:
*treinta y uno* (31), *cuarenta y cinco* (45), *noventa y nueve* (99). Only 16–29 are written as
one word. (The academies also accept rare one-word spellings such as *treintaiuno*, but almost
everyone writes three words, and so does this course.)

Keep *sesenta* (60) and *setenta* (70) apart: *ses-* goes with *seis*, *set-* with *siete*.

*Cien* is exactly 100: *cien años* (a hundred years). Above 100 it becomes *ciento*: *ciento
uno* (101), *ciento veinte* (120). You'll learn the hundreds in Lesson 12.

## Uno, un, una

*Uno* is the number you count with: *uno, dos, tres…* Before a noun it changes: *un* before a
masculine noun, *una* before a feminine one (nouns and their gender are taught in Lesson 5).
Dropping the end of a word before a noun, as *uno* does in *un*, is called **[[apocope]]**:

*un año* — one year · *una letra* — one letter · *veintiún años* — twenty-one years ·
*treinta y una letras* — thirty-one letters

*Veintiún* needs an accent once it loses its last vowel (it ends in *n* and is stressed at the
end). *Cien* is the same kind of shortening, from *ciento*.

## Asking and giving your age

Spanish says your age with "have", not "be": you *have* years.

*¿Cuántos años tienes?* — How old are you? (literally "how many years do you have?", informal)
*¿Cuántos años tiene usted?* — How old are you? (formal)
*Tengo treinta y dos años.* — I'm thirty-two.

Learn *tienes*, *tiene* and *tengo* as part of these phrases; the verb *tener* (to have) comes in
Lesson 6. Never say *Soy treinta*: that means nothing in Spanish. And keep *años* with its tilde:
without it, *anos* is a very different (and rude) word. *La edad* (age) is the word you'll see on
forms: *Edad: 32*.

*Cuántos* (how many) changes to *cuántas* before a feminine noun: *¿Cuántas letras tiene tu
nombre?* — How many letters does your name have?

## Phone numbers

In Mexico every phone number, landline or *celular* (cell phone), has ten digits, and you dial
all ten everywhere in the country (since August 2019). The first two or three digits are the
area: 55 for Mexico City, 33 for Guadalajara, 81 for Monterrey.

Mexicans usually read a number in pairs, so it sounds like a string of numbers from 10 to 99.
The picture shows how:

![A phone number, 55 12 34 07 80, written in five pairs. Under each pair is how it is said: cincuenta y cinco, doce, treinta y cuatro, cero siete, ochenta.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

A pair that starts with 0 is read digit by digit (*cero siete*), and some people read the whole
number one digit at a time; both are fine, and *¿Puede repetir, más despacio?* always is.

To ask for a number: *¿Cuál es tu número?* (What's your number?, informal), *¿Cuál es su
número de teléfono?* (formal: *su* = your, formal). Spanish uses *cuál* (which), not *qué*, when
you ask for one item out of many possible ones: *¿Cuál es tu número?* not *¿Qué es tu número?*

## E-mail addresses

*El correo electrónico* (e-mail), often just *el correo*, is read with these words: *arroba* (@),
*punto* (dot), *guion bajo* (underscore), *guion* (hyphen). Spell any unusual part:

*kate.hughes@correo.mx* — *kate, punto, hughes, arroba, correo, punto, eme, equis*, and then,
for the unusual part, *hughes se escribe hache, u, ge, hache, e, ese*.

*La dirección* means both "address" (where you live, or an e-mail address: *la dirección de
correo*) and "direction".

The picture below shows a phone's contact screen with these details.

![A phone screen showing a contact for Daniel Ruiz. It lists four boxes: Celular 81 23 45 67 90, Correo electrónico daniel_ruiz@correo.mx, Dirección Calle Hidalgo 15, Monterrey, and Edad 24.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Dialogue: signing up at a language school

> Recepcionista: Buenos días. ¿Cómo se llama usted?
>
> Kate: Kate Hughes.
>
> Recepcionista: ¿Cuántos años tiene, señora Hughes?
>
> Kate: Tengo treinta y cuatro años.
>
> Recepcionista: Muy bien. ¿Cuál es su número de celular?
>
> Kate: Es el cincuenta y cinco, setenta y ocho, diecinueve, cero seis, cuarenta y dos.
>
> Recepcionista: Cincuenta y cinco, setenta y ocho… ¿Puede repetir, por favor?
>
> Kate: Cincuenta y cinco, setenta y ocho, diecinueve, cero seis, cuarenta y dos.
>
> Recepcionista: Gracias. ¿Y su correo electrónico?
>
> Kate: kate punto hughes, arroba, correo, punto, eme, equis.
>
> Recepcionista: Perfecto. Y su dirección, ¿cuál es?
>
> Kate: Calle Juárez, número veintiséis.

Good morning. What's your name? — Kate Hughes. — How old are you, Mrs Hughes? — I'm thirty-four.
— Very good. What's your cell number? — It's 55 78 19 06 42. — 55, 78… Can you repeat, please? —
55 78 19 06 42. — Thank you. And your e-mail? — kate dot hughes at correo dot mx. — Perfect. And
your address, what is it? — Juárez Street, number 26.

*Es el…* (it's the…) is a natural way to begin giving a number. *Calle* means street.

## Pronunciation

- *cuatro, cuarenta*: start with "kwa"; *u* before a vowel glides.
- *seis, dieciséis*: *ei* as in "eight": "says", "dyeh-see-SAYS".
- *veinte*: "BAYN-teh"; *v* sounds like *b*.
- *quince*: "KEEN-seh"; the *u* after *q* is silent.
- *cincuenta*: "seen-KWEN-tah".
- *celular*: "seh-loo-LAR", stress at the end (it ends in *r*).
- *teléfono*: stress on *LÉ*, shown by the accent.

## Common mistakes

- Writing 16–29 as separate words. It's *veintidós*, not *veinte y dos*; but *treinta y dos*
  is three words.
- Forgetting the accents on *dieciséis, veintidós, veintitrés, veintiséis*.
- Mixing up *sesenta* (60) and *setenta* (70).
- *Soy veinte años.* Age uses *tener*: *Tengo veinte años.*
- *¿Qué es tu número?* Ask with *cuál*: *¿Cuál es tu número?*
- *Uno año.* Before a noun, *uno* becomes *un* or *una*: *un año*.
- *Anos* for *años*. Always write the tilde.

## Key points

- 0–15 are separate words to learn; 16–19 are *dieci-* + unit, 21–29 *veinti-* + unit, in one word.
- Accents: *dieciséis, veintidós, veintitrés, veintiséis* (and *veintiún*).
- 31–99: ten + *y* + unit, in three words: *cuarenta y ocho*.
- *cien* = 100 exactly; *ciento* from 101.
- *uno* → *un / una* before a noun.
- Age: *¿Cuántos años tienes? — Tengo … años.* (*la edad* = age)
- Mexican phone numbers have ten digits, usually read in pairs.
- *¿Cuál es tu número?* E-mail: *arroba* (@), *punto* (.).

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Pronouns, the present of -ar verbs and asking questions
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

So far you've used verbs as fixed phrases: *soy*, *me llamo*, *vivo en*. In this lesson you'll
learn to make verb forms yourself. Spanish verbs come in three families, by the ending of the
infinitive: *-ar*, *-er* and *-ir*. The *-ar* family is by far the largest, and its present tense
follows one pattern that works for thousands of verbs. You'll also learn all the words for "I,
you, he, she, we, they", how to say "not", and how to ask questions with and without a question
word.

## Subject pronouns

A **[[subject pronoun]]** is a word like "I" or "they" that stands for the person doing the action.
You know *yo*, *tú* and *usted* from Lesson 2. Here are all of them:

| | Singular | Plural |
|---|---|---|
| 1st person | *yo* — I | *nosotros* — we · *nosotras* — we (all female) |
| 2nd person | *tú* — you (informal) · *usted* — you (formal) | *ustedes* — you all |
| 3rd person | *él* — he · *ella* — she | *ellos* — they · *ellas* — they (all female) |

![A grid of subject pronouns with two columns, singular and plural, and three rows. First person: yo; nosotros and nosotras. Second person: tú and usted; ustedes. Third person: él and ella; ellos and ellas. Usted and ustedes are marked as using third-person verb forms.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

- *Nosotros* and *ellos* are for men, or for any mixed group, even nine women and one man.
  *Nosotras* and *ellas* are only for groups of women.
- In Latin America *ustedes* is the only plural "you": friends, children, customers, everyone.
  Spain uses *vosotros / vosotras* for friends and keeps *ustedes* for formal situations. You'll
  see *vosotros* in tables and books from Spain, but this course doesn't ask you to use it.
- *Usted* and *ustedes* take the verb forms of *él* and *ellos*: *usted habla, ustedes hablan*.
  In writing they're often shortened to *Ud.* and *Uds.*
- *Él* (he) has an accent; *el* (the) doesn't (Lesson 1).

Spanish normally uses no word for "it" as a subject: *Es interesante.* — It's interesting.

## The present tense of -ar verbs

Take the infinitive *hablar* (to speak). Remove *-ar* and you have the **[[stem]]**, *habl-*. Add
the **[[ending]]** for each person:

![A chart of the present tense of hablar. The stem habl- is in a box on the left; lines lead to six endings: -o for yo, -as for tú, -a for él, ella and usted, -amos for nosotros, -áis for vosotros (in grey, Spain only), and -an for ellos, ellas and ustedes. The full forms are hablo, hablas, habla, hablamos, habláis, hablan.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

| Person | Ending | hablar | trabajar (to work) |
|---|---|---|---|
| *yo* | *-o* | *hablo* | *trabajo* |
| *tú* | *-as* | *hablas* | *trabajas* |
| *él, ella, usted* | *-a* | *habla* | *trabaja* |
| *nosotros, nosotras* | *-amos* | *hablamos* | *trabajamos* |
| *(vosotros)* | *(-áis)* | *(habláis)* | *(trabajáis)* |
| *ellos, ellas, ustedes* | *-an* | *hablan* | *trabajan* |

A verb whose forms all follow the pattern is a **[[regular verb]]**. Every verb in this lesson is
regular in the present: *estudiar* (to study), *escuchar* (to listen to), *mirar* (to look at,
to watch), *preguntar* (to ask), *contestar* (to answer), *necesitar* (to need), *llegar* (to
arrive), *buscar* (to look for), *tomar* (to take; to drink), *llamar* (to call) and *practicar*
(to practise).

The **[[present tense]]** covers three English tenses: *Hablo español* is "I speak Spanish", "I'm
speaking Spanish" or "I do speak Spanish", depending on context. It also covers the near future:
*Hoy trabajo hasta las cinco* — Today I'm working until five.

### Why you usually leave the pronoun out

Each ending shows the person, so the pronoun is usually dropped: *Hablo inglés* (I speak English),
*Trabajamos aquí* (We work here). Saying *yo* every time sounds heavy, like stressing "*I* speak".
Keep the pronoun for contrast or emphasis, or where *-a* and *-an* could mean several people:

*Yo estudio, pero él trabaja.* — I study, but he works.
*¿Usted habla inglés?* — Do you speak English? (*usted* makes the polite "you" clear)

### Verbs that don't need a preposition

Some verbs include an English preposition in their meaning: *escuchar* (to listen "to"),
*mirar* (to look "at"), *buscar* (to look "for"). Don't translate the preposition:

*Escucho música.* — I listen to music.
*Busco la oficina.* — I'm looking for the office.

*Llamar* is to call someone, on the phone or by name: *Llamo a Daniel.* (The *a* before a person
is explained in Lesson 18.) It's not *llamarse* (to be called) from Lesson 2.

## Saying "not"

Put *no* directly before the verb:

*No hablo francés.* — I don't speak French.
*Ana no trabaja hoy.* — Ana isn't working today.

To answer a question with "no", you often say *no* twice: the first is the answer, the second
makes the verb negative. *¿Estudias ahora? — No, no estudio ahora.* — Are you studying now? — No,
I'm not studying now.

## Asking yes/no questions

A **[[yes/no question]]** has the same words as a statement; only the voice changes, rising at the
end, and the written ¿ … ? marks:

*Hablas español.* — You speak Spanish. (voice falls)
*¿Hablas español?* — Do you speak Spanish? (voice rises)

Spanish has no helper word like "do". You can also put the subject after the verb, which is
common with names and *usted*: *¿Trabaja Daniel aquí? ¿Habla usted inglés?* Adding *¿verdad?*
or *¿no?* at the end asks for agreement: *Estudias mucho, ¿verdad?* — You study a lot, don't you?

## Qué, cuándo, por qué — porque

With a question word, the word comes first, then the verb, then the subject if there is one:

| Question word | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| *¿qué?* | what? | *¿Qué estudias?* — What are you studying? |
| *¿cuándo?* | when? | *¿Cuándo llega Ana?* — When is Ana arriving? |
| *¿por qué?* | why? | *¿Por qué estudias español?* — Why are you studying Spanish? |

The answer to *¿por qué?* starts with *porque* (because): one word, no accent. The question is two
words with an accent; the answer is one word without.

*¿Por qué practicas mucho? — Porque necesito hablar español en mi trabajo.* — Why do you practise
a lot? — Because I need to speak Spanish at my job.

That example shows a useful pattern: *necesitar* + an infinitive means "to need to": *Necesito
estudiar* (I need to study).

## Time and place words

*Ahora* (now), *hoy* (today), *aquí* (here) and *allá* (there, over there; also *allí*) usually go
at the end or the start of the sentence: *Hoy no trabajo. Trabajo aquí, no allá.* After a verb,
*mucho* means "a lot": *Trabajas mucho.* Before a noun, it agrees like an adjective: *muchas
gracias*.

## Dialogue: a phone call

> Daniel: ¿Bueno? Hola, Kate. ¿Qué tal?
>
> Kate: Hola, Daniel. Bien. Oye, ¿trabajas hoy?
>
> Daniel: Sí, trabajo ahora. ¿Por qué?
>
> Kate: Porque necesito practicar español. ¿Cuándo llegas a casa?
>
> Daniel: Llego a las seis. ¿Estudiamos juntos?
>
> Kate: ¡Sí! Yo no hablo mucho, pero escucho mucho.
>
> Daniel: Y yo hablo y pregunto mucho. Tú contestas.
>
> Kate: ¿Qué llevo? ¿Qué estudiamos?
>
> Daniel: Nada. Tomamos un café y hablamos. ¡Hasta luego!

Hello? Hi, Kate. How's it going? — Hi, Daniel. Fine. Listen, are you working today? — Yes, I'm
working now. Why? — Because I need to practise Spanish. When do you get home? — I get there at
six. Shall we study together? — Yes! I don't speak much, but I listen a lot. — And I speak and
ask a lot. You answer. — What do I bring? What shall we study? — Nothing. We'll have a coffee
and talk. See you later!

New in passing: *¿Bueno?* (hello?, on the phone in Mexico), *oye* (listen, hey), *a casa* (home),
*a las seis* (at six), *juntos* (together), *¿qué llevo?* (what do I bring?), *nada* (nothing),
*un café* (a coffee). Notice how *¿Estudiamos juntos?* and *Tomamos un café* use the present
for a suggestion and a plan.

## Pronunciation

- Stress: forms ending in a vowel, *n* or *s* stress the second-to-last syllable: *HA-blo,
  HA-blan, tra-BA-jas*. The *nosotros* form is the same: *ha-BLA-mos*.
- *estudiar*: "es-too-DYAR"; *dia* is one syllable. *Estudio* is "es-TOO-dyo".
- *escuchar*: "es-koo-CHAR".
- *llegar*: *ll* is "y": "yeh-GAR".
- *por qué* and *porque* sound almost the same: *por QUÉ* stresses *qué*, *POR-que* the first
  syllable.
- *ustedes*: "oos-TEH-des".

## Common mistakes

- Adding the pronoun every time. *Yo trabajo, yo estudio, yo hablo* sounds odd; let the ending
  do the work.
- Using *ellas* for a mixed group. Any man in the group makes it *ellos*.
- *Busco para la oficina, escucho a la música.* No preposition: *busco la oficina, escucho
  música*.
- *No* in the wrong place: *Hablo no inglés.* It goes before the verb: *No hablo inglés.*
- Writing *porque* in a question or *por qué* in an answer.
- *¿Tú hablas español?* is fine, but don't add a "do" word: there isn't one.
- Using *vosotros* forms in Latin America. Say *ustedes hablan* to a group.

## Key points

- Pronouns: *yo, tú, usted, él, ella; nosotros/as, ustedes, ellos, ellas*. *Usted(es)* takes
  third-person forms. *Vosotros* is Spain only.
- Usually drop the pronoun; keep it for contrast or clarity.
- -ar present: stem + *-o, -as, -a, -amos, -an*: *hablo, hablas, habla, hablamos, hablan*.
- One present form = "I speak / I'm speaking / I do speak".
- *no* goes right before the verb.
- Yes/no questions: same words, rising voice, ¿ … ?
- *¿qué?, ¿cuándo?, ¿por qué?* — answer *porque*.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Honors: How Spanish sounds across the Americas
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 1 taught the sounds of Mexican Spanish, the standard of this course. But Spanish is the
official language of about twenty countries, and a learner who has only heard one accent can be
lost the first time a Cuban, an Argentine or a Spaniard speaks. This honors lesson shows the
main differences, so you can *recognize* them. You don't need to imitate any of them: a clear
Mexican accent is understood everywhere.

One idea runs through the whole lesson: these are **[[varieties]]**, not mistakes. Spanish has no
single "correct" accent. The language academies of the Spanish-speaking countries treat educated
speech from Mexico City, Bogotá, Buenos Aires, Havana and Madrid as equally correct. A Cuban who
drops an *s* is speaking Cuban Spanish properly, just as a Texan isn't speaking English badly.

You'll also learn how people answer the phone in different countries, and a few words for
talking about pronunciation: *el acento* (accent, way of speaking), *la pronunciación*
(pronunciation), *pronunciar* (to pronounce), *el sonido* (sound), *la sílaba* (syllable) and
*la vocal* (vowel).

## Mexico: the course standard

Central Mexican Spanish, the variety of Mexico City and much of the country, has the features you
already know: *seseo* (*z* and *ce, ci* sound like *s*) and *yeísmo* (*ll* and *y* sound the
same). Two more things are typical of it:

- The *s* is strong and clear, even at the end of a syllable: *buenas tardes, ¿cómo estás?* —
  every *s* is heard.
- In fast speech, an unstressed vowel next to an *s* can become very short, so *buenas noches*
  may sound almost like "buen's noch's". The vowel is still there, just quick.

Northern Mexico sounds a little different again (the *ch* of *mucho* can soften toward "sh"), but
the differences inside Mexico are smaller than those you'll meet below.

## The Caribbean: the *s* that turns into a breath

In Cuba, Puerto Rico and the Dominican Republic, and on the Caribbean coasts of Venezuela,
Colombia and Panama, an *s* at the end of a syllable is often softened to a breathy "h", or not
pronounced at all. This is called **[[aspiration]]** of the *s*. You'll also hear it in much of
Central America (Honduras, El Salvador, Nicaragua), in Chile, Argentina and southern Spain.

| Written | Mexico | Caribbean (typical) |
|---|---|---|
| *¿Cómo estás?* | "KOH-mo es-TAHS" | "KOH-mo eh-TAH" |
| *los niños* (the children) | "los NEE-nyos" | "loh NEE-nyoh" |
| *más o menos* | "MAHS oh MEH-nos" | "MAH oh MEH-noh" |

A tip for listening: when the *s* disappears, the plural is often still clear from the article or
from a slightly more open vowel. Don't listen for each *s*; listen for the whole phrase. Puerto
Rican Spanish may also turn an *r* at the end of a syllable into something like an *l*
(*puerta*, door, can sound like "PWEL-tah"). Speech is also fast, so *¿Puede repetir?* is your
friend.

## Argentina and Uruguay: *sh*, and *vos*

The Spanish of the Río de la Plata region (Buenos Aires, Montevideo and much of Argentina and
Uruguay) has two features you'll notice at once.

First, **[[sheísmo]]**: *ll* and *y* sound the same, as everywhere, but the sound is "sh" (or, more
traditionally, the "zh" of English *measure*): *me llamo* sounds like "me SHAH-mo", *yo* like
"sho", *calle* (street) like "KAH-sheh". The "sh" is spreading among younger speakers, the "zh"
is older.

Second, *vos*. Instead of *tú*, people use *vos* for "you" (informal), with its own verb forms,
stressed at the end:

| With *tú* (this course) | With *vos* (Río de la Plata) | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| *tú eres* | *vos sos* | you are |
| *tú hablas* | *vos hablás* | you speak |
| *tú estudias* | *vos estudiás* | you study |
| *¿Cómo te llamas?* | *¿Cómo te llamás?* | What's your name? |

Using *vos* is called **[[voseo]]**. It's normal, educated speech in Argentina and common in Uruguay,
and it's also used in Paraguay and much of Central America (Guatemala, Honduras, El Salvador,
Nicaragua, Costa Rica), and in parts of Colombia, Venezuela and Chile, with forms that vary by
region. Recognize it; keep using *tú* yourself. Everyone who says *vos* understands *tú*.

## The Andes: clear consonants

In the highlands of Peru, Bolivia and Ecuador, and in parts of Colombia, the consonants are
strong and every *s* is pronounced, often very crisply. Vowels next to an *s* can be short, as in
central Mexico. Two features you may notice:

- The *rr* (and an *r* at the start of a word) can sound like a buzzing "zh" rather than a roll:
  *perro* may sound close to "PEH-zho". This is common in the Andes and also heard in Mexico,
  Guatemala, Costa Rica and Chile.
- Some speakers, especially older and rural ones in the Andes and in Paraguay, still
  pronounce *ll* differently from *y*: *ll* like the "lli" in *million*. For them, *calló* (fell
  silent) and *cayó* (fell) sound different.

## Spain: *th* and *vosotros*

Most of Spain has a sound that Latin America doesn't use: *z*, and *c* before *e* or *i*, are said like
the "th" in English *think*, while *s* stays "s". This is called **[[distinción]]**, because it
distinguishes *casa* (house) from *caza* (hunting).

| Written | Latin America | Central and northern Spain |
|---|---|---|
| *gracias* | "GRAH-syahs" | "GRAH-thyahs" |
| *cinco* | "SEEN-ko" | "THEEN-ko" |
| *zeta* | "SEH-tah" | "THEH-tah" |
| *seis* | "says" | "says" (*s* doesn't change) |

It is not a lisp. A lisp would turn the *s* into "th" as well, and Spaniards keep their *s*. The
Spanish *j* is also often rougher, further back in the throat, than the Mexican one.

Spain also uses *vosotros* (you all, informal) with its own forms: *¿Vosotros habláis inglés?* —
Do you all speak English? You learned in Lesson 4 that Latin America uses *ustedes* for every
group. Recognize *vosotros* in books, films and exams from Spain; answer with *ustedes*.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: A rough guide to placing an accent by ear
  accDescr: A simplified decision chart for guessing where a speaker is from. First, are z and ce, ci said like English th? If yes, the speaker is probably from central or northern Spain. If not, do ll and y sound like sh or zh? If yes, probably Argentina or Uruguay. If not, does the s at the end of a syllable become a breath or disappear? If yes, probably the Caribbean or a coast, or much of Central America, Chile or southern Spain. If not, the speaker is probably from Mexico, the Andes, Guatemala or Costa Rica. The chart is a simplification, since many features overlap.
  A["You hear a Spanish speaker"] --> B{"z and ce, ci like English th?"}
  B -- "yes" --> S["Probably central or northern Spain"]
  B -- "no" --> C{"ll and y like sh or zh?"}
  C -- "yes" --> R["Probably Argentina or Uruguay"]
  C -- "no" --> D{"s at the end of a syllable fades to a breath?"}
  D -- "yes" --> K["Probably the Caribbean or a coast (also much of Central America, Chile, southern Spain)"]
  D -- "no" --> M["Probably Mexico, the Andes, Guatemala or Costa Rica"]
```

The chart is only a first guess: features overlap, people move, and one speaker can sound
different at home and at work.

## Answering the phone

Every country has its own way of picking up the phone. All of them are said as a question:

| Where | Answering the phone |
|---|---|
| Mexico (also El Salvador and Nicaragua) | *¿Bueno?* |
| Peru, Chile, Venezuela, Ecuador and others | *¿Aló?* |
| Spain | *¿Diga?* or *¿Dígame?* (literally "say?", "tell me?") |
| Argentina and Uruguay | *¿Hola?* |
| Colombia | *¿Aló?*, and also *¿A ver?* ("let's see?") |

![Four phones, each with a speech bubble. The first, marked México, says ¿Bueno? The second, marked Perú, Chile and Venezuela, says ¿Aló? The third, marked España, says ¿Diga? The fourth, marked Argentina and Uruguay, says ¿Hola?](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

A few more phrases for phone calls (*la llamada*, the call):

- *¿De parte de quién?* — Who's calling? (literally "on behalf of whom?"). Answer: *De parte de
  Kate.*
- *Número equivocado* — wrong number. *Equivocado* means "wrong, mistaken".
- *colgar* — to hang up: *Ahora cuelgo* — I'm hanging up now. (It changes *o* to *ue* in some
  forms, a pattern taught in Lesson 15.)

### Example 1: Reading one sentence in four accents

Take the sentence *Yo me llamo Cecilia y soy de aquí.* (My name is Cecilia and I'm from here.)
Work through it feature by feature.

1. *Yo, llamo*: the *ll* and *y* sound. Mexico, the Caribbean, the Andes and Spain: "yo, YAH-mo".
   Río de la Plata: "sho, SHAH-mo".
2. *Cecilia*: the two *c*s before *e* and *i*. Latin America: "seh-SEE-lyah". Spain:
   "theh-THEE-lyah".
3. *soy*: here the *s* starts a syllable, so even Caribbean speakers keep it: "soy".
4. Put it together. Mexico: "yo me YAH-mo seh-SEE-lyah ee soy deh ah-KEE". Buenos Aires: "sho me
   SHAH-mo seh-SEE-lyah…". Madrid: "yo me YAH-mo theh-THEE-lyah…".

Conclusion: only the features from this lesson change; the words, the grammar and the stress
stay exactly the same.

### Example 2: Where is the caller from?

You answer the phone and hear: "*¿Aló? Hola, ¿cómo ehtá? … Sí, sí, mah o meno. … ¿Uhtede hablan
inglé?*" Reason it out:

1. The caller says *¿Aló?*, so probably not Mexico or Spain.
2. *estás* sounds like "ehtá", *más o menos* like "mah o meno", *ustedes* like "uhtede": the *s* at
   the end of each syllable is aspirated or dropped.
3. *ll* and *y* don't occur, and no "th" sound is heard.
4. A good guess: the Caribbean coast, for example Venezuela, or a country with the same features.
   It's only a guess, and the right thing to do is ask: *¿De dónde es usted?*

### Example 3: Recognizing *vos*

A message from an Argentine friend: *Hola, ¿cómo estás? ¿Vos hablás inglés? Yo estudio inglés y
necesito practicar. Vos sos de Estados Unidos, ¿no?* Translate *vos* forms into the *tú* forms you
know: *vos hablás* = *tú hablas*, *vos sos* = *tú eres*. Notice that *¿cómo estás?* looks the same
in both. Then answer with your own forms: *Sí, hablo inglés. Soy de Denver. ¿Y tú?* — your friend
understands perfectly.

## Reading: four friends, one call

> Rosa (Mexico City): ¿Bueno? ¡Hola, Martín! ¿Cómo estás?
>
> Martín (Buenos Aires): ¡Hola, Rosa! Bien, ¿y vos? Oíme, ¿Javier está con vos?
>
> Rosa: Sí, aquí está. Y Lucía, de Madrid, también.
>
> Lucía (Madrid): Hola, Martín. ¿Vosotros estudiáis inglés hoy?
>
> Javier (San Juan, Puerto Rico): ¡Sí, ahora! Necesitamos practicar.
>
> Martín: ¿Inglés? ¡Pero hablamos español!
>
> Rosa: Sí, con cuatro acentos. Muy bien, ¿no?

Hello? Hi, Martín! How are you? — Hi, Rosa! Fine, and you? Listen, is Javier with you? — Yes, he's
here. And Lucía, from Madrid, too. — Hi, Martín. Are you all studying English today? — Yes, now! We
need to practise. — English? But we're speaking Spanish! — Yes, with four accents. Very good,
isn't it?

Each speaker uses the forms of home: Rosa *¿Bueno?* and *tú*, Martín *vos* and *oíme* (the *vos*
form of *oye*, listen), Lucía *vosotros estudiáis*. New in passing: *está* (is, of place; Lesson 9)
and *con* (with). Read the dialogue aloud in a Mexican accent, then try Martín's
lines with "sh" and Lucía's with "th".

## Common mistakes

- Calling an accent "wrong" or "lazy". Aspiration, *sheísmo* and *distinción* are regular patterns
  with long histories, used by educated speakers.
- Mixing features. If you decide to say *gracias* with "th", you'd also need *vosotros* and many
  Spain words; it's simpler to keep one variety, and this course uses Mexico's.
- Thinking the Spanish *th* is a lisp. The *s* stays "s".
- Answering *vos* with *vos* forms you half know. Keep *tú*: it's understood everywhere.
- Answering the phone in Mexico with *¿Aló?* It's understood, but *¿Bueno?* sounds local.

## Key points

- Spanish has many correct accents; this course uses central Mexico's.
- Caribbean and coastal Spanish: a syllable-final *s* becomes a breath or disappears.
- Río de la Plata: *ll* and *y* as "sh" or "zh"; *vos* instead of *tú* (*vos sos, vos hablás*).
- The Andes: crisp consonants; a buzzing *rr* in some areas; *ll* distinct from *y* for some
  speakers.
- Spain: *z* and *ce, ci* like "th" (*distinción*), and *vosotros* for "you all" among friends.
- On the phone: *¿Bueno?* (Mexico), *¿Aló?* (much of South America), *¿Diga?* (Spain), *¿Hola?*
  (Argentina, Uruguay). *¿De parte de quién?* — Who's calling?

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Honors: Two surnames, titles and politeness
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

In Lesson 1 you learned *el nombre* (first name) and *el apellido* (surname), and in Lesson 2
*tú*, *usted*, *señor* and *señora*. In Mexico and the rest of the Spanish-speaking world, names
and forms of address carry more information than in English: almost everyone has two surnames,
older people may be called *don* or *doña*, and a lawyer or engineer is often addressed by a
professional title. This honors lesson shows how all of it works, how to read a name on a form
or a business card, and how and when people move from *usted* to *tú*.

## Two surnames

A Mexican's full name, *el nombre completo*, usually has three parts: one or two first names,
then two surnames. The first surname is *el apellido paterno* (the father's surname), the second
*el apellido materno* (the mother's).

![A small family diagram. The father is José López Ramírez and the mother is Ana Ortiz Vega. An arrow from the father's first surname, López, and an arrow from the mother's first surname, Ortiz, lead to their daughter, María Fernanda López Ortiz. Under her name, brackets mark María Fernanda as nombre, López as apellido paterno and Ortiz as apellido materno.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Each parent passes on their *first* surname, usually the one they got from their own father. So the
father's second surname (*Ramírez*) and the mother's second surname (*Vega*) don't reach the
daughter. In two generations a surname can drop out of a family's names.

Many people have two first names: *María Fernanda*, *José Luis*, *Ana Sofía*. The second one is
*el segundo nombre* (middle name), but unlike English middle names it's often used every day:
María Fernanda is "María Fernanda" to her friends, or "Fer", not "María".

### Which surname do people use?

In daily life, one surname is enough, and it's the first one: María Fernanda López Ortiz is *la
señora López* or *la licenciada López*. Both surnames appear on official documents, on forms,
and when there could be confusion between two people called López.

When a woman marries in Mexico, she legally keeps her own surnames. In the past many women added
*de* + the husband's surname (*María López de García*), and some still do socially, but it is
much less common today.

### Is the order fixed?

Traditionally the father's surname comes first. This is changing: in Spain, since 2017, parents
choose the order, and there is no default for the father. In Mexico the Supreme Court has ruled
that requiring the father's surname first discriminates, so parents who agree can ask for the
mother's surname first; in practice most families still follow the traditional order, and
details depend on each state's civil registry. Treat the "paternal then maternal" pattern as the
usual one, not a law of nature.

### Names on forms and lists

Mexican forms often have three boxes: *Apellido paterno*, *Apellido materno* and *Nombre(s)*.
Lists of students or patients are usually sorted by the first surname, written first, often in
capitals: *LÓPEZ ORTIZ, María Fernanda*. If you have only one surname, leave *apellido materno*
empty (or write what the clerk asks for).

The reverse happens in the US, where forms have only "Last name": many Latin Americans write
both surnames with a hyphen (*López-Ortiz*) so a computer doesn't treat *López* as a middle name.

## Don and doña

*Don* (for a man) and *doña* (for a woman) are **[[honorifics]]**: words that show respect. They go
before the *first* name (or the full name), not the surname alone, and are used for older people, neighbours you
respect, the owner of the corner shop:

*Buenos días, don Javier.* — Good morning, (Mr) Javier.
*Doña Carmen es muy amable.* — Doña Carmen is very kind.

There's no English equivalent: *don Javier* is respectful and warm at the same time. In careful
speech *don* and *doña* always come with a name; without one, use *señor* or *señora*. (In casual
Mexican speech you'll hear them alone, as in a market: *¿Qué le doy, doña?*, "What can I get you, ma'am?")

## Professional titles

In Mexico, a university degree often becomes part of how people address you, at work and in
offices, both spoken and on business cards and e-mails:

| Title | Short form | For |
|---|---|---|
| *licenciado / licenciada* | *Lic.* | a university graduate: law, business, communications… |
| *ingeniero / ingeniera* | *Ing.* | an engineer |
| *arquitecto / arquitecta* | *Arq.* | an architect |
| *doctor / doctora* | *Dr. / Dra.* | a medical doctor (and, formally, a PhD) |
| *maestro / maestra* | *Mtro. / Mtra.* | a teacher, or someone with a master's degree |

Use the title with the first surname, or alone: *Buenos días, licenciado.* *El ingeniero Pérez
llega a las diez.* On an e-mail or a door: *Lic. Ana Gómez*. Using the title is polite, and many
Mexicans expect it in professional settings. *Licenciado* in particular is used so widely for
people with a degree, and with lawyers and officials, that you'll hear it all the time.

## From usted to tú

Lesson 2 said to start with *usted* and wait. Here's how the switch happens. Using *tú* with
someone is called **[[tuteo]]**, and the verb is *tutear* (to address someone as *tú*). Usually the
older person, or the one with more status (the boss, the host, the teacher), offers it:

*¿Nos tuteamos?* — Shall we use *tú* with each other?
*Háblame de tú, por favor.* — Please call me *tú*. (Mexico: *hablar de tú*, to address as *tú*)

The natural answer is *¡Claro!* (Of course!) and then switching at once. If you're the younger or
junior person, it's safest to wait for the offer. Some families keep *usted* for parents or
grandparents, out of respect, all their lives, and at work some people keep *usted* with *el
jefe* or *la jefa* (the boss) even after years.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: How people usually move from usted to tú
  accDescr: Two people meet. If they are young people in a casual setting, they often use tú from the start. Otherwise, the older person or the person with more status, such as the boss, the host or the teacher, may offer tú by saying Nos tuteamos? or Háblame de tú. If the offer is made, the other person answers Claro and both use tú. If no one offers, they keep using usted, which is normal and respectful.
  A["Two people meet"] --> B{"Young people, casual setting?"}
  B -- "yes" --> T["tú from the start"]
  B -- "no" --> C{"Does the older or senior person offer tú?"}
  C -- "yes: ¿Nos tuteamos? / Háblame de tú" --> D["Answer: ¡Claro! Both use tú"]
  C -- "no" --> E["Keep usted: normal and respectful"]
```

### A note on Colombia: usted among friends

In parts of Colombia, for example in Bogotá and Antioquia, many people use *usted* with
close friends, partners and even their children. This **[[ustedeo]]** is not cold there: it can sound
warm and familiar. A Colombian friend who says *usted* to you isn't keeping their distance.

## Worked examples

### Example 1: Reading a business card

The card says: *Lic. José Luis Hernández Rivera — Abogado*. Take it apart:

1. *Lic.* = *licenciado*: he has a university degree. *Abogado* (lawyer) confirms it.
2. *José Luis*: two first names, and he probably uses both.
3. *Hernández*: his *apellido paterno*, the one used every day.
4. *Rivera*: his *apellido materno*.
5. How to greet him: *Buenos días, licenciado* or *Buenos días, licenciado Hernández*, with
   *usted*. Not "licenciado Rivera", and not "señor José".

### Example 2: Filling in a Mexican form with an English name

Kate Elizabeth Hughes is from the US, and her mother's surname is Brown. The form at a gym in
Puebla asks for *Apellido paterno, Apellido materno, Nombre(s)*.

1. *Apellido paterno*: *Hughes*, her only legal surname.
2. *Apellido materno*: nothing, since Brown isn't part of her legal name. She leaves it empty,
   or asks: *¿Es obligatorio?* (Is it required?)
3. *Nombre(s)*: *Kate Elizabeth*.
4. On the class list she'll appear as *HUGHES, Kate Elizabeth*, and the staff will call her
   *Kate* or *la señora Hughes*.

### Example 3: Choosing how to address three people

Kate starts a job in Puebla.

1. Her new boss, an engineer called Laura Ramos: *usted* and the title: *Buenos días,
   ingeniera.* She waits until Laura offers *tú*.
2. The older woman who sells newspapers on the corner, Carmen: *Buenos días, doña Carmen*, with
   *usted*.
3. Pablo, a colleague of her own age, who says *¿Nos tuteamos?* on the first day: *¡Claro!*, and
   from then on *tú*: *Pablo, ¿trabajas mañana?*

## Reading: the first day

> Ingeniera Ramos: Buenos días. Usted es la señora Hughes, ¿verdad?
>
> Kate: Sí, buenos días, ingeniera. Mucho gusto.
>
> Ingeniera Ramos: Mucho gusto. Mi nombre completo es Laura Ramos Téllez, pero aquí todos
> hablan de tú. ¿Nos tuteamos?
>
> Kate: ¡Claro! Entonces… Laura, ¿dónde trabajo hoy?
>
> Laura: Aquí, con el licenciado Hernández. Es el abogado de la oficina. Él es muy formal: con él,
> usted, por favor.
>
> Kate: Muy bien. ¿Y la señora de recepción?
>
> Laura: Es doña Lupe. Es muy amable. Ella habla de tú con todos.

Good morning. You're Mrs Hughes, aren't you? — Yes, good morning, (engineer). Nice to meet you. —
Nice to meet you. My full name is Laura Ramos Téllez, but here everyone uses *tú*. Shall we use
*tú*? — Of course! So… Laura, where am I working today? — Here, with Mr Hernández (*licenciado*).
He's the office's lawyer. He's very formal: with him, *usted*, please. — Very good. And the lady
at reception? — That's Doña Lupe. She's very kind. She uses *tú* with everyone.

New in passing: *todos* (everyone), *entonces* (so, then), *amable* (kind), *el abogado* (lawyer),
*recepción* (reception). Notice that after *¿Nos tuteamos?* Kate switches straight away, and that
*Lupe* is a common nickname for *Guadalupe*.

## Common mistakes

- Using the second surname as the "last name": *el señor Rivera* for José Luis Hernández Rivera.
  In daily use it's the first surname: *el señor Hernández*.
- *Don López.* *Don* and *doña* go with the first name: *don José*.
- Switching to *tú* with a senior person before they offer it.
- Thinking a Colombian's *usted* means distance. It can be warm.
- Writing *Lic.* or *Ing.* for yourself without the degree. The titles describe real
  qualifications.
- Dropping the accent in surnames: *Hernández, Ramírez, López* all need it (they end in *z* and
  stress the second-to-last syllable).

## Key points

- Full name = first name(s) + *apellido paterno* + *apellido materno*; everyday use is the first
  surname.
- Children usually take the first surname of each parent; Spain (since 2017) and Mexican courts
  now let parents choose the order.
- Forms: *Apellido paterno / Apellido materno / Nombre(s)*; lists sort by the first surname.
- *Don / doña* + first name: respect for older people.
- Titles as address: *licenciado, ingeniero, arquitecto, doctor, maestro*, with the surname or
  alone.
- Moving to *tú*: *¿Nos tuteamos? Háblame de tú.* — *¡Claro!* Wait for the senior person to offer.
- In parts of Colombia, *usted* (*ustedeo*) is used among friends and family.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Nouns, gender and articles
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

In Module 1 you learned to greet people, say who you are, count and use *-ar* verbs. Now you
start talking about *things*: the pen on the table, the keys in your backpack, the map on the
classroom wall. To do that in Spanish you need three facts about every noun: its gender, the
word for "the" or "a" that goes with it, and its plural.

By the end of this lesson you can point at something and ask *¿Qué es esto?* (What's this?),
answer *Es una llave* (It's a key), and talk about more than one: *Son unas llaves* (They're
some keys).

## Every noun is masculine or feminine

Every Spanish noun has a **[[gender]]**: it is either **[[masculine]]** or **[[feminine]]**. This is a label
on the word, not a fact about the thing. A table isn't female and a book isn't male; *la mesa*
and *el libro* simply belong to two different groups. The gender matters because the little
words around a noun have to match it: "the" and "a" now, and adjectives in Lesson 8.

The word for "the" is the **[[definite article]]**. In the singular it has two forms:

| Gender | "the" | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| masculine | *el* | *el libro* (the book), *el cuaderno* (the notebook), *el lápiz* (the pencil) |
| feminine | *la* | *la mesa* (the table), *la silla* (the chair), *la puerta* (the door) |

The golden rule: learn every noun with its article. Don't learn *mesa = table*; learn *la mesa
= the table*, and say it aloud as one unit: *lamesa, ellibro*. Your vocabulary reviews always
show nouns with *el* or *la*, and you'll type the article too.

Here is a classroom. Each label is coloured by gender: light blue for masculine words, pink for
feminine ones.

![A classroom. On the wall: la ventana (window), el mapa (map), el reloj (clock) and la puerta (door). On la mesa (table): la computadora (computer), los lentes (glasses) on top of el libro (book), el cuaderno (notebook) with la pluma (pen) on it. Next to the table la silla (chair), and on the floor la mochila (backpack). Masculine labels are light blue, feminine labels pink.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### Clues from the ending

Spanish is kind to learners here, because the ending of a noun usually tells you its gender.

- Nouns ending in *-o* are usually masculine: *el libro, el cuaderno, el niño* (the boy).
- Nouns ending in *-a* are usually feminine: *la mesa, la silla, la mochila* (the backpack),
  *la ventana* (the window), *la cosa* (the thing).
- Nouns ending in *-ción* and *-dad* are always feminine: *la dirección* (the address,
  Lesson 3), *la ciudad* (the city, Lesson 2), *la universidad* (Lesson 7).
- Nouns ending in *-e* or a consonant can go either way, so you simply learn them:
  *el papel* (the paper), *el reloj* (the clock), *el hombre* (the man), *la llave* (the key),
  *la mujer* (the woman).

A handful of very common words break the -o/-a rule. Learn them early, because you'll use them
every day:

| Masculine, ending in -a | Feminine, ending in -o |
|---|---|
| *el mapa* (the map) | *la foto* (the photo; short for *la fotografía*) |
| *el día* (the day, Lesson 13) | *la mano* (the hand, Lesson 20) |
| *el problema* (the problem, Lesson 23) | |
| *el idioma* (the language, Lesson 7) | |

*Problema* and *idioma* come from Greek words in *-ma*, and most nouns of that kind are
masculine. *Foto* is feminine because the full word, *fotografía*, ends in *-a*.

For people, the gender usually follows the person: *el niño* (the boy), *la niña* (the girl).
Some pairs are completely different words: *el hombre* (the man), *la mujer* (the woman).

When you meet a new noun, run through these checks:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Masculine or feminine?
  accDescr: First, if you already know the noun with its article, use that article. If not, check whether it is one of the exceptions, such as el mapa, el día, el problema, el idioma, la mano or la foto; if so, use the article you learned for it. Otherwise, a noun ending in -ción or -dad is feminine, la. A noun ending in -o is usually masculine, el. A noun ending in -a is usually feminine, la. Any other ending, -e or a consonant, can be either, so look it up and learn it with its article.
  A["New noun: el or la?"] --> B{"Do you know it with its article?"}
  B -- yes --> C["Use that article"]
  B -- no --> D{"One of the exceptions? el mapa, el día, la mano, la foto"}
  D -- yes --> C
  D -- no --> E{"Ends in -ción or -dad?"}
  E -- yes --> F["la (feminine)"]
  E -- no --> G{"Ends in -o or -a?"}
  G -- "-o" --> H["usually el (masculine)"]
  G -- "-a" --> I["usually la (feminine)"]
  G -- "other" --> J["Look it up and learn it with its article"]
```

## A or an: un and una

The **[[indefinite article]]** means "a" or "an". It also has a masculine and a feminine form, and
they're the forms of the number one you met in Lesson 3:

| Gender | "the" | "a, an" |
|---|---|---|
| masculine | *el cuaderno* | *un cuaderno* |
| feminine | *la mochila* | *una mochila* |

- *Es un mapa.* — It's a map.
- *Es una computadora.* — It's a computer.
- *Necesito un lápiz.* — I need a pencil.
- *Busco una llave.* — I'm looking for a key.

## More than one: plurals

To make a noun **[[plural]]**, look at how it ends.

| The singular ends in | Add | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| a vowel | *-s* | *el libro → los libros*, *la silla → las sillas*, *el café → los cafés* (coffee) |
| a consonant | *-es* | *el papel → los papeles*, *el reloj → los relojes*, *la mujer → las mujeres* |
| *-z* | *z* becomes *c*, then *-es* | *el lápiz → los lápices* |

The *z → c* change is only spelling: Spanish almost never writes *ze* or *zi*, so
the sound stays the same. In Latin America *z* and *c* (before *e, i*) both sound like *s*.

### Accents that appear or vanish

Adding a syllable doesn't move the stress: the same vowel is still the loud one. But that vowel
is now one syllable further from the end of the word, so the rule from Lesson 1 may give a
different answer, and the written accent can appear or disappear.

- *la canción → las canciones* (the song → the songs). *Canción* ends in *n* but is stressed on
  the last syllable, so it needs an accent. *Canciones* ends in *s* and is stressed on the
  second-to-last syllable, *-cio-*, which is what the rule expects: no accent.
- *el joven → los jóvenes* (the young man → the young people). *Joven* follows the rule
  (*JO-ven*). *Jóvenes* is stressed three syllables from the end, and every word like that
  needs an accent.
- *el lápiz → los lápices*. *Lápiz* needs its accent (stress on *LÁ-*, ending in *z*), and so
  does *lápices* (three syllables from the end). The accent stays.

### The plural articles

In the plural, "the" becomes *los* (masculine) or *las* (feminine). The plural of *un* and *una*
is *unos* and *unas*, which mean "some" or "a few".

| | masculine | feminine |
|---|---|---|
| the (singular) | *el* | *la* |
| the (plural) | *los* | *las* |
| a, an | *un* | *una* |
| some | *unos* | *unas* |

- *los cuadernos* (the notebooks), *las llaves* (the keys)
- *unos papeles* (some papers), *unas fotos* (some photos)

### Mixed groups take the masculine

When a group mixes masculine and feminine, Spanish uses the masculine plural. *Los niños* can
mean "the boys" or "the children" (boys and girls together). A room with nine girls and one boy
is full of *niños*. Only a group that is entirely female is *las niñas*.

### Words that are already plural

*Los lentes* (glasses) is plural, just like English "glasses", and you use it for one pair:
*Necesito los lentes* (I need my glasses). In Spain the word is *las gafas*.

## One more twist: el agua

A few feminine nouns begin with a stressed *a-* sound, such as *agua* (water, Lesson 11). Saying
*la agua* would run two *a* sounds together, so Spanish uses *el* in the singular: *el agua*.
The word is still feminine, and you'll see that later when adjectives agree with it (*el agua
fría*, the cold water) and in the plural (*las aguas*). For now, just recognise it.

## ¿Qué es esto?

To ask about something you can't name, point and say *¿Qué es esto?* (What's this?). *Esto*
(this) never changes, because you don't know the noun yet, so you don't know its gender. The
answer uses *es* (it is) from Lesson 2, or *son* (they are) for several things:

- *¿Qué es esto?* — *Es un reloj.* — What's this? — It's a clock.
- *¿Y esto?* — *Es una pluma.* — And this? — It's a pen.
- *¿Y esto?* — *Son unos lentes.* — And this? — They're glasses. (*Son* = they are; you'll learn
  the plural of *ser* in Lesson 6.)

Spanish has no word for "it" in *Es un reloj*: the verb *es* is enough.

## Dialogue: the first day of class

Valeria, a new student, arrives early in a language school in Guadalajara. The teacher,
Mr Ortega, is already in the classroom.

> Valeria: *Buenos días. Perdón, ¿qué es esto?*
>
> Sr. Ortega: *Buenos días. Es un mapa de México.*
>
> Valeria: *¿Y esto? ¿Es una computadora?*
>
> Sr. Ortega: *Sí, es la computadora del salón. Y las plumas, los lápices y los cuadernos son
> para los estudiantes.*
>
> Valeria: *¡Gracias! Necesito un cuaderno y una pluma.*
>
> Sr. Ortega: *Aquí hay cuadernos. ¿Y las fotos? ¿Son de usted?*
>
> Valeria: *No, no son mías. Y la mochila tampoco.*
>
> Sr. Ortega: *Ah, la mochila es de Daniel. Y las llaves también.*

Translation:

> Valeria: Good morning. Excuse me, what's this?
>
> Mr Ortega: Good morning. It's a map of Mexico.
>
> Valeria: And this? Is it a computer?
>
> Mr Ortega: Yes, it's the classroom computer. And the pens, the pencils and the notebooks are for
> the students.
>
> Valeria: Thanks! I need a notebook and a pen.
>
> Mr Ortega: There are notebooks here. And the photos? Are they yours?
>
> Valeria: No, they're not mine. And the backpack isn't either.
>
> Mr Ortega: Ah, the backpack is Daniel's. And the keys too.

A few new bits to recognise: *del salón* = of the classroom (*de* + *el* becomes *del*; Lesson
18), *para* = for, *hay* = there are (Lesson 10), *de usted* = yours, *mías* = mine (said of feminine things, here *las fotos*; words like this come at A2),
*tampoco* = not either (Lesson 11). Spanish shows who owns something with *de*: *la mochila de
Daniel* is Daniel's backpack. There is no *'s*.

## Pronunciation

- *llave*: in Mexico and most of Latin America *ll* sounds like the *y* in "yes": *YA-ve*.
- *lápiz*, *lápices*: *z* and *ce* both sound like *s*. Stress the first syllable: *LA-pis*,
  *LA-pi-ses*.
- *reloj*: the final *j* is soft, like a light *h*, and many speakers barely say it: *re-LO*.
- *hombre*: the *h* is always silent: *OM-bre*.
- *niño, niña*: *ñ* is like the *ny* in "canyon": *NI-nyo*.
- *silla*, *mochila*: *ll* is a *y* sound, but *ch* is as in "church": *SI-ya*, *mo-CHI-la*.
- *computadora*: stress on *-DO-*: *com-pu-ta-DO-ra*.

## Common mistakes

- Trusting the ending over the article. *La mujer* ends in *r* and *el día* ends in *a*; the
  article you learned always wins over the ending.
- Forgetting the exceptions: ~~la mapa~~ → *el mapa*; ~~el foto~~ → *la foto*.
- Plurals of consonant nouns with only *-s*: ~~los papels~~ → *los papeles*; ~~los relojs~~ →
  *los relojes*.
- Forgetting *z → c*: ~~los lápizes~~ → *los lápices*.
- Keeping the accent from the singular: ~~las canciónes~~ → *las canciones*.
- Saying ~~el lente~~ for glasses. One pair of glasses is *los lentes*.
- Using *las* for a mixed group: a class of boys and girls is *los niños*.
- Adding *'s* for owners: ~~Daniel's mochila~~ → *la mochila de Daniel*.

## Key points

- Every noun is masculine or feminine. Learn each one with *el* or *la*.
- Usually -o → masculine, -a → feminine; -ción and -dad → always feminine. Learn the exceptions:
  *el mapa, el día, el problema, el idioma, la mano, la foto*.
- The articles: *el, la, los, las* (the); *un, una* (a); *unos, unas* (some).
- Plurals: vowel + *s*; consonant + *es*; *z → ces*. Written accents can appear or vanish.
- Mixed groups take the masculine plural: *los niños*.
- *¿Qué es esto?* — *Es un…* / *Es una…* (one thing), *Son unos…* / *Son unas…* (several).

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Family, tener and possessives
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Family is one of the first things people talk about when they meet, in Mexico as anywhere:
*¿Tienes hermanos? ¿Tus papás viven aquí?* In this lesson you learn the family words, the verb
*tener* (to have), and the small words *mi, tu, su, nuestro* (my, your, his/her, our). You also
learn the plural of *ser* (*somos, son*), so you can say who people are: *Son mis abuelos.*

## The family

Here is Lucía's family. Each box shows a first name and, in italics, what that person is to
Lucía.

![Lucía's family tree. Top row: Jorge (el abuelo) and Carmen (la abuela). Middle row: their son Roberto (el padre, papá) with his wife Elena (la madre, mamá), and their daughter Patricia (la tía) with her husband Andrés (el tío). Bottom row: Lucía (yo) and her brother Diego (el hermano), children of Roberto and Elena; Sofía (la prima) and Mateo (el primo), children of Patricia and Andrés.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Most family words come in pairs, *-o* for a man and *-a* for a woman, just as you saw in
Lesson 5:

| Man | Woman | English |
|---|---|---|
| *el padre* | *la madre* | father, mother |
| *el papá* | *la mamá* | dad, mom |
| *el hijo* | *la hija* | son, daughter |
| *el hermano* | *la hermana* | brother, sister |
| *el abuelo* | *la abuela* | grandfather, grandmother |
| *el esposo* | *la esposa* | husband, wife |
| *el tío* | *la tía* | uncle, aunt |
| *el primo* | *la prima* | cousin |
| *el novio* | *la novia* | boyfriend, girlfriend |
| *el amigo* | *la amiga* | friend |

*El bebé* (the baby) is used for any baby, and *la bebé* is also common for a girl. Two
adjectives describe whether someone is married: *casado* (married) and *soltero* (single), with
*-a* for a woman: *Mi tía es soltera.* With *casado*, Mexicans usually say *está casado*, with
the verb *estar* of Lesson 9; *es casado* is also heard.

### Plurals for mixed groups

In Lesson 5 you learned that a mixed group takes the masculine plural. Family words show why
that matters:

| Masculine plural | Can mean |
|---|---|
| *los padres* | the parents (mother and father), or the fathers |
| *los hermanos* | the brothers, or brothers and sisters |
| *los hijos* | the sons, or the children |
| *los abuelos* | the grandparents |
