| *los tíos* | the uncles, or uncles and aunts |
| *los primos* | the cousins |

So *¿Tienes hermanos?* means "Do you have any brothers or sisters?", and a woman with one
brother and two sisters answers *Sí, tengo tres hermanos.*

In Mexico, adults usually call their parents *mamá* and *papá* all their lives, and *mis
papás* is an everyday way to say "my parents", alongside *mis padres*. Watch the accent: *el
papá* (dad) is stressed at the end, while *la papa* (Lesson 11) is a potato.

## Tener: to have

*Tener* is one of the most useful verbs in Spanish, and it's irregular, so learn its forms by
heart:

| Person | tener | English |
|---|---|---|
| *yo* | *tengo* | I have |
| *tú* | *tienes* | you have |
| *él, ella, usted* | *tiene* | he/she has, you have |
| *nosotros, nosotras* | *tenemos* | we have |
| *(vosotros)* | *(tenéis)* | (you all have, Spain) |
| *ellos, ellas, ustedes* | *tienen* | they have, you all have |

Two things are irregular. The *yo* form adds a *g*: *tengo*. And in the *tú*, *él* and *ellos*
forms, where the stress falls on the stem, *e* becomes *ie*: *tienes, tiene, tienen*. *Tenemos* keeps the plain *e*
because the stress falls on the ending (*te-NE-mos*). Lesson 15 shows that many verbs change
their stem like this.

- *Tengo dos hermanos y una hermana.* — I have two brothers and a sister.
- *¿Tienes hijos?* — Do you have children?
- *Mis abuelos tienen un perro y dos gatos.* — My grandparents have a dog and two cats.
- *No tenemos carro.* — We don't have a car.

With *tener*, things people usually have only one of often drop the article in questions and
after *no*: *No tengo novio* (I don't have a boyfriend), *¿Tienes perro?* (Do you have a dog?).

### Tener … años: saying your age

In Lesson 3 you learned *¿Cuántos años tienes? — Tengo … años* as a fixed phrase. Now you can
see how it works: Spanish says you *have* years, where English says you *are* an age.

- *¿Cuántos años tiene tu abuela?* — *Tiene ochenta y dos años.* — How old is your
  grandmother? — She's eighty-two.
- *Mi hermano y yo tenemos veinte años; somos gemelos.* — My brother and I are twenty; we're
  twins.
- *El bebé tiene un año.* — The baby is one year old.

## Who? Ser in the plural

You know *soy, eres, es* from Lesson 2. Here is the whole verb *ser*:

| Person | ser |
|---|---|
| *yo* | *soy* |
| *tú* | *eres* |
| *él, ella, usted* | *es* |
| *nosotros, nosotras* | *somos* |
| *(vosotros)* | *(sois)* |
| *ellos, ellas, ustedes* | *son* |

Use it to say who people are. The question *¿Quién es?* (Who is it?) has a plural, *¿Quiénes
son?* (Who are they?):

- *¿Quién es?* — *Es mi hermana Ana.* — Who's that? — It's my sister Ana.
- *¿Quiénes son?* — *Son mis primos.* — Who are they? — They're my cousins.
- *Somos cinco en mi familia.* — There are five of us in my family.

## My, your, his, our: possessive adjectives

A **[[possessive adjective]]** says whose something is. It goes before the noun, with no article:

| Owner | one thing | several things |
|---|---|---|
| *yo* | *mi* hermano | *mis* hermanos |
| *tú* | *tu* hermano | *tus* hermanos |
| *él, ella, usted* | *su* hermano | *sus* hermanos |
| *nosotros, nosotras* | *nuestro* hermano, *nuestra* hermana | *nuestros* hermanos, *nuestras* hermanas |
| *ellos, ellas, ustedes* | *su* hermano | *sus* hermanos |

![A chart of possessive adjectives. For yo: mi hermano, mis hermanos. For tú: tu hermano, tus hermanos. For él, ella, usted: su hermano, sus hermanos. For nosotros, nosotras: nuestro hermano and nuestra hermana, nuestros hermanos and nuestras hermanas. For ellos, ellas, ustedes: su hermano, sus hermanos. Below: the ending matches the thing owned, not the owner.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The key idea: the ending matches the thing owned, not the owner. *Mis* has an *-s* because
there are several brothers, not because there are several owners. Two brothers talking about
their sister say *nuestra hermana*: two owners, but one sister, and *hermana* is feminine. Only *nuestro*
has separate masculine and feminine forms; *mi, tu* and *su* only add *-s*.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Choosing a possessive adjective
  accDescr: First ask who owns it. If the owner is yo, use mi. If tú, use tu. If él, ella, usted, ellos, ellas or ustedes, use su. If nosotros or nosotras, use nuestro, and if the thing owned is feminine, change it to nuestra. Finally, if there are several things owned, add -s, giving mis, tus, sus, nuestros or nuestras.
  A["Who owns it?"] --> B["yo: mi"]
  A --> C["tú: tu"]
  A --> D["él, ella, usted, ellos, ellas, ustedes: su"]
  A --> E["nosotros, nosotras: nuestro"]
  E --> F{"Is the thing feminine?"}
  F -- yes --> G["nuestra"]
  F -- no --> H["nuestro"]
  B --> I{"Several things?"}
  C --> I
  D --> I
  G --> I
  H --> I
  I -- yes --> J["add -s: mis, tus, sus, nuestras, nuestros"]
  I -- no --> K["keep the form"]
```

### Su: his, her, their or your

*Su* has many owners: *él, ella, usted, ellos, ellas, ustedes*. *Su perro* can be his, her,
their or your dog. Usually the conversation makes it clear. When it doesn't, use *de* + the
person instead:

- *el perro de él* (his dog), *el perro de ella* (her dog), *el perro de usted* (your dog)
- *la casa de ellos* (their house)

The same *de* gives you "'s" with names, which Spanish doesn't have: *la hermana de Lucía*
(Lucía's sister), *los hijos de Roberto* (Roberto's children).

*Tu* (your) has no accent; *tú* (you) has one, as you saw in Lesson 1: *Tú tienes tu libro.*
— You have your book.

## Dialogue: photos on the phone

Lucía shows her new colleague, Tom, some photos on her phone during a break at work.

> Tom: *¿Quiénes son?*
>
> Lucía: *Son mis papás, Roberto y Elena. Y el muchacho alto es mi hermano Diego.*
>
> Tom: *¿Cuántos años tiene tu hermano?*
>
> Lucía: *Tiene veinticinco. Es soltero, pero tiene novia.*
>
> Tom: *¿Y la señora con el perro?*
>
> Lucía: *Es mi tía Patricia. Su perro se llama Chispa. Y los niños son sus hijos, mis primos
> Sofía y Mateo.*
>
> Tom: *Tu familia es muy grande.*
>
> Lucía: *Sí, y los domingos estamos todos en la casa de mis abuelos. ¿Y tú? ¿Tienes
> hermanos?*
>
> Tom: *No, no tengo hermanos. Somos tres: mis padres y yo. Y nuestro gato, claro.*

Translation:

> Tom: Who are they?
>
> Lucía: They're my parents, Roberto and Elena. And the tall young man is my brother Diego.
>
> Tom: How old is your brother?
>
> Lucía: He's twenty-five. He's single, but he has a girlfriend.
>
> Tom: And the lady with the dog?
>
> Lucía: That's my aunt Patricia. Her dog is called Chispa. And the children are her kids, my
> cousins Sofía and Mateo.
>
> Tom: Your family is very big.
>
> Lucía: Yes, and on Sundays we're all at my grandparents' house. And you? Do you have any
> brothers or sisters?
>
> Tom: No, I don't have any. There are three of us: my parents and me. And our cat, of course.

New words to recognise: *el muchacho* (young man), *alto* and *grande* (tall, big; Lesson 8),
*pero* (but), *se llama* (is called, Lesson 2), *los domingos* (on Sundays, Lesson 13),
*estamos todos* (we're all; *estar*, Lesson 9), *la casa* (house, Lesson 10), *claro* (of
course, Lesson 14).

## Pronunciation

- *mamá, papá*: stress the last syllable: *ma-MÁ, pa-PÁ*. *Bebé* too: *be-BÉ*.
- *tío, tía*: two syllables, *TÍ-o, TÍ-a*. The accent stops *-io* from blending into one
  syllable.
- *hijo, hija*: the *h* is silent and *j* is a breathy sound, like a strong English *h*:
  *I-ho, I-ha*.
- *tengo* vs *tienes*: in *tienes* the *ie* is one syllable, like "yeah" quickly: *TIE-nes*.
- *abuelo*: *ue* is one syllable, like "way": *a-BUE-lo*.

## Common mistakes

- Using *ser* for age: ~~Soy treinta años~~ → *Tengo treinta años*.
- Matching the possessive to the owner: a woman talking about her brothers says *mis
  hermanos*; a man talking about his and his wife's daughter says *nuestra hija*, not
  ~~nuestro hija~~.
- Putting an article before a possessive: ~~la mi casa~~ → *mi casa*.
- Writing *tú* for "your": ~~tú hermano~~ → *tu hermano*.
- Reading *los padres* as "the fathers" every time. It usually means "the parents".
- Forgetting the *g* in *tengo*, or the *ie* in *tienes, tiene, tienen*: ~~teno~~,
  ~~tenes~~ → *tengo, tienes*.

## Key points

- Family words come in pairs (*el hermano / la hermana*), and the masculine plural covers mixed
  groups: *los hermanos* = siblings, *los padres* = parents. In Mexico *mis papás* is very
  common.
- *Tener*: *tengo, tienes, tiene, tenemos, tienen*. Age uses *tener*: *Tengo 30 años.*
- *Ser* in the plural: *somos, son*. *¿Quién es? ¿Quiénes son?*
- Possessives: *mi(s), tu(s), su(s), nuestro/a(s)*. The ending matches the thing owned.
- *Su* can mean his, her, their or your; use *de él, de ella, de usted* to be clear, and *de*
  + a name for "'s": *el perro de Ana*.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Jobs, countries, languages and -er/-ir verbs
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

After your name and your family, people want to know what you do, where you're from and which
languages you speak. This lesson gives you the words for jobs, countries, nationalities and
languages, and it completes the present tense: in Lesson 4 you learned the *-ar* verbs; now come
the *-er* verbs (*aprender*, to learn) and the *-ir* verbs (*vivir*, to live).

From this lesson on, the conjugation drills on the Vocabulary tab practise the present tense of
every verb you've learned so far, including *ser* and *tener*.

## The present tense of -er and -ir verbs

Every Spanish infinitive ends in *-ar*, *-er* or *-ir*. You make the present tense the same way
for all three: take off the ending to find the stem, then add the endings for each person. The
*-er* and *-ir* endings use *e* where *-ar* verbs use *a*.

![A chart of the present tense endings. Columns: -ar (hablar), -er (aprender), -ir (vivir). Rows: yo hablo, aprendo, vivo; tú hablas, aprendes, vives; él, ella, usted habla, aprende, vive; nosotros hablamos, aprendemos, vivimos; ellos, ustedes hablan, aprenden, viven. The endings are underlined, and the nosotros forms aprendemos and vivimos are highlighted. Note below: -er and -ir share every ending except nosotros, -emos and -imos; vosotros (Spain only) habláis, aprendéis, vivís.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

| | -ar: *hablar* | -er: *aprender* | -ir: *vivir* |
|---|---|---|---|
| *yo* | *hablo* | *aprendo* | *vivo* |
| *tú* | *hablas* | *aprendes* | *vives* |
| *él, ella, usted* | *habla* | *aprende* | *vive* |
| *nosotros, nosotras* | *hablamos* | *aprendemos* | *vivimos* |
| *(vosotros)* | *(habláis)* | *(aprendéis)* | *(vivís)* |
| *ellos, ellas, ustedes* | *hablan* | *aprenden* | *viven* |

Look at the *-er* and *-ir* columns: they're identical except in the *nosotros* form (and the
*vosotros* form of Spain). So once you know *aprender*, you know *vivir* too; just remember
*vivimos* with *i*.

The other verbs of this lesson work the same way:

- *comprender* (to understand): *No comprendo la pregunta.* — I don't understand the question.
- *leer* (to read): *leo, lees, lee, leemos, leen*. The stem *le-* plus the ending gives two
  *e*'s in a row, and you pronounce both: *Leemos un libro en clase.* — We're reading a book in
  class.
- *vivir*: *¿Dónde vives? — Vivo en Chicago, pero mis padres viven en Puebla.* In Lesson 2
  *vivo en* was a fixed phrase; now you can make every form.
- *aprender*: *Aprendemos español.* — We're learning Spanish.

As with *-ar* verbs, the Spanish present covers both "I learn" and "I'm learning", and you
usually leave out the subject pronoun: *Leo mucho* = I read a lot.

## Ser: who you are and what you do

You've now seen every form of *ser*: *soy, eres, es, somos, (sois), son*. Use it for your job and
your nationality, the two things in this lesson that describe who you are.

### Jobs: no article

To say what someone does, use *ser* + the job with no article:

- *Soy maestra.* — I'm a teacher. (Not ~~Soy una maestra~~.)
- *Mi hermano es ingeniero.* — My brother is an engineer.
- *¿Ustedes son estudiantes?* — Are you students?

English needs "a" here; Spanish doesn't. (When you add a description, the article comes back:
*Es una maestra muy buena*, She's a very good teacher. That's Lesson 8.)

Most job words follow the *-o/-a* pattern, or add *-a* to a consonant:

| Man | Woman | English |
|---|---|---|
| *el maestro* | *la maestra* | teacher |
| *el ingeniero* | *la ingeniera* | engineer |
| *el mesero* | *la mesera* | waiter, server |
| *el cocinero* | *la cocinera* | cook |
| *el doctor* | *la doctora* | doctor |
| *el vendedor* | *la vendedora* | salesperson |
| *el estudiante* | *la estudiante* | student |
| *el policía* | *la policía* | police officer |

*Estudiante* and *policía* change only the article. *La policía* also means "the police" as a
whole: *Llamo a la policía.* — I'm calling the police.

To ask about someone's job: *¿En qué trabajas?* (What do you do? literally "In what do you
work?") or, a little more formally, *¿A qué se dedica usted?* Places to work: *Trabajo en una
oficina / en una escuela / en la universidad.*

In Mexico *maestro* is the everyday word for a schoolteacher, and people also use *profesor* /
*profesora*, especially at secondary school and university. Spain says *camarero* for a waiter.

## Countries and nationalities

Here are the countries in this lesson. Spanish is the main language in four of them.

```map
base: world
title: The countries in this lesson
view: fit
labels: on
region: Mexico, Colombia, Argentina, Spain | Spanish is the main language
region: United States, Canada | English is the most widely spoken language
caption: México, Colombia, Argentina and España; Estados Unidos and Canadá. Country names start with a capital letter in Spanish, as in English.
```

A **[[nationality adjective]]** says where someone or something is from: *mexicano* (Mexican),
*canadiense* (Canadian). Like other adjectives it agrees with the person (Lesson 8 explains
agreement fully), and there are three patterns:

| Country | Man | Woman | Pattern |
|---|---|---|---|
| *México* | *mexicano* | *mexicana* | -o → -a |
| *Colombia* | *colombiano* | *colombiana* | -o → -a |
| *Argentina* | *argentino* | *argentina* | -o → -a |
| *España* | *español* | *española* | consonant + -a |
| *Estados Unidos* | *estadounidense* | *estadounidense* | -ense: no change |
| *Canadá* | *canadiense* | *canadiense* | -ense: no change |

When a nationality ends in a consonant, the woman's form adds *-a*. If the man's form has an
accent on its last syllable, the accent disappears: the stressed syllable is now second-to-last,
where the rule from Lesson 1 expects it: *inglés → inglesa* (English), *francés → francesa* (French), *alemán → alemana*
(German). For groups, add *-s* or *-es*: *mexicanos, españoles, canadienses, ingleses*.

- *Soy estadounidense, de Texas.* — I'm American, from Texas.
- *Mi esposa es española.* — My wife is Spanish.
- *Somos canadienses.* — We're Canadian.

Nationalities and languages are written with a small letter in Spanish: *Es mexicana. Hablo
inglés.* Only the country has a capital: *México, España.*

A note on "American": in Latin America *americano* can mean anyone from the Americas, from
Canada to Chile, so the neutral word for someone from the United States is *estadounidense*.
You'll still hear *americano* for the US, and in Mexico also *gringo*, which is informal and can
sound rude.

## Languages

A language is a masculine noun, usually the same word as the man's nationality: *el español, el
inglés, el francés, el alemán, el chino* (Chinese). After *hablar* the article usually drops:

- *¿Qué idiomas hablas?* — What languages do you speak?
- *Hablo inglés y español.* — I speak English and Spanish.
- *Hablo un poco de español.* — I speak a little Spanish.
- *El español es muy útil.* — Spanish is very useful. (Subject: article needed.)

*El idioma* (language) ends in *-a* but is masculine, one of the exceptions from Lesson 5. You'll
also hear *Hablo español e inglés*: before a word that starts with an *i* sound, *y* (and)
becomes *e* so the two vowels don't merge (Lesson 23). The language is also called *el
castellano*, especially in Spain and parts of South America.

## Dialogue: a language exchange in Mexico City

Every Thursday a café in Mexico City holds an *intercambio*, where people practise languages
with each other. Paul meets Daniela and Andrés.

> Daniela: *Hola, soy Daniela. ¿Cómo te llamas?*
>
> Paul: *Me llamo Paul. Soy estadounidense, pero vivo aquí en la Ciudad de México.*
>
> Daniela: *¡Qué bien! ¿En qué trabajas?*
>
> Paul: *Soy ingeniero. Trabajo en una oficina en el centro. ¿Y tú?*
>
> Daniela: *Soy maestra de inglés en una escuela. Él es Andrés, mi amigo. Es colombiano.*
>
> Andrés: *Mucho gusto. Yo soy estudiante. Aprendo francés en la universidad.*
>
> Paul: *¿Qué idiomas hablan ustedes?*
>
> Daniela: *Hablamos español, claro, e inglés. Y Andrés lee y comprende francés.*
>
> Andrés: *Comprendo mucho, pero hablo poco.*

Translation:

> Daniela: Hi, I'm Daniela. What's your name?
>
> Paul: My name's Paul. I'm American, but I live here in Mexico City.
>
> Daniela: That's great! What do you do?
>
> Paul: I'm an engineer. I work in an office downtown. And you?
>
> Daniela: I'm an English teacher at a school. This is Andrés, my friend. He's Colombian.
>
> Andrés: Nice to meet you. I'm a student. I'm learning French at the university.
>
> Paul: What languages do you speak?
>
> Daniela: We speak Spanish, of course, and English. And Andrés reads and understands French.
>
> Andrés: I understand a lot, but I speak little.

New bits: *¡Qué bien!* (great!), *en el centro* (downtown), *poco* (little, not much), *claro*
(of course, Lesson 14). *Maestra de inglés* means "English teacher": the subject comes after
*de*.

## Pronunciation

- *México, mexicano*: the *x* sounds like Spanish *j*, a breathy *h*: *MÉ-hi-co,
  me-hi-CA-no*. This old spelling is kept in the country's name.
- *Canadá*: stress at the end, *ca-na-DÁ*. *Inglés*: *in-GLÉS*.
- *estadounidense*: long but regular: *es-ta-dou-ni-DEN-se*.
- *leer, leemos*: say both *e*'s: *le-ER, le-E-mos*.
- *policía*: *po-li-CÍ-a*, four syllables; the accent keeps *-ía* apart.
- *ingeniero*: *g* before *e* is the breathy *j* sound: *in-he-NIE-ro*.

## Common mistakes

- Adding an article to a bare job: ~~Soy un estudiante~~ → *Soy estudiante*.
- Capital letters on nationalities and languages: ~~Soy Canadiense~~, ~~hablo Español~~ →
  *Soy canadiense, hablo español*.
- Using *-emos* for *-ir* verbs: ~~vivemos~~ → *vivimos*.
- Using *-a-* endings for *-er/-ir* verbs: ~~aprendas~~ → *aprendes*; ~~vivan~~ → *viven*.
- Keeping the accent in the feminine: ~~inglésa~~ → *inglesa*.
- Saying ~~la idioma~~ → *el idioma*.
- Adding *-a* to *-ense*: ~~canadiensa~~ → *canadiense*.

## Key points

- *-er*: *-o, -es, -e, -emos, -en*. *-ir*: *-o, -es, -e, -imos, -en*. They differ only in
  *nosotros* (and Spain's *vosotros*).
- Jobs: *ser* + job, no article: *Soy ingeniera.*
- Nationalities: *-o → -a* (*mexicana*), consonant + *-a* (*española*), *-ense* unchanged
  (*canadiense*). Lowercase, like languages; countries have a capital.
- Languages are masculine: *el español, el inglés*. *¿Qué idiomas hablas? — Hablo inglés y un
  poco de español.*
- *Estadounidense* is the neutral word for someone from the United States.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Describing people and things: adjective agreement and colours
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

You can now name people and things: *el libro, mi hermana, un ingeniero mexicano*. In this
lesson you learn to describe them: big or small, new or old, easy or difficult, red or blue.
Spanish adjectives change their endings to match the noun they describe, so this lesson builds
directly on gender and plurals from Lesson 5. You'll also learn to ask *¿Cómo es?* (What is it
like?) and to make a description stronger or softer with *muy, bastante* and *un poco*.

## Adjectives come after the noun

In English the adjective comes first: "a new book". In Spanish it usually comes after the noun:

- *un libro nuevo* — a new book
- *una ciudad interesante* — an interesting city
- *un perro pequeño* — a small dog

Put it the other way round and it sounds wrong or poetic, so make "noun first, adjective
second" your habit. A few adjectives can come before the noun; you'll meet *buen, mal* and *gran*
below.

## Adjectives agree with the noun

A Spanish adjective takes the gender and number of its noun. This matching is called
**[[agreement]]**. How many forms an adjective has depends on how its masculine singular form ends.

![A grid showing adjective agreement. Rows: el libro, la mochila, los libros, las mochilas. Columns: an -o adjective (nuevo), an -e adjective (grande) and a consonant adjective (azul). The forms are nuevo, nueva, nuevos, nuevas; grande, grande, grandes, grandes; azul, azul, azules, azules. Note: -o adjectives have four forms; -e and consonant adjectives have two.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Adjectives in -o have four forms. Change *-o* to *-a* for the feminine, and add *-s* for the
plural:

| | masculine | feminine |
|---|---|---|
| singular | *un gato negro* | *una silla negra* |
| plural | *unos gatos negros* | *unas sillas negras* |

Adjectives in -e have two forms, singular and plural. They don't change for gender:

- *un libro interesante, una clase interesante* — *libros interesantes, clases interesantes*
- *un carro verde, una puerta verde* — *carros verdes, puertas verdes*

Adjectives ending in a consonant also have two forms. The plural adds *-es*:

- *un cuaderno azul, una pluma azul* — *cuadernos azules, plumas azules*
- *un examen fácil, una pregunta fácil* — *exámenes fáciles, preguntas fáciles*
- *un gato gris, una silla gris* — *gatos grises, sillas grises*
- *un hombre joven, una mujer joven* — *hombres jóvenes, mujeres jóvenes*

(*el carro* = car, Lesson 18; *la clase* = class; *el examen* = exam; *la pregunta* = question.)

The plural spelling rules are the ones you learned for nouns. A final *-z* becomes *-ces*:
*feliz* (happy, Lesson 9) → *felices*. A written accent can appear: *joven → jóvenes*. And
*fácil, difícil* keep theirs: *fáciles, difíciles*.

The main exception is the group you met in Lesson 7: nationalities ending in a consonant do add
*-a* (*español → española, inglés → inglesa*). A few other adjectives do too, mainly those in
*-or* (*trabajador → trabajadora*, hard-working); you'll meet them later.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Making an adjective agree
  accDescr: Start from the masculine singular form of the adjective. If it ends in -o, use -o or -a for gender, and add -s for the plural, giving four forms such as nuevo, nueva, nuevos, nuevas. If it ends in -e, it is the same for both genders, and the plural adds -s, as in grande, grandes. If it ends in a consonant, it is the same for both genders, unless it is a nationality such as español, española; the plural adds -es, as in azul, azules, and a final z becomes ces, as in feliz, felices.
  A["Masculine singular form"] --> B{"How does it end?"}
  B -- "-o" --> C["Four forms: nuevo, nueva, nuevos, nuevas"]
  B -- "-e" --> D["Two forms: grande, grandes"]
  B -- "consonant" --> E{"A nationality?"}
  E -- yes --> F["Add -a: español, española"]
  E -- no --> G["Two forms: azul, azules; z to ces: feliz, felices"]
```

### Two nouns, one adjective

When one adjective describes a masculine and a feminine noun together, it takes the masculine
plural, just like a mixed group of people in Lesson 5:

- *El libro y la mochila son nuevos.* — The book and the backpack are new.
- *Mi hermano y mi hermana son altos.* — My brother and sister are tall.

## Ser + adjective: what something is like

To describe what someone or something is like, use *ser* + adjective. The adjective still
agrees with the subject:

- *Mi casa es pequeña.* — My house is small.
- *Mis primos son muy simpáticos.* — My cousins are very nice.
- *La lección es fácil.* — The lesson is easy.

To ask for a description, use *¿Cómo es…?* (What is … like?):

- *¿Cómo es tu ciudad?* — *Es grande y bastante bonita.* — What's your city like? — It's big
  and quite pretty.
- *¿Cómo son tus maestros?* — *Son jóvenes e inteligentes.* — What are your teachers like? —
  They're young and smart. (*y* becomes *e* before *inteligentes*, as in Lesson 7.)

Notice the difference from Lesson 2: *¿Cómo estás?* asks how you are feeling today; *¿Cómo
eres?* asks what you are like as a person.

Here are the adjectives of this lesson, most of them in pairs of opposites:

| Adjective | Opposite |
|---|---|
| *grande* — big | *pequeño* — small |
| *nuevo* — new; *joven* — young | *viejo* — old |
| *bonito* (*lindo*) — pretty | *feo* — ugly |
| *bueno* — good | *malo* — bad |
| *alto* — tall | *bajo* — short (height) |
| *largo* — long | *corto* — short (length) |
| *fácil* — easy | *difícil* — difficult |
| *interesante* — interesting | *aburrido* — boring |

Two more for people: *simpático* (nice, friendly) and *inteligente* (intelligent, smart).

*Lindo* is very common in Latin America for "pretty" or "lovely". For people, *viejo* can sound
blunt; *mayor* (older) is more polite: *una señora mayor*.

## Muy, bastante, un poco

Three words change the strength of an adjective. They never change their own form.

- *muy* (very): *La película es muy larga.* — The film is very long.
- *bastante* (quite, fairly): *El español es bastante fácil.* — Spanish is quite easy.
- *un poco* (a little, a bit): *El libro es un poco aburrido.* — The book is a bit boring.

*Un poco* goes with negative or unwelcome qualities: *un poco caro* (a bit expensive, Lesson
12), *un poco difícil*. To soften a positive word, use *bastante*, or say *no muy*: *No es muy
interesante.* — It isn't very interesting.

## Buen, mal, gran: short forms before a noun

*Bueno* and *malo* can go before the noun, and then they drop their *-o* before a masculine
singular noun. Lesson 3 called this shortening **[[apocope]]** (like *uno → un*):

- *un buen amigo* — a good friend (but *una buena amiga*, *unos buenos amigos*)
- *un mal día* — a bad day (but *una mala idea*)

*Grande* becomes *gran* before any singular noun, and its meaning changes from "big" to
"great":

- *una ciudad grande* — a big city
- *una gran ciudad* — a great city
- *un gran maestro* — a great teacher

## Colours

The question is *¿De qué color es…?* (What colour is…?). Colours are adjectives, so they follow
the noun and agree with it.

![Eight colour squares: rojo (red), azul (blue), verde (green), amarillo (yellow), negro (black), blanco (white), gris (grey) and café (brown).](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

| Pattern | Colours | Example |
|---|---|---|
| -o: four forms | *rojo, amarillo, negro, blanco* | *una mochila roja, los gatos negros* |
| -e or consonant: two forms | *verde, azul, gris* | *una puerta verde, dos plumas azules* |
| often doesn't change | *café* | *unos zapatos café* (or *cafés*) |

*Café* (brown) means "coffee-coloured". It is the same for both genders (*una silla café*), and
in the plural you'll hear both *unos zapatos café* and *unos zapatos cafés* (shoes, Lesson 20);
in Mexico *ojos cafés* (brown eyes) is very common. Both are correct. Spain and some other
countries say *marrón* (plural *marrones*) instead. *El color* itself is masculine: *¿De qué color es tu carro? — Es gris.*

## Dialogue: lost and found

Martín calls the university's lost-and-found office (*objetos perdidos*).

> Empleada: *Objetos perdidos, buenas tardes.*
>
> Martín: *Buenas tardes. Busco una mochila. Es azul y bastante grande.*
>
> Empleada: *Tenemos tres mochilas azules. ¿Cómo es la mochila?*
>
> Martín: *Es vieja y un poco fea, pero es muy buena. Tiene una computadora pequeña y dos
> cuadernos.*
>
> Empleada: *¿De qué color son los cuadernos?*
>
> Martín: *Un cuaderno es rojo y el otro es amarillo. Y hay unos lentes negros.*
>
> Empleada: *Mmm… aquí hay una mochila azul con unos lentes café.*
>
> Martín: *No, mis lentes son negros. Y mis llaves son de la casa de mis padres: son tres llaves
> grises.*
>
> Empleada: *¡Ah! Sí, aquí está. Es una mochila azul, vieja, con un cuaderno rojo y uno
> amarillo.*
>
> Martín: *¡Qué buena noticia! ¡Muchas gracias!*

Translation:

> Employee: Lost and found, good afternoon.
>
> Martín: Good afternoon. I'm looking for a backpack. It's blue and quite big.
>
> Employee: We have three blue backpacks. What's the backpack like?
>
> Martín: It's old and a bit ugly, but it's very good. It has a small computer and two notebooks
> in it.
>
> Employee: What colour are the notebooks?
>
> Martín: One notebook is red and the other is yellow. And there are some black glasses.
>
> Employee: Hmm… here's a blue backpack with some brown glasses.
>
> Martín: No, my glasses are black. And my keys are for my parents' house: they're three grey
> keys.
>
> Employee: Ah! Yes, here it is. It's an old blue backpack with a red notebook and a yellow one.
>
> Martín: What good news! Thank you very much!

New bits: *la empleada* (the employee), *el otro* (the other one, Lesson 12), *hay* (there is,
there are; Lesson 10), *aquí está* (here it is; *estar*, Lesson 9), *con* (with), *la noticia*
(news). Notice *un cuaderno rojo y uno amarillo*: *un* becomes *uno* when the noun is left out.

## Pronunciation

- *rojo*: the *r* at the start of a word is the strong rolled *r* (like *rr*), and *j* is a
  breathy *h*: *RRO-ho*.
- *amarillo*: one tap of the tongue for the single *r*, and *ll* as *y*: *a-ma-RI-yo*.
- *azul*: *z* sounds like *s*: *a-SUL*.
- *fácil, difícil*: the accents show stress that breaks the rule: *FÁ-sil, di-FÍ-sil*.
- *café*: stress on the last syllable, *ca-FÉ*, for the colour and for coffee.
- *simpático*: *sim-PÁ-ti-co*; every word stressed three syllables from the end has an accent.

## Common mistakes

- Putting the adjective first: ~~una roja mochila~~ → *una mochila roja*.
- Forgetting to agree: ~~las sillas negro~~ → *las sillas negras*; ~~los libros interesante~~
  → *los libros interesantes*.
- Adding *-a* to *-e* or consonant adjectives: ~~una clase interesanta~~, ~~una pluma azula~~ →
  *interesante, azul*.
- Dropping the accent in the plural of *café*: ~~ojos cafes~~ → *ojos cafés* (or *ojos café*).
- *Bueno* before a masculine noun: ~~un bueno libro~~ → *un buen libro* (or *un libro bueno*).
- False friends: *largo* = long (not large); *simpático* = nice, friendly (not sympathetic).
- *Un poco* with a positive word: ~~un poco bonito~~ → *bastante bonito*.

## Key points

- Adjectives usually follow the noun and agree with it in gender and number.
- -o adjectives: four forms (*nuevo, nueva, nuevos, nuevas*). -e and consonant adjectives: two
  (*grande, grandes; azul, azules*). Nationalities in a consonant add *-a*.
- A masculine and a feminine noun together take a masculine plural adjective.
- *Ser* + adjective for what someone or something is like: *¿Cómo es? — Es alta y simpática.*
- *Muy* (very), *bastante* (quite), *un poco* (a bit, with negative qualities).
- *buen, mal* before a masculine singular noun; *gran* before any singular noun = great.
- Colours agree like other adjectives; *café* never changes for gender, and its plural can be
  *café* or *cafés* (Spain: *marrón*).

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Honors: The Spanish-speaking world
lessons.body:
## Twenty countries, one language

In Lesson 7 you learned six countries and four nationality adjectives: *mexicano, español,
estadounidense, canadiense*. But Spanish isn't only the language of Mexico and Spain. It's the
main language of most of the Americas south of the United States, and Instituto Cervantes counted
more than 500 million native speakers in its 2025 yearbook, more than 635 million people who
speak it at any level. Mexico has more Spanish speakers than any other country.

This honors lesson takes you around that world. You'll learn which countries speak Spanish, how
to form the nationality adjective for each one, and their capital cities, and you'll read short
texts about people from different countries. Along the way you'll practise everything from
Module 2: articles, *ser*, *tener*, *-er/-ir* verbs and adjective agreement.

## Where Spanish is official

Spanish is the **[[official language]]**, or the main national language, of 20 countries. This
is the count you'll find in most reference books and in Spanish-language schools:

- North and Central America (7): México, Guatemala, Honduras, El Salvador, Nicaragua, Costa
  Rica and Panamá.
- The Caribbean (2): Cuba and República Dominicana (Dominican Republic).
- South America (9): Colombia, Venezuela, Ecuador, Perú, Bolivia, Chile, Argentina, Uruguay
  and Paraguay.
- Europe (1): España.
- Africa (1): Guinea Ecuatorial (Equatorial Guinea), a former Spanish colony in Central
  Africa.

Add Puerto Rico, a territory of the United States where Spanish and English are both
official and Spanish is the everyday language of most people. Puerto Rico isn't an independent
country, so it isn't in the 20.

```map
base: world
title: Where Spanish is official
view: fit
region: Mexico, Guatemala, Honduras, El Salvador, Nicaragua, Costa Rica, Panama | North and Central America
region: Cuba, Dominican Republic, Puerto Rico | The Caribbean
region: Colombia, Venezuela, Ecuador, Peru, Bolivia, Chile, Argentina, Uruguay, Paraguay | South America
region: Spain, Equatorial Guinea | Europe and Africa
caption: The 20 countries where Spanish is the official or main national language, plus Puerto Rico (a US territory). Brazil, the biggest country in South America, speaks Portuguese.
```

A few details make "official" more interesting than it sounds:

- "Official" by law or in practice. In Mexico, Argentina, Chile and Uruguay no law declares
  Spanish the official language; it's simply the language of government, schools and the
  courts. Mexico's language law of 2003 calls Spanish and the country's Indigenous languages
  *lenguas nacionales* (national languages) with equal validity.
- Shared with other languages. Paraguay has two official languages, Spanish and Guaraní,
  and most Paraguayans speak some Guaraní. Bolivia's 2009 constitution makes Spanish and all
  the Indigenous languages of the country official. Peru adds Quechua, Aymara and other
  Indigenous languages where they're spoken by most people. Equatorial Guinea also has French
  and Portuguese as official languages.
- The count can change. In May 2026 the government of Antigua and Barbuda, an
  English-speaking Caribbean country, approved a policy to make Spanish its "official second
  language". When this lesson was written (November 2026) it was a government policy, not a
  law, and the country isn't Spanish-speaking, so the usual count stays at 20. Some websites
  already say 21.
- The United States has one of the largest Spanish-speaking populations in the world, but
  Spanish isn't official there. Lesson 93 looks at Spanish in the US.

## Nationality adjectives

Each country has a **[[nationality adjective]]** (in Spanish, *el gentilicio*). You know the rules
from Lessons 7 and 8: the adjective agrees with the person, it's written with a small letter,
and the masculine form is also the noun for a man (*un chileno*, a Chilean man). Here are all of
them, with the capital cities:

| País (country) | Capital | Nationality (m., f.) |
|---|---|---|
| México | Ciudad de México | mexicano, mexicana |
| Guatemala | Ciudad de Guatemala | guatemalteco, guatemalteca |
| Honduras | Tegucigalpa | hondureño, hondureña |
| El Salvador | San Salvador | salvadoreño, salvadoreña |
| Nicaragua | Managua | nicaragüense |
| Costa Rica | San José | costarricense |
| Panamá | Ciudad de Panamá | panameño, panameña |
| Cuba | La Habana | cubano, cubana |
| República Dominicana | Santo Domingo | dominicano, dominicana |
| Puerto Rico (US territory) | San Juan | puertorriqueño, puertorriqueña |
| Colombia | Bogotá | colombiano, colombiana |
| Venezuela | Caracas | venezolano, venezolana |
| Ecuador | Quito | ecuatoriano, ecuatoriana |
| Perú | Lima | peruano, peruana |
| Bolivia | Sucre (the government sits in La Paz) | boliviano, boliviana |
| Chile | Santiago | chileno, chilena |
| Argentina | Buenos Aires | argentino, argentina |
| Uruguay | Montevideo | uruguayo, uruguaya |
| Paraguay | Asunción | paraguayo, paraguaya |
| España | Madrid | español, española |
| Guinea Ecuatorial | Ciudad de la Paz (since 2026; before, Malabo) | ecuatoguineano, ecuatoguineana |

Two capitals need a note. Bolivia's constitution names Sucre as the capital, but the president,
the government and the congress are in La Paz, so both cities are often called capitals.
Equatorial Guinea made Ciudad de la Paz, a new city on the mainland, its capital by a decree of
January 2026, replacing Malabo on the island of Bioko; the government's offices were given a
year to move, so older books and maps still show Malabo.

### The patterns

The endings look like a long list, but they fall into a few groups:

| Ending | Nationalities |
|---|---|
| *-ano / -ana* | *mexicano, cubano, dominicano, colombiano, venezolano, ecuatoriano, peruano, boliviano, ecuatoguineano* |
| *-eño / -eña* | *hondureño, salvadoreño, panameño, puertorriqueño* |
| *-ino, -eno, -ayo* | *argentino, chileno, uruguayo, paraguayo* |
| *-ense* (no change) | *nicaragüense, costarricense* (and *canadiense, estadounidense*) |
| others | *guatemalteco, español* |

All of them except the *-ense* group have four forms, like *nuevo*: *un chico peruano, una
chica peruana, unos turistas peruanos, unas doctoras peruanas*. The *-ense* adjectives have two,
like *grande*: *un doctor costarricense, unas maestras costarricenses*.

Look at the spelling of two of them. *Nicaragüense* keeps the two dots on the *ü*, because the
*u* is pronounced: *ni-ca-ra-GÜEN-se*. *Puertorriqueño* writes *rr* inside the word, because a
single *r* between vowels would be a soft tap, and the *r* of *Rico* is the strong one.

You'll also hear informal names: *tico, tica* for Costa Ricans and *boricua* for Puerto Ricans,
which many people use proudly about themselves. The standard forms in the table are always
safe.

## Reading: four people, four countries

> *Me llamo Sofía y soy chilena. Vivo en Santiago, la capital de Chile. Soy ingeniera y trabajo
> en una oficina muy grande. Hablo español y un poco de inglés.*
>
> *Yo soy Mateo. Soy cubano, pero vivo en España, en Madrid. Tengo veintiocho años y soy
> cocinero en un restaurante. Mi esposa es española.*
>
> *Somos Ana y Luis y vivimos en Guatemala. Ana es guatemalteca y Luis es salvadoreño. Somos maestros en
> una escuela pequeña. Nuestros hijos aprenden español y kaqchikel, un idioma maya.*
>
> *Hola, soy Kevin. Soy puertorriqueño y vivo en San Juan. Soy estudiante en la universidad.
> En Puerto Rico hablamos español y también inglés.*

Translation:

> My name is Sofía and I'm Chilean. I live in Santiago, the capital of Chile. I'm an engineer
> and I work in a very big office. I speak Spanish and a little English.
>
> I'm Mateo. I'm Cuban, but I live in Spain, in Madrid. I'm twenty-eight and I'm a cook in a
> restaurant. My wife is Spanish.
>
> We're Ana and Luis and we live in Guatemala. Ana is Guatemalan and Luis is Salvadoran. We're teachers
> at a small school. Our children are learning Spanish and Kaqchikel, a Mayan language.
>
> Hi, I'm Kevin. I'm Puerto Rican and I live in San Juan. I'm a student at the university. In
> Puerto Rico we speak Spanish and English too.

Notice *Somos maestros* for a man and a woman together: the masculine plural, as always for a
mixed group. Kaqchikel is one of the more than twenty Mayan languages spoken in Guatemala.

## Worked examples

### Example 1: from a country to a sentence

Write "My friends (two women) are from Costa Rica" using a nationality adjective.

1. Find the adjective: Costa Rica → *costarricense*.
2. Check its pattern: *-ense*, so it doesn't change for gender, only for number.
3. The subject is plural (*mis amigas*), so add *-s*: *costarricenses*.
4. Use *ser* in the plural, *son*, and keep the adjective lowercase: *Mis amigas son
   costarricenses.*

Compare *Mis amigas son peruanas*: *peruano* is an *-o* adjective, so the feminine plural is
*-as*.

### Example 2: capital, country, nationality

Read *La capital de Ecuador es Quito* and write a sentence about a man from that city.

1. The country is Ecuador; its adjective is *ecuatoriano* (an *-ano* adjective, four forms).
2. A man: masculine singular, *ecuatoriano*.
3. *Él es de Quito. Es ecuatoriano.* Or in one sentence: *Es un hombre ecuatoriano de Quito.*
   (With *un hombre*, the adjective follows the noun, as in Lesson 8.)

### Example 3: capital letters

Which words in this sentence need a capital: *mi esposa es española y vive en madrid, la capital
de españa*?

1. The first word of the sentence: *Mi*.
2. Names of cities and countries: *Madrid, España*.
3. Not the nationality adjective: *española* stays lowercase, and so does *la capital*.

Answer: *Mi esposa es española y vive en Madrid, la capital de España.*

## Common mistakes

- Capitalising nationalities: ~~Soy Colombiana~~ → *Soy colombiana*.
- Making *-ense* adjectives feminine with *-a*: ~~costarricensa~~ → *costarricense*.
- Spelling *puertorriqueño* with one *r* (~~puertoriqueño~~), or *nicaragüense* without the
  dots.
- Saying ~~el capital de Perú~~ for the city. The city is *la capital*; *el capital* means money
  invested in a business.
- Assuming every country south of the United States speaks Spanish: Brazil speaks Portuguese, Guyana English and
  Suriname Dutch, and in Central America Belize's official language is English.
- Forgetting the article in *El Salvador* and *La Habana*, which are part of the names: *Soy de
  El Salvador. Vivo en La Habana.*

## Key points

- Spanish is the official or main national language of 20 countries: 18 in the Americas, plus
  Spain and Equatorial Guinea. Puerto Rico (a US territory) also has Spanish as an official
  language.
- In some countries Spanish shares official status with Indigenous or other languages (Paraguay,
  Bolivia, Peru, Equatorial Guinea); in Mexico, Argentina, Chile and Uruguay it's official in
  practice rather than by law.
- Nationality adjectives are lowercase and agree like other adjectives: *-ano, -eño, -ino* and
  similar endings have four forms; *-ense* has two.
- Watch the spelling of *puertorriqueño* and *nicaragüense*, and say *la capital* for a capital
  city.
- Capitals change sometimes: Equatorial Guinea moved its capital from Malabo to Ciudad de la Paz
  in 2026.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Honors: Family words, diminutives and affection
lessons.body:
## Beyond mamá and papá

In Lesson 6 you met the close family: *padres, hermanos, abuelos, tíos, primos*. In real
conversations in Mexico you'll hear many more family words, and you'll hear the family words you
know in new shapes: *mi abuelita, mi hermanito, mijo*. This honors lesson covers three things:
the wider family, including the in-laws and the godparents, who play a big part in Mexican
family life; the **[[diminutive]]** endings *-ito* and *-ita*, which make words small or
affectionate; and the ways people speak to those they love.

## In-laws, grandchildren, nephews and nieces

| Man | Woman | English |
|---|---|---|
| *el suegro* | *la suegra* | father-in-law, mother-in-law |
| *el cuñado* | *la cuñada* | brother-in-law, sister-in-law |
| *el yerno* | *la nuera* | son-in-law, daughter-in-law |
| *el nieto* | *la nieta* | grandson, granddaughter |
| *el sobrino* | *la sobrina* | nephew, niece |

The plurals work like Lesson 6: *mis suegros* (my parents-in-law), *los nietos* (the
grandchildren), *mis sobrinos* (my nephews and nieces). Spanish has no single word for
"in-laws"; *la familia política* (literally "the political family") is the standard term, but
in everyday speech people just say *mis suegros* or *la familia de mi esposo*.

- *Mi suegra vive con nosotros.* — My mother-in-law lives with us.
- *El esposo de mi hermana es mi cuñado.* — My sister's husband is my brother-in-law.
- *Mis abuelos tienen doce nietos.* — My grandparents have twelve grandchildren.

## Godparents and compadres

In many Mexican families, most of them Catholic, a baby gets godparents at the baptism (*el
bautizo*): *el padrino* (godfather) and *la madrina* (godmother), together *los padrinos*. The
child is their *ahijado* (godson) or *ahijada* (goddaughter). Godparents are expected to stay
close to the child all their life, with presents, advice and help.

The baptism also creates a bond between the adults. The parents and the godparents become each
other's *compadres* (men, or a mixed group) and *comadres* (women). This relationship, called
*el compadrazgo*, is taken seriously: compadres often treat each other almost as family, and
they address each other as *compadre* and *comadre* for life.

![A diagram of compadrazgo. At the top left, Ana and Luis, the parents of baby Sofía; at the top right, Marta and Javier, Sofía's padrinos. A two-way arrow between the couples is labeled compadres / comadres, co-parents to each other. Arrows from both couples go down to Sofía, la ahijada (the goddaughter): one labeled papá y mamá, the other padrino y madrina (godfather, godmother).](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

So in the picture, Luis calls Javier *compadre*, Ana calls Marta *comadre*, and Sofía calls Marta
*madrina*. *Mi compadre* is also used more loosely in Mexico for a close male friend, and *mi
comadre* for a close female friend, without any baptism behind it.

Godparents aren't only for baptisms. Families also choose *padrinos* for a first communion (*la
primera comunión*), a girl's fifteenth-birthday party (*los quince años*) and weddings (*la
boda*). At many Catholic weddings in Mexico several couples are *padrinos*, each sponsoring one
part: the *lazo* (a cord placed around the couple's shoulders), the *arras* (thirteen coins), or
even the cake. These celebrations are big family events; this lesson only names them.

## The diminutive: -ito and -ita

Add *-ito* or *-ita* to a noun and you get a small version of it, or a friendlier one:

- *el perro → el perrito* (the little dog, the doggy)
- *la casa → la casita* (the little house)
- *la abuela → la abuelita* (grandma, granny)

The diminutive is extremely common in Mexico, and it usually carries a feeling as well as a
size. *Mi abuelita* isn't a small grandmother; she's a dearly loved one. *¿Quieres un cafecito?*
is a warm way to offer a coffee, not a promise of a tiny cup. Diminutives also soften requests
and make speech sound friendly, which is why you'll hear them all day in shops and homes.

### How to form it

The noun keeps its gender, so the article doesn't change. The main patterns:

| The word ends in | Do this | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| *-o* or *-a* | drop it, add *-ito / -ita* | *hermano → hermanito, abuela → abuelita, Ana → Anita* |
| *-e*, or *-n* / *-r* (two or more syllables) | add *-cito / -cita* | *café → cafecito, Carmen → Carmencita, amor → amorcito* |
| another consonant | add *-ito / -ita* | *papel → papelito, reloj → relojito, Luis → Luisito* |

Words that end in *-a* but are masculine keep *-a*, because the gender stays: *el mapa → el
mapita*, *el problema → el problemita*.

Spelling changes keep the sound, just as in plurals:

- *c → qu* before *i*: *chico → chiquito* (small one), *poco → poquito* (a tiny bit).
- *g → gu* before *i*: *amigo → amiguito*.
- *z → c* before *i*: *lápiz → lapicito*. The accent disappears, because the stress moves to
  *-ci-*.

Some forms don't follow these patterns, especially with names, and you learn them as you hear
them: *Juan → Juanito, Carlos → Carlitos*. In some regions you'll hear other diminutive endings,
such as *-illo* in Spain and *-ico* in Costa Rica and parts of the Caribbean (often given as the
reason Costa Ricans are called *ticos*).

Adjectives can take the diminutive too: *chiquito* (tiny), *bonito → bonitito* (really cute),
*pequeño → pequeñito*.

### Names and nicknames

Besides the diminutive, many Spanish names have a short form, an *apodo* (nickname) that
families use. They're often far from the full name, so it helps to know the common ones in
Mexico:

| Name | Nickname | Name | Nickname |
|---|---|---|---|
| José | Pepe | Guadalupe | Lupe, Lupita |
| Francisco | Paco, Pancho | Jesús | Chuy |
| Guillermo | Memo | Eduardo | Lalo |
| Ignacio | Nacho | Antonio | Toño |

## Talking to people you love

Spanish speakers use many **[[terms of endearment]]** with family and partners. Here are the ones
you'll hear most in Mexico:

- *mijo, mija*: short for *mi hijo, mi hija*. Parents use them with their children of any age,
  and older people often use them with younger people who aren't their children: *Mija, ¿ya
  comiste?* (Honey, have you eaten?).
- *mi amor* (my love), *mi vida* (my life), *corazón* (heart): to partners and children.
- *cariño*: affection, and also "darling" when you speak to someone: *Cariño, ¿vienes?* (heard
  in Mexico, though *mi amor* is more usual there; very common in Spain). At the end of a letter,
  *con cariño* means "with love".
- *abuelito, abuelita, mamita, papito*: diminutives as terms of affection.

Some are friendly only inside a family or a friendship. In many Mexican families *gordo, gorda*
(literally "fat") or *viejo, vieja* ("old") are loving names for a partner, but used by a
stranger they can offend. Learn to recognise them; use them only when people use them with you.

## Reading: Lupita's family

> *Me llamo Guadalupe, pero en mi familia soy Lupita. Tengo dos hijos y una casita en Puebla.
> Mi esposo se llama Francisco, pero todos dicen Paco. Mis suegros viven con nosotros: mi suegra
> es muy simpática y cocina muy bien. Mi cuñado Memo es el padrino de mi hija; él y Paco son
> compadres y también buenos amigos. Los domingos mi mamá llega con un pastelito y dice:
> "¿Dónde están mis nietos?"*

Translation:

> My name is Guadalupe, but in my family I'm Lupita. I have two children and a little house in
> Puebla. My husband is called Francisco, but everyone says Paco. My parents-in-law live with
> us: my mother-in-law is very nice and cooks very well. My brother-in-law Memo is my daughter's
> godfather; he and Paco are compadres and good friends too. On Sundays my mom arrives with a
> little cake and says, "Where are my grandchildren?"

New words to recognise: *dicen* (they say; *decir*, Lesson 22), *cocina* (cooks; *cocinar*,
Lesson 16), *el pastel* (cake), *¿Dónde están…?* (where are…?, Lesson 9).

## Worked examples

### Example 1: forming diminutives

Make the diminutive of *el gato, la mesa, el amor, el reloj, el chico* and *el mapa*.

1. *el gato* ends in *-o*: drop it, add *-ito*: *el gatito*.
2. *la mesa* ends in *-a*: *la mesita*. (In Mexico *la mesita* is also a small side table.)
3. *el amor* ends in *-r* and has two syllables: add *-cito*: *el amorcito*.
4. *el reloj* ends in another consonant: add *-ito*: *el relojito*.
5. *el chico* ends in *-o*, but *c* before *i* must become *qu*: *el chiquito*.
6. *el mapa* is masculine though it ends in *-a*. The ending keeps the *-a* and the article
   stays *el*: *el mapita*.

### Example 2: who is who?

Lupita's husband is Paco, and Paco's parents live with them. What is each person to the others?

1. Paco's parents are Lupita's *suegros*: *el suegro* and *la suegra*.
2. Lupita is their *nuera* (daughter-in-law); Paco is *el yerno* of Lupita's parents.
3. Paco's brother Memo is Lupita's *cuñado*, and Lupita is Memo's *cuñada*.
4. Lupita's children are *los nietos* of both sets of grandparents, and *los sobrinos* of Memo.

### Example 3: padrino or compadre?

Memo is the godfather of Lupita's daughter, Sofía. What does each person call Memo?

1. Sofía is Memo's goddaughter, so she calls him *padrino*: *¡Hola, padrino!*
2. Sofía's parents, Lupita and Paco, are Memo's co-parents in the *compadrazgo*: Paco calls him
   *compadre*, and so does Lupita (a woman calls her child's godfather *compadre*, and he calls
   her *comadre*).
3. Memo is still Lupita's *cuñado* too: one person can have several family roles.

## Common mistakes

- Changing the gender with the diminutive: ~~la mapita~~ → *el mapita*.
- Forgetting the spelling change: ~~chicito~~ → *chiquito*; ~~amigito~~ → *amiguito*.
- Thinking a diminutive always means small. *Un cafecito* is often a normal cup of coffee,
  offered warmly.
- Mixing up *padrino* and *compadre*: the child says *padrino*; the parents say *compadre*.
- Mixing up *nieto* (grandson) and *sobrino* (nephew).
- Using family nicknames like *gordo* or *vieja* with people outside the family.

## Key points

- In-laws: *suegro/a, cuñado/a, yerno, nuera*. *Nieto/a* = grandchild, *sobrino/a* =
  nephew, niece.
- *Padrino* and *madrina* are godparents; the parents and godparents are *compadres* and
  *comadres* to each other, a lasting bond in many Mexican families.
- The diminutive *-ito / -ita* (*-cito* after *-e* and many words in *-n, -r*) adds smallness
  or affection, keeps the gender, and changes spelling to keep the sound (*chiquito,
  amiguito*).
- Many names have nicknames: *Pepe, Paco, Lupe, Chuy, Memo*.
- Terms of endearment: *mijo, mija, mi amor, mi vida, cariño*. Some are only for family.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Estar: where you are and how you feel (ser or estar?)
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Since lesson 2 you have used *ser* to say who you are, where you're from, what you do and what people and things are like: *Soy Laura. Es de Monterrey. Mi hermano es ingeniero. La casa es grande.* You have also used one phrase with a second verb that means "to be": *¿Cómo estás?* — How are you?

That second verb is *estar*. Spanish has two verbs for English "to be", and choosing between them is one of the first real decisions a learner makes. The good news is that at A1 the choice follows a small number of clear uses. In this lesson you learn *estar* in full, use it for *where* people and things are and for *how* they are right now (tired, happy, open, dirty), and then put the two verbs side by side so you can choose with confidence. You'll also pick up *con* (with), *sin* (without) and *cerca / lejos* (near / far).

## Estar: the forms

*Estar* is irregular in the present, but only a little. Four of its six forms carry a written accent on the ending (*estás, está, estáis, están*), and the *yo* form ends in *-oy*, like *soy*.

| Person | estar | English |
|---|---|---|
| yo | estoy | I am |
| tú | estás | you are (friend) |
| él, ella, usted | está | he / she is, you are (formal) |
| nosotros, nosotras | estamos | we are |
| (vosotros) | (estáis) | (you all are: Spain only) |
| ellos, ellas, ustedes | están | they are, you all are |

The accents are not decoration. *Está* (he is) and *esta* (this, lesson 12) are different words, and *estan* without the accent is simply a misspelling of *están* (they are). Say the stress on the end: es-TOY, es-TÁS, es-TÁ, es-TA-mos, es-TÁN.

- *Estoy en la oficina.* — I'm at the office.
- *¿Estás bien?* — Are you OK?
- *La profesora está en la clase.* — The teacher is in class.
- *Estamos un poco cansados.* — We're a bit tired.
- *¿Dónde están ustedes?* — Where are you all?

## Use 1: where someone or something is

To say where a person or a thing is, Spanish always uses *estar*. The question is *¿Dónde está…?* — Where is…?

- *¿Dónde está el baño?* — Where is the bathroom? (*el baño*, lesson 10)
- *Mi mamá está en el trabajo.* — My mom is at work.
- *Los niños están aquí.* — The children are here.
- *La universidad está en el centro.* — The university is downtown.

This is true even when the place never changes. A city doesn't move, but it still takes *estar*: *Guadalajara está en México. Bogotá está en Colombia.* Don't think "temporary"; think "location". Location is *estar*, full stop.

Two useful words tell you how far something is: *cerca* (near, close) and *lejos* (far). Used alone, they stand on their own: *La escuela está cerca.* — The school is close. To say near or far *from* something, add *de*:

- *Mi casa está cerca de la universidad.* — My house is near the university.
- *Canadá está lejos de Argentina.* — Canada is far from Argentina.
- *Es un lugar muy bonito, pero está lejos.* — It's a very pretty place, but it's far away.

### One exception: events

There is one case where a place goes with *ser*: when the subject is an event, something that *happens*, like a party, a class or a concert. *La fiesta es en mi casa* — The party is (takes place) at my house. Compare: *Mis amigos están en mi casa* — My friends are at my house (location of people).

## Use 2: how someone or something is right now

The second big use of *estar* is for states and feelings: how a person feels, or what condition a thing is in. The adjective agrees with the person or thing, exactly as you learned in lesson 8: *cansado* for a man, *cansada* for a woman, *cansados / cansadas* for several.

Here are five faces you'll meet every day:

![Five cartoon faces in a row, each labeled. Cansado (tired): half-closed eyes and a yawn. Contento (happy): a big smile. Triste (sad): a downturned mouth and a tear. Enojado (angry): slanted eyebrows and a frown, with a red face. Nervioso (nervous): wide eyes, a wavy mouth and a drop of sweat.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| cansado | tired |
| contento | happy, pleased |
| feliz (plural felices) | happy |
| triste | sad |
| enfermo | sick, ill |
| nervioso | nervous |
| ocupado | busy |
| enojado (Spain: enfadado) | angry, annoyed |
| preocupado | worried |
| tranquilo | calm, relaxed |
| listo | ready |

- *Estoy cansada.* — I'm tired. (a woman speaking)
- *¿Estás nervioso?* — Are you nervous? (to a man)
- *Mi papá está enojado.* — My dad is angry.
- *Estamos muy contentos.* — We're very happy.
- *Ana y Lucía están preocupadas.* — Ana and Lucía are worried.
- *Mi abuelo es una persona tranquila, pero hoy está nervioso.* — My grandfather is a calm person, but today he's nervous. (*la persona* is always feminine, even for a man, so *tranquila* agrees with *persona*.)

Things have states too. A shop can be open or closed today; the soup can be hot now and cold in ten minutes:

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| abierto | open |
| cerrado | closed |
| limpio | clean |
| sucio | dirty |
| caliente | hot (temperature) |
| frío | cold |
| lleno | full |

- *La tienda está cerrada.* — The shop is closed.
- *El café está frío.* — The coffee is cold. (*el café*, lesson 11)
- *La mesa está sucia.* — The table is dirty.
- *El salón de clases está lleno.* — The classroom is full.

This is why the greeting *¿Cómo estás?* uses *estar*: it asks how you are *now*. The answer uses *estar* too: *Estoy bien, gracias. Estoy un poco cansado.*

## Ser or estar?

Now put the two verbs side by side. Ask what the sentence is about.

| The sentence says… | Verb | Example |
|---|---|---|
| who or what something is (name, identity) | ser | *Es mi hermana.* |
| where someone is from | ser | *Somos de Puebla.* |
| someone's job | ser | *Eres doctora.* |
| what someone or something is like | ser | *La clase es interesante.* |
| where an event takes place | ser | *La fiesta es en el centro.* |
| where someone or something is | estar | *El libro está en la mesa.* |
| how someone feels | estar | *Estoy contenta.* |
| what condition something is in now | estar | *La puerta está abierta.* |

The same questions fit in a small chart. Work from the top:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Ser or estar? A decision chart for A1
  accDescr: Start with your sentence. First ask: does it say where someone or something is? If yes, ask whether the subject is an event such as a party or a class. An event takes ser; a person or thing takes estar. If the sentence is not about location, ask: does it describe a feeling or a condition right now, like tired, sad, open or dirty? If yes, use estar. If no, it is about identity, origin, job or what something is like, so use ser.
  A["Your sentence"] --> B{"Does it say WHERE someone or something is?"}
  B -- yes --> C{"Is the subject an event, like la fiesta?"}
  C -- yes --> S1["ser: La fiesta es en mi casa."]
  C -- no --> E1["estar: Mi casa está en el centro."]
  B -- no --> D{"Is it a feeling or a condition right now?"}
  D -- yes --> E2["estar: Estoy cansado. La tienda está cerrada."]
  D -- no --> S2["ser: identity, origin, job, what it is like"]
```

You may have heard the shortcut "ser is permanent, estar is temporary". It works often, but it fails at the very first hurdle: *Guadalajara está en México* never changes, and *Soy estudiante* may last only a year. The questions in the chart are more reliable.

### Example 1: choosing the verb

Fill in *ser* or *estar*: *Mi hermano ___ ingeniero, pero hoy ___ en casa porque ___ enfermo.*

1. *ingeniero* is a job → *ser*: *es ingeniero*. (No article before a bare job, lesson 7.)
2. *en casa* says where he is, and he's a person, not an event → *estar*: *está en casa* (at home).
3. *enfermo* is how he is today → *estar*: *está enfermo*.

So: *Mi hermano es ingeniero, pero hoy está en casa porque está enfermo.* — My brother is an engineer, but today he's at home because he's sick.

### Example 2: same adjective, different verb

Some adjectives work with both verbs, and the verb changes the meaning:

| Adjective | with ser | with estar |
|---|---|---|
| aburrido | *La película es aburrida.* — The film is boring. | *Estoy aburrido.* — I'm bored. |
| listo | *Tu hija es muy lista.* — Your daughter is very clever. | *¿Estás lista?* — Are you ready? |
| tranquilo | *Mi perro es tranquilo.* — My dog is a calm dog (by nature). | *Hoy el perro está tranquilo.* — Today the dog is calm. |

Be careful with *aburrido*: *Soy aburrido* means "I'm a boring person", which is probably not what you want to say after a long meeting. Say *Estoy aburrido* (I'm bored).

*Feliz* is the most common feeling word used with both verbs: *Soy feliz* (I'm a happy person, I'm happy in my life) and *Estoy feliz* (I'm happy right now) are both natural. *Contento* goes with *estar*: *Estoy muy contento.*

## Con and sin

*Con* means "with" and *sin* means "without". You'll use them for people and for food and drink:

- *Estoy en el centro con mi amiga.* — I'm downtown with my friend.
- *Un café con leche, por favor.* — A coffee with milk, please. (*la leche*, lesson 11)
- *Té sin azúcar.* — Tea without sugar. (*el té* = tea, *el azúcar* = sugar)

After *sin*, the noun usually has no article: *sin azúcar, sin problema* (no problem).

## Dialogue: ¿Dónde estás?

Sofía calls her friend Diego on a Saturday morning.

> Sofía: Hola, Diego, ¿cómo estás? ¿Dónde estás?
>
> Diego: Hola, Sofía. Estoy en el centro, en una cafetería con mi hermana. Estoy un poco cansado.
>
> Sofía: ¿Cansado? ¿Por qué?
>
> Diego: Porque trabajo mucho. La oficina está lejos de mi casa y estoy muy ocupado. ¿Y tú? ¿Estás en la universidad?
>
> Sofía: No, hoy estoy en casa. Estoy enferma y un poco triste. La fiesta de Marta es hoy, y yo estoy aquí sin mis amigos.
>
> Diego: ¡Ay, no! ¿Estás sola?
>
> Sofía: No, mi mamá está aquí conmigo. Ella es doctora y es muy tranquila. Estoy bien, no estoy preocupada.
>
> Diego: Qué bueno. ¿Y dónde es la fiesta?
>
> Sofía: Es en la casa de Marta. Está cerca de la escuela.
>
> Diego: Bueno, la cafetería está cerca también. Mi hermana y yo estamos listos para la fiesta… ¡pero sin ti no es igual!

In English:

> Sofía: Hi, Diego, how are you? Where are you?
>
> Diego: Hi, Sofía. I'm downtown, in a café with my sister. I'm a bit tired.
>
> Sofía: Tired? Why?
>
> Diego: Because I work a lot. The office is far from my house and I'm very busy. And you? Are you at the university?
>
> Sofía: No, today I'm at home. I'm sick and a bit sad. Marta's party is today, and I'm here without my friends.
>
> Diego: Oh no! Are you alone?
>
> Sofía: No, my mom is here with me. She's a doctor and she's very calm. I'm fine, I'm not worried.
>
> Diego: Good. And where is the party?
>
> Sofía: It's at Marta's house. It's near the school.
>
> Diego: Well, the café is close too. My sister and I are ready for the party… but without you it's not the same!

Look at the verbs. Every location of a person or a building uses *estar* (*estoy en el centro, la oficina está lejos, está cerca de la escuela*). Every feeling uses *estar* (*cansado, enferma, triste, preocupada, listos*). But *Ella es doctora* (job), *es muy tranquila* (her character) and *¿dónde es la fiesta?* (an event) use *ser*. (*la cafetería* = café, *en casa* = at home, *sola* = alone, *conmigo* = with me, *sin ti* = without you, *no es igual* = it isn't the same.)

## Pronunciation

- Stress the end of *estar* forms: es-TOY, es-TÁS, es-TÁ, es-TÁN. Only *estamos* is stressed in the middle: es-TA-mos.
- *estoy* ends in a *y* that sounds like the *i* in *soy*: es-TOI.
- *tranquilo*: *qu* is a plain *k* sound and the *u* is silent: tran-KEE-lo.
- *lleno* and *feliz* follow the Latin American sounds from lesson 1: *ll* like English *y* (YE-no), and *z* like *s* (fe-LEES).
- *enojado* has the Spanish *j*, a breathy sound from the throat, like a strong English *h*: e-no-HA-do.
- *frío* has a written accent on the *í*: it's two syllables, FREE-o, not one.

## Common mistakes

- *Soy cansado.* — Feelings take *estar*: *Estoy cansado.*
- *Estoy de México.* — Origin takes *ser*: *Soy de México.*
- *Estoy estudiante.* — A job or role takes *ser*: *Soy estudiante.*
- *El baño es aquí.* — Where a thing is takes *estar*: *El baño está aquí.* (But an event: *La fiesta es aquí.*)
- *Ana está cansado.* — The adjective agrees: *Ana está cansada.*
- *Esta en la oficina.* — Without the accent, *esta* means "this". Write *está*.
- *Soy aburrido* when you mean "I'm bored" — say *Estoy aburrido*.
- *Mi casa está cerca la escuela.* — "Near the school" needs *de*: *Mi casa está cerca de la escuela.*

## Key points

- *estar*: *estoy, estás, está, estamos, están*. Write the accents.
- Use *estar* for where people and things are (*¿Dónde está…?*), even places that never move.
- Use *estar* for feelings and conditions right now: *Estoy cansada. La tienda está cerrada.*
- Use *ser* for identity, origin, job and what something is like, and for where an event takes place: *La fiesta es en mi casa.*
- Some adjectives change meaning: *es aburrido* (boring) / *está aburrido* (bored), *es listo* (clever) / *está listo* (ready).
- *cerca de* (near), *lejos de* (far from); *con* (with), *sin* (without).

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete the lesson.

lessons.title: At home: hay, estar and where things are
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

In lesson 9 you used *estar* to say where people and things are: *El libro está en la mesa.* In this lesson you move into the home. You'll learn the rooms and the furniture, the little word *hay* (there is, there are), the difference between *hay* and *está*, and the **[[prepositions of place]]** that say exactly where something is: on top of, under, next to, between, behind. By the end you can describe your house or apartment and understand an ad for a place to rent.

As always, Mexican words are the standard here, and a short table near the end gives the words you'll hear in Spain.

## The rooms of a house

![A cross-section of a two-storey house with a garden on the left. Downstairs, from left to right: a kitchen with a refrigerator and a stove (la cocina), a dining room with a table and chairs (el comedor) and a living room with a sofa (la sala). A staircase (la escalera) rises at the right end of the living room, next to the sofa. Upstairs: a bedroom with a bed (el cuarto) and a bathroom with a toilet and a shower (el baño). A tree stands in the garden (el jardín). Each part is labeled.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| la casa | house, home |
| el departamento | apartment |
| el cuarto | room; bedroom |
| la cocina | kitchen |
| el baño | bathroom |
| la sala | living room |
| el comedor | dining room |
| el jardín | garden, yard |
| la escalera | stairs, staircase |
| el piso | floor, storey |
| la pared | wall |

And in the rooms:

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| la cama | bed |
| el sofá (plural los sofás) | sofa, couch |
| el clóset | closet, built-in wardrobe |
| el refrigerador | refrigerator, fridge |
| la estufa | stove (for cooking) |

A few notes on these words:

- *El cuarto* is any room, and in everyday Mexican Spanish it very often means the bedroom: *Mi cuarto es pequeño.* In Mexico you'll also hear *la recámara* for a bedroom, especially in ads.
- *La cocina* means both the kitchen and a cuisine: *la cocina mexicana* is Mexican cooking.
- *El piso* is a floor of a building, a storey: *Vivo en el tercer piso* (I live on the third floor; *tercer* = third). It is also the floor you walk on: *El gato está en el piso.*
- In casual speech the fridge is often *el refri*.
- *En casa* (with no article) means "at home": *Estoy en casa.*

## Hay: there is, there are

*Hay* means "there is" or "there are". It comes from the verb *haber*, but you only need this one form, and it never changes: one sofa or ten sofas, it's *hay*.

- *Hay un sofá en la sala.* — There's a sofa in the living room.
- *Hay dos baños.* — There are two bathrooms.
- *En el comedor hay una mesa y seis sillas.* — In the dining room there's a table and six chairs.
- *No hay refrigerador.* — There's no fridge.
- *¿Hay jardín?* — Is there a garden?

The pronunciation is simple: the *h* is silent and *ay* sounds like English "eye". *Hay* sounds exactly like the exclamation *¡ay!*

*Hay* goes with *un, una, unos, unas*, with numbers, with *mucho*, or with no article at all. In questions and negative sentences the article usually disappears: *¿Hay jardín? No hay estufa.*

To ask how many, use *¿Cuántos…? / ¿Cuántas…?* (lesson 3) with *hay*, matching the gender of the noun:

- *¿Cuántos cuartos hay?* — How many rooms are there? — *Hay tres.*
- *¿Cuántas sillas hay en la cocina?* — How many chairs are there in the kitchen? — *Hay cuatro.*

## Hay or está?

Both can tell you where something is, but they answer different questions.

- *Hay* introduces something new: it says that something exists in a place. *Hay un sofá en la sala.* — There's a sofa in the living room.
- *Está / están* tells you where a particular thing is, one you already know about: *El sofá está en la sala.* — The sofa is in the living room.

The test is the word in front of the noun:

| Before the noun | Verb | Example |
|---|---|---|
| *un, una, unos, unas*, a number, *mucho*, nothing | hay | *Hay una cama. Hay dos clósets. Hay sillas.* |
| *el, la, los, las*, *mi, tu, su…*, or a name | está / están | *La cama está en el cuarto. Mis llaves están aquí. Ana está en la cocina.* |

So you never say *hay el sofá* or *hay mi cama*. And with plural things, use *están*: *Las sillas están en el comedor.* (*Hay* never changes, but *estar* agrees.)

### Example 1: describing a room

You want to describe your kitchen. Start with what's in it, then say where the known things are.

1. Introduce things with *hay*: *En mi cocina hay un refrigerador, una estufa y una mesa pequeña.*
2. Now they're known, so use *el / la* and *estar*: *El refrigerador está al lado de la estufa. La mesa está enfrente de la ventana.*
3. Add *no hay* for what's missing: *No hay sillas.*

Together: *En mi cocina hay un refrigerador, una estufa y una mesa pequeña. El refrigerador está al lado de la estufa, y la mesa está enfrente de la ventana. No hay sillas.* — In my kitchen there's a fridge, a stove and a small table. The fridge is next to the stove, and the table is in front of the window. There are no chairs.

## Where exactly? Prepositions of place

You already know *en* (in, on, at), *cerca de* and *lejos de*. Here are six more. The picture shows five of them, plus *en*, with a cat and a box (*la caja*); the sixth, *enfrente de*, is in the table:

![Six small pictures of a cat and a box, each labeled. En la caja: the cat's head pokes out of an open box. Encima de la caja: the cat sits on top of the box. Debajo de la mesa: the cat lies under a table. Al lado de la caja: the cat sits next to the box. Detrás de la caja: only the top of the cat's head, its ears and its tail show behind a big box. Entre las cajas: the cat sits between two boxes.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| en | in, on, at |
| encima de | on top of, on |
| debajo de | under, underneath |
| al lado de | next to, beside |
| enfrente de | in front of, opposite, across from |
| detrás de | behind |
| entre | between, among |

All of them except *en* and *entre* end in *de*. That *de* is part of the phrase: *debajo de la cama* (under the bed), not *debajo la cama*. *Entre* takes no *de*: *entre la cocina y la sala* (between the kitchen and the living room).

*Enfrente de* covers both "in front of" and "across from": *La tienda está enfrente de mi casa* usually means it's across the street from my house.

### De + el = del

When *de* meets the masculine article *el*, the two words join into *del*. This happens with every phrase that ends in *de*:

- *al lado del sofá* — next to the sofa (de + el sofá)
- *debajo del refrigerador* — under the fridge
- *enfrente del comedor* — opposite the dining room
- *cerca del centro* — near downtown

With *la, los, las* nothing joins: *al lado de la cama, debajo de los libros*. And the *al* in *al lado* is itself a joined form: *a* + *el* = *al*. You'll use *al* and *del* much more in lesson 14; for now, learn *al lado del…* as one chunk.

### Example 2: where is everything?

Look at the picture of the house and answer *¿Dónde está el sofá?*

1. The sofa is a particular, known thing (*el sofá*), so use *está*.
2. It's in the living room: *en la sala*.
3. Be more exact: in the picture the sofa stands right beside the stairs. *Escalera* is feminine, so there's no *del*: *El sofá está en la sala, al lado de la escalera.*

Now *¿Hay una cama en la sala?* — *No, no hay cama en la sala. La cama está en el cuarto, en el segundo piso.* (*segundo* = second.)

## Describing a home

Three new adjectives, plus the ones from lessons 8 and 9, are enough to describe a place:

- *cómodo* — comfortable: *El sofá es muy cómodo.*
- *oscuro* — dark: *El baño es un poco oscuro.*
- *moderno* — modern: *La cocina es moderna.*

Remember the verb choice from lesson 9: what a place is like takes *ser* (*La casa es grande y moderna*), its condition now takes *estar* (*La casa está limpia hoy*).

## Renting a place

In Mexico you pay *la renta* (the rent) and you *rentar* (rent) a house or apartment. *Rentar* is a regular -ar verb: *rento, rentas, renta, rentamos, rentan.* On signs you'll see *Se renta* — For rent.

> SE RENTA DEPARTAMENTO en el centro. Segundo piso, muy cerca de la universidad. Dos cuartos con clóset, un baño, sala-comedor y cocina con estufa y refrigerador. No hay jardín. Departamento moderno y cómodo. Renta: 9,500 pesos al mes.

In English: FOR RENT: APARTMENT downtown. Second floor, very close to the university. Two bedrooms with closets, one bathroom, a combined living and dining room, and a kitchen with stove and fridge. There's no garden. Modern, comfortable apartment. Rent: 9,500 pesos a month. (*al mes* = a month, per month; *sala-comedor* = a living room and dining room in one space.)

## Dialogue: El departamento nuevo

Valeria shows her friend Tomás the apartment she rents.

> Valeria: ¡Pasa, Tomás! Esta es la sala.
>
> Tomás: ¡Qué bonita! El sofá es muy cómodo. ¿Cuántos cuartos hay?
>
> Valeria: Hay dos cuartos y un baño. Mi cuarto está al lado del baño.
>
> Tomás: ¿Y dónde está la cocina?
>
> Valeria: Está detrás de la sala. Es pequeña pero moderna. Hay una estufa nueva, pero no hay refrigerador.
>
> Tomás: ¿No hay refri? ¿Y la leche?
>
> Valeria: La leche está en la casa de mi mamá. Ella vive enfrente.
>
> Tomás: ¡Qué práctico! ¿Y la renta es cara?
>
> Valeria: No, el departamento está lejos del centro, entonces la renta es barata. Pero la sala es un poco oscura.
>
> Tomás: Bueno, hay una ventana grande entre el clóset y la pared. Con una lámpara, perfecto.

In English:

> Valeria: Come in, Tomás! This is the living room.
>
> Tomás: How pretty! The sofa is very comfortable. How many rooms are there?
>
> Valeria: There are two bedrooms and one bathroom. My room is next to the bathroom.
>
> Tomás: And where's the kitchen?
>
> Valeria: It's behind the living room. It's small but modern. There's a new stove, but there's no fridge.
>
> Tomás: No fridge? What about the milk?
>
> Valeria: The milk is at my mom's house. She lives across the street.
>
> Tomás: How practical! And is the rent expensive?
>
> Valeria: No, the apartment is far from downtown, so the rent is cheap. But the living room is a bit dark.
>
> Tomás: Well, there's a big window between the closet and the wall. With a lamp, perfect.

(*¡Pasa!* = come in, *esta* = this, *¡Qué…!* = how…!, *entonces* = so, *la lámpara* = lamp. *Caro* and *barato*, expensive and cheap, are lesson 12 words.) Notice *hay una estufa* (new information) but *la cocina está detrás de la sala* (a known room), and *lejos del centro* with *de* + *el*.

## Mexico and Spain

| Mexico (this course) | Spain | English |
|---|---|---|
| el departamento | el piso | apartment, flat |
| el cuarto, la recámara | el dormitorio, la habitación | bedroom |
| el clóset | el armario | closet, wardrobe |
| el refrigerador, el refri | la nevera, el frigorífico | fridge |
| la estufa | la cocina (the stove), el fogón | stove |
| la renta, rentar | el alquiler, alquilar | rent, to rent |

Two traps: in Spain *el piso* is also the apartment itself, and *la estufa* is a heater, not a stove. Many Latin American countries also use *el apartamento* and *alquilar*, and you'll be understood everywhere with them.

## Pronunciation

- *hay* = "eye". The *h* is always silent.
- *jardín*: the *j* is the breathy throat sound, har-DEEN, with the stress on the accented *í*.
- *sofá* and *clóset* have written accents that tell you the stress: so-FÁ, CLÓ-set.
- *debajo*: de-BA-ho. *detrás*: de-TRÁS, with a tapped *r* after the *t*.

## Common mistakes

- *Hay el sofá en la sala.* — *Hay* doesn't take *el / la*. Say *Hay un sofá en la sala* or *El sofá está en la sala.*
- *Están dos baños en la casa.* — To say that something exists, use *hay*: *Hay dos baños en la casa.*
- *Las sillas está en el comedor.* — *estar* agrees: *Las sillas están en el comedor.*
- *Debajo la cama.* — Keep the *de*: *debajo de la cama.*
- *Al lado de el sofá.* — *De* + *el* joins: *al lado del sofá.*
- *Entre de la sala y la cocina.* — *Entre* takes no *de*: *entre la sala y la cocina.*
- *Rento un piso* in Mexico sounds like Spain; say *Rento un departamento.*

## Key points

- *Hay* = there is / there are; one form for everything; with *un/una*, numbers or no article.
- *Hay* introduces something new; *está / están* says where a known thing is: *Hay un sofá. El sofá está en la sala.*
- *¿Cuántos cuartos hay?* — *Hay tres.*
- Prepositions of place: *en, encima de, debajo de, al lado de, enfrente de, detrás de, entre*.
- *de* + *el* = *del*: *al lado del sofá*.
- Mexico: *el departamento, el cuarto / la recámara, el clóset, el refrigerador, la estufa, la renta, rentar*.
