The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Food, drink and gustar
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Food is where most people first want to use a new language: at the table, in a restaurant, at a friend's house. In this lesson you learn the everyday words for food and drink, and the verb Spanish uses to say what you like: *gustar*. *Gustar* works backwards compared with English "like", so it gets a careful explanation. You'll also learn *encantar* (to love something), *querer* (to want) and the polite *quisiera* for ordering, and how to agree with *A mí también* and *A mí tampoco*.

## Food and drink

The picture shows a Mexican table at midday, with some of the most common foods.

![A table set for a Mexican midday meal, each item labeled. On the left a cloth-covered basket of corn tortillas (las tortillas), then a bowl of beans (los frijoles), a plate of rice (el arroz) with a fried egg (el huevo) on top, a glass of orange juice (el jugo) and a cup of coffee (el café). A bowl of fruit with a banana and an apple (la fruta) stands at the right.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

| Food | English | Food | English |
|---|---|---|---|
| el pan | bread | el huevo | egg |
| la tortilla | tortilla | el queso | cheese |
| los frijoles | beans | la fruta | fruit |
| el arroz | rice | la manzana | apple |
| la carne | meat | el plátano | banana |
| el pollo | chicken | la papa | potato |
| el pescado | fish (as food) | la verdura | vegetable(s) |

| Drink | English |
|---|---|
| el agua | water |
| el café | coffee |
| la leche | milk |
| el jugo | juice |

Notes on the words:

- In Mexico *la tortilla* is the thin, round flatbread of corn (or wheat flour) that goes with almost every meal. In Spain *una tortilla* is a thick potato omelette, a completely different food.
- *Los frijoles* (beans) is almost always plural: *Me gustan los frijoles.*
- *El pescado* is fish you eat. A live fish in the water is *el pez* (not a word for this lesson).
- *La verdura* is often plural: *Como muchas verduras.* — I eat a lot of vegetables.
- *El agua* is feminine, but it takes *el* in the singular because it starts with a stressed *a-* (lesson 5): *el agua fría*, *las aguas*. The same is true of *el hambre* (hunger): *Tengo mucha hambre.*
- Spain uses different words for some of these: *el zumo* (juice), *la patata* (potato), *las judías* or *las alubias* (beans). In much of South America, *la banana* is the fruit and *el plátano* is often a cooking plantain.

### Meals and eating

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| la comida | food; (in Mexico) the main midday meal |
| el desayuno | breakfast |
| la cena | dinner, supper (the evening meal) |
| comer | to eat; (in Mexico) to have the midday meal |
| cenar | to have dinner |
| beber | to drink |

In Mexico the biggest meal of the day is usually *la comida*, eaten in the early afternoon, often between 2 and 4 pm, and *la cena* in the evening is often lighter. That's why *¿A qué hora comes?* (at what time do you eat?) asks when you have your main meal, and *la comida* can mean both "food" and "lunch". (Habits vary by family and job; the honors lesson 12h1 says more.)

*Beber* means to drink, but in everyday Mexican Spanish people more often say *tomar* (lesson 4): *¿Qué quieres tomar?* — What would you like to drink?

### Hungry and thirsty: tener hambre, tener sed

Spanish doesn't say "I am hungry". It says "I have hunger", with *tener* (lesson 6):

- *Tengo hambre.* — I'm hungry.
- *¿Tienes sed?* — Are you thirsty?
- *Tenemos mucha hambre.* — We're very hungry. (*Mucha*, because *hambre* is feminine.)

And when the food is good, it's *rico* — tasty, delicious: *¡Qué rico!* — How delicious! *La sopa está muy rica.* — The soup is really good. (*la sopa* = soup) Careful: about a person, *es rico* means "he's rich".

## Gustar: what you like

English says "I like coffee": I am the subject, coffee is the object. Spanish turns this around. *Gustar* means "to please", so *Me gusta el café* says, literally, "coffee pleases me". The thing you like is the subject, and the verb agrees with it:

- one thing → *gusta*: *Me gusta el café.* — I like coffee.
- several things → *gustan*: *Me gustan los tacos.* — I like tacos.

The person who likes it is shown by a small word in front: *me* (to me), *te* (to you), and so on. These are **[[indirect object pronouns]]**: they say to whom the coffee is pleasing.

![A chart in two columns. On the left, me gusta in a box, with arrows to things in the singular: el café, la fruta, and an infinitive, comer. On the right, me gustan in a box, with arrows to things in the plural: los tacos, las manzanas. A note at the bottom says that the verb agrees with the thing you like, not with the person.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

| Who likes it | Pronoun | + one thing or an action | + several things |
|---|---|---|---|
| (a mí) | me | *me gusta el pan* | *me gustan los huevos* |
| (a ti) | te | *te gusta la leche* | *te gustan las papas* |
| (a él, a ella, a usted) | le | *le gusta el pollo* | *le gustan los frijoles* |
| (a nosotros) | nos | *nos gusta el queso* | *nos gustan las verduras* |
| (a ellos, a ellas, a ustedes) | les | *les gusta la carne* | *les gustan las frutas* |

Notice that the noun after *gustar* almost always has its article: *Me gusta el café*, not *Me gusta café*. You're talking about coffee in general, and Spanish uses *el* for that.

To like *doing* something, use the infinitive, which always takes *gusta*, even with two actions:

- *Me gusta cocinar.* — I like cooking. (*cocinar*, lesson 16)
- *Nos gusta comer y hablar.* — We like eating and talking.

To say you don't like something, put *no* in front of the pronoun: *No me gusta el pescado.* — I don't like fish.

### A mí, a ti: for emphasis, contrast and clarity

You can add *a mí, a ti, a él…* in front. It doesn't change the meaning; it adds emphasis or contrast, and with *le / les* it says who you mean:

- *A mí me gusta el café, pero a ti te gusta el té.* — I like coffee, but you like tea. (contrast; *el té* = tea)
- *¿A usted le gusta la comida mexicana?* — Do you like Mexican food? (*le* alone could be him, her or you)
- *A mi papá le gustan las papas.* — My dad likes potatoes. (*a* + the person)

*A mí* has an accent (*mí* = me); *a ti* has none.

### Example 1: gusta or gustan?

Complete: *¿Te ___ las manzanas?* and *A Laura le ___ el pan.*

1. Find the thing liked. In the first sentence it's *las manzanas*: plural, so *gustan*. *¿Te gustan las manzanas?*
2. In the second it's *el pan*: singular, so *gusta*. *A Laura le gusta el pan.*
3. Don't let the person mislead you: *Laura* is one person, but it doesn't matter. *A mis padres les gusta el pan* — still *gusta*, because the bread is one thing.

## Encantar: to love it

*Encantar* works exactly like *gustar*, but it's stronger: "to love" a thing or an activity.

- *Me encanta la fruta.* — I love fruit.
- *¿Te encantan los tacos?* — Do you love tacos?
- *A mi hermana le encanta cocinar.* — My sister loves cooking.

Because *encantar* already means "a lot", people usually don't add *mucho* to it: say *Me gusta mucho* or *Me encanta*. (You will hear *Me encanta mucho* in casual speech, but many speakers find it redundant, so don't copy it.) (For people you love, Spanish uses *querer*: *Te quiero.*)

## Agreeing and disagreeing: también, tampoco

When someone says what they like, you can agree or disagree in three words:

| They say | You agree | You disagree |
|---|---|---|
| *Me gusta el café.* (yes) | *A mí también.* — Me too. | *A mí no.* — I don't. |
| *No me gusta el pescado.* (no) | *A mí tampoco.* — Me neither. | *A mí sí.* — I do. |

*Tampoco* is the negative partner of *también*: "not … either", "neither". Use *también* after a yes and *tampoco* after a no.

## Querer and quisiera: wanting and ordering

*Querer* (to want) changes its stem: the *e* becomes *ie* in every form except *nosotros*. Lesson 15 shows many verbs that work like this; for now, learn *querer*.

| Person | querer |
|---|---|
| yo | quiero |
| tú | quieres |
| él, ella, usted | quiere |
| nosotros | queremos |
| (vosotros) | (queréis) |
| ellos, ustedes | quieren |

- *Quiero un café.* — I want a coffee.
- *¿Quieres agua?* — Do you want some water?
- *Queremos comer.* — We want to eat. (*querer* + infinitive)

*Quiero…* is fine with friends and family, but it can sound blunt to a waiter or in a shop. The polite form is *quisiera* — I would like. Learn it as a fixed phrase:

- *Quisiera un jugo de naranja, por favor.* — I'd like an orange juice, please. (*la naranja* = orange)
- *Quisiera pollo con arroz.* — I'd like chicken with rice.

### Example 2: ordering politely

You want coffee with milk and bread with cheese. Build the order:

1. Start with the polite chunk: *Quisiera…*
2. Add the first thing with *con*: *un café con leche*.
3. Add the second with *y*: *y pan con queso*.
4. Finish with *por favor*: *Quisiera un café con leche y pan con queso, por favor.*

## Dialogue: La comida en casa de los Ramírez

Ryan, a student from Canada, lives with a family in Puebla, Mrs. Ramírez and her son Diego. It's three in the afternoon.

> Sra. Ramírez: Ryan, ¿tienes hambre? La comida está lista.
>
> Ryan: Sí, tengo mucha hambre. ¡Y también tengo sed!
>
> Sra. Ramírez: Hay agua y jugo. ¿Qué quieres tomar?
>
> Ryan: Agua, por favor. Mmm, ¿qué es esto?
>
> Sra. Ramírez: Es pollo con arroz y frijoles. ¿Te gusta el pollo?
>
> Ryan: Sí, me encanta. Y me gustan mucho los frijoles.
>
> Diego: A mí no me gustan los frijoles. Me gusta el arroz.
>
> Ryan: ¿No? A mí sí. En Canadá no comemos muchos frijoles, pero aquí me encantan.
>
> Sra. Ramírez: ¿Quieres más tortillas?
>
> Ryan: Sí, gracias. Todo está muy rico. ¿Y la cena?
>
> Diego: La cena es pequeña: pan, fruta o un café con leche. A mi papá no le gusta cenar mucho.
>
> Ryan: A mí tampoco.

In English:

> Mrs. Ramírez: Ryan, are you hungry? Lunch is ready.
>
> Ryan: Yes, I'm very hungry. And I'm thirsty too!
>
> Mrs. Ramírez: There's water and juice. What would you like to drink?
>
> Ryan: Water, please. Mmm, what's this?
>
> Mrs. Ramírez: It's chicken with rice and beans. Do you like chicken?
>
> Ryan: Yes, I love it. And I really like beans.
>
> Diego: I don't like beans. I like the rice.
>
> Ryan: No? I do. In Canada we don't eat many beans, but here I love them.
>
> Mrs. Ramírez: Do you want more tortillas?
>
> Ryan: Yes, thanks. Everything is really tasty. And dinner?
>
> Diego: Dinner is small: bread, fruit or a coffee with milk. My dad doesn't like to eat much in the evening.
>
> Ryan: Me neither.

(*todo* = everything, *más* = more, *o* = or; *Sra.* is short for *señora*.) Look at *La comida está lista* — the meal is ready, *estar* + *listo* from lesson 9. *Me gustan los frijoles* is plural, *me gusta el pollo* singular, and *a mi papá no le gusta cenar* uses *le* for a third person.

## Pronunciation

- *gusta, gustan*: a hard *g* as in "go". *Quiero, quieres*: *qu* = *k*, KYEH-ro.
- *frijoles*: free-HO-les. The *j* is the throat sound.
- *huevo*: the *h* is silent, and *hue* sounds like English "weh": WEH-vo.
- *arroz*: the double *rr* is a strong trill, and the *z* is an *s*: a-RROS.
- *pollo*: *ll* like *y*: PO-yo. *Tortilla*: tor-TEE-ya.
- *queso, quisiera*: *qu* before *e* and *i* is a plain *k* sound (the *u* is silent). *Rico* has a *k* sound too, spelled *c*, and starts with the strong trilled *r*: RREE-ko.

## Common mistakes

- *Yo gusto el café.* — The thing liked is the subject: *Me gusta el café.*
- *Me gusta los tacos.* — Plural thing, plural verb: *Me gustan los tacos.*
- *Me gustan comer y bailar.* — Infinitives take *gusta*: *Me gusta comer y bailar.*
- *Me gusta café.* — Add the article: *Me gusta el café.*
- *A mí también* after a negative sentence. After *No me gusta…*, agree with *A mí tampoco.*
- *Me encanta mucho.* — *Encantar* is already strong, so this sounds redundant to many speakers: *Me encanta* or *Me gusta mucho.*
- *Estoy hambre / Soy hambre.* — Use *tener*: *Tengo hambre.*
- *Tengo mucho hambre.* — *Hambre* is feminine: *mucha hambre*.

## Key points

- *Me gusta* + one thing or an infinitive; *me gustan* + several things. The verb agrees with the thing liked.
- Pronouns: *me, te, le, nos, les*; add *a mí, a ti, a él…* for emphasis, contrast or clarity.
- *Encantar* works like *gustar* and means "to love (something)".
- *A mí también* (after yes), *A mí tampoco* (after no), *A mí sí / A mí no* to disagree.
- *querer*: *quiero, quieres, quiere, queremos, quieren*; order politely with *Quisiera…*
- *Tengo hambre / Tengo sed*; good food is *rico*.
- In Mexico *la comida* is also the main meal of the day, in the early afternoon.

lessons.title: Shopping, prices and comparing
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

You can now say what's in a house and what you like to eat. The next step is buying things. In this lesson you learn the numbers from 100 up to a million, how to ask and understand prices in pesos, how Mexico writes numbers, the words for "this" and "that" (*este, ese*), and how to compare two things: *más barato que* (cheaper than), *tan caro como* (as expensive as), *mejor* (better). By the end you can choose between two backpacks in a shop, ask the price and pay.

## Shops, money and paying

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| la tienda | shop, store |
| el mercado | market |
| el supermercado | supermarket |
| el dinero | money |
| el peso | peso (the currency of Mexico) |
| el precio | price |
| la cuenta | bill, check; account |
| la tarjeta | card (credit or debit) |
| el efectivo | cash |
| caro | expensive |
| barato | cheap, inexpensive |

Three verbs do most of the work:

- *comprar* — to buy: *Compro pan en la tienda.* — I buy bread at the shop.
- *pagar* — to pay, to pay for: *Pago la cuenta.* — I'll pay the bill. *Pagar* already means "pay for", so there's no extra word: *Pago el café* (I'm paying for the coffee). You pay *con tarjeta* (by card) or *en efectivo* (in cash).
- *costar* — to cost. Like *querer* in lesson 11, it changes its stem, here *o → ue*: *cuesta, cuestan*. In shops you only need those two forms.

## ¿Cuánto cuesta?

The question is *¿Cuánto cuesta?* — How much does it cost? — for one thing, and *¿Cuánto cuestan?* for several. The verb agrees with the thing, not with you:

- *¿Cuánto cuesta la mochila?* — How much is the backpack? — *Cuesta quinientos pesos.*
- *¿Cuánto cuestan los lentes?* — How much are the glasses? — *Cuestan mil doscientos pesos.*

You can also ask *¿Cuál es el precio?* — What's the price? — but *¿Cuánto cuesta?* is far more common. And if the answer is too high: *No tengo mucho dinero.* — I don't have much money.

For a total at the till, Mexicans also ask *¿Cuánto es?* — How much is it? — and the answer uses *ser*: *Son trescientos pesos.*

## Numbers from 100

| | | |
|---|---|---|
| 100 cien | 400 cuatrocientos | 800 ochocientos |
| 101 ciento uno | 500 quinientos | 900 novecientos |
| 200 doscientos | 600 seiscientos | 1,000 mil |
| 300 trescientos | 700 setecientos | 2,000 dos mil |

The rules:

- *Cien* or *ciento*? Exactly 100 is *cien*, alone or before a noun: *cien pesos*. Before another number it's *ciento*: *ciento uno, ciento cincuenta* (150). Never *cien y cincuenta*.
- Three irregular hundreds: *quinientos* (500), *setecientos* (700), *novecientos* (900). The others are regular: *dos + cientos = doscientos*, *seis + cientos = seiscientos*.
- Hundreds agree with a feminine noun: *doscientas personas, quinientas tortillas*. With *pesos* (masculine) they stay masculine: *quinientos pesos*.
- *Mil* is never *un mil*: *mil pesos, dos mil, diez mil*. It doesn't become plural: *tres mil* (3,000), not *tres miles*.
- *Un millón* (a million) is a noun, so it takes *de* before the thing counted: *un millón de pesos, dos millones de personas*.
- *Y* only goes between tens and units, as in lesson 3: *ciento veinticinco* (125), *mil quinientos* (1,500), *trescientos cuarenta y dos* (342). Never *mil y quinientos*.

### Example 1: reading a price

How do you say 1,875 pesos?

1. Split it: 1,000 + 800 + 75.
2. 1,000 = *mil* (not *un mil*).
3. 800 = *ochocientos*; *peso* is masculine, so it stays *-os*.
4. 75 = *setenta y cinco* (lesson 3).
5. Together: *mil ochocientos setenta y cinco pesos.*

And 2,450? *dos mil cuatrocientos cincuenta*. And 515? *quinientos quince*.

## How Mexico writes prices

Mexico writes numbers like the United States: a comma separates thousands, and a point separates pesos from *centavos* (cents). Spain and many other countries do the opposite: 1.500,50.

![A price tag for a backpack (Mochila) reading 1,250.50 MXN. Four lines point to the comma, the point, the 50 and the letters MXN.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

So 1,250.50 is *mil doscientos cincuenta pesos con cincuenta centavos*. In a shop people often shorten it: *mil doscientos cincuenta con cincuenta*. On real price tags in Mexico, the peso has a symbol that looks just like the dollar sign; in this course we write "pesos" or "MXN" instead, the international code for the Mexican peso.

## Este, ese: this and that

To point at things, Spanish uses **[[demonstratives]]**. They agree with the noun like any adjective:

| | masculine | feminine | English |
|---|---|---|---|
| singular, near me | este | esta | this |
| plural, near me | estos | estas | these |
| singular, near you or a bit away | ese | esa | that |
| plural, near you or a bit away | esos | esas | those |

- *Esta mochila es cara.* — This backpack is expensive.
- *¿Cuánto cuestan esos lentes?* — How much are those glasses?
- *Este reloj es bonito, pero ese es más barato.* — This watch is nice, but that one is cheaper.

As in the last example, you can drop the noun when it's clear: *ese* = "that one". For something far away from both of you, there is a third word, *aquel / aquella* (that one over there), which you'll hear but don't need yet.

When you don't know what something is, or you mean an idea, use the forms without gender, *esto* (this) and *eso* (that), which you met in *¿Qué es esto?* (lesson 5):

- *¿Qué es eso?* — What's that?
- *Eso es muy caro.* — That's very expensive.

*Esta* (this) has no accent. *Está* (he / she / it is) does. *Esta tienda está cerrada* — This shop is closed — uses both.

## Comparing: más, menos, tan … como

![A bar chart comparing the price of three backpacks. The red backpack (la roja) and the blue one (la azul) both cost 650 pesos, so their bars are the same height, labeled tan cara como. The green backpack (la verde) costs 490 pesos, with a shorter bar labeled más barata que.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

To compare two things, put *más* (more) or *menos* (less) before the adjective and *que* (than) after it:

- *La mochila azul es más cara que la verde.* — The blue backpack is more expensive than the green one.
- *La verde es menos cara que la azul.* — The green one is less expensive than the blue one.
- *El mercado es más barato que el supermercado.* — The market is cheaper than the supermarket.

The adjective agrees with the first thing: *la mochila azul* is feminine, so *más cara*.

To say two things are equal, use *tan … como* (as … as):

- *La roja es tan cara como la azul.* — The red one is as expensive as the blue one.
- *Este café no es tan bueno como ese.* — This coffee isn't as good as that one.

Two adjectives have their own **[[comparative]]** forms, so you don't add *más*:

| Adjective | Comparative | Example |
|---|---|---|
| bueno | mejor (better) | *Esta tienda es mejor que esa.* |
| malo | peor (worse) | *Este café es peor que el café de mi mamá.* |

*Mejor* and *peor* have no feminine form; only the plural changes: *mejores, peores*. (You may hear *más bueno* or *más malo* about a person's character, but for quality, price or taste use *mejor* and *peor*.)

Before a number, "more than" is *más de*, not *más que*: *Cuesta más de mil pesos.* — It costs more than a thousand pesos.

### Otro: another, other

*Otro / otra* means "another" or "other", and it never takes *un / una* in front:

- *Quisiera otro café, por favor.* — I'd like another coffee, please.
- *¿Hay otra tienda cerca?* — Is there another shop nearby?
- *Los otros lentes son mejores.* — The other glasses are better.

### Example 2: making a comparison

Compare a watch at 900 pesos with one at 1,200 pesos.

1. Name the first thing: *Este reloj* (masculine).
2. It costs less, so: *es más barato que* … or *es menos caro que* …
3. Name the second with *ese*: *ese*.
4. Result: *Este reloj es más barato que ese.* The difference is 1,200 − 900 = 300 pesos: *Cuesta trescientos pesos menos.* — It costs three hundred pesos less.

## Dialogue: En la tienda

Mariana is shopping for a backpack for university.

> Vendedor: Buenas tardes. ¿Qué busca?
>
> Mariana: Buenas tardes. Busco una mochila para la universidad. ¿Cuánto cuesta esta mochila roja?
>
> Vendedor: Cuesta seiscientos cincuenta pesos.
>
> Mariana: Mmm, es un poco cara. ¿Y esa azul?
>
> Vendedor: Esa también cuesta seiscientos cincuenta. Es tan cara como la roja, pero es más grande.
>
> Mariana: ¿Hay otra más barata?
>
> Vendedor: Sí, esta verde. Cuesta cuatrocientos noventa pesos. Es más barata que las otras, pero es más pequeña.
>
> Mariana: Mmm… La azul es mejor. Necesito una mochila grande para mi computadora. ¿Pago con tarjeta?
>
> Vendedor: Con tarjeta o en efectivo, como usted prefiera.
>
> Mariana: En efectivo. Aquí tiene: setecientos pesos.
>
> Vendedor: Y aquí está su cambio: cincuenta pesos. ¡Gracias!

In English:

> Salesman: Good afternoon. What are you looking for?
>
> Mariana: Good afternoon. I'm looking for a backpack for university. How much is this red backpack?
>
> Salesman: It's six hundred fifty pesos.
>
> Mariana: Hmm, it's a bit expensive. And that blue one?
>
> Salesman: That one is also six hundred fifty. It's as expensive as the red one, but it's bigger.
>
> Mariana: Is there another cheaper one?
>
> Salesman: Yes, this green one. It's four hundred ninety pesos. It's cheaper than the others, but it's smaller.
>
> Mariana: Hmm… The blue one is better. I need a big backpack for my computer. Shall I pay by card?
>
> Salesman: By card or in cash, as you prefer.
>
> Mariana: In cash. Here you are: seven hundred pesos.
>
> Salesman: And here's your change: fifty pesos. Thank you!

(*como usted prefiera* = as you prefer; *aquí tiene* = here you are; *el cambio* = change.) The arithmetic checks out: 700 − 650 = 50. *Esa azul* and *la verde* drop the noun *mochila* because it's clear; *otra más barata* is "another, cheaper one", with no *una* before *otra*.

## Pronunciation

- *cuesta*: KWES-ta, one syllable for *cue*.
- *quinientos*: kee-NYEN-tos; *setecientos*: se-te-SYEN-tos; *novecientos*: no-ve-SYEN-tos. With seseo, *ci* is always "see".
- *doscientos* and *trescientos* have an *s* + *c* that sound like one long *s*: do-SYEN-tos.
- *efectivo*: e-fek-TEE-vo, with a *b*-like *v* (lesson 1).
- *mejor*: me-HOR, with the throat *j*.
- *supermercado*: the stress is on *ca*: su-per-mer-CA-do.

## Common mistakes

- *Cien cincuenta.* — Before another number, use *ciento*: *ciento cincuenta.*
- *Cinco cientos, siete cientos, nueve cientos.* — These three are irregular: *quinientos, setecientos, novecientos.*
- *Un mil pesos.* — Just *mil pesos.*
- *¿Cuánto cuesta los lentes?* — Plural thing: *¿Cuánto cuestan los lentes?*
- *Más bueno que.* — Use *mejor que* for "better than" (and *peor que* for "worse than").
- *Tan caro que.* — Equal comparisons use *como*: *tan caro como.*
- *Un otro café.* — No *un*: *otro café.*
- *Pago por la cuenta.* — *Pagar* already includes "for": *Pago la cuenta.*
- *Esta cara.* — If you mean "it's expensive", that's *Está cara* (it is) or *Es cara*; *esta* without an accent means "this".

## Key points

- *¿Cuánto cuesta?* (one thing) / *¿Cuánto cuestan?* (several); *¿Cuánto es?* for the total.
- *cien* alone, *ciento* + another number; *quinientos, setecientos, novecientos*; *mil* without *un*; *un millón de*.
- Mexico writes 1,250.50 (comma for thousands, point for centavos); Spain writes 1.250,50.
- *este / esta / estos / estas* (this, these), *ese / esa / esos / esas* (that, those), *esto / eso* for unknown things.
- *más … que, menos … que, tan … como*; *mejor, peor*; *más de* + number.
- *otro* never takes *un*.
- Pay *con tarjeta* or *en efectivo*.

lessons.title: Honors: La comida mexicana — eating the Mexican way
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

In lesson 11 you learned the words for food and drink, *me gusta*, and the polite *quisiera*. In lesson 12 you learned to ask prices and pay. This honors lesson puts those pieces together in the place where you'll use them most: a Mexican table. You'll see how a typical day of meals is organized, meet *antojitos* and the words that go with tacos, learn why a Mexican shopper buys *jitomates* and not *tomates*, and order like a local in a *fonda* with *¿Me da…?* and *¿Me trae…?*. You'll also learn what to say when other people are eating, and how tipping works.

A note before we start: everything here about "how Mexicans eat" is a generalization. Mexico is a large country with very different regions, and habits differ between cities and villages, families, jobs and generations. Treat these descriptions as a starting point, not a rule.

## A day of meals

![A timeline of a typical day of meals in Mexico, from 7 in the morning to 11 at night. El desayuno, between about 7 and 10: a cup of coffee and a plate of eggs. La comida, between about 2 and 4 in the afternoon, the biggest block: a bowl of soup, a plate of rice and a main dish, and tortillas. La cena, between about 8 and 10 at night, a small block labeled ligera (light): a sweet bread roll and a cup of coffee. A note says the times are a common pattern, not a rule.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

- *El desayuno* (breakfast) can be quick on a workday: coffee, fruit, a *pan dulce* (sweet bread roll). On weekends many families sit down to a big breakfast with eggs, beans and tortillas.
- *La comida* is the main meal, usually eaten in the early afternoon, often between about 2 and 4 pm. In many families it has several courses: a soup, then rice or pasta, then a main dish (*el guisado*, a stew or cooked dish) with beans and tortillas, and something sweet or a coffee at the end. Office workers and students often eat it at a small restaurant near work.
- *La cena* (dinner) in the evening is often light, especially after a big *comida*: bread and coffee or milk, a few *tacos*, or leftovers. But many people, especially in cities, also go out for tacos at night.

Some people also have a mid-morning snack or a late breakfast called *el almuerzo*. Be careful: in Spain *el almuerzo* is often lunch. When a Mexican friend invites you *a comer*, they usually mean the afternoon meal.

## Antojitos and tacos

*Un antojito* comes from *el antojo*, a craving, and literally means "a little craving". It's the word for the many snacks and small dishes made mostly from corn dough: *tacos, quesadillas, tamales, sopes, tostadas*. You eat them at a street stand (*un puesto*), in a market, or at home. Most of them are eaten with your hands.

A taco is a tortilla folded around a filling. The filling is named with *de*:

- *un taco de pollo* — a chicken taco
- *tacos de carne* — meat tacos
- *tres tacos de frijoles con queso* — three tacos of beans with cheese

This **[[noun + de + noun]]** pattern is everywhere on Mexican menus. Where English puts one noun in front of another ("chicken taco", "orange juice"), Spanish puts the main thing first and joins the second with *de*: *jugo de naranja, agua de limón* (water with lime: a fresh drink), *sopa de verduras*.

### Example 1: reading a taco stand sign

A sign at a stand says: *Tacos de pollo — 18 pesos. Tacos de carne — 22 pesos. Quesadillas de queso — 30 pesos.*

1. Find the main thing first: *tacos*, *tacos*, *quesadillas*.
2. The word after *de* is the filling: chicken, meat, cheese.
3. You want three meat tacos and a cheese quesadilla: 3 × 22 = 66 pesos, plus 30 = 96 pesos.
4. To order: *Tres tacos de carne y una quesadilla de queso, por favor.*

## The words on the table

![A table with six things to eat, each labeled. A halved avocado with its pit (el aguacate), an ear of corn on a stick (el elote), two red tomatoes (el jitomate), three small green tomatillos in their papery husks (el tomate verde), a stack of corn tortillas (las tortillas) and a small clay bowl of red sauce (la salsa).](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

- *La salsa* is a sauce, and on a Mexican table it usually means a spicy one, often *salsa roja* (red) or *salsa verde* (green). Before you put it on everything, ask *¿Pica?* — Is it spicy? (literally "Does it sting?"). An honest answer is often *Pica poquito* (it's a little bit spicy), which may mean quite a lot.
- *El aguacate* is the avocado, and mashed with lime, onion and chile it becomes *el guacamole*.
- *El elote* is an ear of fresh corn, often sold at street stands, boiled or roasted, with mayonnaise, cheese, chile and lime. Dried corn as a grain is *el maíz*.
- *El jitomate* and *el tomate*: in central and southern Mexico, including Mexico City, the red tomato is *el jitomate*, and *el tomate* or *el tomate verde* is the small green tomatillo used for green salsa. In northern Mexico and in the rest of the Spanish-speaking world, the red one is simply *el tomate*. If you ask for *tomates* in a Mexico City market, you may get green ones.

Many of these words came into Spanish from Nahuatl, the language of the Aztecs, which is still spoken by more than a million people in Mexico. A **[[Nahuatl loanword]]** is a Spanish word borrowed from Nahuatl: *aguacate* (from *ahuacatl*), *elote* (from *elotl*), *jitomate* (from *xitomatl*), *tomate* (from *tomatl*) and *chile*. English later borrowed several of them in turn, through Spanish: avocado, tomato, chili.

## Ordering in a fonda

*Una fonda* is a small, simple restaurant, often family-run, the kind of place where office workers eat at midday. Many offer *la comida corrida*: a set lunch at a fixed price, with a few courses and a drink. A typical one has a soup, then rice or pasta, a main dish chosen from two or three options, tortillas, the drink of the day (*el agua del día*, a fresh fruit drink) and sometimes a small dessert. Prices vary a lot by city and neighbourhood.

### ¿Me da…? ¿Me trae…?

In lesson 11 you learned *Quisiera…*, which is always polite. In everyday Mexican Spanish people more often order with a short question:

- *¿Me da un agua de limón, por favor?* — Can I have a lime water, please? (literally "Do you give me…?")
- *¿Me trae la cuenta, por favor?* — Could you bring me the check, please? (literally "Do you bring me…?")
- *¿Me da dos tacos de pollo?* — Can I have two chicken tacos?

The *me* is the same little word as in *me gusta*: "to me". *Da* is the *usted* form of *dar* (to give, lesson 21) and *trae* the *usted* form of *traer* (to bring). You don't need the whole verbs yet: learn *¿Me da…?* and *¿Me trae…?* as chunks. A question in the present tense is the normal, friendly way to make a **[[polite request]]** in Mexico; with *por favor* and a smile it's perfect.

When you order food to go, you'll hear one question at the counter: *¿Para aquí o para llevar?* — For here or to go? Answer *Para aquí* (to eat here) or *Para llevar* (to take away).

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Ordering in a fonda, step by step
  accDescr: You arrive and greet the server with Buenas tardes. The server asks what you would like, Qué le traigo? You order with Me da la comida corrida, por favor. The server asks which main dish, pollo o carne? You choose, for example pollo. At the end you ask for the check with Me trae la cuenta, por favor, and pay. On the way out you say Provecho to the people still eating.
  A["You: Buenas tardes."] --> B["Server: ¿Qué le traigo?"]
  B --> C["You: ¿Me da la comida corrida, por favor?"]
  C --> D["Server: ¿De guisado, pollo o carne?"]
  D --> E["You: Pollo, por favor."]
  E --> F["You: ¿Me trae la cuenta, por favor?"]
  F --> G["On the way out: ¡Provecho!"]
```

### Example 2: building an order

You're in a fonda. You want the set lunch with chicken, and a lime water.

1. Start with the chunk for "can I have": *¿Me da…?*
2. Add the set lunch: *¿Me da la comida corrida…?*
3. The server asks *¿De guisado?* (Which main dish?). Answer with the dish: *Pollo, por favor.*
4. For the drink, the *comida corrida* includes *el agua del día*. If you want something else: *¿Me da un agua de limón en lugar del agua del día?* (*en lugar de* = instead of). Or simply accept: *Sí, está bien.*
5. At the end: *¿Me trae la cuenta, por favor?*

## ¡Buen provecho!

When you pass people who are eating, or when you leave a restaurant and walk past other tables, it's very common in Mexico to say *¡Provecho!* or *¡Buen provecho!* — Enjoy your meal! — even to strangers. A host may say it to start the meal. The usual answer is simply *Gracias*. If you walk into a small office or a family kitchen and people are eating, *¡Provecho!* is the polite thing to say. Some people think it's a little old-fashioned, but you'll hear it every day.

## La propina: tipping

*La propina* is the tip. In sit-down restaurants and *fondas* in Mexico, a tip of about 10 to 15 percent of the bill is a common guide; around 10 percent is usual, more for very good service. Mexico's consumer agency, Profeco, says a tip is voluntary: a restaurant may not add one to your bill without your agreement. At a street taco stand, many people leave no tip or just a few coins. Rules of thumb like these change with time and place, so watch what people around you do.

To give a tip when you pay in cash, say how much you want to pay in all, or say *Quédese con el cambio* — Keep the change. With a card, the server often asks *¿Cuánto le agrego de propina?* (How much should I add as a tip?) and you give a number or a percentage.

### Example 3: working out the tip

Two people's *comida corrida* comes to 380 pesos.

1. 10 percent of 380 is 38 pesos; 15 percent is 57 pesos.
2. Something in between, rounded to a friendly number, is fine: 40 or 50 pesos.
3. With 40 pesos, the total is 380 + 40 = 420 pesos. Hand over a 500-peso bill and say: *Son cuatrocientos veinte, por favor.* You get 500 − 420 = 80 pesos back.

## Reading: Mi fonda favorita

> Trabajo en una oficina en el centro de Puebla. A las dos y media, mis compañeros y yo comemos en la fonda de doña Rosa. Es pequeña, pero la comida es muy rica y no es cara. La comida corrida cuesta ciento veinte pesos. Primero hay sopa de verduras, después arroz, y de guisado hay pollo en salsa verde o carne con papas. El agua del día es de limón o de jamaica. Doña Rosa siempre pregunta: "¿Para aquí o para llevar?" Yo como allí, porque me gusta hablar con mis compañeros. Al final, pido la cuenta y dejo una propina de quince pesos. Cuando salgo, digo "¡Provecho!" a las otras mesas. En la noche, ceno poquito: un pan dulce y un café con leche.

In English:

> I work in an office downtown in Puebla. At half past two, my coworkers and I eat at doña Rosa's fonda. It's small, but the food is very good and it isn't expensive. The set lunch costs one hundred twenty pesos. First there's vegetable soup, then rice, and for the main dish there's chicken in green salsa or meat with potatoes. The drink of the day is lime or hibiscus water. Doña Rosa always asks: "For here or to go?" I eat there, because I like talking with my coworkers. At the end, I ask for the check and leave a fifteen-peso tip. When I leave, I say "¡Provecho!" to the other tables. At night I have a very light dinner: a sweet roll and a coffee with milk.

(*los compañeros* = coworkers, *doña* = a respectful title before a woman's first name, *primero, después* = first, then (lesson 16), *la jamaica* = hibiscus, *pido* = I ask for (*pedir*, lesson 15), *dejo* = I leave (a tip), *salgo* = I leave, go out (*salir*, lesson 16), *poquito* = a little bit.) Check the tip: 15 pesos on 120 is 12.5 percent, right in the usual range.

## Pronunciation

- *aguacate*: a-gwa-KA-te; *gua* sounds like "gwa".
- *jitomate*: hee-to-MA-te, with the throat *j*. *Elote*: e-LO-te.
- *antojito*: an-to-HEE-to.
- *provecho*: pro-VE-cho; the *ch* is as in English "church".
- *¿Me trae…?*: TRA-e, two syllables. *Propina*: pro-PEE-na.
- *Para llevar*: in fast speech it sounds like "pa-ra-ye-VAR"; you'll also hear *pa' llevar*.

## Common mistakes

- *Un pollo taco* or *un taco pollo.* — Spanish puts the main thing first and joins with *de*: *un taco de pollo.*
- *¿Puedo tener un taco?* — A word-for-word "Can I have…?" sounds strange. Say *¿Me da un taco?* or *Quisiera un taco.*
- *Dame la cuenta.* — "Give me the check" with *tú* to a waiter you don't know sounds rude. Use *usted*: *¿Me trae la cuenta, por favor?*
- Asking for *tomates* in Mexico City and expecting red ones. Ask for *jitomates*.
- *Almuerzo* for the main afternoon meal in Mexico. That meal is *la comida*.
- Leaving without a word when people are eating. A quick *¡Provecho!* is friendlier.

## Key points

- A common Mexican pattern: *desayuno* in the morning, *la comida* (the main meal) in the early afternoon, a light *cena* at night. These are generalizations.
- *Antojitos* are corn-based snacks; fillings are named with *de*: *tacos de pollo*.
- *Jitomate* = red tomato in central and southern Mexico; *tomate (verde)* = tomatillo there.
- Many food words are Nahuatl loanwords: *aguacate, elote, jitomate, tomate, chile*.
- Order with *¿Me da…?* and ask for the check with *¿Me trae la cuenta?*; *¿Para aquí o para llevar?*
- Say *¡Provecho!* or *¡Buen provecho!* to people who are eating.
- A tip of about 10–15 percent is a common guide in restaurants; it's voluntary.

lessons.title: Honors: At the market — quantities, change and bargaining
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

In lesson 12 you learned the big numbers, *¿Cuánto cuesta?*, *este / ese* and comparisons, and you bought a backpack in a shop. Shops have price tags. Markets are different: prices are said out loud, food is sold by the kilo and the dozen, the vendor may not have change for a big bill, and in some places you can ask for a better price. This honors lesson takes you to a Mexican market. You'll learn to ask for half a kilo or a dozen, understand a market price with *¿A cómo está…?*, read a receipt, handle *el cambio* and *los centavos*, bargain politely, and read the large numbers in rents and car ads.

As in 12h1, the descriptions of how people shop are generalizations: they hold in many places in Mexico, not everywhere, and they change over time.

## Two kinds of market: el mercado and el tianguis

*El mercado* is a market in a permanent building, open every day or most days, with fixed stalls: fruit and vegetables, meat, cheese, flowers, kitchen things, and small places to eat. Most neighbourhoods in Mexican cities have one.

*El tianguis* (the same form in the plural: *los tianguis*) is a street market that sets up on a fixed day of the week, often in the same street every week, and is taken down in the evening. You'll find fresh food, clothes, used goods, toys and stands selling tacos and fresh drinks. The word comes from Nahuatl *tianquiztli*, "market", and these markets go back to before the Spanish conquest.

Each stall is *un puesto*. As you walk past, vendors call out *¡Pásele, pásele!* (come on in, take a look) and *¿Qué le damos?* or *¿Qué va a llevar?* (What can we get you? What will you take?).

## Quantities: kilos, halves and dozens

Mexico uses the metric system, so fruit, vegetables, meat, cheese and even tortillas are sold by weight: *el kilo* (kilogram) and its parts.

| Spanish | Amount | Example |
|---|---|---|
| un kilo | 1 kg | *un kilo de jitomates* |
| medio kilo | ½ kg = 500 g | *medio kilo de queso* |
| un cuarto de kilo | ¼ kg = 250 g | *un cuarto de kilo de jamón* (ham) |
| kilo y medio | 1½ kg | *kilo y medio de papas* |
| una docena | 12 | *una docena de huevos* |
| media docena | 6 | *media docena de plátanos* |

Three things to notice:

- Spanish always joins the quantity and the food with *de*: *un kilo de manzanas*, where English says "a kilo of apples" too, but also *una docena de huevos*, where English says "a dozen eggs".
- *Medio* (half) agrees with its noun and never takes *un* before it: *medio kilo* (masculine), *media docena* (feminine). Don't say *un medio kilo*.
- *Un cuarto* here is a quarter, not a room. The context always makes it clear: *un cuarto de kilo*.

### ¿A cómo está…? Prices that change

In lesson 12 you asked *¿Cuánto cuesta?*. In a Mexican market, where food prices go up and down with the season, you'll also hear *¿A cómo está…?* (What's the price of… today?), and the answer uses *estar a*:

- *¿A cómo está el jitomate?* — How much are the tomatoes today? — *Está a veintiocho el kilo.* — It's twenty-eight a kilo.
- *¿A cómo están los aguacates?* — *Están a sesenta el kilo.*

The vendor often leaves out *pesos*, and says *el kilo* for "per kilo". *Estar* fits here for the same reason as in lesson 9: the price is the condition of the moment, not a fixed fact.

### Example 1: working out a market order

You need half a kilo of cheese, which is at 180 pesos a kilo, and a quarter kilo of ham at 160 pesos a kilo.

1. Half of 180 is 90: *medio kilo de queso* costs 90 pesos.
2. A quarter of 160 is 40: *un cuarto de kilo de jamón* costs 40 pesos.
3. Total: 90 + 40 = 130 pesos.
4. To order: *¿Me da medio kilo de queso y un cuarto de kilo de jamón, por favor?* The vendor may ask *¿Algo más?* (Anything else?), and you finish with *Es todo, gracias.* — That's all, thanks.

## Money: billetes, monedas, centavos and el cambio

The peso is divided into 100 *centavos*. Money comes as *billetes* (banknotes) and *monedas* (coins). The Bank of Mexico listed bills of 20, 50, 100, 200, 500 and 1,000 pesos in 2026, and the everyday coins are 1, 2, 5 and 10 pesos, plus a few small centavo coins and a 20-peso coin. In supermarkets, prices like 23.90 are common; in markets, prices are usually whole pesos or end in .50.

*El cambio* is the change you get back. It's the same word as in lesson 12's dialogue, and small vendors care about it a lot: early in the morning, a stall may not have change for a 500-peso bill. Useful phrases:

- *¿Tiene cambio de quinientos?* — Do you have change for five hundred?
- *No tengo cambio. ¿No tiene más chico?* — I don't have change. Don't you have a smaller bill? (*más chico* = smaller, an everyday Mexican word for *más pequeño*)
- *¿Cuánto le debo?* — How much do I owe you? (a very common way to ask for the total)

### Reading a receipt

In a supermarket or a small grocery (*la tienda de abarrotes*), you get a receipt, which in Mexico is usually called *el ticket*. The picture shows one. Like Mexican price tags, it uses the peso symbol, which looks just like a dollar sign. (In the lessons we write "pesos" or MXN instead.)

![A shop receipt (ticket) from Abarrotes Doña Lupe. Four lines: 1.000 KG JITOMATE 28.00; 0.500 KG QUESO OAXACA 95.00; 1 DOC HUEVO 42.00; 0.250 KG JAMON 38.50. Then TOTAL 203.50, EFECTIVO 250.00 and CAMBIO 46.50. Each amount has the peso sign in front of it, and the receipt ends with GRACIAS POR SU COMPRA.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Read it line by line: *un kilo de jitomate, 28 pesos; medio kilo de queso Oaxaca, 95 pesos; una docena de huevos, 42 pesos; un cuarto de kilo de jamón, 38.50.* The total is 203.50. The customer paid *en efectivo* with 250 pesos, and *el cambio* was 46.50. (*Queso Oaxaca* is a soft, stringy cheese from Oaxaca; *DOC* is short for *docena*; *Gracias por su compra* = thank you for your purchase.)

### Example 2: checking the change

Check the receipt's sums.

1. Add the items: 28.00 + 95.00 + 42.00 + 38.50 = 203.50. ✓
2. Subtract from what was paid: 250.00 − 203.50 = 46.50. ✓
3. Say the change aloud: *cuarenta y seis pesos con cincuenta centavos*, or in quick speech *cuarenta y seis cincuenta*.

## Bargaining: regatear

*Regatear* means to bargain, to haggle. It's a regular -ar verb: *regateo, regateas, regatea*. In Mexico it's normal in some places and impolite in others.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Should you bargain? A rough guide for Mexico
  accDescr: A rough guide, with generalizations. Is there a printed price tag, or is it a supermarket, chain store, pharmacy or restaurant? If yes, don't bargain; you can only ask whether there is a discount, Hay descuento? If no, is it a craft market, a souvenir stall or a stall selling clothes or used goods? If yes, polite bargaining is often expected, for example Me lo deja en trescientos? If no, it is probably cheap everyday food such as tortillas, fruit or tacos, and most people pay the price asked.
  A["You want to buy something"] --> B{"Price tag, supermarket, chain store, pharmacy or restaurant?"}
  B -- yes --> C["Don't bargain. You can ask: ¿Hay descuento?"]
  B -- no --> D{"Crafts, souvenirs, clothes or used goods at a market?"}
  D -- yes --> E["Polite bargaining is often fine: ¿Me lo deja en trescientos?"]
  D -- no --> F["Everyday food stall: most people pay the price asked"]
```

The usual way to bargain politely is to ask the seller to "leave it" to you at a lower price:

- *¿Me lo deja en trescientos?* — Will you let me have it for three hundred?
- *¿Me la deja en doscientos?* — (for a feminine thing, such as *la bolsa*, the bag)
- *¿Me los deja en quinientos?* — (for several masculine things)
- *¿Me hace un descuento?* — Can you give me a discount? (*hacer*, lesson 16)
- *¿Cuál es su último precio?* — What's your best price? (literally "your last price")

The small words *lo, la, los, las* mean "it" or "them". They are **[[direct object pronouns]]**, and they agree with the thing you're buying: *el sombrero* (hat) → *lo*, *la bolsa* → *la*. You'll learn them fully at A2; for now, use *¿Me lo deja en…?* as a chunk and change *lo* to *la* for a feminine thing if you can. Like *me* in *¿Me da…?*, they go before the verb.

Bargaining is a friendly conversation, not a fight. Start a little below what you're happy to pay, smile, and if the price is fair, accept. Many people feel that bargaining hard over a few pesos with someone selling cheap food is not right, and supermarkets and shops with price tags have fixed prices: there you can only ask about *una oferta* (a special offer) or *un descuento* (a discount).

## Big numbers: rents and cars

Lesson 12 stopped at a million. Rents and car prices use the same numbers, and ads write them the Mexican way, with commas:

- *Renta: 12,500 al mes* — *doce mil quinientos al mes* (12,500 a month).
- *Carro usado: 185,000* — *ciento ochenta y cinco mil pesos* (a used car).
- *Casa: 2,350,000* — *dos millones trescientos cincuenta mil pesos*.

Remember: *millón* takes *de* only when the noun comes right after it: *dos millones de pesos*, but *dos millones trescientos cincuenta mil pesos*. And the hundreds work the same in front of *mil* as anywhere else: *ciento* before another number (*ciento ochenta y cinco mil*, 185,000), but *cien* alone (*cien mil*, 100,000).

### Example 3: reading a car ad

An ad says: *Se vende carro, modelo 2019, 210,000 pesos. Precio a tratar.*

1. *Se vende* = for sale (like *Se renta* in lesson 10).
2. 210,000 = 210 × 1,000: *doscientos diez mil pesos*.
3. *Precio a tratar* means "price negotiable", so here you may bargain: *¿Me lo deja en doscientos mil?* — ten thousand pesos less.

## Dialogue: En el tianguis

Lucía is buying avocados, flowers and a bag at the Tuesday *tianguis*.

> Vendedor: ¡Pásele, güerita! ¿Qué le damos?
>
> Lucía: Buenos días. ¿A cómo están los aguacates?
>
> Vendedor: A sesenta el kilo. Están muy buenos.
>
> Lucía: ¿Me da medio kilo, por favor? Y una docena de rosas.
>
> Vendedor: Medio de aguacate, treinta, y la docena de rosas, cien. ¿Algo más?
>
> Lucía: Es todo, gracias. ¿Cuánto le debo?
>
> Vendedor: Son ciento treinta.
>
> Lucía: Perdón, solo tengo un billete de quinientos. ¿Tiene cambio?
>
> Vendedor: Sí, sí. Aquí está su cambio: trescientos setenta.

Then, at a stall selling bags:

> Lucía: ¿Cuánto cuesta esta bolsa?
>
> Vendedora: Trescientos cincuenta. Es de piel.
>
> Lucía: Es muy bonita. ¿Me la deja en trescientos?
>
> Vendedora: Mmm… se la dejo en trescientos veinte.
>
> Lucía: Bueno, trescientos veinte. ¡Gracias!

In English:

> Vendor: Come on over, miss! What can we get you?
>
> Lucía: Good morning. How much are the avocados today?
>
> Vendor: Sixty a kilo. They're really good.
>
> Lucía: Can I have half a kilo, please? And a dozen roses.
>
> Vendor: Half of avocado, thirty, and the dozen roses, a hundred. Anything else?
>
> Lucía: That's all, thanks. How much do I owe you?
>
> Vendor: That's a hundred thirty.
>
> Lucía: Sorry, I only have a five-hundred bill. Do you have change?
>
> Vendor: Yes, yes. Here's your change: three hundred seventy.
>
> Lucía: How much is this bag?
>
> Vendor: Three hundred fifty. It's leather.
>
> Lucía: It's very pretty. Will you let me have it for three hundred?
>
> Vendor: Hmm… I'll let you have it for three hundred twenty.
>
> Lucía: OK, three hundred twenty. Thanks!

(*güerita* is a friendly word vendors use for a light-haired or light-skinned woman, and often for any young female customer; *medio de aguacate* is market shorthand for *medio kilo de aguacate*; *las rosas* = roses; *solo* = only; *de piel* = made of leather; *se la dejo* = I'll let you have it.) The sums: 30 + 100 = 130, and 500 − 130 = 370. The bag went from 350 to 320, a discount of 30 pesos.

## Pronunciation

- *tianguis*: TYAN-gees. The *u* after *g* is silent before *i*, as in *guitarra*.
- *docena*: do-SE-na; *centavo*: sen-TA-vo (seseo).
- *regatear*: re-ga-te-AR, four syllables; *e* and *a* stay separate.
- *billete*: bee-YE-te; *ll* like *y*.
- *ticket* is said the Spanish way: TEE-ket.
- *¿A cómo está?* is often run together: a-KO-moes-TÁ.

## Common mistakes

- *Un medio kilo.* — No *un*: *medio kilo.* And for feminine nouns: *media docena.*
- *Una docena huevos.* — Keep *de*: *una docena de huevos.*
- *Dos millones de trescientos mil.* — *De* only after a bare million: *dos millones de pesos*, but *dos millones trescientos mil pesos*.
- Bargaining in a supermarket or a pharmacy. Prices there are fixed.
- *¿Me lo deja en trescientos?* about *la bolsa*. Strictly, it's *¿Me la deja…?* (*la* for a feminine thing), though a vendor will understand you either way.
- Paying for a 20-peso snack with a 500-peso bill at a small stall without asking *¿Tiene cambio?* first.

## Key points

- *El mercado* is a permanent market; *el tianguis* is a weekly street market (from Nahuatl *tianquiztli*).
- *un kilo, medio kilo, un cuarto de kilo, una docena, media docena* + *de* + food.
- *¿A cómo está / están…?* — *Está a veinte el kilo*: market prices with *estar a*.
- *el billete, la moneda, el centavo, el cambio*; *¿Tiene cambio?*, *¿Cuánto le debo?*
- Bargain politely where it's normal: *¿Me lo deja en…?*, *¿Me hace un descuento?* Not in supermarkets or shops with price tags.
- *dos millones de pesos*, but *dos millones trescientos mil pesos*.

lessons.title: Telling the time and the days of the week
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

You can count to a million (lessons 03 and 12) and talk about what you do with the present tense (lessons 04 and 07). This module is about your day and your plans, and it starts with the clock and the calendar: how to ask *¿Qué hora es?* (What time is it?), how to say when something happens (*a las nueve*, at nine), the parts of the day, the days of the week, and how often you do things (*siempre, a veces, nunca*). Mexico and most of Latin America tell the time a little differently from Spain, and you'll learn both.

## ¿Qué hora es? — Es la una, son las dos

To ask the time, say *¿Qué hora es?* — What time is it? (*la hora* = the hour, the time on the clock). The answer uses *ser*, and the verb agrees with the number:

| Time | Spanish | Why |
|---|---|---|
| 1:00 | *Es la una.* | one hour: singular |
| 2:00 | *Son las dos.* | two hours: plural |
| 7:00 | *Son las siete.* | |
| 12:00 | *Son las doce.* | |

The little *la / las* stands for *la hora / las horas*, which is why it's feminine and why *uno* becomes *una*. Never leave it out: *Son las cinco*, not *Son cinco*. And it's always *es* with one o'clock and the minutes around it (*Es la una y diez, Es la una menos cuarto*), *son* with every other hour.

In Mexico and other parts of Latin America you'll also hear the plural question *¿Qué horas son?* in everyday speech. Both are fine; *¿Qué hora es?* is the one to use in writing.

### Minutes past the hour: y

From the hour up to half past, add the minutes with *y* (and):

- *Son las tres y cinco.* — It's 3:05.
- *Son las tres y diez.* — It's 3:10.
- *Son las tres y cuarto.* — It's quarter past three. (*un cuarto* = a quarter)
- *Son las tres y veinte.* — It's 3:20.
- *Son las tres y media.* — It's half past three. (*media* = half)

You can also just read the digits, as on a phone screen: *las tres y quince, las tres y treinta, las tres cuarenta*. That is common and always understood, especially for train and bus times.

### Minutes to the hour: menos, or para in Latin America

After half past, Spanish usually counts down to the next hour. There are two ways to do it.

- Everywhere, with *menos* (minus): *Son las cuatro menos cuarto.* — It's quarter to four (3:45). *Son las cuatro menos diez.* — It's ten to four (3:50).
- In Mexico and much of Latin America, with *para* (to, for): *Es un cuarto para las cuatro.* — It's a quarter to four. *Son diez para las cuatro.* — It's ten to four. You'll also hear *Faltan diez para las cuatro* — literally "ten are missing until four" (*faltar* = to be missing).

In Mexico the *para* version is the everyday one; *menos* is understood everywhere and is what you'll read in books from Spain. Learn to recognize both and use whichever comes naturally.

![Four clock faces in a row. The first shows 3:15 with the caption Son las tres y cuarto. The second shows 3:30, Son las tres y media. The third shows 2:45, Son las tres menos cuarto, and under it, Es un cuarto para las tres. The fourth shows 1:00, Es la una.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

This chart sums up the choices:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: How to say the time in Spanish
  accDescr: First look at the hour. If it is one o'clock, start with Es la una; for any other hour start with Son las and the number, such as Son las tres. Then look at the minutes. From 1 to 30 minutes past, add y and the minutes: y cinco, y cuarto, y media. From 31 to 59, count to the next hour: with menos, as in Son las cuatro menos cuarto, or in Latin America with para, as in Es un cuarto para las cuatro.
  A["Look at the hour"] --> B{"Is it one o'clock?"}
  B -- yes --> C["Es la una"]
  B -- no --> D["Son las + number: Son las tres"]
  C --> E{"How many minutes?"}
  D --> E
  E -- "1 to 30" --> F["y + minutes: y cinco, y cuarto, y media"]
  E -- "31 to 59" --> G["Count to the next hour"]
  G --> H["menos: Son las cuatro menos cuarto"]
  G --> I["para (Latin America): Es un cuarto para las cuatro"]
```

## Morning, afternoon and night

A clock time alone can be morning or evening. Spanish adds the part of the day with *de*:

| Spanish | English | Roughly |
|---|---|---|
| *las siete de la mañana* | 7 a.m. | from midnight to noon |
| *las doce del día* / *el mediodía* | noon | 12:00 |
| *las cuatro de la tarde* | 4 p.m. | from noon until it gets dark, about 7 or 8 p.m. |
| *las diez de la noche* | 10 p.m. | from dark until midnight |
| *la medianoche* | midnight | 00:00 |

The borders are a guide, not a rule: 7 p.m. is *las siete de la tarde* for most people and *de la noche* for some. After midnight you say *de la mañana* (*las dos de la mañana*, 2 a.m.); you'll also hear *de la madrugada* for the small hours.

Notice that *mañana* and *tarde* each have two meanings, which are separate words in your vocabulary:

- *la mañana* (noun) = the morning; *mañana* (adverb, no article) = tomorrow. *Mañana por la mañana* = tomorrow morning.
- *la tarde* (noun) = the afternoon; *tarde* (adverb) = late. *Llego tarde* = I'm late. Its opposite is *temprano* (early).

### At what time? a las…

To say when something happens, use *a*: *a la una, a las ocho, a las nueve y media*. The question is *¿A qué hora…?* (At what time…?), which you'll practise more in lesson 16:

- *¿A qué hora es la clase? — A las nueve.* — What time is the class? — At nine.
- *Trabajo de las ocho de la mañana a las cuatro de la tarde.* — I work from 8 a.m. to 4 p.m.
- *Estudio hasta la medianoche.* — I study until midnight. (*hasta* = until)

### de la mañana or por la mañana?

Use *de la mañana / tarde / noche* after a clock time, and *por la mañana / la tarde / la noche* when there's no clock time:

- *Tomo café a las siete de la mañana.* — I have coffee at seven in the morning.
- *Tomo café por la mañana.* — I have coffee in the morning.

(*En la mañana* is also very common in Mexico and much of Latin America: *Estudio en la mañana.* Spain prefers *por*. Both are correct.)

## The days of the week

| Spanish | English | Named after |
|---|---|---|
| *el lunes* | Monday | the moon (*la luna*) |
| *el martes* | Tuesday | Mars |
| *el miércoles* | Wednesday | Mercury |
| *el jueves* | Thursday | Jupiter |
| *el viernes* | Friday | Venus |
| *el sábado* | Saturday | the Sabbath |
| *el domingo* | Sunday | the Lord's day (Latin *dominicus*) |

Three things to remember:

1. No capital letters. Days (and months) are lowercase in Spanish unless they start a sentence: *Hoy es martes.*
2. They are masculine, and the article does the job of English "on": *el lunes* = on Monday (this one), *los lunes* = on Mondays (every Monday). There is no *en*: *Trabajo el sábado*, not *en el sábado*.
3. The plural only changes for the weekend days. *el lunes → los lunes, el jueves → los jueves* (no change, because they already end in -s), but *el sábado → los sábados, el domingo → los domingos*.

After *ser* with today's day, there's no article: *Hoy es viernes.* — Today is Friday. *¿Qué día es hoy?* — What day is it today?

*La semana* is the week and *el fin de semana* the weekend: *Este fin de semana estudio.* — This weekend I'm studying. *El día* is the day; it ends in *-a* but it's masculine (lesson 05): *todo el día*, all day.

Here is one learner's week as she wrote it in her planner:

![A weekly planner page titled Mi semana, with one row per day. lunes: trabajo, 9:00 a 17:00. martes: clase de español, 19:00. miércoles: trabajo; gimnasio, 18:30. jueves: clase de español, 19:00. viernes: trabajo hasta las 15:00; cena con Pablo, 20:30. sábado: mercado por la mañana. domingo: comida con mi familia, 14:00.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Planners, timetables and opening hours usually use the 24-hour clock (17:00 = *las cinco de la tarde*). In conversation people almost always use the 12-hour clock with *de la tarde / de la noche*. The honors lesson 16h1 covers the 24-hour clock.

## How often? siempre, normalmente, a veces, nunca

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| *siempre* | always |
| *todos los días* | every day |
| *normalmente* | usually, normally |
| *a veces* | sometimes |
| *nunca* | never |

- *Siempre* and *normalmente* usually go before the verb or at the start: *Siempre llego temprano. Normalmente como a las dos.*
- *A veces* and *todos los días* go at the start or the end: *A veces estudio por la noche. / Estudio por la noche a veces.*
- *Nunca* goes before the verb, and then there is no *no*: *Nunca trabajo los domingos.* — I never work on Sundays. If *nunca* comes after the verb, Spanish needs *no* in front of the verb as well: *No trabajo nunca los domingos.* That double negative is correct and normal in Spanish, though English avoids it.
- *Todos los* works with any day: *todos los lunes* (every Monday), *todos los fines de semana*.

### el tiempo and la hora

English "time" has two Spanish words here. *La hora* is clock time; *el tiempo* is time in general, a quantity you have or don't have (and also the weather, in lesson 19):

- *¿Qué hora es?* — What time is it?
- *No tengo tiempo.* — I don't have time.
- *¿Tienes tiempo mañana?* — Do you have time tomorrow?

## Dialogue: ¿Tienes tiempo mañana?

> Sofía: Perdón, ¿qué hora es?
>
> Daniel: Es un cuarto para las nueve.
>
> Sofía: ¡Uf! Llego tarde. Mi clase de inglés es a las nueve.
>
> Daniel: ¿Tienes clase todos los días?
>
> Sofía: No, solo los lunes, miércoles y viernes. Los martes y jueves trabajo en una oficina hasta las seis de la tarde.
>
> Daniel: ¿Y el fin de semana?
>
> Sofía: El sábado por la mañana estudio con una amiga. Los domingos nunca trabajo: como con mi familia a las tres.
>
> Daniel: Yo normalmente trabajo los sábados, de la mañana a la noche. Pero mañana no. ¿Tienes tiempo para un café?
>
> Sofía: Sí. ¿A las cinco y media?
>
> Daniel: Perfecto. ¡Hasta mañana!

In English:

> Sofía: Excuse me, what time is it?
>
> Daniel: It's a quarter to nine.
>
> Sofía: Oh! I'm late. My English class is at nine.
>
> Daniel: Do you have class every day?
>
> Sofía: No, only on Mondays, Wednesdays and Fridays. On Tuesdays and Thursdays I work in an office until six in the evening.
>
> Daniel: And at the weekend?
>
> Sofía: On Saturday morning I study with a friend. On Sundays I never work: I eat with my family at three.
>
> Daniel: I usually work on Saturdays, from morning till night. But not tomorrow. Do you have time for a coffee?
>
> Sofía: Yes. At half past five?
>
> Daniel: Perfect. See you tomorrow!

(*solo* = only; you'll meet it as a word in lesson 14. *¡Uf!* is a sigh of annoyance.) Sofía uses the present *llego* for something happening right now: Spanish often does this where English says "I'm late".

## Pronunciation

- *hora*: the *h* is silent: "OH-ra". *¿Qué hora es?* runs together: "keh-OH-ra-ES".
- *mañana*: *ñ* as in "canyon": "ma-NYA-na", stress on the middle syllable.
- *miércoles* and *sábado* carry written accents because they're stressed on the third syllable from the end: MYER-co-les, SA-ba-do. *lunes, martes, jueves, viernes* are stressed on the first syllable and need no accent.
- *cuarto*: *cua* is one syllable, like "kwar-to". *y media*: the *y* is a vowel sound here, "ee": "ee-MEH-dya".
- *medianoche* and *mediodía*: four syllables each, *me-dia-no-che*, *me-dio-dí-a*. The accent on *día* keeps the *i* and *a* apart.

## Common mistakes

- *Son la una.* — One o'clock is singular: *Es la una.*
- *Son tres.* — Keep the article: *Son las tres.*
- *Es las tres y media.* — Only one o'clock takes *es*: *Son las tres y media.*
- *Son las tres y tres cuartos.* — Standard Spanish doesn't say "three quarters past": say *las cuatro menos cuarto*, *un cuarto para las cuatro* or simply *las tres cuarenta y cinco*.
- *en el lunes* or *en lunes*. — No preposition: *el lunes, los lunes.*
- *Lunes, Martes* with capitals. — Lowercase: *lunes, martes.*
- *Yo no nunca trabajo.* — Either *Nunca trabajo* or *No trabajo nunca*, never both before the verb.
- *No tengo hora.* — For "I don't have time" use *tiempo*: *No tengo tiempo.*

## Key points

- *¿Qué hora es? — Es la una. / Son las dos, las tres…*
- Minutes past with *y*: *y cinco, y cuarto, y media*. Minutes to with *menos* (*las cuatro menos cuarto*) or, in Latin America, *para* (*un cuarto para las cuatro, diez para las cuatro*).
- *a las…* = at…: *a las nueve*. *de la mañana / tarde / noche* after a clock time; *por la mañana* (or *en la mañana*) without one.
- *la mañana* = morning, *mañana* = tomorrow; *la tarde* = afternoon, *tarde* = late.
- Days are lowercase and masculine: *el lunes* = on Monday, *los lunes* = on Mondays.
- *siempre, normalmente, a veces, nunca*; *nunca* before the verb, or *no … nunca*.
- *la hora* = clock time; *el tiempo* = time you have.

lessons.title: Going out: ir, venir and plans with ir a
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

In lesson 13 you learned to say when things happen: *el sábado, a las ocho, esta semana*. Now you'll say where you're going and what you're going to do. Two very common irregular verbs, *ir* (to go) and *venir* (to come), carry most of this lesson. With *ir* you also get the easiest way to talk about the future in Spanish, **[[ir a + infinitive]]** (*Voy a ver una película*, I'm going to see a film), and you'll learn to invite someone out and to say yes or no politely.

## ir: to go

*Ir* is irregular in almost every form. Learn it as a set:

| | ir |
|---|---|
| yo | voy |
| tú | vas |
| él, ella, usted | va |
| nosotros, nosotras | vamos |
| (vosotros) | (vais) |
| ellos, ellas, ustedes | van |

The endings look like those of an -ar verb (*-oy* like *estoy*, then *-as, -a, -amos, -an*), so once you know *voy* the rest follows. *Vamos* also means "let's go": *¡Vamos!*

### ¿Adónde vas? — Voy al cine

You go *to* a place with *a*, and the question is *¿Adónde?* (to where?): *¿Adónde vas?* — Where are you going? Compare *¿Dónde estás?* — Where are you? *Dónde* asks where something is; *adónde* asks where someone is going. (It may also be written as two words, *a dónde*, and in everyday speech you'll hear *¿Dónde vas?* too.)

When *a* meets the masculine article *el*, the two join: *a + el = al*. You met it in lesson 10 (*al lado del sofá*); with *ir* you'll use it all the time, and it is not optional:

| Place | Voy… |
|---|---|
| *el cine* (cinema) | *Voy al cine.* |
| *el parque* (park) | *Voy al parque.* |
| *el museo* (museum) | *Vamos al museo.* |
| *el gimnasio* (gym) | *Va al gimnasio.* |
| *el teatro* (theatre) | *Van al teatro.* |
| *la fiesta* (party) | *Voy a la fiesta.* (no change with *la*) |
| *la cafetería* (café) | *Vamos a la cafetería.* |
| *los conciertos* (concerts) | *Voy a los conciertos.* (no change with *los*) |

*Casa* usually has no article in these phrases: *Voy a casa.* — I'm going home.

![Six picture tiles of places in town, each with its name: el cine, a screen showing a film; el teatro, two masks on a stage; el museo, a building with columns; el parque, a tree and a bench; el gimnasio, a dumbbell; el restaurante, a plate with a fork and knife.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## venir: to come

*Venir* has an irregular *yo* form and an *e → ie* change, just like *tener* (lesson 06):

| | venir |
|---|---|
| yo | vengo |
| tú | vienes |
| él, ella, usted | viene |
| nosotros, nosotras | venimos |
| (vosotros) | (venís) |
| ellos, ellas, ustedes | vienen |

You come *from* a place with *de*, and *de + el = del*: *Vengo del gimnasio.* — I'm coming from the gym. *¿Vienes de la fiesta?* — Are you coming from the party?

### ir or venir?

Spanish is stricter than English. *Venir* means moving toward the place where the speaker is. *Ir* means going anywhere else, including toward the person you're talking to:

- *¿Vienes a mi fiesta?* — Are you coming to my party? (the party is at the speaker's place)
- Your friend calls you from the kitchen. You answer *¡Ya voy!* — I'm coming! Not *¡Ya vengo!*, because you are going to where *they* are.

## ir a + infinitive: plans

To say what you're going to do, put *ir* in the present, then *a*, then the infinitive (the verb as it is in the dictionary):

| ir | a | infinitive | |
|---|---|---|---|
| *Voy* | *a* | *ver* | *una película.* — I'm going to see a film. |
| *¿Vas* | *a* | *estudiar* | *esta noche?* — Are you going to study tonight? |
| *Mi hermana va* | *a* | *visitar* | *el museo.* — My sister is going to visit the museum. |
| *Vamos* | *a* | *pasear* | *por el parque.* — We're going to take a walk in the park. |
| *Mis padres van* | *a* | *comer* | *en un restaurante.* — My parents are going to eat in a restaurant. |

Only *ir* changes; the infinitive never does. For a negative, *no* goes before *ir*: *No voy a trabajar mañana.* — I'm not going to work tomorrow.

*Ir a* + infinitive is the everyday way to talk about the future in Latin America, much like English "going to". Spanish also has a future tense (*veré*, I will see), which you'll meet at A2; at this level *ir a* does the job.

Plans need time words. These point forward from today:

- *esta noche* — tonight
- *mañana* — tomorrow; *mañana por la tarde* — tomorrow afternoon
- *este fin de semana* — this weekend (*este* from lesson 12)
- *el próximo sábado* — next Saturday (*próximo* = next; also *la próxima semana*, next week)

![A timeline arrow running from left to right. At the left end, a dot labeled hoy, ahora. Along the arrow, four flags: esta noche, mañana, este fin de semana, el próximo sábado. Above the arrow the pattern ir + a + infinitive; below it the example Voy a ver una película el próximo sábado.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## ver: to see, to watch

*Ver* is short and has an irregular *yo* form: *veo, ves, ve, vemos, (veis), ven*. You *ver* films, matches and TV: *ver una película* (to see a film), *ver un partido* (to watch a game), *ver la tele* (to watch TV; *la tele* is short for *la televisión*). *Mirar* (lesson 04) means to look at something on purpose: *Mira el mapa.* — Look at the map. For shows and films, Spanish uses *ver*.

## Invitations: ¿Quieres…?

*Querer* (lesson 11) + infinitive is the friendly way to invite someone:

- *¿Quieres ir al cine esta noche?* — Do you want to go to the cinema tonight?
- *¿Quieres venir a mi fiesta el sábado?* — Do you want to come to my party on Saturday?

*Invitar* is to invite: *Te invito a mi fiesta.* — I'm inviting you to my party. In Mexico, *Te invito* or *Yo invito* at a café or restaurant often means "it's on me, I'm paying", so it's a generous phrase.

To answer, use one of these:

| Yes | No |
|---|---|
| *¡Claro!* — Of course! | *Lo siento, no puedo.* — I'm sorry, I can't. |
| *¡Sí, claro!* — Yes, of course! | *Hoy no puedo, pero el sábado sí.* — I can't today, but on Saturday I can. |
| *¡Qué buena idea!* — What a good idea! | *Gracias, pero voy a estudiar.* — Thanks, but I'm going to study. |

*Lo siento* (I'm sorry; lesson 23) and *puedo* (I can; lesson 15) are used here as a fixed chunk. A short reason after *no puedo* is polite, and suggesting another day is even better.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Inviting someone and answering
  accDescr: Person A invites with Quieres plus an infinitive, for example Quieres ir al cine esta noche. Person B either accepts with Claro or Qué buena idea and then asks the time with A qué hora, or declines with Lo siento, no puedo, gives a reason such as Voy a estudiar, and suggests another day such as El sábado sí.
  A["¿Quieres ir al cine esta noche?"] --> B{"Can you go?"}
  B -- yes --> C["¡Claro! / ¡Qué buena idea!"]
  C --> D["¿A qué hora?"]
  B -- no --> E["Lo siento, no puedo."]
  E --> F["A reason: Voy a estudiar."]
  F --> G["Another day: ¿El sábado?"]
```

## Together, alone, people

- *juntos* (together) agrees like an adjective: *Vamos juntos* (a mixed or male group), *Vamos juntas* (all women).
- *solo* (alone) agrees too: *Voy solo* (a man), *Voy sola* (a woman). As an adverb, *solo* means "only": *Solo tengo una hora.* — I only have an hour.
- *la gente* (people) is singular in Spanish, so its verb is singular: *La gente va al parque los domingos.* — People go to the park on Sundays. Not *la gente van*.

*Visitar* is to visit a place: *visitar un museo, visitar la ciudad*. For people Spanish adds *a* before the person: *visitar a mis abuelos* (lesson 18 explains why). *Pasear* means to go for a walk or a ride for pleasure: *Los domingos paseamos por el centro.* — On Sundays we go for a walk downtown.

## Dialogue: ¿Qué planes tienes?

> Toño: Hola, Mariana. ¿Qué planes tienes para este fin de semana?
>
> Mariana: El sábado por la mañana voy a visitar el museo con mi hermano. ¿Por qué?
>
> Toño: Esta noche hay un concierto en el parque. ¿Quieres venir?
>
> Mariana: ¿Esta noche? Lo siento, no puedo. Voy a ver una película con mis primos.
>
> Toño: ¿Y el próximo viernes? Voy a invitar a unos amigos a mi casa. Va a ser una fiesta pequeña, con música y comida.
>
> Mariana: ¡Claro! ¡Qué buena idea! ¿A qué hora?
>
> Toño: A las ocho. ¿Vienes sola?
>
> Mariana: No, voy con mi hermano. ¿Está bien?
>
> Toño: ¡Claro! ¡Entre más, mejor!

In English:

> Toño: Hi, Mariana. What plans do you have for this weekend?
>
> Mariana: On Saturday morning I'm going to visit the museum with my brother. Why?
>
> Toño: Tonight there's a concert in the park. Do you want to come?
>
> Mariana: Tonight? I'm sorry, I can't. I'm going to watch a film with my cousins.
>
> Toño: And next Friday? I'm going to invite some friends to my house. It's going to be a small party, with music and food.
>
> Mariana: Of course! What a good idea! What time?
>
> Toño: At eight. Are you coming alone?
>
> Mariana: No, I'm going with my brother. Is that OK?
>
> Toño: Of course! The more the merrier!

Notice *¿Vienes sola?* from Toño (the party is at his place) and *voy con mi hermano* from Mariana (she is going to Toño's). *Va a ser* is *ir a* + *ser*: it's going to be. *¡Entre más, mejor!* is a set phrase heard across Latin America (*mejor* = better, lesson 12); Spain says *cuantos más, mejor*.

## Pronunciation

- *voy*: one syllable, like English "boy" with a soft b/v: "boy". Spanish *v* sounds like *b* (lesson 01).
- *vengo, vienes*: *ie* is one syllable, "VYEH-nes".
- *adónde*: stress and accent on *dón*: "a-DON-de".
- *teatro*: three syllables, *te-a-tro*; *museo*: *mu-se-o*; *idea*: *i-de-a*. Keep each vowel clear.
- *gimnasio*: the *g* before *i* is the throaty *j* sound: "heem-NA-syo".
- *película*: stressed on the third-to-last syllable, so it has an accent: "pe-LEE-ku-la".
- *al* is said together with the next word: *voy al cine* = "boy-al-SEE-ne".

## Common mistakes

- *Voy a el cine.* — Contract it: *Voy al cine.*
- *Voy al la fiesta.* — No contraction with *la*: *Voy a la fiesta.*
- *Voy ver una película.* — Don't forget the *a*: *Voy a ver una película.*
- *Voy a veo.* — The second verb stays in the infinitive: *Voy a ver.*
- *¿Adónde estás?* — For a location use *dónde*: *¿Dónde estás?* For a destination, *¿Adónde vas?* (*¿Dónde vas?* is common in speech, but write *adónde*).
- *¡Vengo!* when someone calls you. — Say *¡Voy!* or *¡Ya voy!*
- *La gente son simpáticos.* — *Gente* is singular: *La gente es simpática.*
- *Yo vo* or *yo vamos.* — *yo voy, nosotros vamos.*

## Key points

- *ir*: *voy, vas, va, vamos, van*. *venir*: *vengo, vienes, viene, venimos, vienen*.
- *a + el = al* (*Voy al parque*), *de + el = del* (*Vengo del gimnasio*); no change with *la, los, las*.
- *¿Adónde vas?* asks for a destination; *¿Dónde estás?* asks for a location.
- *venir* = come to where the speaker is; to go to the listener, use *ir* (*¡Ya voy!*).
- *ir a + infinitive* for plans: *Voy a ver una película el próximo sábado.*
- Invite with *¿Quieres + infinitive?*; accept with *¡Claro! / ¡Qué buena idea!*; decline with *Lo siento, no puedo* + a reason.
- *la gente* takes a singular verb; *juntos* and *solo* agree (*juntas, sola*).
