lessons.title: Free time and stem-changing verbs
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

You already know a few verbs whose vowel changes in the present: *tener* (*tienes*), *venir* (*vienes*), *querer* (*quiero*) and *costar* (*cuesta*). They aren't oddities. They belong to a large, regular family, the **[[stem-changing verbs]]**, and many of the most useful verbs in Spanish are in it: *poder* (can), *jugar* (to play), *dormir* (to sleep), *empezar* (to begin), *pedir* (to ask for). This lesson shows the pattern once, so that every new verb in the family is easy, and uses it to talk about sports, music and what you do in your free time (*el tiempo libre*).

## The pattern: the "boot"

The **[[stem]]** of a verb is the infinitive without *-ar, -er, -ir* (*quer-*, *pod-*, *ped-*). In a stem-changing verb, the last vowel of the stem changes when it is stressed. In the present, the stress falls on the stem in four persons (*yo, tú, él, ellos*) and on the ending in *nosotros* (and *vosotros*). So:

- *QUIEro, QUIEres, QUIEre, QUIEren*: stress on the stem, the *e* becomes *ie*.
- *queREmos*: stress on the ending, the *e* stays.

The endings are perfectly regular. If you shade the four changed forms in the usual table, the shape looks like a boot, which is why teachers call these "boot verbs":

![Three verb tables side by side, each with the singular persons in the left column and the plural persons in the right. A boot-shaped outline goes around the whole left column and the bottom-right cell. querer, e to ie: quiero, quieres, quiere, and quieren inside the boot; queremos outside. poder, o to ue: puedo, puedes, puede, pueden inside; podemos outside. pedir, e to i: pido, pides, pide, piden inside; pedimos outside. The vosotros forms (queréis, podéis, pedís) are in brackets, outside the boot. A note says: nosotros and vosotros keep the vowel of the infinitive.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

There are three kinds of change (and one verb with a fourth).

### e → ie

| | pensar | empezar | entender | preferir |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| yo | pienso | empiezo | entiendo | prefiero |
| tú | piensas | empiezas | entiendes | prefieres |
| él, ella, usted | piensa | empieza | entiende | prefiere |
| nosotros | pensamos | empezamos | entendemos | preferimos |
| ellos, ustedes | piensan | empiezan | entienden | prefieren |

Also *cerrar* (to close: *cierro, cierras…*) and *perder* (to lose, to miss: *pierdo, pierdes…*). Notice that *preferir* has two *e*'s: only the last one in the stem changes (*pref-e-r → prefiero*).

- *pensar* = to think; *pensar en* = to think about; *pensar* + infinitive = to plan to: *Pienso estudiar esta noche.* — I'm planning to study tonight.
- *empezar* = to begin, to start; before an infinitive it takes *a*: *La clase empieza a las ocho. Empiezo a trabajar a las nueve.*
- *preferir* + noun or infinitive: *Prefiero el béisbol. Prefiero nadar.*
- *perder* = to lose (a game, a thing) or to miss (a bus): *Mi equipo siempre pierde.* — My team always loses.

### o → ue

| | poder | dormir | volver | almorzar |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| yo | puedo | duermo | vuelvo | almuerzo |
| tú | puedes | duermes | vuelves | almuerzas |
| él, ella, usted | puede | duerme | vuelve | almuerza |
| nosotros | podemos | dormimos | volvemos | almorzamos |
| ellos, ustedes | pueden | duermen | vuelven | almuerzan |

- *poder* + infinitive = can, to be able to: *¿Puedes venir?* — Can you come? *No puedo dormir.* — I can't sleep. Now you see where *Lo siento, no puedo* (lesson 14) comes from.
- *volver* = to come back, to return: *Vuelvo a casa a las seis.* — I come back home at six.
- *almorzar* = to have lunch in most of Latin America. In Mexico *el almuerzo* is often a late, hearty breakfast or brunch, and the main meal of the day is *la comida* (lesson 11), so Mexicans more often say *comer* for "to have lunch".

### u → ue: jugar

*Jugar* (to play a game or sport) is the only verb with this change: *juego, juegas, juega, jugamos, juegan*. It's an *o → ue*-style boot on a *u*.

### e → i

| | pedir | repetir |
|---|---|---|
| yo | pido | repito |
| tú | pides | repites |
| él, ella, usted | pide | repite |
| nosotros | pedimos | repetimos |
| ellos, ustedes | piden | repiten |

This change only happens in -ir verbs. *Pedir* is to ask for something or to order (food): *Pido un café.* — I'll have a coffee. To ask a question is *preguntar* (lesson 04). *Repetir* is to repeat, as in *¿Puede repetir, por favor?* from lesson 01.

### How do I know which verbs change?

You can't tell from the infinitive: *pensar* changes but *pasar* doesn't, *volver* changes but *comer* doesn't. Dictionaries mark them, usually as *pensar (ie), volver (ue), pedir (i)*, and in this course every stem-changing verb has its forms in its vocabulary card. Learn the change together with the word. The chart below is how to find a form once you know the verb's type:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Finding the present form of a stem-changing verb
  accDescr: Start with the infinitive and take off -ar, -er or -ir to find the stem. If the person is nosotros, or vosotros, keep the stem as it is, as in podemos. For yo, tú, él or ellos, change the last vowel of the stem by the verb's type: e to ie as in quiero, o to ue as in puedo, u to ue in jugar as in juego, or e to i in some -ir verbs as in pido. Then add the regular ending.
  A["Infinitive: poder"] --> B["Stem: pod-"]
  B --> C{"Which person?"}
  C -- "nosotros" --> D["Keep the stem: podemos"]
  C -- "yo, tú, él, ellos" --> E{"Which type?"}
  E -- "e → ie" --> F["quiero, pienso"]
  E -- "o → ue" --> G["puedo, duermo"]
  E -- "u → ue" --> H["juego"]
  E -- "e → i" --> I["pido, repito"]
  F --> J["Add the regular ending"]
  G --> J
  H --> J
  I --> J
```

## Free time: sports, music and hobbies

*¿Qué haces en tu tiempo libre?* — What do you do in your free time? (*haces* is from *hacer*, lesson 16.) A hobby is *un pasatiempo*.

### jugar or tocar?

English "play" is two verbs in Spanish:

- *jugar* for games and sports: *jugar fútbol, jugar básquetbol, jugar videojuegos*.
- *tocar* for musical instruments: *tocar la guitarra, tocar el piano*. (*Tocar* also means to touch.)

With a sport, standard Spanish says *jugar al fútbol* (*a + el = al*, lesson 14). In Mexico and much of Latin America people usually leave it out: *Juego fútbol los sábados.* Both are correct; the honors lesson 16h2 says more.

| Sport | In Mexico | Spain |
|---|---|---|
| football (soccer) | *el futbol* (said fut-BOL), also written *fútbol* | *el fútbol* |
| baseball | *el beisbol* (beis-BOL), also *béisbol* | *el béisbol* |
| basketball | *el básquetbol* or *basquetbol* | *el baloncesto* |

The Spanish Academy accepts both spellings. In Mexico the words are usually stressed on the last syllable and written without an accent (*futbol, beisbol*). Spain and many other countries say and write *fútbol*; *beisbol* is also the usual form in several baseball countries (Cuba, Venezuela, the Dominican Republic: see 16h2), while others say *béisbol*. This course writes *el fútbol, el béisbol, el básquetbol* and accepts the Mexican spellings. *El deporte* is sport in general: *¿Qué deporte practicas?* — What sport do you do? (*practicar*, lesson 04). *El equipo* is a team: *Mi equipo juega el domingo.*

### Verbs for hobbies

These are regular -ar and -er verbs, so no surprises: *nadar* (to swim), *correr* (to run), *caminar* (to walk), *cantar* (to sing), *bailar* (to dance), *dibujar* (to draw). For a bicycle, Mexico says *andar en bicicleta* (to ride a bike; *andar* = to go about) and Spain *montar en bicicleta*; *la bici* is the short form everywhere.

![Six picture tiles of free-time activities, each with a caption: a soccer ball in front of a goal, jugar fútbol; a baseball bat and ball, jugar béisbol; a basketball hoop and ball, jugar básquetbol; a swimmer in waves, nadar; a guitar, tocar la guitarra; a bicycle, andar en bicicleta.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Dialogue: ¿Juegas mañana?

> Lucía: Oye, Beto, ¿juegas fútbol mañana con el equipo?
>
> Beto: No, mañana no puedo. Empiezo a trabajar a las siete y vuelvo a casa muy tarde.
>
> Lucía: ¡Qué pena! ¿Y el domingo? Siempre jugamos a las diez.
>
> Beto: El domingo sí. Pero los domingos duermo hasta las nueve…
>
> Lucía: No hay problema. Primero corremos un poco en el parque, y después jugamos.
>
> Beto: Perfecto. ¿Y tú qué prefieres, el fútbol o el béisbol?
>
> Lucía: Prefiero el béisbol, pero aquí casi todos juegan fútbol. ¿Tú tocas la guitarra, no?
>
> Beto: Sí, un poco. ¿Por qué?
>
> Lucía: Mi hermana canta y busca un guitarrista. Pienso invitarlos a los dos a mi casa.
>
> Beto: ¡Claro! ¿Podemos almorzar juntos también?
>
> Lucía: ¡Sí! Yo pido unas pizzas.

In English:

> Lucía: Hey, Beto, are you playing football tomorrow with the team?
>
> Beto: No, I can't tomorrow. I start work at seven and I come back home very late.
>
> Lucía: What a shame! And on Sunday? We always play at ten.
>
> Beto: Sunday, yes. But on Sundays I sleep until nine…
>
> Lucía: No problem. First we run a bit in the park, and then we play.
>
> Beto: Perfect. And what do you prefer, football or baseball?
>
> Lucía: I prefer baseball, but here almost everybody plays football. You play the guitar, don't you?
>
> Beto: Yes, a little. Why?
>
> Lucía: My sister sings and she's looking for a guitarist. I'm planning to invite you both to my place.
>
> Beto: Of course! Can we have lunch together too?
>
> Lucía: Yes! I'll order some pizzas.

(*Oye* = hey, listen; *¡Qué pena!* = what a shame; *No hay problema* = no problem; *casi todos* = almost everybody; *invitarlos a los dos* = to invite you both. *Primero* and *después* are from lesson 16.) Notice *jugamos* and *podemos*: the nosotros forms keep the stem vowel. And *¿… no?* at the end of a sentence works like English "don't you?", "isn't it?".

## Pronunciation

- *ie* and *ue* are one syllable each: *quie-ro* "KYEH-ro", *pue-do* "PWEH-do", *jue-go* "HWEH-go". Don't split them into two vowels.
- *juego, jugar*: the *j* is the throaty sound in "loch", softer in Mexico, almost like an English h.
- *empiezo, almuerzo*: in Latin America *z* sounds like *s*: "em-PYEH-so", "al-MWER-so".
- *guitarra*: the *u* is silent after *g* before *i*, and the *g* is hard as in "get": "ghee-TA-rra", with a rolled *rr*.
- *béisbol*: in Mexico you'll hear "beis-BOL"; *fútbol* "fut-BOL".
- *videojuego*: *vi-de-o-jue-go*, five syllables.

## Common mistakes

- *Nosotros puedemos, duermimos, juegamos.* — The nosotros form never changes: *podemos, dormimos, jugamos, pedimos.*
- *Yo jugo, yo repeto.* — Keep the change in yo: *juego, repito.*
- *Jugar la guitarra.* — Instruments take *tocar*: *tocar la guitarra*.
- *Tocar fútbol.* — Sports take *jugar*: *jugar (al) fútbol*.
- *Puedo a nadar.* — No *a* after *poder*: *Puedo nadar.* But *empezar a*: *Empiezo a trabajar.*
- *Pregunto un café.* — To ask for something is *pedir*: *Pido un café.*
- *Prefero, prefieremos.* — Only the last stem *e* changes, and not in nosotros: *prefiero, preferimos.*

## Key points

- Stem-changing verbs change the stressed stem vowel in yo, tú, él, ellos; nosotros keeps the infinitive's vowel: the "boot".
- e → ie: *querer, pensar, preferir, empezar, entender, cerrar, perder*.
- o → ue: *poder, dormir, volver, almorzar* (and *costar*); u → ue: *jugar* only.
- e → i (-ir verbs only): *pedir, repetir*.
- *poder* + infinitive (no *a*); *empezar a* + infinitive; *pensar* + infinitive = to plan to.
- *jugar* (al) fútbol for sports and games; *tocar* la guitarra for instruments.
- Mexico: *futbol, beisbol, basquetbol* stressed at the end; Spain says *baloncesto*.

lessons.title: A day in my life: reflexive verbs and irregular yo forms
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

With the clock (lesson 13), *ir a* (lesson 14) and the stem-changing verbs (lesson 15) you can already say a lot about your week. This lesson fills in the day itself: getting up, showering, getting dressed, going out, cooking and cleaning, going to bed. Many of these actions use **[[reflexive verbs]]** (*me levanto*, I get up), and several common verbs have an **[[irregular yo form]]** (*hago, salgo, pongo, sé*). You'll also learn the little words that put a day in order: *primero, luego, después, más tarde, finalmente*.

## Reflexive verbs: doing something to yourself

Compare these two sentences:

- *Lavo el carro.* — I wash the car.
- *Me lavo.* — I wash (myself).

In the second, the person who washes and the person who gets washed are the same. Spanish marks this with a **[[reflexive pronoun]]** (*me* = myself) before the verb. You already know one reflexive verb: *llamarse*, in *Me llamo Ana* (literally "I call myself Ana", lesson 02).

A reflexive verb is listed in the dictionary with *-se* on the end: *levantarse*, to get up. The *-se* moves to the front and changes with the person:

| | levantarse (to get up) |
|---|---|
| yo | *me* levanto |
| tú | *te* levantas |
| él, ella, usted | *se* levanta |
| nosotros, nosotras | *nos* levantamos |
| (vosotros) | (*os* levantáis) |
| ellos, ellas, ustedes | *se* levantan |

The verb itself is conjugated as usual (here a regular -ar verb); only the pronoun is new. *Se* serves for *él, ella, usted* and *ellos, ellas, ustedes*.

Many actions are reflexive in Spanish but not in English, so learn each verb with its *-se*:

| Verb | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| *levantarse* | to get up | *Me levanto a las seis y media.* |
| *despertarse* (e → ie) | to wake up | *Me despierto muy temprano.* |
| *bañarse* | to shower, to bathe | *¿Te bañas por la mañana o por la noche?* |
| *lavarse* | to wash (yourself) | *Me lavo los dientes.* — I brush my teeth. |
| *vestirse* (e → i) | to get dressed | *Mi hijo se viste solo.* — My son gets dressed by himself. |
| *irse* | to leave, to go away | *Me voy.* — I'm off, I'm leaving. |
| *quedarse* | to stay | *Hoy me quedo en casa.* — Today I'm staying home. |
| *acostarse* (o → ue) | to go to bed | *Nos acostamos a las once.* |

Stem changes from lesson 15 still apply: *me despierto, te despiertas; me acuesto, te acuestas; me visto, te vistes*; and as always the nosotros form keeps its vowel: *nos despertamos, nos acostamos, nos vestimos*. *Irse* is just *ir* with the pronoun: *me voy, te vas, se va, nos vamos, se van*.

Three Mexican notes. *Bañarse* in Mexico usually means to take a shower, and the shower is *la regadera* (Spain: *la ducha*, *ducharse*). For teeth you'll hear both *lavarse los dientes* and *cepillarse los dientes* (to brush). And with parts of the body Spanish uses *el / la / los*, not *mi*: *Me lavo los dientes*, not *mis dientes*; the *me* already says whose they are (lesson 20 returns to this).

### Reflexive or not?

The same verb often comes in both versions. Ask whether the action goes back to the subject:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Choosing between a reflexive and a non-reflexive verb
  accDescr: Ask who receives the action. If it is the subject itself, use the reflexive verb with me, te, se, nos: Me lavo, Me levanto, Me baño. If it is something or someone else, use the verb without the pronoun and name the object: Lavo el carro, Baño al perro.
  A["Who gets the action?"] --> B{"The subject itself?"}
  B -- yes --> C["Reflexive: me lavo, me levanto, me baño"]
  B -- "no, something else" --> D["Not reflexive: lavo el carro, baño al perro"]
```

*Lavar* without *-se* is a chore: *lavar la ropa* (to do the laundry; *la ropa* = clothes), *lavar los platos* (to wash the dishes). *Baño al perro* has *al* because the dog is a living being (lesson 18).

## Where does the pronoun go?

With one conjugated verb, the pronoun goes right before it: *Me levanto. No me levanto. ¿A qué hora te levantas?* (*no* goes before the pronoun.)

With an infinitive, as in *ir a* + infinitive, there are two correct places:

- attached to the end of the infinitive: *Voy a bañarme.* — I'm going to take a shower.
- before the conjugated verb: *Me voy a bañar.* — the same meaning.

Both are equally common. What you can't do is put it between: never *Voy me a bañar*. The pronoun still matches the subject: *Vas a bañarte, va a bañarse, vamos a bañarnos, van a bañarse*.

![A chart with three rows. Row 1, one verb: me before levanto, with the note: before the conjugated verb. Row 2, ir a plus infinitive, first way: voy a levantarme, with me joined to the end of levantar. Row 3, second way: me voy a levantar, with me before voy. A crossed-out box below shows the wrong order voy me a levantar.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Putting a day in order

These words tell a sequence. They usually start their sentence or clause:

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| *primero* | first |
| *luego* | then, next |
| *después* | afterwards, then |
| *más tarde* | later |
| *finalmente* | finally |

*Primero me levanto, luego me baño y después me visto.* — First I get up, then I shower and afterwards I get dressed.

To link two actions in one sentence, use *antes de* (before) or *después de* (after) + **[[infinitive]]**, where English uses "-ing":

- *Desayuno antes de bañarme.* — I have breakfast before showering. (*desayunar*: to have breakfast, from *el desayuno*)
- *Después de comer, me lavo los dientes.* — After eating, I brush my teeth.

With a reflexive verb, the pronoun is attached to the infinitive and matches the subject: *antes de acostarme* (me), *antes de acostarte* (you), *después de levantarnos* (us).

## hago, salgo, pongo, sé: irregular yo forms

Some verbs are regular except in the *yo* form:

| | hacer (to do, to make) | salir (to go out, to leave) | poner (to put) | saber (to know) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| yo | *hago* | *salgo* | *pongo* | *sé* |
| tú | haces | sales | pones | sabes |
| él, ella, usted | hace | sale | pone | sabe |
| nosotros | hacemos | salimos | ponemos | sabemos |
| ellos, ustedes | hacen | salen | ponen | saben |

Three of them add a *g* in *yo*, like *tengo* and *vengo* (lessons 06 and 14); some teachers call them "yo-go verbs". *Saber* is short: *sé*, with an accent to tell it apart from the pronoun *se*.

- *hacer*: *¿Qué haces el sábado?* — What are you doing on Saturday? *Hago la cama.* — I make the bed. *¿Qué vas a hacer?* — What are you going to do?
- *salir*: to go out (*Salgo con mis amigos*) and to leave a place, with *de* (*Salgo de casa a las siete*). *Irse* is "to leave", usually without saying from where: *Ya me voy.*
- *poner*: *Pongo las llaves en la mesa.* — I put the keys on the table. *Poner la mesa* is to set the table. With *-se* it means to put on clothes: *Me pongo la chamarra* (lesson 20).
- *saber*: to know a fact (*No sé.* — I don't know. *¿Sabes dónde está?*) and to know how to do something, + infinitive (*Sé cocinar.* — I can cook). Knowing a person or a place is a different verb, *conocer* (*conozco*, lesson 18).

## Chores

*Cocinar* (to cook), *limpiar* (to clean), *lavar* (to wash) and *barrer* (to sweep) are regular. *Limpiar* keeps its stress on *LIM*: *limpio, limpias, limpia*.

- *Los sábados limpio la casa y lavo la ropa.* — On Saturdays I clean the house and do the laundry.
- *Mi papá cocina y yo barro la cocina.* — My dad cooks and I sweep the kitchen.

## Reading: La rutina de Valeria

> Me llamo Valeria y vivo en Puebla. De lunes a viernes mi rutina empieza muy temprano. Me despierto a las seis, pero no me levanto hasta las seis y cuarto. Primero me baño: la regadera es mi lugar favorito para cantar. Luego me visto, desayuno café con pan y me lavo los dientes. Salgo de casa a las siete y diez, y a las ocho empiezo a trabajar en una oficina. A las dos y media como con mis compañeros. Después de trabajar, voy al gimnasio o paseo un poco por el centro. Más tarde ceno con mi hermana. Ella cocina y yo lavo los platos. Antes de acostarme, pongo la ropa para mañana en la silla. Finalmente me acuesto a las once. Los sábados son diferentes: me quedo en la cama hasta las nueve, limpio el departamento y barro el balcón. Y los domingos… no hago nada.

In English:

> My name is Valeria and I live in Puebla. From Monday to Friday my routine starts very early. I wake up at six, but I don't get up until a quarter past six. First I shower: the shower is my favourite place to sing. Then I get dressed, have a coffee and bread for breakfast and brush my teeth. I leave home at ten past seven, and at eight I start work in an office. At half past two I have lunch with my colleagues. After work I go to the gym or take a short walk downtown. Later I have dinner with my sister. She cooks and I wash the dishes. Before going to bed, I put tomorrow's clothes on the chair. Finally I go to bed at eleven. Saturdays are different: I stay in bed until nine, clean the apartment and sweep the balcony. And on Sundays… I don't do anything.

(*favorito* = favourite; *mis compañeros* = my colleagues; *el balcón* = the balcony; *no hago nada* = I do nothing, with the double negative of lesson 13's *no … nunca*.)

Here is Valeria's weekday as a strip:

![A cartoon timeline of a weekday in six panels with clock times and captions. 6:00 a woman waking up next to an alarm clock: se despierta. 6:30 a woman under a shower: se baña. 6:45 a woman putting on a jacket: se viste. 7:10 a woman walking out of a door: sale de casa. 21:00 a woman washing dishes at a sink: lava los platos. 23:00 a woman in bed with the moon in the window: se acuesta.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Pronunciation

- *hago, hacer, hora*: the *h* is always silent: "AH-go".
- *me levanto*: say the pronoun and verb as one word, "me-le-BAN-to".
- When a pronoun is attached to an infinitive, the stress stays where it was and no accent is needed: *bañarme* "ba-NYAR-me", *acostarme* "a-cos-TAR-me".
- *despierto, acuesto*: one syllable each for *ie* and *ue*: "des-PYER-to", "a-KWES-to".
- *regadera* has a single *r* in the middle (a quick tap): "re-ga-DE-ra"; the *r* at the start is rolled.
- *sé* (I know) and *se* (himself, herself) sound the same; only the accent tells them apart in writing.

## Common mistakes

- *Yo levanto a las siete.* — Without *me* it means you lift something: *Me levanto a las siete.*
- *Me levanto* for everybody. — Match the pronoun: *te levantas, se levanta, nos levantamos.*
- *Voy a me bañar* or *Voy me a bañar.* — *Voy a bañarme* or *Me voy a bañar.*
- *Me lavo mis dientes.* — Use the article: *Me lavo los dientes.*
- *Después de me bañar.* — After *antes de / después de*, attach the pronoun: *después de bañarme*.
- *Yo hace, yo salo, yo pono, yo sabo.* — *hago, salgo, pongo, sé.*
- *Se* for "I know". — *Sé*, with the accent.
- *Antes de desayuno* for "before having breakfast". — Use the infinitive: *antes de desayunar*.

## Key points

- Reflexive verbs carry a pronoun that matches the subject: *me, te, se, nos, (os), se*: *me levanto, te levantas, se levanta…*
- The pronoun goes before a conjugated verb (*No me levanto*) or on the end of an infinitive (*Voy a levantarme* = *Me voy a levantar*).
- Stem changes still apply: *me despierto, me acuesto, me visto*.
- Body parts take the article: *me lavo los dientes*.
- Sequence words: *primero, luego, después, más tarde, finalmente*; *antes de / después de* + infinitive.
- Irregular yo: *hago, salgo, pongo, sé* (and *tengo, vengo*); the other persons are regular.
- *saber* = know facts, know how to (*Sé nadar*); *conocer* = know people and places (lesson 18).

lessons.title: Ahorita, al rato and the 24-hour clock
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

In lesson 13 you learned to read a clock: *Son las tres y media, un cuarto para las cuatro*. But knowing the time is not the same as knowing what people mean by it. In Mexico, *ahorita* can mean "right now" or "in a while", depending on who says it and how; a party invitation for eight and a work meeting at eight are not the same eight; and the door of a shop or a bus timetable speaks in the **[[24-hour clock]]**. This honors lesson gives you the words for all three: *ahorita, al rato, en un momento, ahora mismo*; what people usually expect about being on time (described as generalizations, because people differ); and how to read timetables and opening hours with *de … a, desde … hasta* and *cada*.

## Ahorita: now, soon, or a little while ago

*Ahorita* is *ahora* (now) with the ending *-ita*, which makes words smaller or softer (*un momentito*, just a moment). Grammars describe its basic meaning as "right now, this very moment", but it also points to moments just before or just after the present. In Mexico it is used constantly, and its meaning stretches with the situation:

| Sentence | Usual meaning |
|---|---|
| *Ahorita estoy en el trabajo.* | right now (at this moment) |
| *Ahorita vengo.* | I'll be back in a moment (said when you step out) |
| *¿Me ayudas? — Sí, ahorita.* | in a moment… or later, depending on the tone |
| *Ahorita llegó Carlos.* | Carlos arrived a moment ago |
| *Ahorita no, gracias.* | not now, thanks (a polite way to decline) |

(*llegó* is the past of *llegar*, from lesson 21: you only need to recognize it here.)

Linguists have studied the change. A 2021 study from El Colegio de México by Daniel Granados compared three generations of speakers in Mexico City and found that younger speakers use *ahorita* in more and more situations that are not about the immediate moment at all, sometimes where older speakers would say plain *ahora*. In short: the word is getting less precise, not more.

So how do you know which *ahorita* you got? Listen for:

- the verb: present for now (*ahorita estoy*), *ir a* or a present about the near future for soon (*ahorita voy*), past for a moment ago;
- the situation: a waiter who says *ahorita* will probably come soon; a friend who answers *ahorita* to "Can you call the landlord?" may mean "some time";
- the tone: a quick, bright *¡Ahorita!* is a promise; a slow, vague *ahorita…* often isn't.

When you need to be clear, use one of these instead:

- *ahora mismo* — right now, this minute: *Lo hago ahora mismo.* — I'll do it right now. (*lo* = it)
- *en un momento* — in a moment: *Te ayudo en un momento.*
- *al rato* — in a while, later on (very common in Mexico): *Al rato te llamo.* — I'll call you in a while. *¡Nos vemos al rato!* — See you later!

You may also hear *luego luego*, a Mexican way to say "right away": *Llegó y luego luego empezó a trabajar.*

### Example 1: Which ahorita is it?

Read each mini-dialogue and decide what *ahorita* means.

1. *—¿Dónde estás? —Ahorita estoy en el súper.* The verb is the present *estoy* with a place, and the question is "where are you now". Meaning: right now. (*el súper* = the supermarket.)
2. *—Joven, ¿me trae la cuenta? —Sí, ahorita se la traigo.* A waiter is answering a request in the present about an action not done yet. Meaning: in a moment, and in a restaurant you can usually trust it. (*se la traigo* = I'll bring it to you.)
3. *—¿Vas a limpiar tu cuarto? —Ahorita…* A teenager, a slow answer, no time given. Meaning: later, maybe. If you are the parent, ask *¿Cuándo? ¿Ahora mismo?*
4. *—¿Ya llegó Marta? —Sí, ahorita llegó.* A past verb. Meaning: a moment ago.

The method: check the verb first, then the situation, then the tone.

## On time? Social time and work time

*Puntual* means punctual, on time: *Mi jefe es muy puntual.* *Llegar a tiempo* is to arrive on time, and *el retraso* is the delay: *Perdón por el retraso.* — Sorry I'm late (literally "sorry for the delay").

What counts as "on time" depends on the situation. The points below are generalizations, useful as a starting guide; habits differ by city, by family, by profession and by person.

- Work and official appointments — meetings (*una reunión*), the doctor, a bank, a government office, a job interview, a class — are expected to start on time, and you should arrive on time. The US government's business guide for Mexico, for example, says punctuality is the norm for most business and government appointments.
- Social invitations — a dinner at someone's home, a birthday party — are looser. In many places guests arrive half an hour or more after the time on the invitation, and arriving exactly on time at a home can catch the hosts still getting ready. The same guide notes that guests may arrive up to an hour late to social events, but not in the cities of the north, where people tend to be more punctual.
- When in doubt, ask. *¿La fiesta es a las ocho en punto?* (*en punto* = sharp, exactly). Some invitations say *hora exacta* or *puntual* to mean "really at that time".

And mind the lunch hour: since the main meal (*la comida*) is often eaten between about 2 and 4 p.m. (lesson 11), that's not a good time to ask for a meeting.

## The 24-hour clock

Timetables, tickets, opening hours, official letters and phone screens in Spanish-speaking countries usually use the 24-hour clock. You already know the numbers: 13 *trece* to 23 *veintitrés* (lesson 03).

- In writing: *18:00, 18:30 h*. The standard abbreviation is *h* (no period, no plural). In Mexico you'll often see *hrs.* on signs: *9:00 a 18:00 hrs.*
- Read aloud in formal announcements: *Las dieciocho horas.* *El tren sale a las veinte treinta.* — The train leaves at 20:30.
- In conversation people normally convert to the 12-hour clock: 18:00 is *las seis de la tarde*. With the 12-hour clock you may also see *a. m.* and *p. m.*: *6:00 p. m.*

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Turning a 24-hour time into everyday speech
  accDescr: Look at the hour. Hour 0 is medianoche or las doce de la noche, so 0:15 is las doce y cuarto. From 1 to 11, the hour stays the same and you add de la mañana, so 9:30 is las nueve y media de la mañana. At 12 it is mediodía or las doce del día. From 13 to 23, subtract 12 and add de la tarde until about 7 or 8 p.m. and de la noche after that, so 18:45 is un cuarto para las siete de la tarde and 22:00 is las diez de la noche.
  A["A 24-hour time, e.g. 18:45"] --> B{"What is the hour?"}
  B -- "0" --> Z["medianoche / las doce (de la noche): 0:15 = las doce y cuarto"]
  B -- "1 to 11" --> C["Keep it + de la mañana: 9:30 = las nueve y media de la mañana"]
  B -- "12" --> D["mediodía / las doce del día"]
  B -- "13 to 23" --> E["Subtract 12: 18 → 6"]
  E --> F["+ de la tarde or de la noche"]
  F --> G["18:45 = un cuarto para las siete de la tarde"]
```

### Example 2: Converting times

Say each time in everyday Spanish.

1. 15:10. 15 − 12 = 3; it's afternoon. *Las tres y diez de la tarde.*
2. 21:30. 21 − 12 = 9; it's night. *Las nueve y media de la noche.*
3. 13:45. 45 minutes past, so count to the next hour: 14 − 12 = 2. *Un cuarto para las dos de la tarde* (or *las dos menos cuarto*, or simply *la una cuarenta y cinco*).
4. 00:15. Just after midnight: *las doce y cuarto de la noche* (many people also say *de la mañana* for times after midnight).

## Opening hours and timetables: de … a, desde … hasta, cada

*El horario* is a schedule: a shop's opening hours, a timetable, your class schedule. Opening hours use two pairs:

- *de … a* (from … to), the everyday pair: *de nueve a seis, de lunes a viernes*.
- *desde … hasta* (from … until), a little more formal or emphatic: *desde las ocho hasta las diez*. You know *hasta* from lesson 13; *desde* is "from, since".

Note the article: in a full sentence you'll usually hear it with clock times (*Abrimos de las nueve a las seis*; casually also *de nueve a seis*), but signs drop it: *de 9:00 a 18:00 h*.

![A shop door sign titled Horario de atención. Lunes a viernes: 9:00 a 18:00 h. Sábados: 10:00 a 14:00 h. Domingos y días festivos: cerrado. Below it, a smaller note: Pagos y trámites solo en días hábiles.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Two expressions from signs and official messages:

- *el día hábil* — a working day (Monday to Friday, except public holidays): *Su tarjeta llega en cinco días hábiles.* — Your card arrives within five working days.
- *la hora pico* — rush hour (Mexico; Spain *la hora punta*): *En hora pico el metro va lleno.* — At rush hour the metro is full.

*Cada* means each, every. It never changes for gender or number, and it goes right before the noun:

- *cada día* — every day (like *todos los días*)
- *cada hora* — every hour; *cada quince minutos* — every fifteen minutes
- *cada lunes* — every Monday; *cada dos semanas* — every two weeks

### Example 3: Reading a bus timetable

> **Línea 7 — Centro / Universidad**
>
> Lunes a viernes: salidas cada 15 minutos, desde las 5:30 hasta las 23:00 h.
>
> Hora pico (7:00 a 9:00 y 18:00 a 20:00 h): cada 8 minutos.
>
> Sábados, domingos y días festivos: cada 30 minutos, de 7:00 a 22:00 h.

Translation:

> Line 7, Downtown / University. Monday to Friday: departures every 15 minutes, from 5:30 until 23:00. Rush hour (7:00 to 9:00 and 18:00 to 20:00): every 8 minutes. Saturdays, Sundays and public holidays: every 30 minutes, from 7:00 to 22:00.

(*la línea* = line, route; *la salida* = departure, lesson 17; *días festivos* = public holidays.)

Questions and how to answer them:

1. *¿A qué hora sale el último camión el miércoles?* (*el último* = the last; *el camión* = the bus in Mexico.) Wednesday is a weekday: the line runs *hasta las 23:00 h*. Answer: *A las once de la noche.*
2. *¿Cada cuánto pasa el camión el martes a las 8:15?* (*¿Cada cuánto?* = how often?) 8:15 falls between 7:00 and 9:00, so it's rush hour. Answer: *Cada ocho minutos.*
3. *¿Hay camiones el domingo a las 6:30?* On Sundays the first one is at 7:00. Answer: *No, empiezan a las siete.*

## Dialogue: ¿Nos vemos a las ocho?

> Andrés: Oye, Paula, mañana a las ocho tenemos reunión con el cliente.
>
> Paula: ¿A las ocho de la mañana? ¡Qué temprano!
>
> Andrés: Sí, y el cliente es muy puntual. Mejor llegamos a las ocho menos diez.
>
> Paula: Claro. Y el sábado, ¿vienes a la fiesta de Rosa? La invitación dice "8:00 p. m.".
>
> Andrés: Sí, pero no llego a las ocho en punto. Llego como a las ocho y media.
>
> Paula: Yo también. Oye, ¿me mandas el horario de la reunión?
>
> Andrés: Sí, ahorita te lo mando.
>
> Paula: ¿Ahorita-ahorita o ahorita-al rato?
>
> Andrés: ¡Ahora mismo! Ya está.

In English:

> Andrés: Hey, Paula, tomorrow at eight we have a meeting with the client.
>
> Paula: At eight in the morning? So early!
>
> Andrés: Yes, and the client is very punctual. We'd better arrive at ten to eight.
>
> Paula: Of course. And on Saturday, are you coming to Rosa's party? The invitation says "8:00 p.m."
>
> Andrés: Yes, but I won't arrive at eight sharp. I'll get there at about half past eight.
>
> Paula: Me too. Hey, can you send me the meeting schedule?
>
> Andrés: Yes, I'll send it to you *ahorita*.
>
> Paula: *Ahorita* as in now, or *ahorita* as in later?
>
> Andrés: Right now! Done.

(*mandar* = to send, lesson 23; *te lo mando* = I'll send it to you; *como* = about, roughly; *Ya está* = done, there you go.) Doubling a word, as Paula does, is a playful way to ask "the real one": *ahorita-ahorita* means truly now.

## Pronunciation

- *ahorita*: silent *h*, single tapped *r*: "a-o-REE-ta".
- *horario*: "o-RA-ryo"; *hora pico*: "O-ra PEE-ko".
- *hábil* is stressed on the first syllable, so it has an accent: "A-beel". Plural *hábiles*: "A-bee-les".
- *dieciocho horas*: "dye-see-O-cho O-ras"; the two *o* sounds run together in fast speech.
- *puntual*: *pun-tual*, stress on the last syllable: "poon-TWAL" (the *u* and *a* glide together).

## Common mistakes

- Taking every *ahorita* as a promise. Check the verb, the situation and the tone, and ask *¿Ahora mismo?* if it matters.
- Arriving at a home party exactly on time and being surprised the hosts aren't ready. For social invitations, ask or follow local friends; for work, be on time.
- *Las dieciocho de la tarde.* — Don't mix systems: either *las dieciocho horas* or *las seis de la tarde*.
- *Cadas semanas* or *cada semanas*. — *Cada* never takes a plural noun except after a number: *cada semana, cada dos semanas*.
- *Desde las nueve a las seis.* — Mixed pairs are heard, but the safe choice is to keep each pair together: *de … a* or *desde … hasta*.
- *La hora punta* in Mexico is understood, but the Mexican word is *la hora pico*.

## Key points

- *ahorita* = right now, in a moment, a moment ago, or later: context, verb and tone decide. For clarity: *ahora mismo* (right now), *en un momento* (in a moment), *al rato* (in a while).
- Generalizations: work and official appointments start on time; social invitations are looser in many places; ask *¿en punto?* when it matters.
- Timetables and signs use the 24-hour clock: *18:00 h* = *las dieciocho horas* = *las seis de la tarde*. Mexico often writes *hrs.*
- *de … a* and *desde … hasta* for ranges; *cada* + noun for "every"; *el horario, el día hábil, la hora pico*.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Fútbol, béisbol y música
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

In lesson 15 you learned *jugar* and *tocar*, the stem-changing verbs, and the names of a few sports. This honors lesson takes you into the stands and onto the dance floor: how people in Mexico and across Latin America talk about football and baseball, what the Spanish Academy says about *jugar al fútbol* and *jugar fútbol*, and four musical styles you will certainly hear (mariachi, son jarocho, cumbia and salsa), each with a short text in Spanish.

## Fútbol: the national passion

Football is the most popular sport in Mexico and in most of Latin America. A few things you'll hear:

- *la liga* — the league. Mexico's top men's league is the *Liga MX*. Instead of one long season, it plays two short championships (*campeonatos*) a year, the *Apertura* (opening) and the *Clausura* (closing), so there are two champions a year.
- *el Tri* — the Mexican national team, named after the three colours (*tricolor*) of the flag.
- *el estadio* — the stadium. Mexico City's Estadio Azteca hosted the opening match of the World Cup in 1970, in 1986 and again on 11 June 2026, the first stadium to open three World Cups. In 2025 it took the sponsor's name Estadio Banorte, but many people still call it *el Azteca*.
- *el aficionado, la aficionada* — the fan. *el jugador, la jugadora* — the player.
- *el gol* — the goal (plural *los goles*). Commentators famously stretch it: *¡Goool!*

To talk about a match (*el partido*, lesson 14) you need *ganar* (to win; it's a lesson 21 word, used here with its meaning), *perder* (to lose, lesson 15) and *empatar* (to draw, to tie):

- *¿Quién gana?* — Who's winning?
- *Ganamos dos a uno.* — We're winning / we win two-one.
- *Pierden tres a cero.* — They're losing three-nil.
- *Empatan uno a uno.* — It's one all.

Mexicans ask which team you support with a special use of *ir*: *¿A qué equipo le vas?* — Which team do you support? *Le voy al América.* — I support América (a Mexico City club). *Ser de* also works everywhere: *Soy del Guadalajara.*

### Example 1: Reading a match report

> **Gran partido en el estadio**
>
> El domingo, el equipo de la ciudad juega contra el campeón de la liga. Hay mucha gente en el estadio: más de cuarenta mil aficionados. En el minuto 20, el número 9 mete un gol. ¡Uno a cero! Pero en el minuto 75 el otro equipo empata. Finalmente, en el minuto 89, una jugadora joven de la ciudad mete el segundo gol. ¡Dos a uno! Los aficionados cantan y bailan en el estadio. Ahora el equipo tiene una oportunidad en el campeonato.

Translation:

> **Great match at the stadium.** On Sunday, the city's team plays the league champion. There are a lot of people in the stadium: more than forty thousand fans. In the 20th minute, number 9 scores a goal. One-nil! But in the 75th minute the other team equalizes. Finally, in the 89th minute, a young player from the city scores the second goal. Two-one! The fans sing and dance in the stadium. Now the team has a chance in the championship.

(*meter un gol* = to score a goal, literally "to put in a goal"; *contra* = against; *el campeón* = the champion; *segundo* = second; *la oportunidad* = the chance.) Reports often tell a past match in the present tense like this, to make it vivid.

Questions and how to work them out:

1. *¿Cuántos goles mete el equipo de la ciudad?* Count the goals by the city's team: minute 20 and minute 89. Answer: *Dos.*
2. *¿Quién gana?* The final score is *dos a uno* for the city. Answer: *El equipo de la ciudad.*
3. *¿Quién mete el último gol?* Find *minuto 89*: *una jugadora joven*. Answer: *Una jugadora joven de la ciudad.* (The *-a* of *jugadora* tells you it's a woman.)

## Béisbol: the Caribbean and the north and south of Mexico

Baseball is the top sport in parts of the Caribbean, especially Cuba, the Dominican Republic, Puerto Rico and Venezuela, and very popular in parts of Mexico. The *Liga Mexicana de Béisbol* was founded in 1925 and plays in spring and summer; in winter the *Liga Mexicana del Pacífico* plays in the north-west. Northern Mexico and states of the south-east such as Tabasco and Campeche are known for their fans.

Much of the vocabulary comes from English, written the Spanish way: *el jonrón* (home run, plural *los jonrones*) and *el pícher* (pitcher; also *el lanzador*). In Mexico, Guatemala, Colombia, Venezuela, Cuba and the Dominican Republic the sport is *el beisbol*, stressed on the last syllable; elsewhere, *el béisbol*.

## jugar, jugar a, jugar al: what the Academy says

In lesson 15 you saw that Mexicans usually say *Juego fútbol* and that *Juego al fútbol* is also correct. The *Diccionario panhispánico de dudas* (the Spanish Academy's guide to doubtful usage) puts it this way:

| Form | Status |
|---|---|
| *jugar al fútbol* | the form of careful, standard Spanish everywhere |
| *jugar fútbol* | common in everyday speech in much of Latin America and accepted as valid, because it's rooted in American Spanish; probably a **[[calque]]** of English "play football" |
| *jugar a fútbol* | heard mostly in Spain among speakers of Catalan; not considered good usage |

A calque copies the structure of a phrase from another language, word by word. Either of the first two is fine for you; in formal writing, *jugar al fútbol* is the safe choice.

For games that aren't sports, Mexicans normally keep *a*: *jugar a las cartas* (to play cards), *jugar a las escondidas* (to play hide-and-seek). And *jugar con* is to play with someone or something: *Juego con mi hijo. El perro juega con la pelota.*

## Tocar: instruments

Instruments take *tocar* (lesson 15) and the article: *tocar la trompeta, tocar el violín, tocar el tambor, tocar la guitarra*. *El instrumento* is an instrument: *¿Tocas algún instrumento?* — Do you play an instrument? (*algún* = any). A singer is *el cantante* or *la cantante*, and the beat or rhythm is *el ritmo*.

![Four instruments drawn side by side, each with its name: a trumpet, la trompeta; a violin with its bow, el violín; a drum with two sticks, el tambor; a guitar, la guitarra.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Four styles to know

Read each short text, then the notes below it (facts checked in November 2026).

El mariachi. *El mariachi es música de México. Es del oeste del país, sobre todo del estado de Jalisco. Un grupo de mariachi tiene violines, trompetas, guitarras, una vihuela y un guitarrón. Los músicos cantan y tocan en fiestas, bodas y cumpleaños. En la Ciudad de México, muchos mariachis esperan clientes en la Plaza Garibaldi.*

> Mariachi is music from Mexico. It's from the west of the country, above all the state of Jalisco. A mariachi group has violins, trumpets, guitars, a vihuela and a guitarrón. The musicians sing and play at parties, weddings and birthdays. In Mexico City, many mariachis wait for customers in Plaza Garibaldi.

The *vihuela* is a small, high guitar and the *guitarrón* a large bass guitar. Early mariachi was played on strings only; the trumpet became a standard part of the group in the first half of the 20th century. In 2011 UNESCO added mariachi to its list of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.

El son jarocho. *El son jarocho es de Veracruz, en el sur del estado. Los músicos tocan el arpa, el requinto y la jarana, una guitarra pequeña. En un fandango, la gente canta, toca y baila sobre una tarima de madera: los pies también hacen ritmo.*

> Son jarocho is from Veracruz, in the south of the state. The musicians play the harp, the requinto and the jarana, a small guitar. At a fandango, people sing, play and dance on a wooden platform: the feet make rhythm too.

*Jarocho* is the adjective for people and things from Veracruz. The best-known son jarocho worldwide is "La Bamba", a traditional song that became a rock hit in the US in the late 1950s.

La cumbia. *La cumbia es de Colombia, de la costa del Caribe. Tiene raíces indígenas, africanas y españolas. Hoy es muy popular en México, en Perú y en Argentina. En México, la gente baila cumbia en fiestas y en la calle.*

> Cumbia is from Colombia, from the Caribbean coast. It has Indigenous, African and Spanish roots. Today it's very popular in Mexico, Peru and Argentina. In Mexico, people dance cumbia at parties and in the street.

Cumbia reached Mexico in the 1940s, when the Colombian singer Luis Carlos Meyer worked there with Mexican orchestras, and from the 1960s on Mexican bands and, later, street sound systems (*sonideros*) made their own styles of it. The three-roots origin is the usual account, not the only one.

La salsa. *La salsa es música para bailar. Tiene raíces en la música de Cuba, sobre todo en el son cubano. Los músicos cubanos y puertorriqueños de Nueva York tocan esta música en los años sesenta y setenta. La cantante cubana Celia Cruz es muy famosa.*

> Salsa is music for dancing. It has roots in Cuban music, above all Cuban son. Cuban and Puerto Rican musicians in New York play this music in the sixties and seventies. The Cuban singer Celia Cruz is very famous.

The text tells history in the present tense, as Spanish often does. The sound grew in New York from the 1940s and 1950s and got the name *salsa* (literally "sauce") in the 1960s; it then spread across Latin America. (*famoso* = famous, lesson 22.)

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Where four Latin American music styles come from
  accDescr: Mariachi comes from western Mexico, mainly Jalisco. Son jarocho comes from southern Veracruz in Mexico. Cumbia comes from the Caribbean coast of Colombia and is now popular in Mexico, Peru and Argentina. Salsa grew in New York among Cuban and Puerto Rican musicians, from Cuban son.
  M["Mariachi"] --> M1["Western Mexico: Jalisco"]
  S["Son jarocho"] --> S1["Southern Veracruz, Mexico"]
  C["Cumbia"] --> C1["Caribbean coast of Colombia"]
  C1 --> C2["Today also Mexico, Peru, Argentina"]
  L["Salsa"] --> L1["New York: Cuban and Puerto Rican musicians"]
  L1 --> L2["Roots in Cuban son"]
```

### Example 2: Reading a concert listing

> **Cartelera del fin de semana**
>
> Viernes, 20:30 h — Noche de cumbia en el parque central. Entrada libre.
>
> Sábado, 19:00 h — Mariachi en el Teatro de la Ciudad. Boletos: 350 MXN.
>
> Domingo, 12:00 h — Fandango de son jarocho en la plaza. Lleva tu jarana.

Translation:

> **This weekend's listings.** Friday, 8:30 p.m.: cumbia night in the central park, free entry. Saturday, 7 p.m.: mariachi at the City Theatre, tickets 350 pesos. Sunday, 12 noon: son jarocho fandango in the square. Bring your jarana.

(*la cartelera* = the listings; *entrada libre* = free admission; *el boleto* = the ticket, lesson 18; *lleva* = bring, a *tú* command, lesson 17.)

1. *¿Qué concierto cuesta dinero?* Only Saturday's lists *Boletos: 350 MXN*; Friday's says *entrada libre*. Answer: *El mariachi del sábado.*
2. *¿A qué hora es la cumbia?* 20:30 h = *las ocho y media de la noche* (the 24-hour clock from the honors lesson 16h1).

## Dialogue: ¿Partido o concierto?

> Diego: ¿A qué equipo le vas, Ana?
>
> Ana: Le voy a los Tigres. ¿Y tú?
>
> Diego: Yo no veo mucho fútbol. Prefiero el béisbol. El sábado juegan los Sultanes en el estadio. ¿Quieres ir?
>
> Ana: El sábado no puedo, voy a un concierto de cumbia. Mi primo es el cantante del grupo.
>
> Diego: ¿En serio? ¿Y qué instrumento tocas tú?
>
> Ana: Toco el tambor, pero muy mal. ¿Tú tocas algo?
>
> Diego: La trompeta. Toco con un mariachi los domingos.
>
> Ana: ¡Qué padre! Entonces el domingo voy a escuchar tu mariachi, y el próximo sábado vamos al béisbol.

In English:

> Diego: Which team do you support, Ana?
>
> Ana: I support the Tigres. And you?
>
> Diego: I don't watch much football. I prefer baseball. On Saturday the Sultanes are playing at the stadium. Do you want to go?
>
> Ana: I can't on Saturday, I'm going to a cumbia concert. My cousin is the band's singer.
>
> Diego: Really? And what instrument do you play?
>
> Ana: I play the drum, but very badly. Do you play anything?
>
> Diego: The trumpet. I play with a mariachi band on Sundays.
>
> Ana: How cool! Then on Sunday I'll go and listen to your mariachi, and next Saturday we'll go to the baseball.

(*Tigres* and *Sultanes* are teams from Monterrey, in football and baseball; *¿En serio?* = really?; *algo* = something, anything; *¡Qué padre!* = how cool!, a Mexican expression; *entonces* = then, so.)

## Pronunciation

- *jonrón*: *j* like a strong h, stress on the end: "hon-RON". It comes from English "home run".
- *violín*: *vio-lín*, stress on the last syllable, so it has an accent: "byo-LEEN".
- *aficionado*: "a-fee-syo-NA-do"; *ci* is "see" in Latin America.
- *trompeta*: "trom-PE-ta"; *tambor*: "tam-BOR", stress on the last because it ends in *r*.
- *mariachi*: "ma-RYA-chee"; *jarocho*: "ha-RO-cho".

## Common mistakes

- *Juego la trompeta.* — Instruments take *tocar*: *Toco la trompeta.*
- *Toco béisbol.* — Sports take *jugar*: *Juego béisbol* or *Juego al béisbol.*
- *Juego a fútbol* in Latin America. — Use *jugar fútbol* or *jugar al fútbol*.
- *El aficionado* for a woman. — *La aficionada*; also *la jugadora*, but *la cantante* (no change).
- Treating every origin story as settled fact. Musical styles mix many influences; the facts above are the usual accounts, and books may differ on dates.

## Key points

- Football words: *la liga, el campeonato, el estadio, el aficionado, el jugador, el gol*; *ganar, perder, empatar*; *dos a uno*.
- Mexico: *¿A qué equipo le vas? — Le voy al…*; *el Tri* is the national team.
- Baseball: big in the Caribbean and in northern and south-eastern Mexico; *el jonrón*; Mexico says *beisbol*.
- *jugar al fútbol* (standard everywhere) and *jugar fútbol* (accepted, common in Latin America); *jugar a las cartas*; *jugar con*.
- *tocar* + article + instrument: *la trompeta, el violín, el tambor, la guitarra*.
- Mariachi (western Mexico, Jalisco; UNESCO 2011), son jarocho (southern Veracruz), cumbia (Colombia's Caribbean coast), salsa (New York, from Cuban son).

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete the lesson.

lessons.title: In the city: places, directions and commands
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Module 5 takes you out of the door: into the city, onto buses and planes, through the calendar and the weather, and finally to the doctor. This first lesson gives you the places you find in any Mexican city, the words for asking the way and understanding the answer, and a new verb form, the **[[imperative]]**: the form you use to tell or ask someone to do something. *Siga derecho* — Go straight ahead. *Doble a la derecha* — Turn right. *Toma el metro* — Take the metro.

You already know most of the pieces. The *tú* command is a present-tense form you learned in lesson 4 and lesson 7, and the *usted* command is built from the *yo* form, including the irregular *yo* forms from lessons 6, 14 and 16 (*tengo, vengo, hago, salgo, pongo*).

## Places in the city

| Spanish | English | Spanish | English |
|---|---|---|---|
| *la calle* | street | *el banco* | bank |
| *la avenida* | avenue | *la farmacia* | pharmacy |
| *la plaza* | square | *el hospital* | hospital |
| *la esquina* | corner | *la iglesia* | church |
| *la cuadra* | block | *el edificio* | building |
| *el semáforo* | traffic light | *el puente* | bridge |
| *la parada* | (bus) stop | *el metro* | metro, subway |
| *la entrada* | entrance | *la salida* | exit |

Here is a small city centre. You are at the red star, on the corner of Calle Zaragoza and Avenida Juárez. We will use this map for the directions later in the lesson.

![A street map. Avenida Juárez runs from left to right across the middle. Four streets cross it: Calle Zaragoza, Calle Hidalgo, Calle Morelos and Calle Allende. On the far right a river crosses the avenue under a bridge, el puente. A red star on the corner of Zaragoza and Juárez says Usted está aquí. North of the avenue, from left to right: la parada (a bus stop sign), la iglesia (a church) at the top of la plaza (a square with trees), el semáforo (a traffic light on the corner of Morelos), and la farmacia (a building with a green cross on the corner of Allende). South of the avenue: el metro (an orange M sign) near the star, el edificio (a tall building) between Hidalgo and Morelos, el banco (a building with columns) on the corner of Morelos, and el hospital (a building with a blue H sign) behind the bank.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

*La cuadra* is a city block, and it's the normal way to give distances in Latin America: *El banco está a dos cuadras* — The bank is two blocks away. Spain says *la manzana*. In everyday Mexican speech *la manzana* is "apple", although official maps and some addresses in Mexico also use it for a block (*Mz. 5*).

## Asking the way

Start with a polite word to get someone's attention. *Disculpe* (lesson 1) is the safest. *Oiga* — literally "hear!" — is also common, and it sounds friendlier with *disculpe* after it: *Oiga, disculpe…* Then ask one of three questions:

- *¿Dónde está el hospital?* — Where is the hospital? (lesson 9)
- *¿Hay una farmacia cerca de aquí?* — Is there a pharmacy near here? (*hay*, lesson 10)
- *¿Cómo llego a la plaza?* — How do I get to the square?

*Llego* is the *yo* form of *llegar* (to arrive, to get to), which you know from lesson 4. Remember that *a + el* becomes *al* (lesson 14): *¿Cómo llego al metro?* — How do I get to the metro? *¿Cómo llego al banco?*

If you're lost, say so: *Estoy perdido* (a man) or *Estoy perdida* (a woman). And if you need more help: *¿Me puede ayudar?* — Can you help me?

## Directions: derecha, izquierda, derecho

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| *a la derecha* | to the right, on the right |
| *a la izquierda* | to the left, on the left |
| *derecho* | straight ahead (Spain: *todo recto*) |
| *en la esquina* | on the corner, at the corner |
| *en el semáforo* | at the traffic light |
| *a dos cuadras* | two blocks away |
| *hasta el puente* | as far as the bridge (*hasta*, lesson 13) |
| *enfrente de, al lado de* | opposite, next to (lesson 10) |

Watch the pair *derecha* and *derecho*. *A la derecha* means "to the right"; *derecho*, with *-o* and no article, means "straight ahead". Both come from the same old word for "straight", which is why learners mix them up.

The four verbs of directions:

- *seguir* — to follow, to keep going: *seguir derecho* (to keep going straight). It's an e → i stem-changing verb like *pedir* (lesson 15), with one extra detail: *sigo* has no *u*, because *g* before *o* already sounds hard. *Sigo, sigues, sigue, seguimos, siguen.*
- *doblar* — to turn: *doblar a la izquierda*. Spain usually says *girar*. In Mexico you'll also hear *dar vuelta*: *Dé vuelta a la derecha* — Turn right (*dé* comes from *dar*, to give, lesson 21).
- *cruzar* — to cross: *cruzar la calle, cruzar el puente*.
- *pasar* — to pass, to go past or through: *pasar por la plaza*. It's a very useful verb with other meanings too: *¡Pase!* — Come in! *¿Qué pasa?* — What's happening?

## The imperative: telling people what to do

Spanish has a command for each kind of "you". This lesson teaches the two you'll use and hear most, *tú* and *usted*, in the affirmative (telling someone to do something). Negative commands ("don't turn") use a different form, and you'll meet them at A2.

### The tú command: the él form of the present

For someone you call *tú*, take the present-tense *él/ella* form. That's all:

| Infinitive | él/ella present | tú command |
|---|---|---|
| *tomar* | *toma* | *¡Toma el metro!* — Take the metro! |
| *doblar* | *dobla* | *Dobla a la derecha.* — Turn right. |
| *cruzar* | *cruza* | *Cruza la calle.* — Cross the street. |
| *mirar* | *mira* | *¡Mira!* — Look! |
| *comer* | *come* | *Come algo.* — Eat something. |
| *seguir* | *sigue* | *Sigue derecho.* — Keep going straight. |
| *volver* | *vuelve* | *Vuelve mañana.* — Come back tomorrow. |

Stem changes stay, because the *él* form has them: *sigue, vuelve, cierra* (close), *pide* (ask for).

Eight common verbs have a short, irregular *tú* command. Learn them as a set; most of them are the verbs whose *yo* form is irregular:

| decir | hacer | ir | poner | salir | ser | tener | venir |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| *di* | *haz* | *ve* | *pon* | *sal* | *sé* | *ten* | *ven* |

- *¡Ven aquí!* — Come here!
- *Haz la tarea.* — Do your homework. (*la tarea*, lesson 24)
- *Ve al banco y luego a la farmacia.* — Go to the bank and then to the pharmacy.
- *Ten cuidado.* — Be careful. (literally "have care")
- *Sé paciente.* — Be patient.

*Ve* (go!) looks like *ve* (he sees) from *ver*, and *sé* (be!) looks like *sé* (I know). The sentence always makes clear which one is meant.

### The usted command: the yo form with the "other" vowel

For someone you call *usted*, start from the *yo* form of the present, drop the *-o*, and add the "other" vowel: *-e* for -ar verbs, *-a* for -er and -ir verbs.

| Infinitive | yo present | usted command |
|---|---|---|
| *tomar* | *tomo* | *Tome el metro.* — Take the metro. |
| *doblar* | *doblo* | *Doble a la izquierda.* — Turn left. |
| *mirar* | *miro* | *Mire.* — Look. |
| *comer* | *como* | *Coma.* — Eat. |
| *seguir* | *sigo* | *Siga derecho.* — Go straight ahead. |
| *tener* | *tengo* | *Tenga.* — Here you are. (literally "have") |
| *venir* | *vengo* | *Venga mañana.* — Come tomorrow. |
| *hacer* | *hago* | *Haga una cita.* — Make an appointment. |
| *salir* | *salgo* | *Salga por la puerta principal.* — Go out through the main door. |
| *poner* | *pongo* | *Ponga la maleta aquí.* — Put the suitcase here. |

Starting from the *yo* form carries every irregular *yo* form and stem change into the command: *tengo → tenga, vuelvo → vuelva*.

**Spelling changes.** Before *-e*, *c* and *g* would change their sound, so the spelling changes to keep it: *-car → -que*, *-gar → -gue*. And Spanish spelling writes *c*, not *z*, before *e*: *-zar → -ce*.

- *cruzar → cruce*: *Cruce la avenida.* — Cross the avenue.
- *llegar → llegue*: *Llegue temprano.* — Arrive early.
- *buscar → busque*: *Busque la parada.* — Look for the stop.

**Five irregulars.** Verbs whose *yo* form doesn't end in *-o* need their own form: *ser → sea*, *ir → vaya*, *saber → sepa*, *estar → esté*, *dar → dé*. *Vaya derecho dos cuadras* — Go straight ahead two blocks.

This chart sums up both commands:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: How to make an affirmative command
  accDescr: First ask who you are talking to. For someone you call tú, check whether the verb is one of the eight irregulars: decir di, hacer haz, ir ve, poner pon, salir sal, ser sé, tener ten, venir ven. If it is, use that short form; if not, use the él form of the present, for example toma or sigue. For someone you call usted, check whether the verb is ser, ir, saber, estar or dar; if so, use sea, vaya, sepa, esté or dé. If not, take the yo form of the present, drop the -o and add -e for -ar verbs or -a for -er and -ir verbs, for example tome, siga, tenga, and keep the sound with spelling changes such as cruce, llegue and busque.
  A{"Who are you talking to?"} -- "tú" --> B{"One of the 8 irregulars?"}
  B -- "yes" --> C["di, haz, ve, pon, sal, sé, ten, ven"]
  B -- "no" --> D["él form of the present: toma, sigue"]
  A -- "usted" --> E{"ser, ir, saber, estar or dar?"}
  E -- "yes" --> F["sea, vaya, sepa, esté, dé"]
  E -- "no" --> G["yo form minus -o, plus -e (-ar) or -a (-er, -ir): tome, siga, tenga"]
  G --> H["Keep the sound: cruce, llegue, busque"]
```

### Ustedes: add -n

To give a command to a group (*ustedes*), add *-n* to the *usted* command: *tomen, sigan, crucen, vayan*. You'll see it on signs and hear it from guides, so recognize it: *Sigan a la guía, por favor* — Follow the guide, please. You don't need to produce it yet.

### Commands you already know

Some polite words you learned as fixed phrases are really *usted* commands: *disculpe* (from *disculpar*, to excuse), *oiga* (from *oír*, to hear: *oigo → oiga*), *mire* (from *mirar*) and *pase* (from *pasar*). You may also hear pronouns joined to the end of a command, with an accent to keep the stress: *Dígame* — Tell me, *Ayúdeme* — Help me. At this level, just recognize them.

### Making it polite

Add *por favor*, or ask with *poder* (lesson 15): *¿Me puede ayudar?* is softer than *Ayúdeme*. In directions, though, *usted* commands are normal and perfectly polite.

## Dialogue: ¿Cómo llego a la farmacia?

Daniel is visiting the city and stops a woman at the corner of Zaragoza and Juárez (the red star on the map).

> Daniel: Oiga, disculpe. ¿Hay una farmacia cerca de aquí?
>
> Señora: Sí, claro. Hay una en la esquina de Allende.
>
> Daniel: ¿Y cómo llego?
>
> Señora: Mire, siga derecho por la Avenida Juárez tres cuadras. Pase el semáforo y cruce la calle Morelos.
>
> Daniel: Tres cuadras derecho… ¿y luego?
>
> Señora: La farmacia está a la izquierda, en la esquina de Allende. Antes del puente.
>
> Daniel: ¿Está lejos?
>
> Señora: No, está cerca. Son cinco minutos a pie.
>
> Daniel: Muchas gracias. Es que estoy un poco perdido.
>
> Señora: De nada. ¡Que le vaya bien!

*Daniel: Excuse me, sorry. Is there a pharmacy near here? — Woman: Yes, of course. There's one on the corner of Allende. — Daniel: And how do I get there? — Woman: Look, keep going straight along Avenida Juárez for three blocks. Go past the traffic light and cross Calle Morelos. — Daniel: Three blocks straight on… and then? — Woman: The pharmacy is on the left, on the corner of Allende. Before the bridge. — Daniel: Is it far? — Woman: No, it's close. It's five minutes on foot. — Daniel: Thanks a lot. I'm a bit lost, you see. — Woman: You're welcome. All the best!*

*¡Que le vaya bien!* is a warm Mexican goodbye to someone you call *usted* (to a friend: *¡Que te vaya bien!*). Learn it as a chunk. *A pie* means "on foot".

## A text message: the way to Sofía's place

> ¡Hola, Marco! Para llegar a mi casa, toma el metro y bájate en la estación Coyoacán. Sal por la salida de la Avenida Universidad. Sigue derecho dos cuadras y dobla a la derecha en el semáforo. Mi edificio está a la izquierda, enfrente del banco. Ven a las ocho, ¿sí? ¡Y ten cuidado con los carros!

*Hi, Marco! To get to my place, take the metro and get off at Coyoacán station. Go out through the Avenida Universidad exit. Keep going straight for two blocks and turn right at the traffic light. My building is on the left, opposite the bank. Come at eight, OK? And watch out for the cars!*

(*Bájate* — get off, a *tú* command with a pronoun joined on; *el carro*, *la estación* — car, station, lesson 18.) Sofía writes to a friend, so she uses *tú* commands: *toma, sal, sigue, dobla, ven, ten*.

## Pronunciation

- *izquierda*: three syllables, iz-KYER-da. The *z* sounds like *s* (lesson 1), and *qu* is a plain *k*.
- *semáforo*: the stress is on the second syllable, se-MÁ-fo-ro, so it needs the written accent.
- *sigue, siga*: in *sigue* the *u* is silent and only keeps the *g* hard (SEE-geh); in *siga* there is no *u* to write (SEE-ga).

## Common mistakes

- Mixing up *derecha* and *derecho*. *Doble a la derecha* = turn right; *Siga derecho* = go straight ahead.
- Using the *tú* form of the present as a command. *Tomas el metro* is a statement ("you take the metro"); the command is *Toma el metro*.
- Using the *tú* command with *usted*. *Toma* is for a friend; for a stranger it's *Tome*. The *usted* command swaps the vowel: -ar verbs take *-e*.
- Making regular *tú* commands of the eight irregulars: *Tiene cuidado*, *Hace la tarea* and *Pone la maleta aquí* are wrong; say *Ten cuidado*, *Haz la tarea*, *Pon la maleta aquí*.
- Forgetting the spelling change: *cruze* and *llege* are misspellings of *cruce* and *llegue*.
- Saying *a el*. It's always *al*: *¿Cómo llego al hospital?*
- Turning a command negative by adding *no*: *No dobla* is not a negative command. Negative commands come at A2; for now, use the affirmative.

## Key points

- Places: *la calle, la avenida, la plaza, la esquina, la cuadra, el semáforo, la parada, el banco, la farmacia, el hospital, la iglesia, el edificio, el puente, el metro, la entrada, la salida*.
- Ask: *Disculpe / Oiga, disculpe… ¿Dónde está…? ¿Hay… cerca de aquí? ¿Cómo llego a / al…?*
- Directions: *a la derecha, a la izquierda, derecho, en la esquina, a dos cuadras*; verbs *seguir, doblar, cruzar, pasar*.
- *tú* command = *él* present (*toma, sigue*); eight irregulars: *di, haz, ve, pon, sal, sé, ten, ven*.
- *usted* command = *yo* present minus *-o* plus *-e* (-ar) or *-a* (-er, -ir): *tome, coma, siga, tenga*; spelling changes *cruce, llegue, busque*; irregulars *sea, vaya, sepa, esté, dé*.
- *ustedes*: add *-n* (*tomen, sigan*), for recognition.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Travel, transport and the hotel
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

In lesson 17 you found your way around a city on foot. Now you leave town: by bus, by plane or by train, to the beach, the mountains or a small village. This lesson gives you the words for transport and travel, three small but busy words (*en*, *de … a* and *para*), the verb *conocer* (to know a person or a place) and how it differs from *saber*, and two everyday tasks: buying a bus ticket and checking into a hotel.

## Ways to travel

![Six pictures, each with a caption: el avión (a plane), el autobús (a bus), el tren (a train on a track), el carro (a car), el taxi (a car with a TAXI sign on the roof) and la bicicleta (a bicycle).](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

| Spanish | English | Note |
|---|---|---|
| *el avión* | plane | *el aeropuerto* — airport |
| *el autobús* | bus | Mexico: *el camión* |
| *el tren* | train | *la estación* — station |
| *el carro* | car | Spain: *el coche*; Argentina: *el auto* |
| *el taxi* | taxi | |
| *el metro* | metro (lesson 17) | |
| *la bicicleta* | bicycle (lesson 15) | |

A word about buses in Mexico: people usually call a bus *el camión*, both a city bus and a long-distance one: *Tomo el camión a las siete* — I take the bus at seven. *El autobús* is understood everywhere, and it's the word on many signs, so this course uses *el autobús* as the main word. (*El camión* is also a truck, which can surprise visitors.)

### en + vehicle, but a pie

To say how you travel, use *en* with the vehicle and no article: *en autobús, en avión, en tren, en carro, en taxi, en metro, en bicicleta*. The one exception is on foot: *a pie*.

- *Voy a Oaxaca en autobús.* — I'm going to Oaxaca by bus.
- *¿Vas al trabajo en carro o en metro?* — Do you go to work by car or by metro?
- *La escuela está cerca; voy a pie.* — The school is close; I walk.

### subir, bajar, esperar, manejar

- *subir* — to go up, and to get on (a bus, a train): *Subimos al tren.* — We get on the train. (*a + el = al*.)
- *bajar* — to go down, and to get off: *Bajamos del avión.* — We get off the plane. (*de + el = del*.) You'll often hear it with *se*: *Me bajo aquí* — I'm getting off here.
- *esperar* — to wait, to wait for: *Espero el camión.* — I'm waiting for the bus. There is no word for "for": *esperar por el camión* is a common learner mistake. *Esperar* also means "to hope".
- *manejar* — to drive: *No sé manejar.* — I can't drive. Spain says *conducir*.

## de … a, and para

**De … a** gives the start and end of a trip, just as *de … a* gave the start and end of a time in lesson 13: *de México a Puebla* — from Mexico City to Puebla; *de la estación al hotel* — from the station to the hotel. The articles join with *de* and *a* as usual: *del aeropuerto al centro*.

**Para** has two everyday uses at this level:

1. Destination: *el camión para Puebla* — the bus to (going to) Puebla; *el vuelo para Cancún* — the flight to Cancún (*el vuelo*, flight); *Salgo para Monterrey mañana* — I leave for Monterrey tomorrow.
2. Purpose, with an infinitive, "(in order) to": *Necesito el pasaporte para viajar.* — I need my passport to travel. *Voy a la estación para comprar los boletos.* — I'm going to the station to buy the tickets.

It also means "for" a person or a time: *un boleto para mí* (*mí*, me, after a preposition), *una habitación para dos noches*. You met *por* in lesson 13 (*por la mañana*); *por* and *para* are both "for" in some sentences, and sorting them out fully is A2 work. For now: destination, purpose and "for someone" take *para*.

## Travel words

| Spanish | English | Spanish | English |
|---|---|---|---|
| *el viaje* | trip | *la playa* | beach |
| *viajar* | to travel | *el mar* | sea |
| *las vacaciones* | vacation | *la montaña* | mountain |
| *el turista* | tourist | *el río* | river |
| *el pasaporte* | passport | *el pueblo* | village, small town |
| *la maleta* | suitcase | *la llegada* | arrival |
| *el boleto* | ticket | *la salida* | departure, exit (lesson 17) |

- *Las vacaciones* is always plural: *ir de vacaciones* (to go on vacation), *Estamos de vacaciones* (We're on vacation).
- *El boleto* is the Latin American word for a ticket (bus, train, plane, cinema). Spain says *el billete*, which in Mexico means a banknote.
- *El turista* is the same for a woman: *la turista*. *¡Buen viaje!* — Have a good trip!

## conocer: to know a person or a place

Spanish has two verbs for "to know". You met *saber* in lesson 16: knowing facts and knowing how to do something. The other is *conocer*: knowing a person, or being familiar with a place, from experience.

| conocer | |
|---|---|
| yo | *conozco* |
| tú | *conoces* |
| él, ella, usted | *conoce* |
| nosotros | *conocemos* |
| ellos, ustedes | *conocen* |

Only *yo* is irregular: *conozco* (the *z* sounds like *s*: co-NOS-co).

- *¿Conoces Guadalajara?* — Have you been to Guadalajara? (literally "Do you know Guadalajara?")
- *No conozco el norte de México.* — I've never been to the north of Mexico.
- *Conozco a tu hermano.* — I know your brother.
- *Sé dónde está el hotel, pero no conozco la ciudad.* — I know where the hotel is, but I don't know the city.

*Conocer* also means "to meet" someone for the first time: *Quiero conocer a tus padres.* — I want to meet your parents.

### The personal a

Look again at *Conozco **a** tu hermano*. When the direct object of a verb is a specific person, Spanish puts *a* in front of it. This is the **[[personal a]]**, and it has no translation in English.

- *Conozco a Ana.* — I know Ana. But: *Conozco Puebla.* — I know Puebla (a place: no *a*).
- *Espero a mi amiga.* — I'm waiting for my friend. But: *Espero el camión.* — I'm waiting for the bus.
- *Voy a visitar a mis abuelos.* — I'm going to visit my grandparents.

### saber or conocer?

| saber | conocer |
|---|---|
| facts, information: *Sé su número.* | people: *Conozco a Luis.* |
| question words: *¿Sabes dónde está?* | places: *Conozco Oaxaca.* |
| how to do something: *Sé manejar.* | things you've tried: *Conozco este restaurante.* |

## tener que: having to (a preview)

*Tener que* + infinitive means "to have to". You'll practise it fully in lesson 20, but it's too useful for travelling to leave out: *Tengo que comprar los boletos.* — I have to buy the tickets. *Tenemos que estar en el aeropuerto a las seis.* — We have to be at the airport at six.

## Buying a bus ticket

Long-distance buses are the most common way to travel between Mexican cities, and big cities have several bus stations. This ticket is invented, but the fields are typical:

![An invented bus ticket from a company called Autobuses La Garza. Fields: Origen, Ciudad de México (TAPO); Destino, Puebla; Fecha, 15/03/2026; Salida, 08:30; Llegada, 10:45; Asiento, 23; Pasajero, Ana López; Precio, 320.00 MXN. At the bottom: Ida, Sencillo, Pasajero adulto. A tear-off stub on the right repeats the seat and the departure time.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

*El origen* is where you leave from and *el destino* where you're going; *la salida* is the departure time and *la llegada* the arrival; *el asiento* is your seat. *Sencillo* means a one-way ticket in Mexico (*de ida* elsewhere); a return ticket is *de ida y vuelta*, or in Mexico *viaje redondo*.

> Ana: Buenos días. ¿A qué hora sale el próximo camión para Puebla?
>
> Empleado: Hay uno a las ocho y media. Llega a Puebla a las once menos cuarto.
>
> Ana: Perfecto. Un boleto, por favor.
>
> Empleado: ¿Sencillo o de ida y vuelta?
>
> Ana: Sencillo. Regreso el domingo con mi hermano, en carro.
>
> Empleado: Muy bien. ¿Ventanilla o pasillo?
>
> Ana: Ventanilla, por favor. Me gusta ver las montañas.
>
> Empleado: El asiento veintitrés. Son trescientos veinte pesos.
>
> Ana: Aquí tiene.
>
> Empleado: Gracias. Tiene que estar en la sala de espera quince minutos antes. ¡Buen viaje!

*Ana: Good morning. What time does the next bus to Puebla leave? — Clerk: There's one at half past eight. It gets to Puebla at a quarter to eleven. — Ana: Perfect. One ticket, please. — Clerk: One-way or round-trip? — Ana: One-way. I'm coming back on Sunday with my brother, by car. — Clerk: Very well. Window or aisle? — Ana: Window, please. I like seeing the mountains. — Clerk: Seat twenty-three. That's three hundred and twenty pesos. — Ana: Here you are. — Clerk: Thank you. You have to be in the waiting room fifteen minutes before. Have a good trip!*

(*el empleado* — clerk; *regresar* — to come back, lesson 21; *la ventanilla* — window seat; *el pasillo* — aisle; *la sala de espera* — waiting room.)

## At the hotel

> Recepcionista: Buenas tardes. Bienvenida al Hotel del Río.
>
> Ana: Buenas tardes. Tengo una reservación a nombre de Ana López.
>
> Recepcionista: Sí, aquí está. Una habitación sencilla, dos noches. ¿Me permite su pasaporte, por favor?
>
> Ana: Sí, tenga.
>
> Recepcionista: Gracias. Es la habitación trescientos cinco, en el tercer piso. El desayuno es de siete a diez, en el restaurante.
>
> Ana: ¿Hay elevador?
>
> Recepcionista: Sí, a la derecha. Aquí tiene su llave. ¡Que disfrute su estancia!

*Receptionist: Good afternoon. Welcome to the Hotel del Río. — Ana: Good afternoon. I have a reservation in the name of Ana López. — Receptionist: Yes, here it is. A single room, two nights. May I have your passport, please? — Ana: Yes, here you are. — Receptionist: Thank you. It's room three hundred and five, on the third floor. Breakfast is from seven to ten, in the restaurant. — Ana: Is there an elevator? — Receptionist: Yes, on the right. Here is your key. Enjoy your stay!*

(*la reservación* — reservation, the Mexican word; Spain says *la reserva*. *Sencilla* here means single. *Tercer* — third, before a masculine noun; *el elevador* — elevator, Spain *el ascensor*. *¡Que disfrute su estancia!* is a set phrase.)

To book a room yourself: *Quiero reservar una habitación para dos personas.* *La habitación* is a room in a hotel; a room in your home is *el cuarto* (lesson 10).

## Pronunciation

- *autobús, avión, habitación, estación*: the stress is on the last syllable, so they need an accent. In the plural the accent disappears because a syllable is added: *autobuses, aviones, habitaciones* (lesson 5).
- *habitación, hotel*: the *h* is silent: a-bi-ta-SYON, o-TEL.
- *viaje, viajar*: the *j* is the throaty sound from lesson 1: BYA-he, bya-HAR.
- *conozco*: co-NOS-co, with *z* and *c* both as *s* in Latin America.
- *pueblo*: two syllables, PWE-blo.

## Common mistakes

- Using *por* or a "by" word for transport. It's *en autobús, en tren*, not *por autobús*; and on foot is *a pie*, not *en pie*.
- Putting an article after *en*: *en el avión* means "inside the plane", not "by plane". To say how you travel, use *en avión*.
- Adding "for" after *esperar*: *Espero el camión*, not *Espero por el camión*.
- Using *saber* for people and places: *Sé a Ana* and *Sé Guadalajara* are wrong; say *Conozco a Ana*, *Conozco Guadalajara*.
- Forgetting the personal *a* with people, or adding it with places: *Conozco a mi vecino*, but *Conozco Cancún*.
- Calling a hotel room *el cuarto* in a formal booking. It's understood, but *la habitación* is the normal word in a hotel.

## Key points

- Transport: *el avión, el autobús* (Mexico *el camión*), *el tren, el carro, el taxi*; travel *en* + vehicle, but *a pie*.
- *subir* (to get on), *bajar* (to get off), *esperar* (to wait for: no extra word), *manejar* (to drive).
- *de … a* for from … to; *para* for destination (*el camión para Puebla*), purpose (*para viajar*) and "for" a person.
- *conocer* (*conozco*): people and places; *saber*: facts and skills. Personal *a* before people: *Conozco a Ana*.
- *tener que* + infinitive: to have to.
- Tickets: *sencillo* or *de ida y vuelta*; fields *origen, destino, salida, llegada, asiento*. Hotels: *Tengo una reservación*, *una habitación para dos noches*.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Dates, seasons and the weather
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

You can tell the time and name the days of the week (lesson 13), and you can plan a trip (lesson 18). Now you need the calendar and the sky: the months, how to say a date and a year, birthdays, the seasons, and the weather. Weather in Spanish uses a handful of fixed patterns with *hacer*, *estar* and two special verbs, *llover* and *nevar*, and once you have them you can make small talk anywhere: *¡Qué calor! — Sí, hace mucho calor hoy.*

## The months

| | | | |
|---|---|---|---|
| *enero* — January | *abril* — April | *julio* — July | *octubre* — October |
| *febrero* — February | *mayo* — May | *agosto* — August | *noviembre* — November |
| *marzo* — March | *junio* — June | *septiembre* — September | *diciembre* — December |

Like the days of the week, the months are masculine and written with a small letter: *en enero*, *Mi cumpleaños es en julio*. They take no article when you say "in": *en marzo*, not *en el marzo*. *Setiembre* is an accepted spelling too, used in some countries; in Mexico you'll see *septiembre*.

## Saying the date

A date in Spanish is *el* + number + *de* + month (+ *de* + year). The day comes first, as in most of the world:

- *el 5 de mayo* — the fifth of May, May 5th
- *el 16 de septiembre de 2026* — September 16th, 2026
- *el 24 de diciembre* — December 24th

Use ordinary numbers (*cinco, dieciséis*), not "fifth, sixteenth". The one exception is the first day of the month. In Mexico and most of Latin America it's *el primero*: *el primero de mayo*, *el primero de enero*. Spain usually says *el uno de mayo*. *Primero* is an **[[ordinal number]]**, a number that gives a position in a series (first, second, third). Before a masculine noun it shortens to *primer*: *el primer día de clases* — the first day of school.

Two more details:

- English "on" disappears. *Mi cumpleaños es el 3 de abril.* — My birthday is on April 3rd. Never *en el 3 de abril*.
- In numbers, the day still comes first: 10/11/2026 is the tenth of November, not October 11th. Mexican forms and tickets write dates this way (look at the ticket in lesson 18: 15/03/2026).
