To ask the date: *¿Qué fecha es hoy?* — What's the date today? Answer: *Hoy es 10 de noviembre* or *Hoy es el 10 de noviembre* (both are common). With the day of the week: *Hoy es martes 10 de noviembre*.

### Years

Read a year as an ordinary number (lesson 12), never in pairs as in English:

- 2026 — *dos mil veintiséis*
- 1999 — *mil novecientos noventa y nueve*
- 1810 — *mil ochocientos diez*

"In 2026" is *en 2026* (*en dos mil veintiséis*). Years are written without a comma or point: 2026, not 2,026.

### Birthdays

- *¿Cuándo es tu cumpleaños?* — When is your birthday?
- *Es el 23 de mayo.* — It's on May 23rd.
- *¿Cuántos años vas a cumplir?* — How old are you going to be? (*cumplir años* — to have a birthday, to turn)
- *¡Feliz cumpleaños!* — Happy birthday!

*El cumpleaños* ends in *-s* in the singular too: *el cumpleaños, los cumpleaños*. In Mexico the birthday song is *Las mañanitas*, often sung early in the morning.

### A calendar page

![A calendar page for May 2026, with the weekdays from lunes to domingo across the top. The 1st is a Friday. Four days are coloured and explained in a legend: 1, Día del Trabajo (Labour Day); 5, Batalla de Puebla (the Battle of Puebla); 10, Día de las Madres (Mother's Day); 23, cumpleaños de Ana (Ana's birthday).](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Three of these dates are Mexican: *el primero de mayo* (Labour Day) is an official day off; *el 5 de mayo* remembers the Battle of Puebla in 1862, but it is not one of the official days off in Mexico's labour law (schools, though, often close); and Mexico celebrates Mother's Day on *el 10 de mayo* every year, whatever the weekday. This calendar starts the week on Monday, *lunes*.

## The seasons

| | |
|---|---|
| *la primavera* — spring | *el otoño* — autumn, fall |
| *el verano* — summer | *el invierno* — winter |

- *En verano* or *en el verano* — in summer: both are correct.
- South of the equator the seasons are the other way round: in Argentina and Chile, December is summer and July is winter.
- Much of Mexico thinks in terms of rain more than the four seasons. *La temporada de lluvias*, the rainy season, normally runs from about May or June to October, with heavy afternoon showers in many places; the rest of the year is the dry season, *la temporada de secas*. This is a general pattern: the north is drier, and the south-east wetter.

## The weather: ¿Qué tiempo hace?

To ask about the weather, say *¿Qué tiempo hace?* — What's the weather like? (*el tiempo* also means time, lesson 13.) In Mexico people very often say *el clima* for the weather of the day: *¿Cómo está el clima hoy?* *El clima* also means "climate" everywhere, and it's masculine although it ends in *-a*.

![Six weather pictures with captions: a sun, Hace sol; a cloud with rain, Llueve; a cloud with snowflakes, Nieva; three curling lines, Hace viento; two grey clouds, Está nublado; a thermometer with low blue mercury and a snowflake, Hace frío.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Spanish weather sentences come in three patterns.

**1. hace + noun.** *Hacer* (to make, to do; lesson 16) is used in the *él* form, *hace*, with a noun:

| | |
|---|---|
| *Hace calor.* | It's hot. (*el calor* — heat) |
| *Hace frío.* | It's cold. (*el frío* — the cold) |
| *Hace sol.* | It's sunny. (*el sol* — sun) |
| *Hace viento.* | It's windy. (*el viento* — wind) |
| *Hace buen tiempo.* | The weather is nice. |
| *Hace mal tiempo.* | The weather is bad. |

Because *calor, frío, sol* and *viento* are nouns, "very" is *mucho*, not *muy*: *Hace mucho calor* — It's very hot (literally "it makes much heat"). *Hace muy calor* is a typical mistake.

**2. Weather verbs.** *Llover* (to rain) and *nevar* (to snow) are stem-changing verbs (lesson 15), and for the weather they're used only in the *él* form, with no subject at all:

- *Llueve.* — It rains, it's raining. (o → ue)
- *Nieva.* — It snows, it's snowing. (e → ie)
- *En agosto llueve casi todas las tardes.* — In August it rains almost every afternoon.

They are **[[impersonal verbs]]**: there is no "it" in Spanish, because nobody does the raining. You'll also hear *Está lloviendo* — It's raining (right now); learn it as a chunk for now. The nouns are *la lluvia* (rain) and *la nieve* (snow).

**3. estar + adjective.** *Está nublado.* — It's cloudy. *El cielo está nublado.* — The sky is cloudy (*el cielo*, sky).

To give a temperature, Mexico (like most of the world) uses degrees Celsius: *Hace 30 grados* — It's 30 degrees (*el grado*, degree). *Estamos a 30 grados* is also common.

### hace calor, tengo calor, está caliente

English "hot" and "cold" need three different Spanish patterns:

| Weather | A person | A thing (lesson 9) |
|---|---|---|
| *Hace calor.* — It's hot. | *Tengo calor.* — I'm hot. | *La sopa está caliente.* — The soup is hot. |
| *Hace frío.* — It's cold. | *Tengo frío.* — I'm cold. | *El café está frío.* — The coffee is cold. |

So a person *has* heat or cold (*tener*, like *tener hambre* in lesson 11), the weather *makes* it (*hacer*), and a thing *is* hot or cold (*estar*). *Estoy caliente* about yourself is a mistake to avoid: said of a person, *caliente* usually has a sexual meaning (and in Mexico it can also mean "angry").

## Dialogue: ¿Qué tiempo hace allá?

Laura lives in Mexico City. She calls her cousin Rodrigo in Monterrey, in the north of Mexico.

> Laura: ¡Hola, Rodrigo! ¿Cómo estás?
>
> Rodrigo: Bien, pero con mucho calor. Aquí en Monterrey estamos a treinta y ocho grados.
>
> Laura: ¡Qué horror! Aquí está nublado y llueve todas las tardes. Es la temporada de lluvias.
>
> Rodrigo: ¿Y hace frío?
>
> Laura: No, no hace frío, pero tampoco hace calor. Llevo un suéter en la mochila.
>
> Rodrigo: Oye, ¿cuándo es el cumpleaños de tu mamá? ¿Es en julio?
>
> Laura: No, es el primero de agosto. Va a cumplir sesenta años.
>
> Rodrigo: ¡Sesenta! Entonces voy a viajar a México para la fiesta.
>
> Laura: ¡Qué bueno! Pero trae un paraguas.

*Laura: Hi, Rodrigo! How are you? — Rodrigo: Fine, but very hot. Here in Monterrey it's thirty-eight degrees. — Laura: How awful! Here it's cloudy and it rains every afternoon. It's the rainy season. — Rodrigo: And is it cold? — Laura: No, it isn't cold, but it isn't hot either. I carry a sweater in my backpack. — Rodrigo: Hey, when is your mom's birthday? Is it in July? — Laura: No, it's on the first of August. She's going to be sixty. — Rodrigo: Sixty! Then I'm going to travel to Mexico City for the party. — Laura: Great! But bring an umbrella.*

(*oye* — hey, listen: the *tú* command of *oír*, lesson 17's *oiga* for a friend. *Trae* — bring, a *tú* command of *traer*; *el paraguas* — umbrella. *Llevo* — I carry, from *llevar*, lesson 20. Many Mexicans call Mexico City just *México*.)

## Pronunciation

- *lluvia, llueve, llover*: *ll* sounds like *y* (yeísmo, lesson 1): YU-vya, YWE-be.
- *nieva, viento, invierno*: *ie* is one syllable: NYE-va, BYEN-to, in-BYER-no.
- *otoño, cumpleaños*: *ñ* as in "canyon": o-TO-nyo, cum-ple-A-nyos.
- *septiembre*: many speakers soften or drop the *p*, which is why *setiembre* is also a spelling.
- *frío*: two syllables, FRI-o; the accent keeps the *i* and *o* apart.

## Common mistakes

- Capital letters: *Enero*, *Mayo* are wrong inside a sentence. Write *enero*, *mayo*.
- Saying "on" with dates: *en el 5 de mayo* is wrong; say *el 5 de mayo*.
- English order: *mayo 5* is wrong; say *el 5 de mayo*. And read 10/11 as the 10th of November.
- *el uno de mayo* is Spain's usage; in Mexico say *el primero de mayo*.
- Reading years in pairs: 2026 is *dos mil veintiséis*, not *veinte veintiséis*.
- *Hace muy calor*: with the noun *calor* you need *mucho*: *Hace mucho calor*.
- *Es frío* for the weather: say *Hace frío*. (In Mexico you will also hear *Está frío* or *Está haciendo frío*, but *Hace frío* is the pattern to learn.) For yourself, *Tengo frío*.
- Adding a subject to weather verbs: just *Llueve*, *Nieva*.

## Key points

- Months are lowercase and masculine: *enero … diciembre*. In a month: *en mayo*.
- Dates: *el* + number + *de* + month: *el 5 de mayo*; the 1st is *el primero* in Latin America. No word for "on".
- Years are read as whole numbers: *dos mil veintiséis*; *en 2026*.
- *¿Cuándo es tu cumpleaños? — Es el 23 de mayo. ¡Feliz cumpleaños!*
- Seasons: *la primavera, el verano, el otoño, el invierno*; much of Mexico has a rainy season (about May or June to October) and a dry season.
- Weather: *hace* + *calor, frío, sol, viento, buen / mal tiempo* (very = *mucho*); *llueve, nieva*; *está nublado*.
- Weather *hace*, person *tengo*, thing *está*: *Hace frío. Tengo frío. El café está frío.*

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Body, clothes and feeling ill
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

The last lesson of this module is about you: your body, what you wear, and what to say when you don't feel well. You'll learn the main parts of the body, the verb *doler* (to hurt), which works exactly like *gustar* from lesson 11, the patterns *tener que* and *hay que* for things you must do, the verb *llevar* for clothes, and a visit to the doctor, where everyone uses *usted* and the *usted* commands from lesson 17.

## The body

![A person standing, seen from the front, with labels: la cabeza (the head), el ojo (an eye), la nariz (the nose), la oreja (an ear), la boca (the mouth), el brazo (an arm), el estómago (the stomach), la mano (a hand), la pierna (a leg) and el pie (a foot).](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

| Spanish | English | Spanish | English |
|---|---|---|---|
| *el cuerpo* | body | *el brazo* | arm |
| *la cabeza* | head | *la mano* | hand |
| *el ojo* | eye | *el estómago* | stomach |
| *la oreja* | ear | *la espalda* | back |
| *la nariz* | nose | *la pierna* | leg |
| *la boca* | mouth | *el pie* | foot |

- *La mano* is feminine although it ends in *-o*: *la mano derecha* (the right hand), *las manos*. You met it as an exception in lesson 5.
- *La oreja* is the outside of the ear. For an earache people say *dolor de oído* (*el oído*, the inner ear, hearing).
- *La nariz* has the plural *las narices* (z → c before *-es*, like *el lápiz, los lápices*).
- *A pie* (lesson 18), "on foot", comes from *el pie*.

### The article, not "my"

With parts of the body (and clothes), Spanish usually uses *el, la, los, las* where English uses "my, your, his": the person is already clear from the verb or the pronoun.

- *Me lavo las manos.* — I wash my hands. (lesson 16)
- *Abra la boca, por favor.* — Open your mouth, please.
- *Tengo los ojos verdes.* — I have green eyes.
- *Me duele la cabeza.* — My head hurts.

*Me lavo mis manos* sounds like an English speaker translating word by word.

## doler: it hurts me

*Doler* means "to hurt", but you use it like *gustar*: the part that hurts is the subject, and the person who feels the pain is shown with *me, te, le, nos, les* (lesson 11).

| who hurts | one thing | several things |
|---|---|---|
| (a mí) *me* | *me duele la cabeza* | *me duelen los pies* |
| (a ti) *te* | *te duele el estómago* | *te duelen los ojos* |
| (a él, a ella, a usted) *le* | *le duele la espalda* | *le duelen las piernas* |
| (a nosotros) *nos* | *nos duele la cabeza* | *nos duelen los brazos* |
| (a ellos, a ustedes) *les* | *les duele el estómago* | *les duelen los pies* |

*Doler* is an o → ue stem-changing verb (lesson 15), so the forms you need are *duele* (one thing) and *duelen* (several things). Literally, *Me duele la cabeza* is "the head hurts to me".

- *¿Qué te duele?* — What hurts? (to a friend)
- *¿Le duele algo?* — Does anything hurt? (to someone you call *usted*)
- *A mi papá le duele la espalda.* — My dad's back hurts.
- *Me duele todo el cuerpo.* — My whole body aches.

### tener dolor de, tener fiebre

The noun *el dolor* (pain) gives a second way to say it, with *tener*: *Tengo dolor de cabeza* — I have a headache. *Tengo dolor de estómago* — I have a stomach ache. *Tener* also gives you *tener fiebre* (to have a temperature) and *tener gripa* (to have the flu). *La gripa* is the Mexican and Colombian word; most other countries say *la gripe*. In Mexico *tener gripa* also covers a bad cold.

And you know *estar* for states (lesson 9): *Estoy enfermo / enferma* — I'm ill. *Estoy cansado* — I'm tired.

## tener que and hay que

You previewed *tener que* in lesson 18. It means "to have to", for a particular person:

- *Tengo que ir al doctor.* — I have to go to the doctor.
- *Tienes que descansar.* — You have to rest.
- *Mi hermana tiene que tomar la medicina dos veces al día.* — My sister has to take the medicine twice a day.

*Hay que* + infinitive means "you have to, one must": a general rule, for everybody, with no person at all. It uses *hay* from lesson 10 and never changes.

- *Hay que tomar mucha agua.* — You have to drink lots of water. (*tomar* is the everyday word for "to drink" in Mexico.)
- *Para viajar hay que tener pasaporte.* — To travel you need a passport.
- *Hay que hacer una cita.* — You have to make an appointment.

The difference: *Tienes que descansar* is about you; *Hay que descansar* is advice for anyone.

## Clothes and llevar

![Eight pieces of clothing, each with a caption: el suéter (a sweater), la chamarra (a jacket with a zip), la playera (a T-shirt), el pantalón (a pair of pants), la falda (a skirt), el vestido (a dress), los zapatos (a pair of shoes) and los tenis (a pair of sneakers).](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

| Mexico | Spain and elsewhere | English |
|---|---|---|
| *la playera* | *la camiseta* | T-shirt |
| *la chamarra* | *la chaqueta* | jacket |
| *el suéter* | *el jersey* (Spain) | sweater |
| *el pantalón / los pantalones* | | pants, trousers |
| *los tenis* | *las zapatillas* (Spain) | sneakers |
| *la falda* | | skirt |
| *el vestido* | | dress |
| *el zapato* | | shoe |

*El pantalón* and *los pantalones* both mean one pair of pants. *Los tenis* is plural (*el tenis* is the sport).

To say what someone is wearing, use *llevar*, a regular -ar verb: *Hoy llevo una playera blanca y pantalón negro.* — Today I'm wearing a white T-shirt and black pants. Colours and other adjectives agree with the clothes (lesson 8): *una chamarra negra, unos zapatos negros*. In Mexico you'll also hear *usar* (to use, to wear) for clothes and glasses: *Uso lentes* — I wear glasses.

*Llevar* has other meanings too: "to carry" (*Llevo la maleta*) and "to take someone or something somewhere" (*Te llevo al aeropuerto* — I'll take you to the airport).

## At the doctor's

At the doctor's, both sides use *usted*, and the doctor gives instructions with *usted* commands (lesson 17). A visit usually follows the same steps:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: A visit to the doctor, step by step
  accDescr: The doctor greets the patient and asks Qué tiene or Qué le pasa, meaning what's wrong. The patient describes the problem, for example Me duele la cabeza and Tengo fiebre. The doctor asks Desde cuándo, since when, and the patient answers Desde el lunes. The doctor examines the patient with commands such as Abra la boca. Then the doctor explains: Tiene gripa. Next come the instructions: Tome una pastilla cada ocho horas, and Tiene que descansar. The visit ends with Que se mejore, get well soon.
  A["Doctor: Buenos días. ¿Qué tiene? ¿Qué le pasa?"] --> B["Patient: Me duele la cabeza. Tengo fiebre."]
  B --> C["Doctor: ¿Desde cuándo? — Patient: Desde el lunes."]
  C --> D["Doctor examines: Abra la boca, por favor."]
  D --> E["Doctor explains: Tiene gripa."]
  E --> F["Instructions: Tome una pastilla cada ocho horas. Tiene que descansar."]
  F --> G["¡Que se mejore!"]
```

> Doctora: Buenos días, señor Ruiz. Pase y siéntese, por favor. ¿Qué tiene?
>
> Señor Ruiz: Buenos días, doctora. Me duele mucho la cabeza y tengo fiebre.
>
> Doctora: ¿Desde cuándo?
>
> Señor Ruiz: Desde el lunes. Y también me duele todo el cuerpo.
>
> Doctora: A ver… Abra la boca, por favor. Mmm. ¿Le duele el estómago?
>
> Señor Ruiz: No, el estómago no.
>
> Doctora: Bueno, tiene gripa. Tiene que descansar tres días en casa. Tome una pastilla cada ocho horas, y hay que tomar mucha agua.
>
> Señor Ruiz: ¿Puedo ir a trabajar mañana?
>
> Doctora: No, mañana no. Descanse. Y si la fiebre no baja, llame otra vez para hacer una cita.
>
> Señor Ruiz: Muy bien. Gracias, doctora.
>
> Doctora: De nada. ¡Que se mejore!

*Doctor: Good morning, Mr Ruiz. Come in and sit down, please. What's the matter? — Mr Ruiz: Good morning, doctor. My head hurts a lot and I have a temperature. — Doctor: Since when? — Mr Ruiz: Since Monday. And my whole body aches too. — Doctor: Let's see… Open your mouth, please. Hmm. Does your stomach hurt? — Mr Ruiz: No, not my stomach. — Doctor: Well, you have the flu. You have to rest at home for three days. Take a pill every eight hours, and you need to drink lots of water. — Mr Ruiz: Can I go to work tomorrow? — Doctor: No, not tomorrow. Rest. And if the fever doesn't go down, call again to make an appointment. — Mr Ruiz: Very well. Thank you, doctor. — Doctor: You're welcome. Get well soon!*

(*Siéntese* — sit down, an *usted* command of *sentarse* with the pronoun joined on; *a ver* — let's see; *cada* — every, each; *si* — if; *bajar* — here, to go down, lesson 18.)

To a friend who is ill, say *¡Que te mejores!*; to someone you call *usted*, *¡Que se mejore!* Both mean "get well soon" (literally "may you get better"). Learn them as fixed phrases.

### A message to a friend

> Hola, Paco. Hoy no voy a la clase: tengo gripa y me duelen la cabeza y la espalda. La doctora dice que tengo que descansar. ¿Me mandas la tarea, por favor? Gracias. Laura

*Hi, Paco. I'm not going to class today: I have the flu and my head and back hurt. The doctor says I have to rest. Will you send me the homework, please? Thanks. Laura*

Notice *me duelen la cabeza y la espalda*: two things, so *duelen*. (*Mandar* — to send, lesson 23.)

## Pronunciation

- *estómago*: es-TÓ-ma-go, stress on the second syllable (hence the accent).
- *oreja, ojo*: the *j* is the throaty sound of lesson 1: o-RE-ha, O-ho.
- *suéter*: SWE-ter, two syllables; the accent is there because it ends in *-r* but is stressed on the first part.
- *pierna, fiebre, duele*: *ie* and *ue* are single syllables: PYER-na, FYE-bre, DWE-le.
- *gripa*: GREE-pa, with a tapped *r*.

## Common mistakes

- *Mi cabeza duele* (English word order and "my"). Say *Me duele la cabeza*.
- *Me duele los pies*. Several things need the plural: *Me duelen los pies*.
- *Yo duelo la cabeza*. The person is never the subject of *doler*; use *me, te, le…*
- *Me lavo mis manos*. Use the article: *Me lavo las manos*.
- *Hay que* with a person: *Hay que tú descansas* is wrong. Use *Tienes que descansar* for a person, *Hay que descansar* for everyone.
- *el mano*: it's *la mano*.
- Mixing up *¡Que te mejores!* and *¡Que se mejore!*: *te* for a friend, *se* for *usted*.

## Key points

- Body: *la cabeza, el ojo, la oreja, la nariz, la boca, el brazo, la mano* (feminine), *el estómago, la espalda, la pierna, el pie*.
- Body parts take the article, not "my": *Me lavo las manos. Abra la boca.*
- *doler* works like *gustar*: *me duele* + one thing, *me duelen* + several. Also *tener dolor de…, tener fiebre, tener gripa*.
- *tener que* + infinitive: a person has to; *hay que* + infinitive: everyone has to.
- Clothes with *llevar*: *la playera, la chamarra, el suéter, el pantalón, la falda, el vestido, los zapatos, los tenis*.
- At the doctor's: *¿Qué tiene? ¿Desde cuándo? Abra la boca. Tome… Tiene que descansar. ¡Que se mejore!* (to a friend: *¡Que te mejores!*)

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Honors: Getting around a Latin American city
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

In lesson 17 you asked the way on foot, and in lesson 18 you bought a bus ticket to another city. A big Latin American city needs more: a metro with a dozen lines, buses that don't always have stops, taxis of two or three kinds, bus stations named after the direction they serve, and addresses that look nothing like English ones. This honors lesson uses Mexico City as its example, because it's the largest Spanish-speaking city in the world and its system is typical of the region, and it gives you the words and the reading skills to move around on your own.

Fares, opening hours and line details change. Everything here was checked in November 2026; check again before you travel.

## The Mexico City metro

The metro (*el Metro*, with a capital M when people mean the system) opened in 1969. Today it has 12 lines and 195 stations. Each line has a number or a letter and a colour: line 1 is pink, line 2 blue, line 3 olive green, and so on up to line 12, which is gold; two lines that run far out into the State of Mexico are lettered A and B.

Three things make the metro easy to read once you know them:

1. **Directions are named after the last station.** There is no "northbound" or "eastbound". A sign says *Dirección Pantitlán* or *Dirección Observatorio*: the train goes towards that end of the line. So before you get on, find your line *and* the name of the station at the end you're heading towards.
2. **Transfers are called *correspondencia*.** At a station where two lines meet, signs say *Correspondencia* with the other line's number and colour. (The everyday verb for changing is *transbordar*, and people also say *hacer transbordo*.)
3. **Every station has a picture.** Since the opening, each station has had its own small icon, originally designed by the American designer Lance Wyman. The icon shows something connected with the place's name or history, and it appears on the signs and on the maps in the trains. Wyman later said the icons worked because they didn't need translating, which is also why they help visitors.

Paying is simple: there is one fare for any trip, however far you go and however many times you change lines. In late 2025 the city government said the fare would stay at 5 pesos through 2026. Most people pay with a rechargeable card, the *tarjeta de Movilidad Integrada* (MI card), which also works on the Metrobús and other city services; you can top it up in the stations. On most trains the front carriages are reserved for women and children: look for the signs on the platform (*el andén*).

Here is a simplified diagram of three lines in the city centre. Only some stations are shown.

![A simplified diagram of three Mexico City metro lines. Line 1 (pink) runs left to right: Chapultepec, Insurgentes, Balderas, Salto del Agua, Pino Suárez, with arrows to Observatorio on the left and Pantitlán on the right. Line 3 (olive green) runs top to bottom: Hidalgo, Juárez, Balderas, Centro Médico, with arrows to Indios Verdes at the top and Universidad at the bottom. Line 2 (blue) runs from Cuatro Caminos on the left through Revolución, Hidalgo, Bellas Artes and Allende, then turns down through Zócalo/Tenochtitlan, Pino Suárez and San Antonio Abad towards Tasqueña. Hidalgo, Balderas and Pino Suárez are drawn as larger circles: transfer stations.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### Example 1: From Chapultepec to the Zócalo

You're at Chapultepec (line 1) and want to visit the main square, the Zócalo. Its station is Zócalo/Tenochtitlan on line 2.

1. Find where line 1 meets line 2: Pino Suárez.
2. On line 1, which way is Pino Suárez from Chapultepec? To the right on the diagram, towards the end called Pantitlán. So you take line 1 *dirección Pantitlán*.
3. At Pino Suárez, follow the *Correspondencia Línea 2* signs.
4. On line 2, Zócalo/Tenochtitlan is one stop up, towards Cuatro Caminos. So you take line 2 *dirección Cuatro Caminos* and get off at the first stop.

In Spanish, the directions sound like this: *Tome la línea 1 dirección Pantitlán y bájese en Pino Suárez. Ahí hay correspondencia con la línea 2. Tome la línea 2 dirección Cuatro Caminos y bájese en la siguiente estación.* (*bájese* — get off, the *usted* command of *bajarse*; *la siguiente* — the next.)

### Example 2: From Centro Médico to Bellas Artes

Centro Médico is on line 3; Bellas Artes is on line 2.

1. Lines 3 and 2 meet at Hidalgo.
2. From Centro Médico, Hidalgo is up the line, towards Indios Verdes: *línea 3 dirección Indios Verdes*. You pass Balderas and Juárez and get off at Hidalgo. (The diagram leaves out some stations: on the real line, Hidalgo is the fifth stop.)
3. At Hidalgo, take line 2 towards Tasqueña (Bellas Artes is between Hidalgo and the Zócalo, on the Tasqueña side): *línea 2 dirección Tasqueña*, one stop.

You could also go round by Balderas and Pino Suárez, but that means two changes and more stops. Getting the *dirección* right is the whole skill.

## Buses, peseros and combis

Above ground, a city like this has several kinds of buses:

- *El camión* or *el autobús*: a full-size city bus on a fixed route.
- *El Metrobús*: long buses with their own lanes and closed stations, where you pay with the card before you get on.
- *El pesero*, also called *el micro* or *el microbús*: a smaller, privately run bus on a fixed route. The name comes from *el peso*, the fare these shared rides once cost. The destinations are painted or written on the windscreen, so you read the windscreen, not a timetable.
- *La combi*: a van that works like a small pesero.

On peseros and combis you pay the driver in cash when you get on, and stops are often informal: you wave from the pavement, and to get off you call out to the driver. Two things passengers say are *¡Bajan!* (literally "people are getting off!") and *En la esquina, por favor* — At the corner, please. The fare (*el pasaje*) depends on the distance; after a rise announced in late 2025, the minimum for the first 5 km in Mexico City was 7.50 pesos.

Questions for any bus:

- *¿Este camión va al centro?* — Does this bus go downtown?
- *¿Pasa por la Avenida Reforma?* — Does it go along Avenida Reforma? (*pasar por*, lesson 17)
- *¿Cuánto es el pasaje?* — How much is the fare?
- *¿Dónde me bajo para el museo?* — Where do I get off for the museum?
- *¿Me avisa cuando lleguemos, por favor?* — Will you tell me when we get there, please? (Learn it as a chunk.)

## Taxis and apps

There are three common ways to get a taxi in a big Mexican city:

- *Un taxi de sitio*: from a taxi stand (*el sitio*) with a base and a phone number, often outside hotels, malls and stations. It usually costs a little more.
- *Un taxi libre*: a taxi you stop in the street.
- A ride-hailing app, very widely used in large cities.

Visitors are often advised to use a *sitio* or an app rather than hail one in the street, especially at night; that's a general piece of advice, not a rule, and local people will tell you what they do. In the car: *¿Me lleva a la colonia Roma, por favor?* — Will you take me to Colonia Roma, please? *¿Cuánto me cobra?* — How much will you charge me? (*cobrar*, to charge). *Aquí está bien, gracias.* — Here's fine, thanks.

## Long-distance bus stations

Mexico City has four big long-distance bus stations. Each is named after the direction it serves, so you need to know which one before you buy a ticket:

| Station | Usual name | Serves, for example |
|---|---|---|
| *Terminal del Norte* | Central del Norte | the north: Querétaro, Guanajuato, Monterrey |
| *Terminal del Sur* | Taxqueña (by the metro station spelled Tasqueña) | the south: Cuernavaca, Taxco, Acapulco |
| *Terminal de Oriente* | TAPO | the east and south-east: Puebla, Oaxaca, Veracruz |
| *Terminal del Poniente* | Observatorio | the west: Toluca, Morelia |

*La terminal* is feminine in Mexico and most countries (*la terminal de autobuses*), though Chile, Colombia, Peru and Venezuela prefer *el terminal*. In other Mexican cities you'll often hear *la central de autobuses* or just *la central*. *Oriente* and *poniente* are other words for east and west (also *este* and *oeste*), common in Mexican place names.

## Reading a Mexican address

Mexican addresses follow a fixed order, and two parts surprise visitors: the *colonia* and the inside number.

![An envelope with an invented address, each part underlined in a colour and named on the right. Sra. Laura Méndez Ruiz. Calle Fresno (la calle) 27 (el número exterior), Int. 4 (el número interior). Col. Las Palmas (la colonia). C.P. 62050 (el código postal). Cuernavaca, Morelos (la ciudad, el estado).](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

- *Calle Fresno 27*: the street (or *Av.* for *avenida*) and the building's number, *el número exterior*. The number comes after the name.
- *Int. 4*: *el número interior*, the flat or office inside the building. You'll also see *Depto.* (*departamento*, lesson 10).
- *Col. Las Palmas*: *la colonia*, the named district. It's not optional: many cities have several streets with the same name in different *colonias*, so a taxi driver will always ask *¿En qué colonia?*
- *C.P. 62050*: *el código postal*, five digits.
- *Cuernavaca, Morelos*: the city or municipality and the state. In Mexico City the line has the borough instead, called *la alcaldía*.

Two more abbreviations: *S/N* means *sin número* (no number), common in villages; *esq.* means *esquina*, as in *Hidalgo esq. Morelos* (on the corner of Hidalgo and Morelos). When you give directions to a house, people also say which streets it's between: *entre Juárez y Allende*.

### Example 3: Giving an address to a taxi driver

A friend sends you her address: *Av. Morelos 310, Int. 12, Col. Centro, entre Galeana y Matamoros*. In the taxi you say:

> *Buenas tardes. ¿Me lleva a la Avenida Morelos, número trescientos diez, en la colonia Centro, por favor? Está entre Galeana y Matamoros.*

Notice what you leave out: the inside number (12) is for you, not the driver. And numbers are read as whole numbers (lesson 12): *trescientos diez*, not "three-one-zero".

## Common mistakes

- Looking for "north" or "south" on metro signs. Look for *Dirección* + the last station.
- Getting off at a *correspondencia* station and leaving by the *Salida* signs. To change lines, follow *Correspondencia*.
- Waiting at a bus stop sign for a pesero that stops anywhere, or not calling out to get off. Wave, and say *¡Bajan!* or *En la esquina, por favor.*
- Saying *el terminal* in Mexico. Mexicans say *la terminal* (de autobuses).
- Leaving out the *colonia* in an address. Without it, the driver may not find the street.
- Putting the house number before the street, English-style: *27 Calle Fresno*. In Spanish it's *Calle Fresno 27*.

## Key points

- Metro: lines have a number and a colour; directions are named after the last station (*Dirección Pantitlán*); changes are *correspondencias*; every station has an icon; one flat fare (5 pesos through 2026, per the city government).
- Buses: *el camión / el autobús*, *el Metrobús*, *el pesero* (*micro*), *la combi*. Pay the driver on peseros and combis, and call out *¡Bajan!* to get off. *El pasaje* = the fare.
- Questions: *¿Este camión va a…? ¿Pasa por…? ¿Dónde me bajo? ¿Cuánto es el pasaje?*
- Taxis: *taxi de sitio* (from a stand), *taxi libre* (from the street), or an app.
- Mexico City's long-distance stations are named for directions: Norte, Sur (Taxqueña), Oriente (TAPO), Poniente (Observatorio).
- Addresses: *Calle + número exterior, Int., Col., C.P.*, city and state; *S/N* = no number, *esq.* = corner.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Honors: At the pharmacy and the doctor's
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

In lesson 20 you said what hurts (*Me duele la cabeza*), visited a doctor and heard *Tome una pastilla cada ocho horas*. This honors lesson goes further into a situation every traveller and every resident meets sooner or later: describing symptoms in more detail, understanding what a pharmacist says, reading the instructions on a box or bottle, and knowing where to go and whom to call. It also shows you a very Mexican institution, the doctor's office next to the pharmacy.

This is a language lesson, not medical advice. The doses on the invented label below are there to practise reading; always follow what your own doctor or pharmacist tells you.

## Describing symptoms

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| *la tos* — *tener tos* | cough — to have a cough |
| *toser* | to cough |
| *la garganta* — *me duele la garganta* | throat — I have a sore throat |
| *el catarro* (also *el resfriado*) | cold (the illness) |
| *la alergia* — *tener alergia a…* | allergy — to be allergic to… |
| *mareado* — *estar mareado* | dizzy — to feel dizzy |
| *el síntoma* | symptom (masculine, like *el problema*) |

Some useful patterns:

- *Me siento mal.* — I feel ill. (*sentirse*, to feel; learn *me siento* as a chunk.)
- *Tengo tos y me duele la garganta.* — I have a cough and a sore throat.
- *Estoy un poco mareada.* — I feel a bit dizzy (a woman speaking).
- *Soy alérgico a la penicilina.* / *Tengo alergia a la penicilina.* — I'm allergic to penicillin.
- *Desde hace tres días.* — For three days (literally "since three days ago"). It answers *¿Desde cuándo?* Learn it as a chunk; you'll meet *hace* + time in lesson 21.

In Mexico, *tengo gripa* (lesson 20) is what many people say for any bad cold; *el catarro* or *el resfriado* is a milder cold. And a warning: *estar constipado* is a false friend. In Spain it means having a blocked nose from a cold, not "constipated" (*estreñido*). You'll hear it in Spain more than in Mexico.

A doctor or pharmacist usually starts with *¿Qué tiene?* or *¿Qué le pasa?* — What's the matter? — and then asks:

- *¿Qué síntomas tiene?* — What symptoms do you have?
- *¿Tiene fiebre?* — Do you have a temperature?
- *¿Es alérgico a algún medicamento?* — Are you allergic to any medicine? (*algún* — any)
- *¿Toma alguna medicina?* — Are you taking any medicine?

## At the pharmacy

Mexican pharmacies sell many medicines over the counter, but not all. Since 2010, antibiotics (*los antibióticos*) have been sold only with a doctor's prescription, *la receta* (*receta* also means "recipe"). When the pharmacist asks *¿Tiene receta?*, that's what they mean.

### Example 1: Buying cough syrup

> Farmacéutico: Buenas tardes. ¿Qué le damos?
>
> Clienta: Buenas tardes. Tengo mucha tos desde hace dos días. ¿Tiene algo para la tos?
>
> Farmacéutico: ¿Tiene fiebre?
>
> Clienta: No, fiebre no. Pero me duele un poco la garganta.
>
> Farmacéutico: Mire, este jarabe es muy bueno. Tome diez mililitros cada ocho horas, después de comer.
>
> Clienta: ¿Y si no me siento mejor?
>
> Farmacéutico: Entonces consulte a un médico. Aquí al lado tenemos consultorio.
>
> Clienta: Muy bien, me lo llevo. ¿Cuánto es?
>
> Farmacéutico: Son ciento veinte pesos.

*Pharmacist: Good afternoon. What can we get you? — Customer: Good afternoon. I've had a bad cough for two days. Do you have anything for a cough? — Pharmacist: Do you have a temperature? — Customer: No, no temperature. But my throat hurts a little. — Pharmacist: Look, this syrup is very good. Take ten millilitres every eight hours, after eating. — Customer: And if I don't feel better? — Pharmacist: Then see a doctor. We have a doctor's office right next door. — Customer: Very well, I'll take it. How much is it? — Pharmacist: That's a hundred and twenty pesos.*

Step by step:

1. *¿Qué le damos?* is a typical Mexican shop greeting: literally "What do we give you?"
2. The customer gives the symptom and how long: *tengo mucha tos desde hace dos días*.
3. The pharmacist checks with a question (*¿Tiene fiebre?*) and then gives instructions as *usted* commands: *Mire, tome, consulte*.
4. *Me lo llevo* — I'll take it: a set phrase for buying something (*lo* = it).

## Reading the label

Medicine labels and leaflets use two kinds of instruction. You know the first: the *usted* command (*Tome*, *Consulte a su médico*). The second looks strange at first: *Agítese*, *Consérvese*, *No se deje*. These are commands with *se* joined on, and they don't speak to anyone in particular; they mean "is to be shaken", "is to be kept". This course calls it the **[[impersonal se]]** (grammars often call this use the passive *se*, because the thing, the bottle, is the grammatical subject), and it's typical of labels, signs and instructions. You only need to recognize it.

![The label of an invented cough syrup called TOSINA, 120 ml, marked "producto inventado". Dosis: Adultos: 10 ml cada 8 horas. Niños de 6 a 12 años: 5 ml cada 8 horas. Niños menores de 6 años: consulte a su médico. Agítese antes de usarse. No se deje al alcance de los niños. Consérvese en un lugar fresco y seco. Si los síntomas continúan, consulte a su médico.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### Example 2: What does the label say?

Take the label line by line.

1. *Dosis: Adultos: 10 ml cada 8 horas.* — Dose: adults, 10 ml every 8 hours. (*cada* — every, each.) Every 8 hours means three times a day.
2. *Niños de 6 a 12 años: 5 ml cada 8 horas.* — Children aged 6 to 12: 5 ml every 8 hours.
3. *Niños menores de 6 años: consulte a su médico.* — Children under 6: consult your doctor. (*menores de* — younger than.)
4. *Agítese antes de usarse.* — Shake before use. (*agitar*, to shake; *antes de*, lesson 16.)
5. *No se deje al alcance de los niños.* — Keep out of the reach of children (literally "is not to be left within reach"). This exact sentence is on almost every Mexican medicine.
6. *Consérvese en un lugar fresco y seco.* — Store in a cool, dry place.
7. *Si los síntomas continúan, consulte a su médico.* — If the symptoms continue, see your doctor.

Other phrases you'll see on boxes and prescriptions:

| Label | Meaning |
|---|---|
| *una tableta / una cápsula* | one tablet / one capsule (in speech, *una pastilla*) |
| *por 5 días* | for 5 days |
| *en ayunas* | on an empty stomach |
| *con los alimentos* | with meals (*los alimentos* — food, formal) |
| *antes de dormir* | before going to sleep |
| *Su venta requiere receta médica.* | Sold only with a prescription. |

## The doctor next to the pharmacy

In Mexico many pharmacies, especially the big chains, have a small doctor's office next door or inside: *el consultorio*, officially a *consultorio adyacente a farmacia*. A general doctor sees patients without an appointment, for a low fee (in 2025 reports, often a few dozen pesos; some chains offer it free), and can write a prescription that you then take to the pharmacy counter. The pharmacy association Anafarmex counted about 18,000 of these offices in 2023, giving millions of consultations a month. This is a Mexican pattern; you'll find similar arrangements elsewhere in Latin America, but not everywhere.

People use them for everyday problems: a cold, a sore throat, a stomach upset. For anything serious, a hospital or your own doctor is the place.

## Emergencies: 911

Mexico's national emergency number is **911** (*el nueve once*), the same as in the United States and Canada. It started in 16 states in October 2016 and has covered the whole country since January 2017, replacing several older numbers. It's free and works 24 hours a day for the police, fire and ambulance (*la ambulancia*). In a hospital, the emergency department is called *Urgencias*.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Where to go when you feel ill in Mexico
  accDescr: First ask whether it is an emergency, such as severe pain, an accident or difficulty breathing. If yes, call 911 or go to Urgencias at a hospital. If no, ask whether it is an everyday problem like a cold, a cough or a sore throat. If yes, ask at the pharmacy or see the doctor at the consultorio next to the pharmacy. If no, make an appointment, una cita, with a doctor. If a doctor gives you a receta, take it to the pharmacy.
  A{"Is it an emergency?"} -- "yes" --> B["Call 911 or go to Urgencias"]
  A -- "no" --> C{"An everyday problem: catarro, tos, garganta?"}
  C -- "yes" --> D["Ask at the farmacia, or see the doctor at the consultorio"]
  C -- "no" --> E["Make una cita with a doctor"]
  D --> F["With a receta: buy the medicine at the farmacia"]
  E --> F
```

Phrases for an emergency (*Llame* is an *usted* command, lesson 17):

- *¡Ayuda!* — Help!
- *¡Llame a una ambulancia!* — Call an ambulance!
- *Es una emergencia.* — It's an emergency.
- *Mi amigo está mareado y no puede caminar.* — My friend is dizzy and can't walk.

### Example 3: Calling 911

> Operadora: Nueve once, ¿cuál es su emergencia?
>
> Turista: Buenas noches. Mi esposo está muy mal. Le duele mucho el pecho y está mareado.
>
> Operadora: ¿Dónde están?
>
> Turista: En el hotel Las Flores, Avenida Hidalgo número cuarenta, colonia Centro.
>
> Operadora: Muy bien. La ambulancia va para allá. No cuelgue, por favor.

*Operator: Nine one one, what is your emergency? — Tourist: Good evening. My husband is very ill. His chest hurts a lot and he's dizzy. — Operator: Where are you? — Tourist: At the Hotel Las Flores, Avenida Hidalgo number forty, colonia Centro. — Operator: Very good. The ambulance is on its way. Don't hang up, please.*

(*el pecho* — chest; *va para allá* — is on its way there; *no cuelgue* — don't hang up, a negative command you'll learn at A2.) The tourist gives the three things an operator needs: who, what, and where, with the full address including the *colonia* (lesson 20h1).

## Common mistakes

- *Estoy alergia*. Say *Tengo alergia a…* or *Soy alérgico / alérgica a…*
- *Estoy constipado* for "I'm constipated". In Spain it means you have a cold; constipated is *estreñido*.
- Reading *cada 8 horas* as "8 times a day". It's every 8 hours: three times a day.
- Taking *receta* only as "recipe". At the doctor's and the pharmacy it's a prescription.
- Thinking *Agítese* or *Consérvese* speak to you personally. They're impersonal instructions on labels; when the pharmacist speaks to you, it's *Agite el frasco* (shake the bottle) or *Tome…*
- Assuming you always need an appointment to see a doctor. At a Mexican pharmacy's *consultorio* you usually just wait your turn.

## Key points

- Symptoms: *tengo tos, me duele la garganta, tengo catarro / gripa, estoy mareado, tengo alergia a…, me siento mal*; how long: *desde hace dos días*.
- Doctors and pharmacists ask *¿Qué tiene? ¿Qué le pasa? ¿Tiene fiebre? ¿Es alérgico a algún medicamento?*
- Antibiotics need *una receta* in Mexico (since 2010).
- Labels: *usted* commands (*Tome, Consulte a su médico*) and the impersonal *se* (*Agítese, Consérvese, No se deje al alcance de los niños*); *cada 8 horas, por 5 días, en ayunas, con los alimentos*.
- Many Mexican pharmacies have a *consultorio* next door with a doctor and low fees (a Mexican pattern).
- Emergencies: 911 everywhere in Mexico (since January 2017); hospitals' emergency departments are *Urgencias*.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Talking about the past: the preterite
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Up to now you have talked about the present (*Trabajo en una oficina*), about what you like
(*Me gusta el café*) and about plans (*Voy a visitar a mi abuela*). This module adds the past:
what you did yesterday, where you went on vacation, when you were born.

Spanish has more than one past tense. This lesson teaches the most useful one for Latin
America, the **[[preterite]]** (*el pretérito indefinido*, also called *pretérito perfecto
simple*). It is the past of finished events: *Ayer comí tacos* (Yesterday I ate tacos), *Nací
en 1995* (I was born in 1995), *Fuimos a la playa* (We went to the beach). In Mexico and most
of Latin America it is the everyday past, even for things that happened earlier today. Lesson
22 adds a second past form for experiences, and the honors lesson 24h1 shows you a third one so
it doesn't surprise you in books.

Strictly speaking, the past tenses belong to level A2 in the Instituto Cervantes curriculum.
This course takes the step early because a learner who can't say what they did yesterday is
stuck in very simple conversations. Think of this module as your first step into A2.

## Time words for the past

These words tell you, and the person listening, that a sentence is about finished time:

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| *ayer* | yesterday |
| *anoche* | last night |
| *anteayer* | the day before yesterday |
| *el sábado, el lunes…* | on Saturday, on Monday… (this past one) |
| *la semana pasada* | last week |
| *el mes pasado, el año pasado* | last month, last year |
| *el fin de semana pasado* | last weekend |
| *hace dos días, hace un año* | two days ago, a year ago |
| *en 2020* | in 2020 |
| *una vez* | once, one time |

*Pasado* (last, past) is an adjective, so it agrees with its noun: *el año pasado*, *la
semana pasada*. *Hace* + a length of time means "ago", and the time comes after *hace*: *hace
tres semanas* (three weeks ago). You know *hace* from the weather (*hace calor*); here it is
a fixed pattern, always in the same form.

![A horizontal timeline running from left (long ago) to right (now). Points from left to right: hace dos años, el año pasado, la semana pasada, anteayer, ayer, anoche, and hoy at the right end, where the line meets "now".](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Regular verbs

To make the preterite, take the infinitive, remove *-ar*, *-er* or *-ir*, and add these
endings. The -er and -ir verbs share one set.

| | -ar: *hablar* | -er: *comer* | -ir: *vivir* |
|---|---|---|---|
| yo | hablé | comí | viví |
| tú | hablaste | comiste | viviste |
| él, ella, usted | habló | comió | vivió |
| nosotros | hablamos | comimos | vivimos |
| (vosotros) | (hablasteis) | (comisteis) | (vivisteis) |
| ellos, ellas, ustedes | hablaron | comieron | vivieron |

The *vosotros* forms in brackets are used in Spain; you'll see them in books, but you don't
need to produce them.

![A chart of the regular preterite endings in three columns. -ar: é, aste, ó, amos, aron. -er and -ir share one column: í, iste, ió, imos, ieron. The written accents on é, ó, í and ió are highlighted, with a note that the yo and él forms carry the accent.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Three things to notice:

1. The accents matter. *Hablo* means "I speak", but *habló* means "he spoke" or "you
   (usted) spoke". The only difference is the stress, and the written accent shows it. The
   same goes for *terminé* (I finished) and *termine* (the *usted* command from lesson 17:
   *Termine, por favor*).
2. *Nosotros* looks like the present in -ar and -ir verbs: *hablamos* can be "we speak" or
   "we spoke", *vivimos* "we live" or "we lived". The time words tell you which: *Ayer
   hablamos con Ana* (Yesterday we talked to Ana). The -er verbs differ: *comemos* (we eat),
   *comimos* (we ate).
3. Stem changes disappear in -ar and -er verbs: *encontrar* has *encuentro* in the
   present, but the preterite is regular: *encontré, encontraste, encontró*. The same goes for
   *pensar* (*pensé*), *volver* (*volví*) and *entender* (*entendí*).

Examples:

- *Anoche terminé el libro.* — Last night I finished the book.
- *¿A qué hora regresaste a casa?* — What time did you get back home?
- *Mi hermana ganó un premio en la escuela.* — My sister won a prize at school.
- *Decidimos ir al cine.* — We decided to go to the movies.
- *¿Recibieron mi mensaje?* — Did you (all) get my message?
- *Olvidé las llaves en el carro.* — I forgot the keys in the car.
- *Nací en Guadalajara en 1998.* — I was born in Guadalajara in 1998.

Spanish has no helper word like English "did" in questions or negatives. "Did you finish?" is
just *¿Terminaste?*, and "I didn't finish" is *No terminé*.

### Spelling changes in the yo form

Spanish spelling shows the sound. Before *e*, the letters *c*, *g* and *z* would change their
sound or break a spelling rule, so three groups of -ar verbs adjust their spelling in the *yo*
form only (you saw this in the vocabulary of lessons 04, 12, 15 and 17):

| Verb ends in | yo | the other forms |
|---|---|---|
| -car: *buscar, tocar, practicar* | *busqué, toqué, practiqué* | *buscaste, buscó…* |
| -gar: *llegar, pagar, jugar* | *llegué, pagué, jugué* | *llegaste, llegó…* |
| -zar: *empezar, almorzar, cruzar* | *empecé, almorcé, crucé* | *empezaste, empezó…* |

The sound doesn't change: *busqué* sounds like *busc-* + *é*. Only the spelling does.

### Two smaller patterns

- *i* becomes *y* between vowels in the *él* and *ellos* forms: *leer → leyó, leyeron* (and
  *leí, leíste, leímos* with an accent on the *í*). *Creer* and *oír* do the same.
- -ir verbs that change their stem in the present change again in the preterite, but only
  in the *él* and *ellos* forms, and only by one step: e → i, o → u. *Pedir → pidió,
  pidieron*; *dormir → durmió, durmieron*; *preferir → prefirió*. The other persons are
  regular: *pedí, dormiste*.

## The key irregular verbs

The verbs people use most are irregular in the past, as in English (went, had, did). Learn
them as three groups.

### ser and ir: one set of forms

*Ser* (to be) and *ir* (to go) have the same preterite. The sentence tells you which verb it
is.

| | ser / ir |
|---|---|
| yo | fui |
| tú | fuiste |
| él, ella, usted | fue |
| nosotros | fuimos |
| ellos, ellas, ustedes | fueron |

- *Fui al mercado.* — I went to the market. (*ir*: a place follows with *a*)
- *Fue un día increíble.* — It was an incredible day. (*ser*: a description follows)
- *¿Cómo fue la excursión?* — How was the trip?

### The strong preterite: a new stem, no accents

A group of very common verbs takes a new stem and its own endings, with no written accents at
all. This is the **[[strong preterite]]**. The endings are *-e, -iste, -o, -imos, -ieron*.

| infinitive | new stem | yo | él, ella, usted | ellos |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| *tener* | tuv- | tuve | tuvo | tuvieron |
| *estar* | estuv- | estuve | estuvo | estuvieron |
| *poder* | pud- | pude | pudo | pudieron |
| *venir* | vin- | vine | vino | vinieron |
| *hacer* | hic- | hice | hizo | hicieron |

The full table for *tener*: *tuve, tuviste, tuvo, tuvimos, tuvieron*. The others work the
same way. *Hizo* is written with *z* so that it still sounds like *hic-* (*hico* would sound
like a *k*).

![A chart of the strong preterite. On the left, five verbs with their new stems: tener to tuv-, estar to estuv-, poder to pud-, venir to vin-, hacer to hic-. An arrow joins them to the shared endings -e, -iste, -o, -imos, -ieron, marked "no accents". An example row shows tuve, tuviste, tuvo, tuvimos, tuvieron, and a note says hic- plus -o is spelled hizo.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

- *Ayer tuve mucho trabajo.* — Yesterday I had a lot of work.
- *¿Dónde estuviste el fin de semana?* — Where were you at the weekend?
- *No pude dormir anoche.* — I couldn't sleep last night.
- *Mis primos vinieron de Monterrey.* — My cousins came from Monterrey.
- *¿Qué hiciste el sábado?* — What did you do on Saturday?

### dar and ver: short and plain

*Dar* (to give) and *ver* (to see, to watch) take the -er/-ir endings but with no written
accents: the forms that would carry one (*di, dio, vi, vio*) have only one syllable, and
one-syllable words don't take an accent:

| | dar | ver |
|---|---|---|
| yo | di | vi |
| tú | diste | viste |
| él, ella, usted | dio | vio |
| nosotros | dimos | vimos |
| ellos, ellas, ustedes | dieron | vieron |

- *Le di un regalo a mi mamá.* — I gave my mom a present. (*le* = to her; take it as part of
  the chunk for now)
- *Vimos una película muy divertida.* — We watched a very funny movie.

## Telling what happened

To tell a short story, put the events in order with the words from lesson 16 (*primero,
luego, después, finalmente*) and two new ones: *entonces* (then, so) and *de repente*
(suddenly). *Durante* means "during" or "for": *durante el viaje* (during the trip),
*durante dos horas* (for two hours).

- *Primero fuimos al museo. Luego comimos en el centro. De repente empezó a llover, entonces
  regresamos al hotel.* — First we went to the museum. Then we ate downtown. Suddenly it
  started to rain, so we went back to the hotel.

*Pasarla bien* means "to have a good time" in Mexico and much of Latin America (Spain says
*pasarlo bien*). The *la* stays the same; only *pasar* changes: *La pasé muy bien* (I had a
great time), *¿La pasaron bien?* (Did you all have a good time?).

## Dialogue: Monday morning

Valeria and Andrés work in the same office in Guadalajara.

> Valeria: ¡Hola, Andrés! ¿Qué hiciste el fin de semana?
>
> Andrés: Fui a Tequila con mi familia. Hicimos una excursión en tren.
>
> Valeria: ¡Qué padre! ¿La pasaron bien?
>
> Andrés: Sí, la pasamos muy bien. Vimos los campos de agave y comimos en el pueblo. Fue
> increíble.
>
> Valeria: ¿Y compraste algún recuerdo?
>
> Andrés: Sí, le di una taza a mi papá. ¿Y tú? ¿Saliste?
>
> Valeria: No, el sábado tuve que trabajar. Pero el domingo vino mi hermana y vimos una
> película. Luego, de repente, se fue la luz.
>
> Andrés: ¡No! ¿Y entonces?
>
> Valeria: Entonces jugamos a las cartas durante dos horas. ¡Fue muy divertido!

Translation:

> Valeria: Hi, Andrés! What did you do at the weekend?
>
> Andrés: I went to Tequila with my family. We took a trip by train.
>
> Valeria: Cool! Did you have a good time?
>
> Andrés: Yes, we had a great time. We saw the agave fields and ate in the town. It was
> incredible.
>
> Valeria: And did you buy a souvenir?
>
> Andrés: Yes, I gave my dad a mug. And you? Did you go out?
>
> Valeria: No, on Saturday I had to work. But on Sunday my sister came and we watched a movie.
> Then suddenly the power went out.
>
> Andrés: No! And then?
>
> Valeria: Then we played cards for two hours. It was a lot of fun!

Notes: Tequila is a real town in the state of Jalisco, near Guadalajara, known for its agave
fields and the drink named after it. *¡Qué padre!* is a Mexican way to say "cool!" or "how
great!" (*padre* here has nothing to do with fathers). *Jugar a las cartas* is "to play cards". *Algún* is "some, any" before a
masculine noun. *La taza* is a mug or cup. *Se fue la luz* means "the power went out" (*la
luz* = light, electricity). *Tuve que trabajar* is *tener que* (lesson 20) in the past.

## Pronunciation

- Stress the accented syllable firmly: *ha-BLÓ*, *co-MIÓ*, *ter-mi-NÉ*. Compare *HA-blo*
  (I speak) and *ha-BLÓ* (he spoke). Saying them the same way changes the meaning.
- *-ió* is one syllable: *vi-vió*, *re-ci-bió*, not *re-ci-bi-ó*.
- The strong forms are stressed on the stem, with no accent: *TU-ve*, *TU-vo*, *HI-ce*,
  *PU-de*. Don't say *tu-VÓ*.
- *Anteayer* has four syllables: *an-te-a-YER*. *Increíble* has the stress on the *í*:
  *in-cre-Í-ble*.

## Common mistakes

- Leaving out the accent: *hablo* (I speak) is not *habló* (he spoke). In writing and in
  speech, the stress matters.
- Adding accents to the strong forms: *tuve, hizo, pudo, vino* never have one, and neither do
  *fui, fue, di, dio, vi, vio*.
- Treating *hacer* as regular: not *hací* or *hació*, but *hice* and *hizo*.
- Using "did" thinking: *¿Terminaste?* (not *¿Hiciste terminar?*), *No fui* (not *No hice ir*).
- Forgetting the yo spelling change: *busqué, llegué, empecé* (not *buscé, llegé, empezé*).
- Copying English word order with *hace*: "two days ago" is *hace dos días*, not *dos días
  hace*.

## Key points

- The preterite tells finished events at a finished time. It is the everyday past in Mexico
  and most of Latin America.
- Regular endings: -ar *é, aste, ó, amos, aron*; -er/-ir *í, iste, ió, imos, ieron*. The
  accents on *é, ó, í, ió* change the meaning.
- yo spelling changes: *-qué, -gué, -cé*.
- *Ser* and *ir* share *fui, fuiste, fue, fuimos, fueron*.
- Strong preterite, no accents: *tuve, estuve, pude, vine, hice (hizo)*; and *di*, *vi*.
- Time words: *ayer, anoche, anteayer, la semana pasada, el año pasado, hace dos días*.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson. The past reference sheet has every table from this lesson in one place.

lessons.title: Experiences and today: the present perfect
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

In lesson 21 you learned the preterite for finished events: *Ayer fui al museo* (Yesterday I
went to the museum). This lesson adds a second past form, the **[[present perfect]]** (*el
pretérito perfecto*): *He ido al museo muchas veces* (I have been to the museum many times).

It looks and works much like English "I have done". You use it to talk about experiences in
your life up to now (*¿Has probado el mole?* Have you tried mole?), and with *ya* (already)
and *todavía no* (not yet). You also learn the main difference between Mexico and Spain: in
Spain the perfect is used for things that happened today, while Mexico normally uses the
preterite. Both are correct Spanish, and you'll hear both.

## How the present perfect is built

The present perfect has two parts:

1. a present form of *haber*, the **[[auxiliary verb]]** (a helper verb that carries the person);
2. the **[[past participle]]** of the main verb, which never changes.

| | haber | + participle |
|---|---|---|
| yo | he | hablado |
| tú | has | comido |
| él, ella, usted | ha | vivido |
| nosotros | hemos | estado |
| (vosotros) | (habéis) | |
| ellos, ellas, ustedes | han | ido |

Any form of *haber* goes with any participle: *he hablado, has hablado, ha hablado…*

*Haber* is a new verb, but you met one of its forms long ago: *hay* (there is, there are, from
lesson 10) is a special form of *haber*. In the perfect you only need the five forms in the
table.

### Regular participles

- -ar verbs: stem + *-ado*: *hablar → hablado, estudiar → estudiado, viajar → viajado*
- -er and -ir verbs: stem + *-ido*: *comer → comido, vivir → vivido, tener → tenido, ir →
  ido, ser → sido, estar → estado*

When the stem ends in a vowel (*a, e, o*), the *í* takes a written accent so it is a separate
syllable: *leer → leído, creer → creído, oír → oído*.

### Irregular participles

A short list of common verbs has irregular participles. Learn them as a set; they are among
the most frequent words in Spanish.

| infinitive | participle | | infinitive | participle |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| *hacer* | hecho (done, made) | | *escribir* | escrito (written) |
| *decir* | dicho (said, told) | | *abrir* | abierto (opened) |
| *ver* | visto (seen) | | *volver* | vuelto (come back) |
| *poner* | puesto (put) | | *romper* | roto (broken) |

![A chart showing how the present perfect is built. On the left, the five forms of haber: he, has, ha, hemos, han. A plus sign joins them to the participle. Regular participles: -ar becomes -ado, as in hablado; -er and -ir become -ido, as in comido and vivido. A box of irregular participles lists hecho, dicho, visto, puesto, escrito, abierto, vuelto and roto. A note says the participle never changes.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### Three rules of word order

1. The participle never changes. It doesn't agree with the subject: *Ella ha comido*, *Ellas
   han comido* (not *comida*, *comidas*).
2. Nothing goes between *haber* and the participle. *No* and pronouns go before *haber*: *No
   he comido. ¿Te has levantado?*
3. In questions, the verb usually comes before the subject, if there is one: *¿Ha llegado tu
   hermano?* (Has your brother arrived?)

## Use 1: experiences

The perfect asks and tells about life experience, without saying when: "Have you ever…?",
"I've never…", "I've done it many times".

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| *alguna vez* | ever (once or more) |
| *nunca* | never |
| *una vez* | once |
| *muchas veces* | many times, often |
| *hasta ahora* | so far, until now |

- *¿Has estado alguna vez en el extranjero?* — Have you ever been abroad?
- *Nunca he probado el chile habanero.* — I've never tried habanero chili.
- *Hemos visitado las pirámides de Teotihuacán dos veces.* — We've visited the pyramids of
  Teotihuacán twice.
- *¿Has oído esta canción?* — Have you heard this song?
- *Mi abuelo ha contado esa historia muchas veces.* — My grandfather has told that story many
  times.
- *Hasta ahora, la experiencia ha sido increíble.* — So far, the experience has been
  incredible.

With *nunca* before the verb, no *no* is needed: *Nunca he montado a caballo* (I've never
ridden a horse). If *nunca* comes after, *no* goes first: *No he montado nunca a caballo.*

When you say *when* something happened, switch to the preterite: *¿Has estado en Cuba? —
Sí, fui en 2019.* (Have you been to Cuba? — Yes, I went in 2019.) The perfect asks about the
experience; the preterite tells the finished event at a finished time.

## Use 2: ya and todavía no

*Ya* means "already" (or "yet" in a question); *todavía no* means "not yet".

- *¿Ya has hecho la tarea? — Sí, ya la he hecho.* — Have you already done the homework? —
  Yes, I've already done it.
- *¿Has leído la novela? — Todavía no.* — Have you read the novel? — Not yet.
- *Todavía no les he dicho nada a mis papás.* — I haven't said anything to my parents yet.
  (*les* = to them; Spanish normally adds it even when *a mis papás* follows. Take it as part
  of the chunk for now, like *le* in lesson 21.)

*Todavía* alone means "still": *Todavía vivo con mi familia* (I still live with my family).

In Mexico you will very often hear the preterite with *ya*: *¿Ya comiste?* (Have you eaten
yet?) *Sí, ya comí.* Both *¿Ya comiste?* and *¿Ya has comido?* are correct; the first sounds
more everyday in Mexico.

## Mexico and Spain: which past for today?

This is the biggest difference between Spain's Spanish and Latin American Spanish in the
past tenses.

- In most of Spain, things that happened today, this week or this year usually
  take the perfect: *Hoy he comido paella. Esta mañana he hablado con mi jefe.*
- In Mexico and most of Latin America, any finished event normally takes the preterite, even
  today's: *Hoy comí tacos. Esta mañana hablé con mi jefe.*

Both sides use the perfect for experiences (*¿Has estado en Perú?*) and with *todavía no*.
This course follows Mexican usage: for a finished event, use the preterite. Recognize the
Spain pattern when you hear it (the DELE exam's texts and recordings are mostly
based on Spain's Spanish; see lesson 24).

You may also notice that in Mexico the perfect often describes something that has been going
on or repeating up to now: *Últimamente he trabajado mucho* (I've been working a lot lately).
That is a tendency, not a strict rule.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Preterite or present perfect?
  accDescr: A decision chart. First question: is it about a life experience with no time given, or does it use ya, todavía no, nunca or alguna vez? If yes, use the present perfect, for example he probado or todavía no he terminado. If no, next question: is it a finished event? If yes, use the preterite, for example ayer comí or en 2019 fui. A side note says that in Spain, events of today or this week often take the perfect, for example hoy he comido, while Mexico uses the preterite, hoy comí.
  A["Experience with no time given, or ya / todavía no / nunca / alguna vez?"] -- yes --> P["Present perfect: he probado, todavía no he terminado"]
  A -- no --> B["A finished event (ayer, el sábado, en 2019, hoy...)?"]
  B -- yes --> T["Preterite: ayer comí, en 2019 fui, hoy comí"]
  T -.- N["Spain: today or this week often takes the perfect: hoy he comido"]
```

## The new verbs

*Decir* (to say, to tell) is irregular in the present, the preterite and the participle:

| | present | preterite |
|---|---|---|
| yo | digo | dije |
| tú | dices | dijiste |
| él, ella, usted | dice | dijo |
| nosotros | decimos | dijimos |
| ellos, ellas, ustedes | dicen | dijeron |

Participle *dicho*; *tú* command *di* (*Di la verdad*, Tell the truth). *Decir que* = to say
that: *Dice que el plato es muy picante* (He says that the dish is very spicy).

*Oír* (to hear) has a *g* in *yo* and a *y* in several forms: present *oigo, oyes, oye,
oímos, oyen*; preterite *oí, oíste, oyó, oímos, oyeron*; participle *oído*. *Escuchar*
(lesson 04) is to listen on purpose; *oír* is to hear. *¡Oye!* (Hey! Listen!) is the *tú*
command; *oiga* (lesson 17) is the *usted* one.

*Probar* (to try, to taste) and *contar* (to tell, to count) change o → ue in the present,
like *poder*: *pruebo, pruebas, prueba, probamos, prueban*; *cuento, cuentas, cuenta,
contamos, cuentan*. Their preterites and participles are regular: *probé, probado; conté,
contado*. *Romper* (to break) is regular apart from its participle *roto*: *He roto un plato*
(I've broken a plate).

## Dialogue: have you ever…?

Emily, from Canada, is studying in Mexico City. Her friend Diego asks her about her first
months.

> Diego: Oye, Emily, ¿ya has probado el mole?
>
> Emily: Todavía no. ¿Es muy picante?
>
> Diego: Depende del plato. Mi mamá hace un mole poblano increíble. ¿Y has visitado las
> pirámides de Teotihuacán?
>
> Emily: Sí, fui en marzo con mi curso. Fue una experiencia increíble. ¿Tú has subido a la
> Pirámide del Sol?
>
> Diego: Muchas veces. Mi papá dice que la subí por primera vez a los seis años.
>
> Emily: ¡Qué bonito! Yo nunca he visto un volcán de cerca.
>
> Diego: Desde el centro de la ciudad, en un día claro, se ve el Popocatépetl. ¿No lo has
> visto?
>
> Emily: No, hasta ahora siempre ha estado nublado.
>
> Diego: Bueno, el domingo vamos a comer mole en casa de mi mamá. ¡Y luego al volcán!

Translation:

> Diego: Hey, Emily, have you tried mole yet?
>
> Emily: Not yet. Is it very spicy?
>
> Diego: It depends on the dish. My mom makes an amazing mole poblano. And have you visited
> the pyramids of Teotihuacán?
>
> Emily: Yes, I went in March with my class. It was an incredible experience. Have you climbed
> the Pyramid of the Sun?
>
> Diego: Many times. My dad says I climbed it for the first time when I was six.
>
> Emily: How lovely! I've never seen a volcano up close.
>
> Diego: From downtown, on a clear day, you can see Popocatépetl. Haven't you seen it?
>
> Emily: No, so far it has always been cloudy.
>
> Diego: Well, on Sunday we're going to eat mole at my mom's house. And then to the volcano!

Notes: *mole* is a family of thick Mexican sauces made with chilies and many other
ingredients; *mole poblano* comes from the state of Puebla. Teotihuacán is an ancient city
about 50 km northeast of Mexico City; its Pyramid of the Sun is one of the largest pyramids
in the Americas. Popocatépetl is an active volcano southeast of the city. *Depende de* = it
depends on. *Subir a* = to climb. *A los seis años* = at the age of six. *De cerca* = up
close. *Se ve* = you can see, it can be seen. *Lo* and *la* = it (pronouns that go before the verb).

## Pronunciation

- *H* is silent: *he, has, ha, hemos, han* sound like "eh, ahs, ah, EH-mos, ahn". *Hecho* is
  "EH-cho".
- In Mexico the *d* of *-ado* is kept but said softly, like the "th" in "this": *ha-BLA-do*.
  In Spain and the Caribbean you'll often hear it drop in fast speech (*hablao*); don't copy
  that in writing.
- *Oído* and *leído* have three syllables: *o-Í-do*, *le-Í-do*. The accent keeps the *í* apart.
- *Volcán* and *canción* are stressed on the last syllable, so they need the accent; the
  plurals *volcanes* and *canciones* don't (lesson 01).

## Common mistakes

- Using *tener* as the helper. "I have eaten" is *he comido*, never *tengo comido*.
- Making the participle agree: *Ellas han llegado* (not *llegadas*).
- Splitting the two parts: *Nunca he comido* or *No he comido nunca*, not *He nunca comido*.
- Regular forms for irregular participles: *hecho, dicho, visto, puesto, escrito, abierto,
  vuelto, roto* (not *hacido, decido, vido, ponido*).
- Using the perfect with a finished time in Latin American Spanish: *Ayer fui al cine*, not
  *Ayer he ido al cine* (standard Spanish in Spain doesn't accept it either).

## Key points

- Present perfect = *he, has, ha, hemos, han* + past participle (*-ado*, *-ido*).
- Irregular participles: *hecho, dicho, visto, puesto, escrito, abierto, vuelto, roto*.
- The participle never changes, and nothing goes between the two parts.
- Use it for experiences (*alguna vez, nunca, muchas veces, hasta ahora*) and with *ya* /
  *todavía no*.
- For a finished event, Mexico uses the preterite, even for today (*Hoy comí*); Spain often
  uses the perfect (*Hoy he comido*). Default to the preterite.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Linking ideas and writing short messages
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

So far most of your sentences have been short and separate: *Fui al mercado. Compré fruta.
Regresé a casa.* Real messages join ideas together: "I went to the market, but it was closed, so
I went to the supermarket." This lesson gives you the small words that join ideas, then shows
you how to write the texts an A1 learner writes most: a message or e-mail to a friend, a
polite e-mail to a school or office, and a form with your personal details. These are also
the two kinds of writing in the DELE A1 exam (lesson 24).

## Linking words

A **[[connector]]** is a word that joins two ideas and shows how they relate: adding, contrasting,
giving a reason or a result. You already know several of them.

| connector | meaning | example |
|---|---|---|
| *y* | and | *Compré pan y leche.* |
| *o* | or | *¿Quieres café o té?* |
| *pero* | but | *Es caro, pero es muy bueno.* |
| *porque* | because | *No fui porque tuve que trabajar.* |
| *también* | also, too | *Ana habla inglés. También habla francés.* |
| *tampoco* | not … either, neither | *No me gusta el frío. — A mí tampoco.* |
| *además* | besides, also, what's more | *El hotel es barato. Además, está cerca de la playa.* |
| *entonces* | so, then | *Llovió mucho, entonces nos quedamos en casa.* |

- *Además* adds a stronger, extra point, often at the start of a new sentence, followed by a
  comma.
- *Entonces* gives a result ("so") or the next step in a story ("then"). In writing, *por eso*
  (that's why) is also common; it's two words you know: *por* + *eso*.
- *Porque* (because, one word, no accent) answers *¿por qué?* (why?, two words, accent). Keep
  them apart: *¿Por qué estudias español? — Porque quiero viajar a México.*

### y becomes e, o becomes u

Two small changes keep the words from melting into the next sound:

- *y* becomes *e* before a word that starts with the sound *i* (spelled *i-* or *hi-*):
  *Fernando e Isabel*, *padres e hijos*, *español e inglés*. But *agua y hielo* (ice) keeps *y*,
  because *hie-* starts with a different sound.
- *o* becomes *u* before a word that starts with the sound *o* (*o-* or *ho-*): *siete u
  ocho*, *uno u otro*, *mujeres u hombres*.

### cuando and ¿cuándo?

*Cuando* without an accent means "when" inside a sentence; it joins two events. *¿Cuándo?*
with an accent is the question word from lesson 04.

- *Cuando llegué a casa, llamé a mi mamá.* — When I got home, I called my mom.
- *Me gusta caminar cuando hace buen tiempo.* — I like walking when the weather is nice.
- *¿Cuándo regresaste?* — When did you get back?

The same goes for *que* (that) and *¿qué?* (what?): *Creo que es tarde* (I think that it's
late) but *¿Qué hora es?*

### Giving your opinion: creo que

*Creo que* (I think that, I believe that) introduces an opinion. In Spanish the *que* can't be
left out, as it often is in English ("I think it's late").

- *Creo que el examen es el lunes.* — I think the exam is on Monday.
- *¿Va a llover? — Creo que sí. / Creo que no.* — Is it going to rain? — I think so. / I
  don't think so.

*Creer* is regular in the present (*creo, crees, cree…*), but in the preterite the *i* becomes
*y* like *leer*: *creí, creíste, creyó, creímos, creyeron*. Participle *creído*.

## Messages and e-mails

Every message has the same four parts: a greeting (*el saludo*), the body (*el cuerpo*), a
closing phrase (*la despedida*) and your name or signature (*la firma*).

![An e-mail on a screen. At the top, the fields Para (to) and Asunto (subject). Below, labels at the side mark the subject line (el asunto) and the four parts: the greeting "Querida Sofía:" (el saludo), the body of three short sentences (el cuerpo), the closing "Un abrazo," (la despedida) and the signature "Lucía" (la firma).](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

| | informal (*tú*) | formal (*usted*) |
|---|---|---|
| greeting | *Querida Ana:* / *Querido Pablo:* / *Hola, Ana:* | *Estimado señor:* / *Estimada señora López:* / *A quien corresponda:* |
| closing | *Un abrazo,* / *Saludos,* / *Besos,* | *Atentamente,* / *Saludos cordiales,* |

- After the greeting, Spanish uses a colon, not a comma: *Querida Ana:*, *Estimado señor:*.
  The next line starts with a capital letter. In quick informal messages you'll also see a
  comma, copied from English, but the colon is the standard.
- *Querido* (dear) agrees with the person: *querido Pablo, querida Ana, queridos amigos*. So
  does *estimado*: *estimada señora*, *estimados señores*.
- *A quien corresponda* ("to whom it may concern") is common in Mexico when you don't know the
  person's name.
- *Besos* (kisses) is only for family and close friends. *Un abrazo* (a hug) is warm and safe
  with most friends. *Atentamente* (yours sincerely) ends a formal e-mail.
- Choose *tú* or *usted* at the start and keep it to the end: *¿Cómo estás?* in an informal
  message, *¿Me puede mandar…?* (Could you send me…?) in a formal one.

### An informal e-mail

> Querida Sofía:
>
> ¿Cómo estás? Te mando unas fotos de mi viaje a Oaxaca. Fui con mis papás y la pasamos muy
> bien. Comimos mole y visitamos Monte Albán. Además, compré un regalo para ti. ¿Cuándo
> nos vemos?
>
> Un abrazo,
>
> Lucía

Translation:

> Dear Sofía,
>
> How are you? I'm sending you some photos of my trip to Oaxaca. I went with my parents and we
> had a great time. We ate mole and visited Monte Albán. What's more, I bought a present for
> you. When shall we meet?
>
> Hugs,
>
> Lucía

*Te mando* = I'm sending you; *nos vemos* = we see each other, we meet. Monte Albán is an
ancient Zapotec city on a hilltop near the city of Oaxaca.

### A formal e-mail

> Estimada señora Ramírez:
>
> Me llamo Daniel Harris y quiero estudiar en su escuela. Tengo dos preguntas: ¿cuándo empieza
> el próximo curso de español? ¿Hay clases por la tarde? Trabajo por las mañanas; por eso,
> no puedo estudiar antes de las tres. Gracias por su respuesta.
>
> Atentamente,
>
> Daniel Harris

Translation:

> Dear Mrs Ramírez,
>
> My name is Daniel Harris and I want to study at your school. I have two questions: when does
> the next Spanish course start? Are there classes in the afternoon? I work in the mornings;
> that's why I can't study before three. Thank you for your reply.
>
> Yours sincerely,
>
> Daniel Harris

*Su escuela* is "your school" for *usted* (lesson 06).

### Short messages for every day

- *¡Felicidades!* — Congratulations! (in Mexico also a common way to say "Happy birthday!")
- *Lo siento, no puedo ir.* — I'm sorry, I can't go.
- *Gracias por la invitación.* — Thanks for the invitation.
- *¿Recibiste mi mensaje?* — Did you get my message?
- *Te mando la respuesta mañana.* — I'll send you the answer tomorrow.

*Mandar* (to send) is the everyday Mexican word; *enviar* means the same and is a little more
formal. *El correo* is the mail, and also e-mail; *el correo electrónico* (lesson 03) is the
full name.

## Filling in a form

Forms (*formularios*) ask for the same details again and again. To fill in a form is *llenar
un formulario* in Mexico (Spain: *rellenar*).

![A registration form for a language school. Fields: Nombre, Apellido(s), Fecha de nacimiento with 14/02/1990, Nacionalidad with canadiense, Estado civil with soltera, Dirección, Código postal with 06700, Correo electrónico, Curso with Español A1, and a line for the Firma.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

| field | what to write | example |
|---|---|---|
| *Nombre* | first name | *Emily* |
| *Apellido(s)* | surname(s) | *Clark* |
| *Fecha de nacimiento* | date of birth: day/month/year | *14/02/1990* |
| *Nacionalidad* | nationality, lowercase | *canadiense* |
| *Estado civil* | marital status | *soltera* (single), *casada* (married) |
| *Dirección* | street address | *Calle Durango 25* |
| *Código postal* | postal code (five digits in Mexico) | *06700* |
| *Firma* | signature | (sign your name) |

- Dates are written day first: *14/02/1990* is 14 February 1990, and *05/03/2025* is 5 March
  2025, not May 3.
- Adjectives agree with you: a woman writes *soltera, casada*; a man *soltero, casado*.
- To sign is *firmar*: *Firme aquí, por favor* (Sign here, please).

At the school office, the conversation might go like this:

> Secretaria: Buenos días. ¿Quiere inscribirse en un curso?
>
> Emily: Sí. Ya llené el formulario, pero tengo un problema: no sé qué es "estado civil".
>
> Secretaria: Es si usted es soltera o casada.
>
> Emily: Ah, soltera. ¿Y aquí?
>
> Secretaria: Aquí va su firma. Firme abajo, por favor.

Translation:

> Secretary: Good morning. Would you like to sign up for a course?
>
> Emily: Yes. I've already filled in the form, but I have a problem: I don't know what "estado
> civil" is.
>
> Secretary: It's whether you are single or married.
>
> Emily: Ah, single. And here?
>
> Secretary: Your signature goes here. Sign at the bottom, please.

*Inscribirse* = to sign up, to enroll; *abajo* = below, at the bottom.

## Pronunciation

- *Atentamente* has five syllables, stressed on *-men-*: *a-ten-ta-MEN-te*. All -mente
  adverbs keep the stress of the adjective and add a second one on *-men-*.
- *Felicidades*: *fe-li-ci-DA-des*, with *c* as *s* (Latin American seseo).
- *Además* is stressed on the last syllable, so it has an accent: *a-de-MÁS*.
- *Código* is stressed on the first syllable: *CÓ-di-go*.

## Common mistakes

- A comma after the greeting in a formal letter: write *Estimado señor:*, not *Estimado
  señor,*.
- Leaving out *que*: *Creo que sí*, *Creo que es caro* (not *Creo es caro*).
- *Porque* for questions: *¿Por qué?* asks; *porque* answers.
- Forgetting *y → e* and *o → u*: *Ana e Inés*, *siete u ocho*.
- Mixing *tú* and *usted* in one message: *Estimada señora: ¿Me puedes…?* Choose *usted* and
  stay with it: *¿Me puede…?*
- Writing the date English-style: 02/14/1990 on a Mexican form is read as the 2nd of the
  14th month.

## Key points

- Connectors: *y, o, pero, porque, también, tampoco, además, entonces*. *Y → e* before *i-*,
  *o → u* before *o-*.
- *Cuando* (when, joining two ideas) vs *¿cuándo?* (question). *Creo que* + opinion; keep the
  *que*.
- Messages: greeting with a colon, body, closing, name. Informal: *Querida Ana: … Un abrazo*.
  Formal: *Estimado señor: … Atentamente*.
- Forms: *nombre, apellido, fecha de nacimiento (day/month/year), nacionalidad, estado civil,
  dirección, código postal, firma*.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson.

lessons.title: The DELE A1 exam and review
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

This is the last core lesson of the course. It does four things: it explains what level A1
means and what you can now do; it describes the official A1 exam, the DELE A1 of the
Instituto Cervantes, with strategies for each part; it adds the words you need for exam
instructions and for asking for help; and it reviews the whole course with pointers back to
the lessons. The questions at the end of this lesson cover the whole course, so use them as a
final check.

You don't have to take an exam. But the free official model exam is a good way to see for
yourself whether you have reached A1.

## What A1 means

The levels A1 to C2 come from the Common European Framework of Reference for Languages
(CEFR), which the Instituto Cervantes uses for its exams and its curriculum. A1 is the first
level. In plain words, a learner at A1 can:

- understand and use very common everyday phrases about concrete needs: food, shopping,
  times, directions, prices;
