- introduce themselves and others, and ask and answer simple questions about where someone
  lives, the people they know and the things they have;
- have a simple conversation, as long as the other person speaks slowly and clearly and is
  ready to help.

Nobody expects an A1 speaker to follow fast native conversation; asking for help is part of
the level, and this lesson gives you the words for it.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: The six CEFR levels
  accDescr: Three groups of levels from bottom to top. Basic user: A1 and A2. Then independent user: B1 and B2. Then proficient user: C1 and C2. A note marks A1 as the level this course reaches, with a first step into A2 through the past tenses.
  A["Basic user: A1, A2"] --> B["Independent user: B1, B2"] --> C["Proficient user: C1, C2"]
  Y["This course: A1, plus a first step into A2 (the past tenses)"] -.- A
```

## The DELE A1

The DELE (*Diplomas de Español como Lengua Extranjera*) are the official Spanish diplomas,
awarded by the Instituto Cervantes on behalf of Spain's Ministry of Education. The diplomas
don't expire. There is a separate version of A1 for school students; this lesson describes
the one for adults.

The exam has four tests (*pruebas*). The figures below come from the official exam guide
(version 2020), described in this course's own words.

| test | time | tasks | points |
|---|---|---|---|
| Reading (*Comprensión de lectura*) | 45 minutes | 4 | 25 |
| Listening (*Comprensión auditiva*) | 25 minutes | 4 | 25 |
| Writing (*Expresión e interacción escritas*) | 25 minutes | 2 | 25 |
| Speaking (*Expresión e interacción orales*) | 10 minutes, after 10 minutes to prepare | 3 | 25 |

The four tests give 100 points, but there is no overall pass mark. Instead, the tests are put
into two groups of 50 points:

- group 1: reading + writing;
- group 2: listening + speaking.

To pass you need at least 30 points in each group. The result is simply *Apto* (pass) or
*No apto* (fail); there are no grades. A very good score in one group can't make up for a
weak one in the other: 45 points in group 1 and 28 in group 2 is *No apto*.

![A diagram of the DELE A1. Four boxes: reading, 45 minutes, 25 points; writing, 25 minutes, 25 points; listening, 25 minutes, 25 points; speaking, 10 minutes plus 10 minutes to prepare, 25 points. Reading and writing are grouped as group 1, 50 points; listening and speaking as group 2, 50 points. Under each group: at least 30 points. At the bottom: both groups at 30 or more gives Apto.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### What each test asks, in general terms

- Reading: short real-life texts: a personal letter or e-mail, very short notes and
  notices, small ads, public information. You choose answers or match texts to people or
  statements.
- Listening: short conversations, short messages and announcements, and a longer
  conversation. Some answers are pictures. Each recording is played twice.
- Writing: two tasks: filling in a form with short answers, and writing a short message
  (a postcard, e-mail or note of about 30–40 words) that covers the points the task gives
  you.
- Speaking: a short presentation of yourself and a short talk on an everyday topic, both
  prepared in the 10 minutes before (you may take notes), then a conversation with the
  examiner, in which you also ask a couple of questions.

Which Spanish? The exam's texts and recordings are mostly based on the Spanish of Spain, so
you'll hear *vosotros*, *el ordenador*, *el móvil* and *Hoy he comido*. You don't need to use
them: the guide says any standard variety of Spanish is accepted in your answers, as long as
you use it consistently. Answer in the Latin American Spanish of this course, and recognize
Spain's words when you hear them (the vocabulary notes list them).

Dates, fees, exam centers and details of the format can change. Check the official pages
before you register:

- [DELE: the official page of the Instituto Cervantes](https://cervantes.org/es/examenes/dele)
- [DELE A1 exam guide, version 2020 (PDF)](https://agenda.cervantes.es/sites/default/files/DELE_A1_v2020_Guia-de-examen.pdf)
- [Preparing for the DELE: free model exams with audio and answers](https://agenda.cervantes.es/es/node/27166889)

## Strategies for each test

### Reading

- Look at the kind of text first (a sign, an ad, a message). Then read the question, then
  find the part of the text that answers it. You don't need every word.
- Many wrong options repeat a word from the text but change the meaning: *abierto* vs
  *cerrado*, *antes de* vs *después de*, *todos los días* vs *los lunes*.
- Watch for the small words that change everything: *no, nunca, nada, nadie, sin, solo*.

### Listening

- Read the questions before you listen. They tell you what to listen for: a time, a price, a
  day, a place.
- Numbers, times and days come up again and again (lessons 03, 12, 13 and 19).
- Listen for corrections: *El concierto es el viernes… no, perdón, el sábado.* The second
  piece of information is the one that counts.

### Writing

- In the form, copy names and numbers exactly, with accents. Dates go day/month/year (lesson
  23). Adjectives agree with you: *soltera* or *soltero*.
- In the message, cover every point the task gives you. A missing point costs more than a
  small grammar mistake. Count your words roughly; staying close to the length asked is part
  of the task.
- Use a correct frame: *Querida Ana: … Un abrazo* or *Estimado señor: … Atentamente*. Join
  your sentences with *y, pero, porque, además, entonces*.
- Check at the end: accents on the past forms (*fui, comí, visité*)? *tú* or *usted* all the
  way through? Nouns with the right article?

### Speaking

- Prepare your self-presentation until it is automatic: name, nationality, age, where you
  live, family, work or studies, languages, free time (lessons 02, 03, 06, 07, 15).
- In the short talk, use simple, correct sentences and connectors: *Normalmente… Además…
  Pero…* Add one thing you did (*El fin de semana pasado fui a…*) and one plan (*Voy a…*).
- If you don't understand, ask. That is part of a real conversation, and examiners expect it.

## Words for instructions and for asking for help

Exam and textbook instructions use *usted* commands (lesson 17), so you'll recognize them:

| instruction | meaning |
|---|---|
| *Lea el texto.* | Read the text. |
| *Marque la opción correcta.* | Mark the correct option. |
| *Elija la respuesta.* | Choose the answer. |
| *Complete el formulario.* | Complete the form. |
| *Relacione los textos con las imágenes.* | Match the texts to the pictures. |
| *Fíjese en el ejemplo.* | Look at the example. |

- *Elegir* (to choose) changes e → i and spells *g* as *j* before *o*: *elijo, eliges, elige,
  elegimos, eligen*; preterite *elegí, eligió, eligieron*; commands *elige* (*tú*), *elija*
  (*usted*).
- *Marcar* and *explicar* respell the *yo* preterite: *marqué, expliqué*.
- *Aprobar* (to pass an exam) changes o → ue: *apruebo, apruebas…* The opposite in Mexico is
  *reprobar*; in Spain, *suspender*. *¡Aprobé el examen!* — I passed the exam!
- *El examen* is the whole exam; *la prueba* is one test of it (or any test); *la tarea* is a
  task in the exam, or homework; *la parte* is a part.

For asking for help in any conversation:

- *¿Qué significa "abrazo"?* — What does "abrazo" mean?
- *¿Cómo se dice "souvenir" en español?* — How do you say "souvenir" in Spanish?
- *No entiendo. ¿Me lo puede explicar?* — I don't understand. Could you explain it to me?
- *¿Puede repetir, por favor? Más despacio.* — Could you repeat, please? More slowly. (lesson 01)

### algo, nada, alguien, nadie, todo

| | something / somebody | nothing / nobody |
|---|---|---|
| things | *algo* | *nada* |
| people | *alguien* | *nadie* |

*Todo* is "everything" (or "all": *todo el día*, all day; *todos los días*, every day).

When *nada* or *nadie* comes after the verb, Spanish also needs *no* before it. This
**[[double negative]]** is correct and normal, the same pattern as *no … nunca* in lesson 22:

- *No entiendo nada.* — I don't understand anything. (literally "I don't understand nothing")
- *No hay nadie en la oficina.* — There's nobody in the office.
- *¿Quieres algo? — No, nada, gracias.* — Do you want something? — No, nothing, thanks.
- *¿Llamó alguien? — No, no llamó nadie.* — Did anyone call? — No, nobody called.

If *nadie* or *nada* comes first, there's no *no*: *Nadie llamó. Nada es fácil al
principio.* Like *algo*, these words never change their form.

*Suficiente* (enough) agrees in number only: *tiempo suficiente*, *suficientes puntos*.

## Review of the course

Use this table to go back to the lesson you need.

| topic | the core idea | lessons |
|---|---|---|
| sounds and accents | five pure vowels; stress rules; *sí/si, tú/tu* | 01 |
| *tú* and *usted*, *ser* | *¿Cómo se llama usted? Soy de Canadá.* | 02, 07 |
| numbers and prices | *veintidós, treinta y cinco, quinientos, mil* | 03, 12 |
| present tense | -ar, -er, -ir endings; *no* before the verb | 04, 07 |
| gender and articles | *el/la, un/una*; *el día, la mano, el agua* | 05 |
| possessives, *tener* | *mi, tu, su, nuestro*; *tengo 30 años* | 06 |
| adjectives | agree and usually follow: *casas blancas* | 08 |
| *ser* or *estar* | identity vs location and state | 09 |
| *hay* | *Hay un sofá. El sofá está en la sala.* | 10 |
| *gustar* | *me gusta el café, me gustan los tacos* | 11 |
| comparing | *más caro que, tan alto como* | 12 |
| time and days | *Son las tres y media. El lunes trabajo.* | 13 |
| plans | *ir a* + infinitive: *Voy a viajar.* | 14 |
| stem changes | *quiero, puedo, juego, pido* | 15 |
| reflexive verbs | *me levanto, voy a bañarme*; *hago, salgo* | 16 |
| commands | *toma, ve; tome, vaya* | 17 |
| travel, *para*, *conocer* | *el camión para Puebla; conozco Oaxaca* | 18 |
| dates and weather | *el 5 de mayo; hace calor, llueve* | 19 |
| *doler*, *tener que* | *me duele la cabeza; tengo que descansar* | 20 |
| the past | preterite *comí, fui, tuve*; perfect *he comido* | 21, 22 |
| linking and writing | *pero, además, entonces*; *Estimado señor:* | 23 |

## Dialogue: practising for the speaking test

Carmen and Tom are practising together.

> Carmen: Bueno, Tom, empieza tú. Preséntate, por favor.
>
> Tom: Me llamo Tom Becker. Soy estadounidense, de Chicago, y tengo treinta y cuatro años.
> Vivo en Puebla desde el año pasado. Soy ingeniero y trabajo en una empresa de carros.
>
> Carmen: Muy bien. Ahora el tema: "Mi fin de semana".
>
> Tom: Normalmente los sábados hago deporte y los domingos como con amigos. El fin de semana
> pasado fui a Cholula y subí a la pirámide. Además, probé las cemitas. ¿Qué significa
> "cemita", en realidad?
>
> Carmen: Es un pan típico de Puebla, y también una torta con ese pan.
>
> Tom: ¡Ah! Pues me encantó. El próximo fin de semana voy a visitar un pueblo cerca de aquí.
>
> Carmen: ¡Perfecto! No has olvidado nada: pasado, presente y planes. Vas a aprobar.
>
> Tom: ¡Eso espero!

Translation:

> Carmen: OK, Tom, you start. Introduce yourself, please.
>
> Tom: My name is Tom Becker. I'm American, from Chicago, and I'm thirty-four. I've lived in
> Puebla since last year. I'm an engineer and I work for a car company.
>
> Carmen: Very good. Now the topic: "My weekend".
>
> Tom: Usually on Saturdays I do sport and on Sundays I eat with friends. Last weekend I went
> to Cholula and climbed the pyramid. I also tried cemitas. What does "cemita" actually mean?
>
> Carmen: It's a typical bread from Puebla, and also a sandwich made with that bread.
>
> Tom: Ah! Well, I loved it. Next weekend I'm going to visit a town near here.
>
> Carmen: Perfect! You haven't forgotten anything: past, present and plans. You're going to
> pass.
>
> Tom: I hope so!

Notes: *Preséntate* = introduce yourself (a reflexive *tú* command). *Vivo en Puebla desde el
año pasado* uses the present, where English says "I've lived": Spanish uses the present for
something that started in the past and is still true. *La empresa* = company. Cholula, next
to the city of Puebla, has a huge ancient pyramid with a church on top. *La torta* is a
Mexican sandwich on a bread roll. *En realidad* = actually. *¡Eso espero!* = I hope so!

## Pronunciation

- *Examen* is stressed on *-xa-* and has no accent: *ek-SA-men* (it ends in *n*). The plural
  *exámenes* needs one.
- *Elegir* and *elijo*: *g* before *e* and *j* sound the same, a breathy sound in the throat,
  softer in Mexico than in Spain.
- *Alguien* has two syllables: *AL-guien*; the *u* is silent. *Nadie*: *NA-die*.
- *Opción* has the stress on the last syllable: *op-CIÓN*; plural *opciones*, no accent.

## Common mistakes

- Using *nada* or *nadie* alone after the verb: *No veo nada* (not *Veo nada*).
- Confusing *aprobar* and *probar*: *aprobar un examen* (to pass), *probar la comida* (to try).
- Leaving out a point in the writing task. Tick each point as you write.
- Staying silent in the speaking test. Say *No entiendo* or *¿Puede repetir, por favor?* and
  keep going.

## What comes next

At A2 you will use the past much more: the imperfect for descriptions and habits (honors
lesson 24h1 gives you a preview), object pronouns (*lo, la, le*) as a system, *estar* +
-ndo for actions in progress (*estoy comiendo*), negative commands and more connectors. Keep
your vocabulary reviews going, read the graded readers on the reading list, and listen to
slow Spanish every day.

## Key points

- A1: you can manage simple everyday situations if people speak slowly and help.
- DELE A1: reading 45 min, listening 25 min, writing 25 min, speaking 10 min (plus 10 to
  prepare), 25 points each. Two groups of 50 (reading + writing, listening + speaking): you
  need 30 in each for *Apto*. Diplomas don't expire.
- The exam's texts mostly use Spain's Spanish; you may answer in Latin American Spanish.
- Ask for help: *¿Qué significa…? ¿Cómo se dice…? No entiendo.*
- Double negatives are correct: *No hay nada. No vino nadie.*

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson. ¡Felicidades! You have finished Spanish A1.

lessons.title: Honors: Telling a story in the past
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

In lesson 21 you learned the preterite: the regular endings, the yo spelling changes, *fui*,
and the strong forms *tuve, estuve, pude, vine, hice*. With those you can list what happened.
A story needs a little more: what people wanted, where they put things, what they found out,
what they said and brought. It also needs words that move the listener from the beginning to
the end, and some background ("it was dark, there was a storm") behind the events.

This honors lesson adds five more strong preterites (*querer, poner, saber, decir, traer*),
the words that give a story its shape, and a first look at the **[[imperfect]]**, the past tense
for background, so that you recognize it in graded readers. It ends with a longer story that
puts everything together. Some of this goes beyond A1, and the lesson says so where it does.

## Five more strong preterites

These verbs follow exactly the pattern you know from *tener* (*tuve, tuviste, tuvo*): a new
stem, the endings *-e, -iste, -o, -imos, -ieron*, and no written accents.

| infinitive | stem | yo | tú | él, ella, usted | nosotros | ellos, ustedes |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| *querer* | quis- | quise | quisiste | quiso | quisimos | quisieron |
| *poner* | pus- | puse | pusiste | puso | pusimos | pusieron |
| *saber* | sup- | supe | supiste | supo | supimos | supieron |
| *decir* | dij- | dije | dijiste | dijo | dijimos | dijeron |
| *traer* | traj- | traje | trajiste | trajo | trajimos | trajeron |

One detail: when the stem ends in *j* (*dij-, traj-*), the *ellos* ending is *-eron*, not
*-ieron*: *dijeron, trajeron* (never *dijieron*). Learn *dijeron* as a word, and the rest
follows.

*Traer* (to bring) is new: present *traigo, traes, trae, traemos, traen* (only *yo* is
irregular); participle *traído*. It's the opposite of *llevar* (to take, lesson 20): *traer*
is toward the speaker, *llevar* away. *¿Me traes un café? — Sí, te llevo uno ahora.*

### When the preterite changes the meaning

Two of these verbs mean something slightly different in the preterite, because the preterite
shows a single moment:

- *saber* = to know; *supe* = I found out (the moment I came to know). *Ayer supe que mi
  prima está embarazada.* — Yesterday I found out that my cousin is pregnant.
- *querer* = to want; *quise* = I tried, wanted and acted on it; *no quise* = I refused. *El
  niño no quiso comer.* — The boy refused to eat.

This is usually taught at A2; at A1 it's enough to recognize it. If *supe* feels odd, read it
as "I learned" and the sentence will make sense.

### Example 1: choosing the form

Put the verb in brackets into the preterite: *Anoche mis amigos (traer) pastel y yo (poner)
la mesa.*

1. *Mis amigos* = *ellos*. *Traer* has the stem *traj-*, and after *j* the *ellos* ending is
   *-eron*: *trajeron*.
2. *Yo* + *poner*: stem *pus-* + *-e*: *puse*, no accent.
3. Answer: *Anoche mis amigos trajeron pastel y yo puse la mesa.* — Last night my friends
   brought cake and I set the table.

*Poner la mesa* is "to set the table". *El pastel* is cake (in Spain you'll also hear *la tarta*).

## Giving a story its shape

A story in Spanish usually moves through these words. Most of them you know; the new ones
are *al principio*, *por fin*, *al final* and *por suerte*.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: The shape of a story
  accDescr: Story words in order from top to bottom. Al principio, at first, sets the scene. Primero, first, gives the first event. Luego or después, then or afterwards, give the next events. De repente, suddenly, brings the problem. Entonces, so or then, gives the reaction. Por suerte, luckily, brings help. Por fin or al final, at last or in the end, closes the story.
  A["Al principio (at first): the scene"] --> B["Primero (first): the first event"]
  B --> C["Luego / después (then, afterwards): more events"]
  C --> D["De repente (suddenly): the problem"]
  D --> E["Entonces (so, then): the reaction"]
  E --> F["Por suerte (luckily): help arrives"]
  F --> G["Por fin / al final (at last / in the end): the ending"]
```

- *Al principio* (at first) can also mean "at the beginning": *Al principio no entendí nada*
  (At first I didn't understand anything).
- *Por fin* (at last, finally) shows relief after waiting: *¡Por fin llegó el camión!*
- *Al final* (in the end) closes the story: *Al final, todo salió bien* (In the end,
  everything turned out fine).
- *Por suerte* (luckily) turns a problem around: *Por suerte, alguien nos ayudó.*
- *Finalmente* (lesson 16) is the last step in a list; *al final* and *por fin* sound more
  like storytelling.

### Example 2: joining events into a story

Join these four events with story words: *Perdí el celular. Lo busqué en la casa. Mi hermano
lo encontró en el carro. Me lo dio.*

1. Start with the problem and the first reaction: *Primero perdí el celular y lo busqué en
   toda la casa.*
2. The turn: *Luego, por suerte, mi hermano lo encontró en el carro.*
3. The ending: *Al final, me lo dio y yo le di las gracias.*

Result: *Primero perdí el celular y lo busqué en toda la casa. Luego, por suerte, mi hermano
lo encontró en el carro. Al final, me lo dio y yo le di las gracias.* — First I lost my
phone and looked for it all over the house. Then, luckily, my brother found it in the car.
In the end he gave it to me and I thanked him.

*Lo* = it; *me lo dio* = he gave it to me; *dar las gracias* = to thank. Object pronouns are
A2 grammar; here, read them as chunks.

## A first look at the imperfect

Graded readers and real stories use a second past tense beside the preterite: the
**[[imperfect]]** (*el pretérito imperfecto*). You don't need to produce it at A1, but you will
meet it constantly, so it helps to recognize the most common forms:

| imperfect | from | meaning |
|---|---|---|
| *era* | *ser* | it was, he/she was (description) |
| *estaba* | *estar* | it was, he/she was (place or state) |
| *había* | *haber* (*hay*) | there was, there were |
| *tenía* | *tener* | he/she had, I had |
| *hacía (frío, calor)* | *hacer* | it was (cold, hot) |

The difference in one sentence: the preterite tells what happened, the imperfect describes
what things were like at the time. The imperfect is the scenery; the preterite is the action
in front of it.

![A diagram with a long shaded band across the top labeled "imperfect: the background" with the words era, estaba, había, hacía frío. Below it, a timeline with four separate points labeled "preterite: the events": llegamos, empezó a llover, nos perdimos, encontramos una casa. Arrows from the points go up into the band, showing the events happening against the background.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

- *Era de noche y hacía frío. De repente, alguien abrió la puerta.* — It was night and it was
  cold. Suddenly, somebody opened the door.
- *Había mucha gente en la plaza, pero encontré a mi amiga.* — There were a lot of people in
  the square, but I found my friend.
- *Mi abuela estaba en la cocina cuando llegué.* — My grandmother was in the kitchen when I
  arrived.

In the first sentence, *era* and *hacía* set the scene; *abrió* is the event. If you are not
sure which tense to use when you speak, use the preterite for events and keep descriptions
very short: *Fue un día muy frío* (It was a very cold day) is correct too, because it sums up
the whole day as one finished event.

### Example 3: background or event?

In *Estaba en la playa cuando vi una tortuga*, which verb is the background and which is the
event?

1. *Estaba* (I was) is imperfect: it describes where I was, with no beginning or end.
2. *Vi* (I saw) is preterite: one finished moment.
3. So: I was on the beach (background) when I saw a turtle (event). *La tortuga* = turtle.

## Story: *La tormenta*

> El sábado pasado, mi amiga Paola y yo hicimos una excursión a una cascada cerca de
> Cuernavaca. Al principio todo fue perfecto: hacía sol, el camino era bonito y Paola trajo
> fruta y agua para las dos.
>
> Caminamos durante dos horas. Por fin llegamos a la cascada. Nos sentamos, comimos y
> tomamos muchas fotos. Luego quise ver el río de cerca, y puse mi mochila en una piedra.
>
> De repente, el cielo se puso negro. Empezó una tormenta muy fuerte y en dos minutos
> estábamos mojadas. Buscamos el camino, pero no lo encontramos. Paola estaba asustada y yo
> también. Gritamos: "¿Hay alguien?", pero no había nadie.
>
> Entonces oímos un perro. Por suerte, cerca de allí había una casa. Una señora abrió la
> puerta y nos dijo: "¡Pasen, pasen!" Nos dio café y pan dulce. Su hijo nos explicó el camino
> y, cuando terminó la lluvia, nos llevó en su camioneta al pueblo. Antes de salir, Paola le
> dio su número de teléfono a la señora.
>
> En el camión de regreso, supe que mi celular estaba en la mochila… y la mochila, en la
> piedra junto al río. Casi lloré. Pero al final la historia terminó bien: el domingo la
> señora llamó a Paola. Su hijo encontró la mochila, y el lunes me la trajo a Cuernavaca.
> ¡Qué sorpresa! Ahora tengo una nueva amiga… y un buen recuerdo.

Translation:

> Last Saturday my friend Paola and I went on a trip to a waterfall near Cuernavaca. At first
> everything was perfect: it was sunny, the path was pretty and Paola brought fruit and water
> for both of us.
>
> We walked for two hours. At last we reached the waterfall. We sat down, ate and took lots of
> photos. Then I wanted to see the river up close, and I put my backpack on a rock.
>
> Suddenly the sky went black. A very strong storm started and within two minutes we were
> wet. We looked for the path, but we didn't find it. Paola was scared, and so was I. We
> shouted, "Is anybody there?", but there was nobody.
>
> Then we heard a dog. Luckily, there was a house near there. A woman opened the door and said
> to us, "Come in, come in!" She gave us coffee and sweet bread. Her son explained the way
> to us and, when the rain stopped, took us in his pickup truck to the town. Before leaving,
> Paola gave the woman her phone number.
>
> On the bus back, I realized that my phone was in the backpack… and the backpack was on the
> rock by the river. I almost cried. But in the end the story ended well: on Sunday the woman
> called Paola. Her son had found the backpack, and on Monday he brought it to me in
> Cuernavaca. What a surprise! Now I have a new friend… and a good memory.

Notes: Cuernavaca is a city south of Mexico City, in the state of Morelos. *La cascada* =
waterfall; *la piedra* = rock, stone; *el cielo* = sky; *se puso negro* = went black (*ponerse*
= to become, here); *fuerte* = strong; *¡Pasen!* = come in (the *ustedes* command of *pasar*);
*el pan dulce* = Mexican sweet bread; *la camioneta* = pickup truck, van; *el camión de
regreso* = the bus back; *casi* = almost; *junto a* = next to. The imperfect forms in the
story are *hacía, era, estábamos, estaba, había*; every other past verb is a preterite.

### Example 4: reading the story for events

List the events of the third paragraph in order, and say why *estaba asustada* is different.

1. Events (preterite): *el cielo se puso negro → empezó una tormenta → buscamos el camino → no
   lo encontramos → gritamos*.
2. *Estaba asustada* (she was scared) and *no había nadie* (there was nobody) are imperfect:
   they describe how things were, not a step in the action.

## Common mistakes

- Adding accents to strong forms: *quise, puso, supo, trajo, dijo* (not *quisé, pusó*).
- *Dijieron* and *trajieron*: after *j*, the ending is *-eron*: *dijeron, trajeron*.
- Mixing up *traer* and *llevar*: *traer* is "bring" (toward the speaker), *llevar* is "take"
  (away from the speaker). Think of where the speaker is.
- Using *al final* for a list step: for "finally" in a list of steps, *finalmente* or
  *por último* (lastly) fit better; *al final* is "in the end" of a story.
- Trying to use the imperfect for every past verb because it looks like English "was …ing".
  At A1, tell events with the preterite; recognize the imperfect for background.

## Key points

- Strong preterites: *quise, puse, supe, dije, traje* (stems *quis-, pus-, sup-, dij-,
  traj-*), no accents; *dijeron, trajeron* with *-eron*.
- *Supe* = I found out; *no quise* = I refused (recognize these).
- Story words: *al principio, primero, luego, después, de repente, entonces, por suerte, por
  fin, al final*.
- The imperfect (*era, estaba, había, tenía, hacía*) describes the background; the preterite
  tells the events.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Honors: WhatsApp, e-mail and formal notes
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 23 gave you the frame of a message: greeting, body, closing, name, with *tú* or *usted*
all the way through. This honors lesson takes that frame into three real situations. First,
the quick chat on your phone, with the shorthand and voice notes you'll see every day in
Mexico. Second, the formal e-mail you'll need when something goes wrong at your apartment or
you need something from a school. Third, the DELE A1 writing test, with two practice tasks
written for this course and model answers, worked through step by step.

## Chatting on the phone

In Mexico, as in most of Latin America, people organize much of their lives in chat apps.
WhatsApp is by far the most used: a 2025 Statista consumer survey reported by
Marketing4eCommerce found that 93 % of the people it surveyed in Mexico use it. Families, schools,
landlords and small businesses all chat on it, so you'll be writing and reading short messages
in Spanish from your first week.

### Shorthand you'll see

Chat Spanish drops letters, accents and the opening *¿ ¡*. Here are some common abbreviations.
They are informal and they change over time and from group to group, so treat this list as a
snapshot, not a rule.

| shorthand | full form | meaning |
|---|---|---|
| *q* | *que, qué* | that, what |
| *xq* | *porque, por qué* | because, why |
| *x fa* (also *xfa*) | *por favor* | please |
| *tmb* | *también* | also, too |
| *ntp* | *no te preocupes* | don't worry |
| *bn* | *bien* | well, fine |
| *tqm* | *te quiero mucho* | love you lots |
| *jaja* | (laughter) | haha |

The *x* stands for *por* because the multiplication sign × is read *por* in Spanish (*dos por
tres*, two times three). *Jaja* is Spanish laughter because *j* sounds like English *h*;
*jajaja* is a bigger laugh. In Mexico you'll also see *va* or *¿va?* for "OK" and "OK?".

![A phone screen showing a chat between Ana and Luis. Ana: "Hola!! q haces?" Luis: "nada, en la casa. xq?" Ana: "vamos al cine a las 7?" Luis: "va! tmb viene Sofi?" Ana: "sí. compras los boletos x fa?" Luis: "ntp, ya los compré jaja".](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The chat in full Spanish: *¡Hola! ¿Qué haces? — Nada, en la casa. ¿Por qué? — ¿Vamos al cine
a las siete? — ¡Va! ¿También viene Sofi? — Sí. ¿Compras los boletos, por favor? — No te
preocupes, ya los compré, jaja.* (Hi! What are you doing? — Nothing, at home. Why? — Shall we
go to the movies at seven? — OK! Is Sofi coming too? — Yes. Can you buy the tickets, please?
— Don't worry, I already bought them, haha.)

Notice *en la casa*: in Mexico people often say *en la casa* where Spain says *en casa* (at
home). Both are understood everywhere.

### Voice notes

Many people prefer to send a voice note (*una nota de voz*, in Mexico often just *un audio*)
instead of typing: *Te mando un audio* (I'll send you a voice message). For a learner they are
good listening practice, because you can play them again as often as you like. A generalization
worth knowing: long voice notes are normal among friends and family, but at work a short
written message is usually more polite.

### When not to use shorthand

Never use chat shorthand in an e-mail to a school, an office or a landlord, in a form, or in
the DELE exam. Write every word in full, with accents and the opening *¿ ¡*.

## The formal e-mail

When you write to someone you don't know, or to someone in a position of authority (a
landlord, *el dueño*; a school office; a doctor's practice), use *usted* and a clear structure.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: The structure of a formal e-mail
  accDescr: Six parts from top to bottom. The subject line, asunto, says the topic in a few words. The greeting, for example Estimado señor Morales, ends with a colon. The first sentence says who you are or why you write, for example Le escribo porque. The body gives the facts and the request, for example Puede mandar a un técnico. The closing line is Quedo atento or atenta a su respuesta. The sign-off, Atentamente or Cordialmente, is followed by your name.
  A["Asunto: the topic in a few words"] --> B["Greeting + colon: Estimado señor Morales:"]
  B --> C["Why you write: Le escribo porque..."]
  C --> D["The facts and your request: ¿Puede...?"]
  D --> E["Quedo atento / atenta a su respuesta."]
  E --> F["Atentamente, / Cordialmente, + your name"]
```

- *El asunto* is the subject line. Keep it short and concrete: *Estufa descompuesta,
  departamento 302*.
- *Le escribo porque…* (I'm writing to you because…) or *Le escribo para…* + infinitive (I'm
  writing to…) is the most natural first line. *Le* is "to you" for *usted*.
- Make the request with *¿Puede…?* or *¿Me puede…?* + infinitive. That is polite enough in an
  e-mail when it comes with *por favor* and *gracias*.
- *Quedo atento a su respuesta* (I look forward to your reply) is a set phrase; a woman writes
  *Quedo atenta*. Mexican e-mails often put *Sin más por el momento* (with nothing more for
  now) in front of it.
- *Cordialmente* (cordially) and *Atentamente* (sincerely) are both good formal sign-offs.
- To attach is *adjuntar*: *Le adjunto una foto* (I'm attaching a photo). The attached file
  is *el archivo adjunto*.

### Example 1: an e-mail to the landlord

Situation: you rent apartment 302. The stove hasn't worked since Monday. You want the
landlord, Mr Morales, to send someone this week. You are home after five.

1. Subject line: the problem and where: *Estufa descompuesta, departamento 302*.
2. Greeting with a colon: *Estimado señor Morales:*
3. Why you write, with the facts: *Le escribo porque la estufa del departamento 302 no
   funciona desde el lunes.*
4. What you have done, and the attachment: *Ya revisé el gas y no es el problema. Le adjunto
   una foto.*
5. The request and when you can be reached: *¿Puede mandar a un técnico esta semana? Estoy en
   casa todas las tardes después de las cinco.*
6. Closing and sign-off.

> Asunto: Estufa descompuesta, departamento 302
>
> Estimado señor Morales:
>
> Le escribo porque la estufa del departamento 302 no funciona desde el lunes. Ya revisé el
> gas y no es el problema. Le adjunto una foto. ¿Puede mandar a un técnico esta semana? Estoy
> en casa todas las tardes después de las cinco.
>
> Sin más por el momento, quedo atenta a su respuesta.
>
> Cordialmente,
>
> Rachel Kim

Translation: *Subject: Broken stove, apartment 302. Dear Mr Morales, I'm writing to you
because the stove in apartment 302 hasn't worked since Monday. I've already checked the gas
and that's not the problem. I'm attaching a photo. Could you send a technician this week? I'm
at home every afternoon after five. With nothing more for now, I look forward to your reply.
Kind regards, Rachel Kim.*

*Descompuesto* (broken, out of order) is the Mexican word for machines that stop working
(Spain: *estropeado*); *roto* (lesson 22) is for things that physically break, like a plate.
*Funcionar* is "to work" for machines: *El celular no funciona.* People *trabajan*; machines
*funcionan*. *Revisar* = to check; *el técnico* = technician; *desde el lunes* = since Monday.
Spanish uses the present here (*no funciona desde el lunes*) where English says "hasn't
worked".

### Example 2: from chat to formal

Here is a message to a friend. Rewrite it for the school office.

*hola!! no puedo ir a clase mañana xq tengo cita con el doctor. me mandas la tarea x fa? gracias!!*

1. Change the register: *tú* → *usted*, *me mandas* → *¿Me puede mandar…?*
2. Write every word in full and restore accents and *¿ ¡*: *xq* → *porque*, *x fa* → *por
   favor*.
3. Add the frame: greeting with a colon, the reason, the request, the closing.

> Estimada maestra Ortiz:
>
> Le escribo porque mañana no puedo ir a clase: tengo una cita con el doctor. ¿Me puede mandar
> la tarea por correo, por favor? Muchas gracias.
>
> Atentamente,
>
> Kevin Lee

(Dear Ms Ortiz, I'm writing to you because tomorrow I can't come to class: I have a doctor's
appointment. Could you send me the homework by e-mail, please? Thank you very much. Yours
sincerely, Kevin Lee.) In Mexico, students often address a teacher as *maestra* or *maestro*,
with or without the surname.

## DELE-style writing practice

The DELE A1 writing test (lesson 24) has two tasks: a form with short answers, and a short
message of about 30–40 words. The two tasks below were written for this course in that
style. They are not exam tasks, but they practise the same skills. Give yourself about 10
minutes for each, then compare with the model answers.

### Example 3: a form

*Task: You want to join the sports center in your neighborhood. Fill in the registration
form.*

| field | model answer |
|---|---|
| *Nombre y apellidos* | *Sarah Miller* |
| *Nacionalidad* | *estadounidense* |
| *Fecha de nacimiento* | *09/07/1992* |
| *Teléfono* | *55 1234 5678* |
| *¿Qué deporte quiere practicar?* | *Natación y yoga.* |
| *¿Qué días puede venir?* | *Los martes y los jueves por la tarde.* |
| *¿Por qué quiere hacer deporte?* | *Porque trabajo en una oficina y quiero estar más activa.* |

How the answers were built:

1. Copy the personal data exactly; the date goes day/month/year (9 July 1992), and the
   nationality is lowercase.
2. Answer the questions in short phrases or one sentence. A full sentence is not required,
   but the words must be correct: *los martes* (on Tuesdays) with the article, days lowercase.
3. Answer the question asked, with the word it suggests: *¿Por qué…?* → *Porque…* Agreement:
   Sarah writes *activa* (feminine).

*La natación* = swimming; *activo* = active.

### Example 4: a short e-mail

*Task: Write an e-mail to your friend Marcos (30–40 words). Greet him, tell him what you did
last weekend, invite him to do something on Saturday, and say goodbye.*

Plan first: four points, so about four sentences, one per point. The second point needs the
preterite; the third needs *¿Quieres…?* + an infinitive, or *ir a*.

> Querido Marcos:
>
> ¿Qué tal? El fin de semana pasado fui a Puebla con mi hermana. Visitamos el centro y comimos
> mole. ¡La pasamos muy bien! ¿Quieres ir al cine conmigo el sábado?
>
> Un abrazo,
>
> Ana

That is 35 words, counting the greeting and the name. Check it against the task:

1. Greeting: *Querido Marcos:* with a colon, and *¿Qué tal?* Done.
2. Last weekend: *fui, visitamos, comimos, la pasamos*, all preterite, with accents. Done.
3. Invitation: *¿Quieres ir al cine conmigo el sábado?* (*conmigo* = with me). Done.
4. Goodbye: *Un abrazo, Ana.* Done.

(Dear Marcos, How are you? Last weekend I went to Puebla with my sister. We visited
downtown and ate mole. We had a great time! Do you want to go to the movies with me on Saturday?
Hugs, Ana.) A message with one point missing would lose more than one with a small spelling
slip, so tick the points off before you finish.

## Common mistakes

- Shorthand or missing accents in formal writing or the exam: write *porque*, *por favor*,
  *¿Qué tal?* in full.
- Switching from *usted* to *tú* in the middle: *¿Me puede…?* in the request, then *gracias por
  tu ayuda* at the end. Keep *su ayuda*.
- *Atento* that doesn't agree: a woman writes *Quedo atenta a su respuesta*.
- *Trabajar* for machines: *La estufa no funciona* (not *no trabaja*).
- A long story in a 30–40-word task, and no invitation. Cover every point, briefly.

## Key points

- Chat shorthand (*q, xq, x fa, tmb, ntp, jaja*) is informal and changes; recognize it, but
  never use it in formal writing or the exam.
- Formal e-mail: *Asunto*, *Estimado/a …:*, *Le escribo porque…*, the request with *¿Puede…?*,
  *Quedo atento/a a su respuesta*, *Atentamente* or *Cordialmente*.
- *Funcionar* (machines), *descompuesto* (broken, out of order), *adjuntar* (to attach).
- For a DELE-style message: plan one sentence per point, use the right tense for each point,
  count roughly, and check every point at the end.

lessons.title: El año en fiestas: Día de Muertos, posadas and national holidays
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

In lesson 19 you learned to say dates (*el 16 de septiembre*), in lesson 14 to make plans with
*ir a* (*Vamos a ir al cine*), and in lessons 21 and 22 to talk about the past (*Ayer compré
flores*, *¿Has visto una ofrenda?*). This honors lesson puts all of that to work on one theme:
the holiday year in Mexico, with a glance at other Spanish-speaking countries.

You'll learn when the big days are, read how one family gets ready for *Día de Muertos* (the
Day of the Dead), and practise the skill that holds a longer text together: choosing the tense
from the time words around it. People talk about holidays in all three times: what we did last
year, what we do every year, and what we're going to do this year.

## The holiday year in Mexico

Mexican federal labour law (the *Ley Federal del Trabajo*, article 74, as reformed in 2024)
lists the official days off, the *días de descanso obligatorio*; in everyday Spanish a public
holiday is *un día festivo*. Some fall on a fixed date; three
were moved to a Monday in 2006, so people get a long weekend (*un puente*, literally "a bridge").
Many of the best-known celebrations are not official days off at all.

| Date | Holiday | Official day off? |
|---|---|---|
| *el 1 de enero* | *el Año Nuevo* (New Year's Day) | yes |
| *el 6 de enero* | *el Día de Reyes* (Three Kings' Day): children get presents, families share a *rosca de reyes* (a ring-shaped sweet bread) | no |
| *el primer lunes de febrero* | *el Día de la Constitución* (for 5 February) | yes |
| *el tercer lunes de marzo* | Benito Juárez's birthday (for 21 March) | yes |
| March or April (it moves) | *la Semana Santa* (Holy Week, before Easter) | no, but schools close and many people travel |
| *el 1 de mayo* | *el Día del Trabajo* (Labour Day) | yes |
| *el 16 de septiembre* | *el Día de la Independencia* | yes |
| *el 1 y el 2 de noviembre* | *el Día de Muertos* | no |
| *el tercer lunes de noviembre* | *el Día de la Revolución* (for 20 November) | yes |
| *el 12 de diciembre* | *el Día de la Virgen de Guadalupe*: huge pilgrimages to the Basilica in Mexico City | no |
| *del 16 al 24 de diciembre* | *las posadas* | no |
| *el 25 de diciembre* | *la Navidad* (Christmas) | yes |

The law also gives a day off on federal and local election days, and on 1 October every six
years, when a new president takes office. *Semana Santa* moves with Easter: in 2027, Holy Thursday
and Good Friday fall on 25 and 26 March.

![A year strip of twelve months, January to December, with a coloured marker on each month that has a big holiday: Año Nuevo and Día de Reyes in January, Día de la Constitución in February, Semana Santa in March or April, Día del Trabajo in May, Día de la Independencia in September, Día de Muertos and Día de la Revolución in November, and las posadas and Navidad in December. Markers in one colour show official days off, in another colour celebrations that are not days off.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Two spelling points: holiday names take capital letters (*la Navidad, la Semana Santa, el Día de
Muertos*), but months stay lowercase, as in lesson 19 (*el 25 de diciembre*); and the day comes
first: *el 16 de septiembre*.

### Las fiestas patrias

Mexico's independence war began in the early hours of 16 September 1810, when the priest Miguel
Hidalgo called on the people of Dolores (today Dolores Hidalgo, Guanajuato) to rise up. That call
is remembered as *el Grito de Dolores* (the cry of Dolores). Today the celebration starts the night
before: on 15 September, at about 11 p.m., the president rings a bell on the balcony of the
National Palace and leads the crowd in the shout *¡Viva México!*, and mayors do the same in town
squares all over the country. The 16th brings a military parade (*el desfile*).

Other countries have their own *fiestas patrias*: Argentina on 9 July (1816), Colombia on 20
July (1810), Peru on 28 July (1821). In Spain *el Día de Reyes* (6 January) is a public holiday,
and in many families the Three Kings, not Santa Claus, bring the presents.

## El Día de Muertos

It isn't a sad day, and it isn't Mexican Halloween: families remember the people they have lost and, in the traditional belief,
welcome their souls home for a visit. Celebrations run from the end of October to 2 November.
In much of Mexico, 1 November is for children who have died and 2 November for adults, though
customs vary from region to region and from town to town. In 2008 UNESCO inscribed the
"Indigenous festivity dedicated to the dead" on its list of the intangible cultural heritage of
humanity (it had first been proclaimed in 2003).

At home, families set up *una ofrenda* (an offering, a home altar), often with two or more
levels. What goes on it depends on the family; these are the usual explanations:

- *las flores de cempasúchil*: orange Mexican marigolds. Their colour and their petals, laid in
  a path to the door, help the souls find their way. The name comes from the Nahuatl
  *cempohualxochitl*, usually explained as "twenty flower".
- *las velas*: candles, to light the way.
- *la foto*: a photo of each person the family remembers.
- *el pan de muerto*: a round sweet bread decorated with "bones" made of dough.
- *las calaveras de azúcar*: sugar skulls, often with a name written on the forehead.
- *el papel picado*: coloured tissue paper cut into patterns.
- the person's favourite food and drink, a glass of water (for the long journey) and a little
  salt.

![An ofrenda on a table with three levels. Strings of papel picado hang above it. On the top level stands a framed photo between two candles. On the middle level there are two sugar skulls and a round pan de muerto. On the bottom level there are vases of orange cempasúchil flowers, a glass of water and a plate of food, with a path of orange petals on the floor in front. Labels name las velas, la foto, el pan de muerto, las calaveras de azúcar, el papel picado and el cempasúchil.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Many families also go to the cemetery (*el panteón* in Mexico; *el cementerio* everywhere) to
clean the graves, cover them with flowers and spend time together, sometimes with music. Mexicans usually say *Día de Muertos*; *Día de los Muertos* is common in the United
States and in other countries.

### Las posadas y la Navidad

From 16 to 24 December, on nine nights, many neighbourhoods and families hold *las posadas*.
*Una posada* is an inn, a place to stay: the celebration recalls Mary and Joseph looking for a
place to stay in Bethlehem. Guests walk outside with candles, singing, and "ask for lodging"
(*pedir posada*) at a door; the people inside sing back, refuse at first, then open the door,
and the party begins. There is usually a *piñata*, often a star with seven points, and hot fruit
punch (*el ponche*). The tradition is usually traced to the Augustinian monastery of Acolman,
near Teotihuacán, in the 1580s.

On 24 December, *la Nochebuena* (Christmas Eve), families have a big dinner late in the evening.
The season goes on to *el Día de Reyes* (6 January) and, in many families, to 2 February, *el Día
de la Candelaria*: whoever found the little baby Jesus figure in the *rosca* brings tamales for
everyone.

## Telling it across time

A longer text mixes tenses, and the **[[time markers]]** (*ayer, ahora, todos
los años, mañana, alguna vez*) tell you which one each sentence needs. Read the time word first;
then you know the tense before you look at the verb.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Choosing the tense from the time marker
  accDescr: Start with the time word in the sentence. Finished past time words such as ayer, el año pasado and anoche take the preterite, for example compramos. Present time words such as hoy, ahora and todos los años take the present, for example ponemos. Future time words such as mañana, el 2 de noviembre and el próximo año take ir a plus an infinitive, for example vamos a comprar. Experience words such as alguna vez, nunca and ya take the present perfect, for example has visto.
  A["What is the time word?"] --> B["ayer, anoche, el año pasado"]
  A --> C["hoy, ahora, todos los años"]
  A --> D["mañana, el 2 de noviembre, el próximo año"]
  A --> E["alguna vez, nunca, ya"]
  B --> F["preterite: compramos"]
  C --> G["present: ponemos"]
  D --> H["ir a + infinitive: vamos a comprar"]
  E --> I["perfect: has visto"]
```

### Reading: La ofrenda de mi abuelo

Lucía, sixteen, writes about her family's preparations. New words: *el pétalo* (petal), *el vaso* (glass), *la tumba* (grave), *el mole* (a rich sauce served with
chicken or turkey). *El camino* (path) is from the module 6 honors lesson.

> Hoy es 30 de octubre. El 1 y el 2 de noviembre celebramos el Día de Muertos, y en mi casa estamos muy ocupados. Todos los años mi familia pone una ofrenda en la sala.
>
> Mi abuelo murió en marzo del año pasado. Este año, por primera vez, su foto va a estar en la ofrenda. Ayer mi mamá y yo fuimos al mercado. Compramos flores de cempasúchil, velas y papel picado. También compramos calaveras de azúcar.
>
> Ahora mi papá pone la foto del abuelo en la ofrenda, y mi hermano pequeño hace un camino de pétalos desde la puerta. Yo escribo nuestros nombres en las calaveras.
>
> Mañana vamos a comprar pan de muerto. Mi mamá va a cocinar mole, el plato favorito del abuelo, y vamos a poner un vaso de agua y un poco de sal.
>
> El 2 de noviembre vamos a ir al panteón. Vamos a limpiar la tumba y poner flores. Vamos a comer, escuchar música y contar historias del abuelo. No es un día triste: es un día para recordar.
>
> ¿Y tú? ¿Has visto alguna vez una ofrenda?

*Today is 30 October. On 1 and 2 November we celebrate the Day of the Dead, and at home we're very
busy. Every year my family sets up an ofrenda in the living room. My grandfather died in March last
year. This year, for the first time, his photo is going to be on the ofrenda. Yesterday my mum and I went to the market. We bought
cempasúchil flowers, candles and papel picado. We also bought sugar skulls. Now my
dad is putting Grandpa's photo on the ofrenda, and my little brother is making a path of petals
from the door. I'm writing our names on the skulls. Tomorrow we're going to buy pan de muerto. My
mum is going to cook mole, Grandpa's favourite dish, and we're going to put out a glass of water
and a little salt. On 2 November we're going to go to the cemetery. We're going to clean the grave
and put flowers on it. We're going to eat, listen to music and tell stories about Grandpa. It isn't
a sad day: it's a day for remembering. And you? Have you ever seen an ofrenda?*

Notice *su foto*: *su* means "his" here (lesson 6), and *por primera vez* means "for the first
time" (*la vez*, lesson 21). *Mi papá pone la foto* is a plain present, but in English it's "is
putting": Spanish uses the simple present for what is happening right now.

### Example 1: Sorting the verbs by time

Take the second and fourth paragraphs and sort every verb by its time marker.

1. *en marzo del año pasado* → finished past → preterite: *murió* (from *morir*, o → u in the
   preterite, like *durmió*).
2. *ayer* → preterite: *fuimos* (ir), *compramos* (comprar; *-amos* is the same as the present, and
   *ayer* tells you it's past).
3. *mañana* → *ir a* + infinitive: *vamos a comprar, va a cocinar, vamos a poner*.
4. *este año, por primera vez* → a plan for this year → *ir a*: *va a estar* (from *estar*).

### Example 2: Last year, this year

Lucía's brother writes about the same ofrenda one year later. Turn her plans (*ir a*) into his
past (preterite), keeping the person of each sentence.

| Lucía, 30 October (plan) | Her brother, a year later (past) |
|---|---|
| *Mañana vamos a comprar pan de muerto.* | *El año pasado compramos pan de muerto.* |
| *Vamos a poner un vaso de agua.* | *Pusimos un vaso de agua.* |
| *Vamos a ir al panteón.* | *Fuimos al panteón.* |
| *Mi mamá va a cocinar mole.* | *Mi mamá cocinó mole.* |

Find the infinitive after *vamos a* / *va a* and give its preterite in the same person: regular
*cocinó*, irregular *poner → pusimos*, *ir → fuimos*.

## Pronunciation

- *cempasúchil*: sem-pa-SOO-cheel; the accent marks the stressed syllable. The spelling
  *cempasúchitl* is also used.
- *Muertos*: MWER-tos, one syllable for *ue*. *Nochebuena*: no-che-BWE-na.
- *posada*: po-SA-da, with a soft *d*, close to the *th* in "other".
- *Guadalupe*: gwa-da-LOO-pe. *Reyes*: RRE-yes, with a rolled *r* at the start of the word.

## Common mistakes

- Calling *Día de Muertos* "Mexican Halloween": the dates are close, but it's a family holiday
  for remembering the dead.
- Writing the date the English way: *el 16 de septiembre*, not "septiembre 16"; and *el 1 de
  mayo* or *el primero de mayo* (lesson 19), both fine in Mexico.
- Capitals: holiday names take them (*la Navidad*), months and weekdays don't (*en diciembre*).
- Mixing time words and tenses: *Mañana compramos pan* is possible (the present for a fixed plan),
  but *Ayer vamos a comprar* is wrong: *ayer* needs the preterite, *compramos* or *fuimos a
  comprar*.

## Key points

- Official days off in Mexico (Ley Federal del Trabajo, art. 74): 1 January, the first Monday
  of February, the third Monday of March, 1 May, 16 September, the third Monday of November and
  25 December, plus election days and the change of president every six years.
- Independence: the *Grito* on the night of 15 September, the holiday on the 16th (1810).
- Día de Muertos, from the end of October to 2 November: *la ofrenda* with *velas, flores de
  cempasúchil, pan de muerto, papel picado, calaveras de azúcar* and photos. UNESCO heritage
  since 2008.
- *Las posadas* (16–24 December), *la Nochebuena*, *la Navidad*, *el Día de Reyes* (6 January).
- Read the time marker first: *ayer* → preterite, *todos los años* → present, *mañana* → *ir a*,
  *alguna vez* → perfect.

lessons.title: Una semana en la Ciudad de México
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

This is the capstone reading of the course. Emma, a Canadian student, spends a week in Mexico City
and keeps a diary (*un diario*) in Spanish. Her seven short entries use almost everything you've
learned: the present (lessons 4–16), *ir a* for plans (14), *ser* and *estar* (9), *hay* (10),
*gustar* and *encantar* (11), the preterite (21) and the perfect (22). Read each entry once for
the main idea, then again for the details; the questions at the end of the lesson ask about the
whole week.

Before the diary, two short sections: what you should know about the city, and two useful verbs
for talking about places, *quedar* and *recomendar*.

## La Ciudad de México

Mexico City is the capital of Mexico and one of the largest cities in the Americas. The 2020
census counted about 9.2 million people in the city itself, and the whole metropolitan area has
more than 20 million. It stands about 2,240 metres above sea level, so many visitors feel tired
for the first day or two.

The city is built where Tenochtitlan stood, the capital of the Mexica (often called the Aztecs),
traditionally founded in 1325 on an island in a lake. Spanish forces took Tenochtitlan in 1521
and built the new city on top of it. Until 2016 the capital's official name was *el Distrito
Federal* (*el D.F.*); today it is *la Ciudad de México*, written *CDMX*. People from the city call
themselves *capitalinos*, or, informally, *chilangos*. In 1987 UNESCO listed the historic centre
and Xochimilco, with its canals, as a World Heritage site.

The heart of the old city is *el Zócalo*, officially the *Plaza de la Constitución*. In Mexico
*el zócalo* is the main square of any town, but *el Zócalo* with a capital letter means this one.

![A simplified map of Mexico City's historic centre, not to scale. The Zócalo, a large square, is in the middle right. The Catedral Metropolitana stands on its north side and the Palacio Nacional along its east side. The Templo Mayor is just north-east of the cathedral. Calle Madero runs west from the Zócalo to the Torre Latinoamericana. North of the tower is the Palacio de Bellas Artes, and west of it the Alameda Central park. A compass arrow points north.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Two verbs for places: quedar and recomendar

*Quedar* is the everyday Latin American way to ask where a place is. It works like *estar* for
location, but only for places and buildings that don't move:

- *¿Dónde queda el Templo Mayor?* — Where is the Templo Mayor?
- *Queda al lado de la catedral.* — It's next to the cathedral.
- *El museo queda lejos del centro.* — The museum is a long way from the centre.

*Quedar* is regular (*queda, quedan*). Don't mix it up with *quedarse* (lesson 16), "to stay":
*Me quedo en casa.* — I'm staying at home.

*Recomendar* (to recommend) changes *e → ie* like *pensar* (lesson 15): *recomiendo, recomiendas,
recomienda, recomendamos, recomiendan*. *Te recomiendo el museo* — I recommend the museum (to
you). The *te* here works like the one in *te gusta*.

Two more words you'll meet: *el siglo* (century) is written with Roman numerals and read as a
number: *el siglo XX* = *el siglo veinte*, the twentieth century. *Antiguo* (old, ancient) goes
after the noun for something very old: *una pirámide antigua*.

## El diario de Emma

New words: *el norte, el sur, el este* (north, south, east), *el lado* (side), *el mirador* (lookout), *el cerro* (hill), *el paraguas*
(umbrella), *la trajinera* (a flat, brightly painted boat in Xochimilco), *el elote* (corn on the
cob), *el compañero* (classmate), *entero* (whole), *último* (last), *destruir* (to destroy: *destruyeron*, they destroyed), *construir* (to
build: *construyeron*, they built). *Estaba* means "was (located)"; it's a past form of *estar*
you met for recognition in the module 6 honors lesson.

> Lunes: Hoy llegué a la Ciudad de México. Voy a estudiar español aquí cuatro semanas. Mi familia de intercambio, los Hernández, vive en Coyoacán, un barrio muy bonito en el sur de la ciudad. Su casa es azul y tiene un jardín pequeño. Estoy muy cansada: la ciudad está a 2,240 metros. Esta noche voy a dormir temprano.

*Monday. Today I arrived in Mexico City. I'm going to study Spanish here for four weeks. My host
family, the Hernándezes, live in Coyoacán, a very pretty neighbourhood in the south of the city.
Their house is blue and has a small garden. I'm very tired: the city is at 2,240 metres. Tonight
I'm going to go to bed early.*

> Martes: Esta mañana tomé el metro con Mateo, el hijo de la familia. Fuimos al Zócalo. ¡Es enorme! En el lado norte está la Catedral Metropolitana, y en el lado este, el Palacio Nacional. En el palacio vi los murales de Diego Rivera. Cuentan la historia de México, desde los mexicas hasta el siglo XX. Muchos museos quedan cerca del Zócalo, y mañana vamos a volver.

*Tuesday. This morning I took the metro with Mateo, the family's son. We went to the Zócalo. It's
huge! On the north side is the Metropolitan Cathedral, and on the east side, the National Palace.
In the palace I saw Diego Rivera's murals. They tell the history of Mexico, from the Mexica to the
twentieth century. Lots of museums are near the Zócalo, and tomorrow we're going back.*

> Miércoles: Hoy visitamos el Templo Mayor, al lado de la catedral. Es una pirámide antigua de los mexicas. Aquí estaba Tenochtitlan, su ciudad. En 1521 los españoles destruyeron Tenochtitlan y encima construyeron una ciudad nueva. Después caminamos por la calle Madero hasta la Torre Latinoamericana y subimos al mirador. ¡La vista es increíble! La ciudad no termina.

*Wednesday. Today we visited the Templo Mayor, next to the cathedral. It's an ancient pyramid of
the Mexica. Tenochtitlan, their city, was here. In 1521 the Spanish destroyed Tenochtitlan and
built a new city on top of it. Afterwards we walked along Madero Street to the Torre
Latinoamericana and went up to the lookout. The view is incredible! The city doesn't end.*

> Jueves: Hoy empezó mi curso de español. Mi maestra se llama Rocío y es muy simpática. En mi clase hay estudiantes de Japón, de Brasil y de Alemania. En la tarde llovió mucho. Mateo dice que en julio llueve casi todas las tardes, y ahora siempre llevo un paraguas en la mochila. Ya he aprendido muchas palabras nuevas.

*Thursday. Today my Spanish course started. My teacher is called Rocío and she's very nice. In my
class there are students from Japan, Brazil and Germany. In the afternoon it rained a lot. Mateo
says that in July it rains almost every afternoon, and now I always carry an umbrella in my
backpack. I've already learned lots of new words.*

> Viernes: Hoy las clases terminaron a la una. Después fui con dos compañeros al Bosque de Chapultepec. Es un parque enorme, con un lago y un castillo. El castillo está en un cerro y ahora es un museo de historia. Luego visitamos el Museo Nacional de Antropología y vimos la Piedra del Sol. Recomiendo mucho el museo, pero necesitas un día entero.

*Friday. Today classes finished at one. Afterwards I went with two classmates to Chapultepec Park
(the Bosque de Chapultepec). It's a huge park, with a lake and a castle. The castle is on a hill
and is now a history museum. Then we visited the National Museum of Anthropology and saw the Sun
Stone. I really recommend the museum, but you need a whole day.*

> Sábado: Hoy fuimos a Xochimilco con la familia Hernández. Allí hay canales y trajineras de muchos colores. Paseamos dos horas en una trajinera. Comimos tacos y elotes, y unos músicos tocaron canciones de mariachi en otra trajinera. Mateo cantó con ellos. ¡Qué divertido!

*Saturday. Today we went to Xochimilco with the Hernández family. There are canals and trajineras
in lots of colours there. We rode around in a trajinera for two hours. We ate tacos and corn on the
cob, and some musicians played mariachi songs on another trajinera. Mateo sang with them. What
fun!*

> Domingo: Hoy es el último día de mi primera semana. En la mañana caminamos por Coyoacán y visitamos la Casa Azul, el museo de Frida Kahlo. Esta semana he visto pirámides, palacios, museos y canales, y he probado los chilaquiles y el mole. Nunca he visto una ciudad tan grande. La próxima semana voy a visitar Teotihuacán. ¡Me encanta esta ciudad!

*Sunday. Today is the last day of my first week. In the morning we walked around Coyoacán and
visited the Blue House, Frida Kahlo's museum. This week I've seen pyramids, palaces, museums and
canals, and I've tried chilaquiles and mole. I've never seen such a big city. Next week I'm going
to visit Teotihuacán. I love this city!*

The places are real; the diary and the Hernández family are invented. Opening days and ticket
rules change, so check before you go: as of 2026, for example, the Museum of Anthropology opens
Tuesday to Sunday and is closed on Mondays.

### Example 1: The tenses in one entry

Sunday's entry uses four times. Find the time marker, then the verb.

| Words in the entry | Time marker | Tense |
|---|---|---|
| *Hoy es el último día* | *hoy* | present (*ser*) |
| *caminamos, visitamos* | *en la mañana* (already over) | preterite |
| *he visto, he probado* | *esta semana* (up to now), *nunca* | perfect |
| *voy a visitar* | *la próxima semana* | *ir a* + infinitive |

Notice *caminamos* and *visitamos*: they look like the present, but the morning is over, so they're
preterite. Notice too that Emma uses the perfect for her week as a whole, *esta semana he visto*,
a time that isn't over yet. In Mexico many people would simply say *esta semana vi*; both are
correct (lesson 22).

### Example 2: Answering from the text

Question: *¿Por qué está cansada Emma el lunes?*

1. The question word is *por qué*, so the answer gives a reason, usually with *porque*.
2. Find the place: Monday's entry, the sentence with *cansada*: *Estoy muy cansada: la ciudad está
   a 2,240 metros.* The colon works like *porque*.
3. Answer with the reason in the third person: *Porque la ciudad está a 2,240 metros* (or *Porque
   la ciudad está muy alta*).

The same method works for every question: find the question word, find the entry and the
sentence, then change the person (*estoy → está*, *fui → fue*) when you answer about Emma.

## Pronunciation

- *México, mexicano*: the *x* sounds like Spanish *j* (lesson 1).
- *Xochimilco*: so-chee-MEEL-ko. In many Nahuatl names *x* sounds like "s" or like English "sh":
  *Xola* (SHO-la).
- *Chapultepec*: cha-pool-te-PEK; *Coyoacán*: ko-yo-a-KAN; *Tenochtitlan*: te-noch-TEET-lan.
- *Zócalo*: SO-ka-lo, with the stress on the first syllable, as the accent shows. *Quedar*:
  ke-DAR, with a silent *u*.

## Common mistakes

- *Queda* vs *se queda*: *El hotel queda en el centro* (is located), but *Emma se queda en
  Coyoacán* (is staying).
- *Está* vs *es* for places: *El castillo está en un cerro* (location, *estar* or *quedar*), but
  *El castillo es un museo* (what it is, *ser*).
- Reading *caminamos* or *visitamos* as present when the time marker is past. Look for *hoy en la
  mañana, ayer, el sábado*.
- *Recomendo*: the stem changes in the singular and in *ellos*: *recomiendo*, but *recomendamos*.
- Saying "México City" in Spanish: it's *la Ciudad de México*, *la CDMX*, or just *la ciudad*.
  In Mexico, *México* on its own often means the capital as well as the country.

## Key points

- Mexico City: capital; about 9.2 million people (2020 census), more than 20 million in the
  metropolitan area; about 2,240 m high; built on Tenochtitlan; *Distrito Federal* until 2016.
- The historic centre: *el Zócalo*, *la Catedral*, *el Palacio Nacional* (Diego Rivera's murals),
  *el Templo Mayor*; to the west, *la calle Madero*, *la Torre Latinoamericana*, *Bellas Artes*, *la Alameda*.
- *¿Dónde queda…? — Queda al lado de…*; *quedarse* = to stay. *Recomendar*: *recomiendo*.
- In a long text, find the time marker first: *hoy* (present), *ayer, en la mañana* (preterite),
  *esta semana, nunca* (perfect), *la próxima semana* (*ir a*).

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Leyendas: legends retold in easy Spanish
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

In lesson 21 you learned the preterite for finished events (*llegó, ganó, regresó*), and in the
module 6 honors lesson you told a story in the past with *primero, después, entonces*. This
honors lesson uses those tools to read two traditional legends from Mexico, retold in easy
Spanish for this course: the volcanoes Popocatépetl and Iztaccíhuatl, and the Maya legend of the
hummingbird. You'll also see why the same legend comes in many versions, and a second way to tell
a story: in the present tense.

Both retellings are short versions written for this course. These stories have been told for
generations, in Nahuatl, Maya and Spanish, and no telling is the "real" one.

## What is a legend?

*Una leyenda* (a legend) is a traditional story that people pass on, often about a real place,
animal or custom. Many legends explain why something is the way it is: why a mountain has its
shape, why a bird is so small, why a city stands where it does. That's the difference from *un
cuento* (a story, a tale), which can happen anywhere, and from *un mito* (a myth), which is mostly
about gods and the creation of the world. These are simplified labels: people often mix the
three words.

Legends change as they're retold. A grandmother in Puebla and a schoolbook in Mexico City may tell
the volcano legend differently, and both are "right". When you read a legend, it's normal to find
that the names, the reasons and the ending vary.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: The usual shape of an explaining legend
  accDescr: A legend often starts with a formula such as Había una vez or Hace muchos siglos, long ago. Then it introduces the characters, for example a princess, a warrior or the gods. A problem follows, such as a war, a lie or something missing from the world. Something changes, often through the gods. At the end the legend explains something we can still see today, such as two volcanoes or a hummingbird.
  A["Había una vez … / Hace muchos siglos …"] --> B["The characters: a princess, a warrior, the gods"]
  B --> C["A problem: a war, a lie, something missing"]
  C --> D["A change, often by the gods"]
  D --> E["The end explains something we see today"]
```

*Había una vez* means "once upon a time" (literally "there was once"); it uses *había*, the past of
*hay* that you met for recognition in the module 6 honors lesson. *Hace muchos siglos* means "many
centuries ago", from *hace* + time (lesson 21) and *el siglo* (century, previous lesson).

## Leyenda 1: Popocatépetl e Iztaccíhuatl

Two volcanoes stand south-east of Mexico City, both more than 5,000 metres high, and on clear days
you can see them from the city. *El Popocatépetl* is active: it often sends out smoke and ash, and
people nearby call it *Don Goyo*. *El Iztaccíhuatl* is not active, and its snowy peaks look like
a woman lying on her back. Their names come from Nahuatl: *Popocatépetl* is usually translated as
"smoking mountain" and *Iztaccíhuatl* as "white woman"; many people call her *la Mujer Dormida*
(the Sleeping Woman).

New words: *casarse* (to get married), *celoso* (jealous), *la mentira* (lie), *muerto* (dead, from *morir*, lesson 90),
*la montaña* (lesson 18), *acostar* (to lay down), *la cima* (top, summit), *arrodillarse* (to kneel), *la antorcha*
(torch), *convertir en* (to turn into), *la nieve* (snow), *echar humo* (to send out smoke).

> Había una vez, hace muchos siglos, un rey en el valle de México. Su hija era la princesa Iztaccíhuatl. Un día, la princesa conoció a Popocatépetl, un guerrero joven y valiente, y los dos se enamoraron.
>
> Popocatépetl habló con el rey: "Quiero casarme con su hija." El rey contestó: "Primero tienes que ir a la guerra. Si ganas, puedes casarte con la princesa."
>
> Popocatépetl se fue a la guerra, muy lejos, y la princesa esperó muchos meses. Un día llegó un guerrero celoso con una mentira: "Popocatépetl murió en la guerra." Iztaccíhuatl lloró y lloró. Su corazón estaba muy triste, y poco después ella también murió.
>
> Pero Popocatépetl no murió. Ganó la guerra y regresó a la ciudad, y allí encontró a la princesa muerta.
>
> Con mucho dolor, el guerrero llevó a Iztaccíhuatl a las montañas y acostó a la princesa en la cima de una montaña, como una mujer dormida. Él se arrodilló a su lado con una antorcha en la mano.
>
> Los dioses vieron su gran amor y convirtieron a los dos en volcanes. Desde ese día, Iztaccíhuatl duerme debajo de la nieve, y Popocatépetl, a su lado, todavía echa humo. Así van a estar juntos para siempre.

*Once upon a time, many centuries ago, there was a king in the Valley of Mexico. His daughter was
Princess Iztaccíhuatl. One day the princess met Popocatépetl, a young, brave warrior, and the two
fell in love. Popocatépetl spoke to the king: "I want to marry your daughter." The king answered:
"First you have to go to war. If you win, you can marry the princess." Popocatépetl went off to
war, far away, and the princess waited many months. One day a jealous warrior arrived with a lie:
"Popocatépetl died in the war." Iztaccíhuatl cried and cried. Her heart was very sad, and soon afterwards
she died too. But Popocatépetl hadn't died. He won the war and came back to the city, and there he
found the princess dead. In great pain, the warrior carried Iztaccíhuatl to the mountains and laid
the princess on top of a mountain, like a sleeping woman. He knelt at her side with a torch in his
hand. The gods saw their great love and turned the two of them into volcanoes. Since that day,
Iztaccíhuatl has slept under the snow, and Popocatépetl, at her side, still sends out smoke. So they
will be together forever.*

![A storyboard in four panels. Panel 1: a king with a crown sits on a throne while a princess and a young warrior with a feather headdress stand hand in hand, with a heart above them. Panel 2: the warrior walks away with a shield and spear while the princess cries. Panel 3: the warrior carries the princess towards the mountains. Panel 4: two volcanoes side by side, a snowy one shaped like a lying woman and a taller one sending out smoke, with a small flame like a torch at its foot. Captions in Spanish under each panel: Los dos se enamoran. Él va a la guerra. Él lleva a la princesa a la montaña. Ahora son dos volcanes.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### How the versions differ

This is one telling among many. In some versions the princess's father is a lord of Tlaxcala and
the war is against the Aztecs; in others he is an Aztec emperor. Sometimes the lie comes from a
rival who wants to marry her, sometimes from her father's enemies; in some versions she dies of
sadness without any lie, because the war lasts so long. In some, Popocatépetl comes back and kills the
liar. What almost every version keeps: a warrior, a princess, a
war, her death, and a love that lasts as two volcanoes.

## Telling a story in the present

Spanish speakers often tell a story, a joke or a legend in the present tense, even though it
happened long ago: *Un día la princesa conoce a un guerrero…* This **[[historical present]]** makes
the story feel close and alive, and it's common in retellings for children, in summaries and in
conversation. The time is clear from the start (*hace muchos siglos*), so the present can't be
misunderstood.

The second legend is told this way. New words: *crear* (to create), *el árbol* (tree), *la piedra*
(stone), *el deseo* (wish), *el pensamiento* (thought), *el barro* (clay), *el maíz* (corn),
*la flecha* (arrow), *soplar* (to blow), *rápido* (fast), *la pluma* (here: feather; lesson 5's
*pluma* is a pen, and both meanings are real), *atrapar* (to catch).

## Leyenda 2: El colibrí

This legend is told in Yucatán and across the Maya region, and it's retold everywhere today. In
Yucatec Maya, the hummingbird is *ts'unu'um*.

> Los dioses mayas crean el mundo. Hacen los árboles, las piedras y los animales, y cada animal tiene un trabajo. Pero hay un problema: nadie lleva los deseos y los pensamientos de las personas.
>
> Los dioses ya no tienen barro ni maíz. Entonces toman una piedra de jade y hacen una flecha muy pequeña. Soplan sobre la flecha, y la flecha vuela: es el primer colibrí.
>
> El colibrí es un pájaro muy pequeño y muy rápido, y sus plumas tienen todos los colores del sol. Las personas quieren atrapar al colibrí, pero los dioses dicen: "Nadie puede tener un colibrí en la mano."
>
> Por eso hoy nadie tiene un colibrí en casa. Y si un colibrí vuela cerca de ti, alguien te manda buenos deseos.

*The Maya gods create the world. They make the trees, the stones and the animals, and each animal
has a job. But there's a problem: nobody carries people's wishes and thoughts. The gods have no
clay or corn left. So they take a jade stone and make a very small arrow. They blow on the arrow,
and the arrow flies: it's the first hummingbird. The hummingbird is a very small, very fast bird,
and its feathers have all the colours of the sun. People want to catch the hummingbird, but the gods
say: "Nobody may hold a hummingbird in their hand." That's why nobody keeps a hummingbird at home
today. And if a hummingbird flies near you, someone is sending you good wishes.*

*Volar* (to fly) changes *o → ue* like *poder*: *vuela, vuelan*. *Al colibrí*: animals can take
the personal *a* when the story treats them like people.

### Example 1: From present to preterite

Retell the second paragraph of *El colibrí* in the preterite, as a story that's over.

| Historical present | Preterite | Why |
|---|---|---|
| *no tienen* | *no tuvieron* | *tener*: irregular stem *tuv-* |
| *toman* | *tomaron* | regular -ar |
| *hacen* | *hicieron* | *hacer*: irregular stem *hic-* |
| *soplan* | *soplaron* | regular -ar |
| *vuela* | *voló* | -ar verbs don't change their stem in the preterite |
| *es* | *fue* | *ser*: *fue* |

Result: *Entonces tomaron una piedra de jade e hicieron una flecha muy pequeña. Soplaron sobre la
flecha, y la flecha voló: fue el primer colibrí.* (*Y* becomes *e* before *hi-*: *e hicieron*,
lesson 23.) In books, the first sentence would often be *Ya no tenían barro*, with the imperfect;
you'll learn it at A2.

### Example 2: Comparing two versions

A schoolbook says: *El rey prometió a su hija a Popocatépetl. La guerra duró muchos años, y la
princesa murió de tristeza.* (*prometer* = to promise, *durar* = to last, *la tristeza* =
sadness.) What's different from our telling?

1. Find the shared events: the king, the war, the princess's death. Same.
2. Find the cause of her death: here *murió de tristeza* because the war *duró muchos años*; in
   our telling, *un guerrero celoso* brought *una mentira*.
3. Conclusion: same story, different reason. Neither version is wrong; that's how legends live.

## The founding of Tenochtitlan, in one paragraph

One more legend you'll see every day in Mexico, on the flag and on Mexican coins: the Mexica
travelled for years looking for a sign from their god Huitzilopochtli: an eagle on a cactus (*el
nopal*), eating a snake. They found it on an island in a lake, and there they built Tenochtitlan,
traditionally in 1325. Like the volcanoes, it's a legend that explains something real: why the
capital stands where it does. (Huitzilopochtli's name is usually explained as "hummingbird of the
south" or "of the left": the hummingbird again.)

## Pronunciation

- *-tl* at the end of Nahuatl words is one soft sound, close to the *tl* in English "atlas":
  *Popocatépetl* (po-po-ka-TE-petl), *Iztaccíhuatl* (ees-tak-SEE-watl).
- *guerrero*: ge-RRE-ro; the *u* is silent after *g* before *e*, and *rr* is rolled.
- *colibrí*: ko-lee-BREE, stress on the last syllable (the accent shows it). *Leyenda*: le-YEN-da.
- *valiente*: ba-LYEN-te; *v* sounds like *b* (lesson 1).

## Common mistakes

- *Enamorarse de*, not *con*: *Iztaccíhuatl se enamoró de Popocatépetl*. Together: *se
  enamoraron*.
- *Morir* in the preterite: *murió, murieron* (o → u, like *durmió*). Not "morió".
- *El dios* (a god) and *los dioses* (gods) are lowercase; *Dios* with a capital means God in
  Christianity, Judaism and Islam. A goddess is *la diosa*.
- *Había una vez*, not "Era una vez" (Spanish also has the more literary *Érase una vez*).
- Asking for "the true version" of a legend. Every version is part of the tradition; say *según
  esta versión* (according to this version).

## Key points

- A legend (*una leyenda*) is a traditional story that often explains something real: two
  volcanoes, a small bird, the site of a city. Versions differ, and none is the only true one.
- *Había una vez* = once upon a time; *hace muchos siglos* = many centuries ago.
- Story verbs: *se enamoraron, se fue, esperó, lloró, murió, ganó, regresó, encontró, llevó*.
- The **[[historical present]]** tells a past story in the present (*Los dioses crean el mundo*);
  to retell it in the preterite, change each verb: *hacen → hicieron, vuela → voló, es → fue*.
- *Popocatépetl* ("smoking mountain") and *Iztaccíhuatl* ("white woman", *la Mujer Dormida*).

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: El español en Estados Unidos
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

You don't need a plane ticket to use your Spanish. The United States has one of the largest
Spanish-speaking populations in the world, and Spanish is on its signs, forms, radio stations and
menus. This last honors lesson looks at Spanish in the US: how many people speak it, how it got
there, the words English and Spanish have borrowed from each other, the mix often called
Spanglish, the false friends that trip up English speakers, and how to read the bilingual signs
you can see in shops, stations and offices. The command forms of lesson 17 come back here, because
signs are full of them.

## Spanish in the US: some numbers

Figures change every year, so here they are with their dates and sources:

- People: the US Census Bureau estimated 70.1 million Hispanic or Latino people on 1 July
  2025, about 21% of the population, or one person in five.
- Speakers: in the Bureau's American Community Survey for 2024, nearly 45 million people aged
  5 and over spoke Spanish at home, by far the most common language after English.
- The law: an executive order of 1 March 2025 (Executive Order 14224) designated English as the
  official language of the United States. It says that agencies are not required to stop offering
  documents and services in other languages.

Two cautions. Not every Hispanic person speaks Spanish (many families have spoken English for
generations), and not everyone who speaks Spanish at home is Hispanic. And the Spanish you hear
varies: Mexican in much of the Southwest, Caribbean in Florida and New York, Central American in
many cities, all of them correct.

### Older than English

Spanish arrived in what is now the US before English did. Spain founded St. Augustine, Florida,
in 1565: the National Park Service calls it the oldest continuously occupied European settlement
in the country. Santa Fe, New Mexico, was founded around 1610. Much of today's Southwest belonged
