to Mexico until 1848. In Puerto Rico, a US territory, Spanish and English are both official, and
Spanish is the everyday language.

You can see this history on any map: *Florida* (flowery), *Colorado* (red, reddish, for the reddish
Colorado River), *Nevada* (snowy), *Montana* (from *montaña*), *Los Ángeles* (the angels), *Las
Vegas* (the meadows), *El Paso* (the pass), *Santa Fe* (holy faith).

## Borrowings both ways

A **[[loanword]]** is a word one language takes from another. English and Spanish have swapped
hundreds.

| English words from Spanish | English words that came through Spanish from Nahuatl | Spanish words from English |
|---|---|---|
| patio, plaza, rodeo, mosquito | tomato (*el tomate*, from *tomatl*) | *el fútbol, el béisbol* |
| canyon (*el cañón*), ranch (*el rancho*) | chocolate (*el chocolate*) | *el clóset, el suéter* |
| alligator (*el lagarto*, lizard) | avocado (*el aguacate*) | *el sándwich, el líder* |
| cockroach (*la cucaracha*) | coyote (*el coyote*), chili (*el chile*) | *el email, chatear* |

Loanwords take the other language's sounds and spelling: Spanish *fútbol* has an accent because
its stress breaks the rule of lesson 1 (Mexico usually says and writes *futbol*, stressed on
the last syllable, as lesson 15 explains), and *el suéter* gets a gender like every Spanish noun.

## Spanglish

*Spanglish* is the everyday name for speech that mixes Spanish and English. Linguists usually
describe two different things under that name:

1. **[[Code-switching]]**: moving between the two languages inside one conversation, or one
   sentence, as many bilingual people do: *Mañana tengo un meeting, pero después vamos al cine.*
   It follows patterns and needs good command of both languages; it isn't a sign that the speaker
   knows neither.
2. **Adapted loanwords**: English words given Spanish form, such as *parquear* (to park; also
   heard in parts of Latin America, but Mexico mostly says *estacionar*), *la troca* (truck,
   also in northern Mexico), *el lonche* (lunch).

Some people are proud of Spanglish, some dislike it; it's simply how many bilingual communities
talk. For the DELE, a formal e-mail or a stranger, use the standard words: *estacionar el carro,
la camioneta, la comida*.

> Daniela: ¿Vienes a la fiesta de mi prima el sábado?
>
> Andrés: No sé. El sábado trabajo en la tienda hasta las seis.
>
> Daniela: No hay problema, la fiesta empieza a las siete. ¿Tienes la troca?
>
> Andrés: Sí, pero no hay dónde parquear cerca de tu casa.
>
> Daniela: Hay un estacionamiento enfrente del parque. Es gratis después de las seis.
>
> Andrés: ¡Perfecto! Then I'll see you there. Llevo los refrescos.

*Daniela: Are you coming to my cousin's party on Saturday? Andrés: I don't know. On Saturday I
work at the shop until six. Daniela: No problem, the party starts at seven. Have you got the truck?
Andrés: Yes, but there's nowhere to park near your house. Daniela: There's a car park opposite the
park. It's free after six. Andrés: Perfect! Then I'll see you there. I'll bring the soft drinks.*

(*Gratis* = free of charge; *el refresco* = soft drink.) Notice how Andrés switches to English for
one sentence and back again, and how *la troca* and *parquear* sit next to the standard *el
estacionamiento* in the same conversation.

## False friends

A **[[false friend]]** is a word that looks like an English word but means something else. Most
look-alikes are honest (*la universidad, interesante, el hospital*), so the few false ones are
worth learning by heart.

| Spanish | Means | Not | "Not" in Spanish |
|---|---|---|---|
| *embarazada* | pregnant | embarrassed | *avergonzado*; in Mexico *me da pena* (I'm embarrassed) |
| *el éxito* | success | exit | *la salida* |
| *la carpeta* | folder, binder | carpet | *la alfombra* |
| *la librería* | bookshop | library | *la biblioteca* |
| *actual* | current, present-day | actual (real) | *real, verdadero*; "actually" = *en realidad* |
| *realizar* | to carry out, to make happen | to realize | *darse cuenta (de)* |

*Realizar* is formal: *realizar un examen* (to take or give an exam), *realizar un sueño* (to make a
dream come true). *Me di cuenta de mi error* is "I realized my mistake".

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: What to do with a Spanish word that looks like English
  accDescr: When a Spanish word looks like an English word, first ask whether it is on your false-friend list, such as embarazada, éxito, carpeta, librería, actual or realizar. If yes, use its real meaning. If no, it is probably a true cognate like universidad, but check that the meaning fits the sentence.
  A["A Spanish word looks like English"] --> B{"On the false-friend list?"}
  B -- yes --> C["Use the real meaning: éxito = success"]
  B -- no --> D["Probably a true cognate: universidad"]
  D --> E["Check that the meaning fits the sentence"]
```

## Reading bilingual signs

Public signs in the US are often in English and Spanish. A sign with words is *un letrero* (Spain
usually says *el cartel*), and one in two languages is *un letrero bilingüe*. Spanish signs give
orders in three ways, all of which you know:

- an **usted command** (lesson 17): *Empuje* (push), *Jale* (pull), *Espere aquí* (wait here);
- *no* + infinitive, or an infinitive alone: *No fumar* (no smoking), *No estacionarse* (no
  parking);
- a noun or adjective phrase: *Salida* (exit), *Piso mojado* (wet floor), *Prohibido el paso* (no
  entry), *Peligro* (danger), *Solo personal autorizado* (staff only).

*Jalar* (to pull) is the word in Mexico and much of Latin America; Spain says *tirar*, so its doors
say *Tire*. US signs usually follow Latin American Spanish.

![Six bilingual signs, each with an English line above a Spanish line: Push / Empuje on a door plate, Pull / Jale on a door plate, Exit / Salida over a doorway, Wet floor / Piso mojado on a yellow warning stand, No parking / No estacionarse with a crossed-out P, and Danger / Peligro with a warning triangle.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### Example 1: Decoding a command on a sign

A door says *Empuje*. Where does the form come from?

1. It ends in *-e*, and the infinitive is probably an *-ar* verb: *usted* commands swap the vowel
   (lesson 17: *tome, doble*).
2. Take off the *-e* and add *-ar*: *empujar*, "to push". Check: yo *empujo* → *empuj-* → *empuje*.
3. So *Empuje* = "(you) push". On the other side, *Jale* comes the same way from *jalar*: pull.

### Example 2: Spotting the false friend

Marta, from Texas, writes to a friend in Mexico: *Ayer en la escuela tuve un problema muy actual:
olvidé mi carpeta en la librería y estaba muy embarazada.* What does each word really say, and what
did she mean?

1. *actual* = current, but she meant "real": *un problema real*, or simply *un problema*.
2. *la carpeta* = folder. That one is right: she forgot her folder.
3. *la librería* = bookshop. At school she probably meant *la biblioteca*, the library.
4. *embarazada* = pregnant! She meant *me dio mucha pena* (Mexico) or *estaba muy avergonzada*.

Fixed: *Ayer en la escuela tuve un problema: olvidé mi carpeta en la biblioteca y me dio mucha
pena.*

## Pronunciation

- *bilingüe*: bee-LEEN-gwe. The two dots on *ü* (lesson 1) tell you to pronounce the *u*.
- *Jale*: HA-le, with the Spanish *j*. *Empuje*: em-POO-he.
- US place names in Spanish: *Los Ángeles* (los AN-he-les), *Nevada* (ne-BA-da), *Texas* (TE-has;
  the *x* is the old spelling of the *j* sound, as in *México*).
- Loanwords keep Spanish sounds: *el béisbol* (BEIS-bol; in Mexico usually *beisbol*, beis-BOL), *el suéter* (SWE-ter).

## Common mistakes

- *Estoy embarazada* for "I'm embarrassed": it means "I'm pregnant". Say *Me da pena* (Mexico) or
  *Estoy avergonzado/a*.
- *La librería* for the library: a library is *la biblioteca*.
- *Realizar* for "to realize": use *darse cuenta*: *Me di cuenta de que…*
- *Actualmente* means "currently", not "actually": *Actualmente vivo en Chicago* = I currently live
  in Chicago.
- Thinking code-switching is "bad Spanish": it's normal among bilinguals, but in formal writing
  use one language.

## Key points

- US Census Bureau: 70.1 million Hispanic people (1 July 2025, about 21%); nearly 45 million
  people aged 5+ speak Spanish at home (2024). English was designated the official language by an
  executive order of 1 March 2025.
- Spanish came early: St. Augustine (1565), Santa Fe (about 1610), the Southwest (Mexican until
  1848); place names like *Colorado, Nevada, Los Ángeles*.
- **[[Loanwords]]** go both ways (*patio, rodeo*; *el fútbol, el suéter*); **[[code-switching]]** and
  adapted loans (*parquear, la troca*) are what people usually call Spanglish.
- False friends: *embarazada* (pregnant), *el éxito* (success), *la carpeta* (folder), *la librería*
  (bookshop), *actual* (current), *realizar* (to carry out).
- Signs give orders with *usted* commands (*Empuje, Jale*), infinitives (*No fumar*) and phrases
  (*Salida, Peligro*).

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

sections.name: Casa, comida y compras (home, food and shopping)
Mi día y mis planes (my day and my plans)
La ciudad, los viajes y la salud (town, travel and health)
El pasado y el DELE A1 (the past and the A1 exam)
Honors: Cultura y vida cotidiana (culture and everyday life)

questions.stem: On what date is the Independence Day holiday in Mexico?
questions.explanation: The holiday is on 16 September, the day in 1810 when Hidalgo called the people of Dolores to rise up. The night before, 15 September, is when the Grito ceremony takes place, but the day off is the 16th. 5 May (Cinco de Mayo) remembers the Battle of Puebla of 1862, and 20 November the Revolution.

questions.stem: Which of these is NOT an official day off under Mexico's federal labour law (Ley Federal del Trabajo, article 74)?
questions.explanation: Día de Muertos is celebrated everywhere, but it isn't on the law's list of days off. The Revolution (third Monday of November), Christmas (25 December) and Labour Day (1 May) all are.

questions.stem: Which of these usually go on an ofrenda for Día de Muertos? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Candles, cempasúchil flowers, pan de muerto and photos of the people being remembered are the classic parts of an ofrenda. A piñata belongs to the posadas and birthdays, and a Christmas tree to Christmas.

questions.stem: Name the numbered parts of this ofrenda.

image.alt: An ofrenda on three levels with papel picado above, a photo between two candles, sugar skulls, a pan de muerto and vases of orange flowers. Six parts are numbered.

questions.explanation: 1 is the papel picado hanging above, 2 the photo, 3 a candle (las velas), 4 a sugar skull (las calaveras de azúcar), 5 the round pan de muerto with its dough "bones", and 6 the orange cempasúchil flowers. La piñata and el ponche belong to the posadas.

questions.stem: Match each celebration to its date.
questions.explanation: Reyes: 6 January. Posadas: the nine nights from 16 to 24 December. Día de Muertos: 1 and 2 November (with celebrations from the end of October). Christmas: 25 December. The Grito: the night of 15 September. 5 May is the Battle of Puebla, not one of these.

questions.stem: Ayer mi mamá y yo ___ al mercado.
questions.explanation: "Ayer" (yesterday) is a finished past time, so the preterite: "fuimos" (ir, nosotros). "Vamos a ir" is a plan, "vamos" is the present, and "hemos ido" (perfect) doesn't go with "ayer".

questions.stem: Mañana ___ pan de muerto.
questions.explanation: "Mañana" points to the future, so "ir a" + infinitive: "vamos a comprar". "Compraron" is the preterite (they bought), "hemos comprado" the perfect, and "ayer" contradicts "mañana".

questions.stem: Last year we put up an ofrenda. Type the preterite of poner (nosotros): El año pasado ___ una ofrenda en la sala.
questions.explanation: "Poner" has the irregular preterite stem "pus-": puse, pusiste, puso, pusimos, pusieron. "El año pasado" (last year) calls for the preterite.

questions.stem: In Lucía's text, what is her father doing at the moment she writes?
choices: Buying pan de muerto at the market
Putting the grandfather's photo on the ofrenda
Cleaning the grave at the cemetery
questions.explanation: "Ahora mi papá pone la foto del abuelo en la ofrenda": "ahora" (now) + the present. The bread and the mole are plans for tomorrow (vamos a comprar, va a cocinar), and the cemetery is for 2 November.

questions.stem: What is the usual explanation for the path of cempasúchil petals from the door to the ofrenda?
choices: It keeps insects away from the food
It shows visitors the way to the cemetery
It decorates the house for Christmas
It helps the souls find their way home
questions.explanation: In the traditional belief the souls visit their families, and the bright orange petals and their path guide them to the ofrenda. Customs vary by family and region, but this is the explanation you'll hear most.

questions.stem: Put these holidays in calendar order, starting in December.
questions.explanation: Las posadas start on 16 December; la Nochebuena is the 24th and la Navidad the 25th; el Año Nuevo is 1 January, el Día de Reyes 6 January, and el Día de la Candelaria 2 February, when whoever found the figure in the rosca brings tamales.

questions.stem: Build the sentence in Spanish.
questions.prompt: We're going to go to the cemetery on 2 November.
questions.explanation: "Vamos a ir" is ir a + infinitive for a plan; "al" is a + el. The date can go at the start, at the end, or after "ir" (Vamos a ir el 2 de noviembre al panteón).

questions.stem: Which sentence is written correctly?
choices: La Navidad es el 25 de diciembre.
La navidad es el 25 de Diciembre.
La Navidad es el 25 de Diciembre.
questions.explanation: Holiday names take a capital (la Navidad), months don't (diciembre), and the day comes before the month: el 25 de diciembre.

questions.stem: What happens at a posada?
choices: Families build an altar with photos of the dead
Guests sing to ask for a place to stay, then there's a party, often with a piñata
The president rings a bell and shouts ¡Viva México!
Children find a figure of the baby Jesus in a sweet bread
questions.explanation: A posada recalls Mary and Joseph looking for somewhere to stay: guests ask for lodging (pedir posada) in song, the door opens and the party begins. The altar is Día de Muertos, the bell is the Grito, and the figure in the bread is the rosca de reyes.

questions.stem: Why is Emma tired on Monday?
choices: Because the city is at 2,240 metres
Because the plane arrived at midnight
Because she walked all the way to Coyoacán
questions.explanation: "Estoy muy cansada: la ciudad está a 2,240 metros." The colon gives the reason. Nothing in the entry says she studied, arrived at midnight or walked.

questions.stem: According to Emma's diary and the map, on which side of the Zócalo is the Palacio Nacional?
questions.explanation: "En el lado norte está la Catedral Metropolitana, y en el lado este, el Palacio Nacional." The cathedral is on the north side; calle Madero comes in from the west.

questions.stem: Name the numbered places on this map of Mexico City's historic centre.

image.alt: A simplified map of Mexico City's historic centre with a large square, a cathedral, a long palace, a small pyramid and a tower on a street corner. Five places are numbered.

questions.explanation: The big square is el Zócalo; on its north side stands la Catedral, along its east side el Palacio Nacional, and to the north-east el Templo Mayor. La Torre Latinoamericana is at the west end of calle Madero, on Eje Central. Bellas Artes is the domed building further west (not numbered), and the Castillo is in Chapultepec, far from the centre.

questions.stem: Where did Emma see the Piedra del Sol (the Sun Stone)?
choices: In the Museo Nacional de Antropología
questions.explanation: Friday: "Luego visitamos el Museo Nacional de Antropología y vimos la Piedra del Sol." In the Palacio Nacional she saw Rivera's murals; the Casa Azul is Frida Kahlo's museum.

questions.stem: Match each day of Emma's week to what she did.
choices: el Zócalo y los murales de Rivera
el Templo Mayor y la Torre Latinoamericana
Chapultepec y el Museo de Antropología
questions.explanation: Tuesday: the Zócalo and the murals. Wednesday: the Templo Mayor and the tower. Friday: Chapultepec and the Museum of Anthropology. Saturday: a trajinera in Xochimilco. Sunday: the Casa Azul. Teotihuacán is a plan for next week.

questions.stem: Which sentence means "The museum is near the park"?
choices: El museo se queda cerca del parque.
El museo queda cerca del parque.
El museo hay cerca del parque.
El museo queda cerca de el parque.
questions.explanation: "Quedar" gives the location of a place: "queda cerca del parque". "Se queda" means it stays (quedarse); "hay" doesn't take a subject like "el museo"; and "de + el" must become "del".

questions.stem: Type the right form of recomendar: Yo te ___ el Museo de Antropología.
questions.explanation: "Recomendar" changes e → ie in the yo form: recomiendo (like pienso). Only nosotros keeps the e: recomendamos.

questions.stem: In Sunday's entry Emma writes "Esta semana he visto pirámides". Why the present perfect?
choices: It's a plan for next week
It happened at a fixed time yesterday
The time, "esta semana", isn't over yet
It's something she does every week
questions.explanation: "Esta semana" (this week) includes the present, so the perfect fits; many Mexicans would also say "esta semana vi". A plan would use ir a, a fixed past time ("ayer") the preterite, and a habit the present.

questions.stem: What is Emma going to do next week?
questions.explanation: "La próxima semana voy a visitar Teotihuacán." She stays four weeks in all, her course started on Thursday, and she went to Xochimilco on Saturday.

questions.stem: Which statements about Mexico City are true, according to the lesson? Select all that apply.
choices: It stands about 2,240 metres above sea level.
Its official name was el Distrito Federal until 2016.
It was built where Tenochtitlan stood.
The 2020 census counted about 20 million people in the city itself.
The Zócalo's official name is Plaza de la Independencia.
questions.explanation: The city is about 2,240 m high, was officially the Distrito Federal until 2016, and was built where Tenochtitlan stood. The 2020 census counted about 9.2 million people in the city itself (the metropolitan area has more than 20 million), and the Zócalo's official name is Plaza de la Constitución.

questions.stem: Put these events of Emma's week in order.
choices: Vio los murales de Diego Rivera.
questions.explanation: Monday she arrived; Tuesday she saw Rivera's murals; Wednesday she went up the Torre Latinoamericana; Thursday her course started; Saturday she rode a trajinera; Sunday she visited the Casa Azul.

questions.stem: Build the sentence in Spanish.
questions.prompt: Lots of museums are near the Zócalo.
questions.explanation: "Quedan" agrees with "muchos museos" (plural). The place phrase can also come first: "Cerca del Zócalo quedan muchos museos."

questions.stem: Sunday's entry says "En la mañana caminamos por Coyoacán." Which tense is "caminamos" here, and how do you know?
choices: Preterite: the morning is already over
Present perfect: it's still this week
Future: she's going to walk later
questions.explanation: The -amos form of -ar verbs is the same in the present and the preterite. Here "en la mañana" of a day she's writing about in the evening is finished, so it's the preterite ("we walked"). The perfect would be "hemos caminado" and the future plan "vamos a caminar".

questions.stem: Which sentence is correct?
choices: El castillo es en un cerro.
El castillo está en un cerro.
El castillo estar en un cerro.
questions.explanation: Location takes "estar" (or "quedar"): "está en un cerro". "Es en" is used for events, not buildings; what something is takes "ser" ("es un museo"); and "estar" must be conjugated.

questions.stem: What does the name Iztaccíhuatl usually mean?
questions.explanation: Iztaccíhuatl is usually translated from Nahuatl as "white woman", for its snowy peaks; people also call it la Mujer Dormida. "Smoking mountain" is Popocatépetl.

questions.stem: In this course's telling of the volcano legend, why does the princess die?
choices: A jealous warrior tells her Popocatépetl has died
Her father gives her to another prince
questions.explanation: "Un día llegó un guerrero celoso con una mentira: Popocatépetl murió en la guerra." She is so sad that she dies. In other versions the lie comes from her father's enemies, or there is no lie and the war simply lasts too long; that's why legends are "one telling among many".

questions.stem: Name the numbered characters and things in the storyboard.

image.alt: A four-panel storyboard of the volcano legend without captions: a king, a princess and a warrior; the warrior leaving; the warrior carrying the princess; two volcanoes with a torch. Six parts are numbered.

questions.explanation: In panel 1, 1 is the king (el rey) with his crown, 2 the princess and 3 the warrior with his feather headdress. In panel 4, 4 is el Iztaccíhuatl, the snowy volcano shaped like a lying woman, 5 el Popocatépetl, the smoking one, and 6 the torch (la antorcha) at its foot. The hummingbird is from the other legend.

questions.stem: Put the events of the legend in order, as this lesson tells it.
choices: El rey dijo: "Primero tienes que ir a la guerra."
Un guerrero celoso llegó con una mentira.
Popocatépetl ganó la guerra y regresó.
Los dioses convirtieron a los dos en volcanes.
questions.explanation: They fall in love; the king sets the condition of the war; the lie arrives; the princess dies; Popocatépetl wins and comes back; the gods turn them into volcanoes.

questions.stem: Retell in the preterite: "Los dioses hacen una flecha."
choices: Los dioses han hacido una flecha.
questions.explanation: "Hacer" has the irregular preterite stem "hic-": hice, hiciste, hizo, hicimos, hicieron. "Hacieron" adds regular endings to the infinitive stem; "hizo" is singular; the perfect would be "han hecho", never "hacido".

questions.stem: Type the preterite of volar: Los dioses soplaron sobre la flecha, y la flecha ___.
questions.explanation: "Volar" changes o → ue only in the present (vuela). In the preterite -ar verbs never change their stem: voló, like "habló".

questions.stem: Choose the correct sentence.
choices: La princesa se enamoró con un guerrero.
La princesa enamoró de un guerrero.
La princesa se enamoró de un guerrero.
La princesa se enamora a un guerrero.
questions.explanation: The verb is reflexive and takes "de": enamorarse de alguien. "Con" is a common English-influenced mistake, and the "se" can't be left out.

questions.stem: Match each word to its meaning.
questions.explanation: el guerrero = warrior, la princesa = princess, el dios = god (la diosa = goddess), la leyenda = legend, el colibrí = hummingbird. A queen is la reina; the sky is el cielo.

questions.stem: In the Maya legend, why did the gods make the hummingbird?
choices: To carry people's wishes and thoughts
questions.explanation: "Nadie lleva los deseos y los pensamientos de las personas": the hummingbird is made for that job. That's why, the legend says, a hummingbird near you means someone is sending you good wishes.

questions.stem: Which description of a legend fits this lesson?
choices: A traditional story, often about something real, that changes from one telling to another
A true historical report with one correct version
A story only about gods, with no real places
A modern short story by one known author
questions.explanation: Legends are passed on by many people, so they come in many versions, and many explain something real: two volcanoes, a small bird, where a city stands. A story mostly about gods and creation is closer to a myth.

questions.stem: Which details change between versions of the volcano legend, according to the lesson? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: The lesson lists differences in who the father is (a lord of Tlaxcala or an Aztec emperor), why the princess dies, and whether there is a lie at all. What almost every version keeps is the ending: the two become volcanoes.

questions.stem: Build the sentence in Spanish.
questions.prompt: The princess fell in love with a brave warrior.
questions.explanation: Enamorarse takes "de", not "con". The adjective normally follows the noun ("un guerrero valiente"); before it ("un valiente guerrero") it sounds more literary but is also correct.

questions.stem: Which sentence is in the historical present?
choices: Hace muchos siglos, los dioses crearon el mundo.
Hace muchos siglos, los dioses crean el mundo.
Los dioses van a crear el mundo.
Los dioses han creado el mundo.
questions.explanation: The historical present tells a past story in the present: "hace muchos siglos" shows it's long ago, but the verb "crean" is present. "Crearon" is the preterite, "van a crear" a future plan, "han creado" the perfect.

questions.stem: According to the legend of the founding of Tenochtitlan, what sign did the Mexica look for?
choices: An eagle on a cactus, eating a snake
A sleeping woman made of snow
questions.explanation: Their god Huitzilopochtli told them to settle where they found an eagle on a nopal cactus eating a snake. They found it on an island in a lake, and the scene is on Mexico's flag today.

questions.stem: What does "Estoy embarazada" mean?
questions.explanation: "Embarazada" is a classic false friend: it means pregnant. "I'm embarrassed" is "Estoy avergonzado/a" or, in Mexico, "Me da pena". Busy is "ocupado", tired "cansado".

questions.stem: Match each false friend to what it really means.
questions.explanation: embarazada = pregnant, el éxito = success, la carpeta = folder, la librería = bookshop, actual = current, realizar = to carry out. A library is la biblioteca and an exit la salida.

questions.stem: These signs are missing their Spanish. Choose the Spanish line for each numbered sign.

image.alt: Six signs with only their English line: Push, Pull, Exit, Wet floor, No parking and Danger. The Spanish line of each is numbered.

questions.explanation: Push = Empuje and Pull = Jale (usted commands of empujar and jalar); Exit = Salida; Wet floor = Piso mojado; No parking = No estacionarse; Danger = Peligro. Entrada is "entrance" and Baños "restrooms".

questions.stem: A door in a US store says "Pull". Type the word on its Spanish sign: ___
questions.explanation: "Jale" is the usted command of jalar (to pull), the Latin American word. Spain says "Tire" (from tirar), and that is accepted too.

questions.stem: According to the US Census Bureau, about how many people aged 5 and over spoke Spanish at home in 2024?
questions.explanation: The American Community Survey for 2024 counted nearly 45 million. About 70 million is the Bureau's estimate of the Hispanic population (1 July 2025), and not every Hispanic person speaks Spanish at home.

questions.stem: Which city did Spain found in 1565, now called the oldest continuously occupied European settlement in the US?
questions.explanation: Pedro Menéndez de Avilés founded St. Augustine in 1565. Santa Fe came around 1610; Los Angeles and San Antonio were founded in the 1700s.

questions.stem: Which of these English words came from Spanish, directly or through Spanish from Nahuatl? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Patio, rodeo and canyon (cañón) come from Spanish; chocolate came into English through Spanish from Nahuatl. Window comes from Old Norse and kindergarten from German.

questions.stem: Andrés says: "¡Perfecto! Then I'll see you there. Llevo los refrescos." What is this?
questions.explanation: He moves from Spanish to English and back inside one turn: code-switching. An adapted loanword is a single English word given Spanish form, like "parquear".

questions.stem: A sign says "No estacionarse". What does it mean?
questions.explanation: "Estacionarse" means to park (in Mexico), so "No estacionarse" is "No parking". Signs often give orders with no + infinitive, like "No fumar".

questions.stem: Put these events in the history of Spanish in the US in order.
choices: Santa Fe, New Mexico, is founded.
Much of the Southwest stops being part of Mexico.
An executive order designates English as the official language.
questions.explanation: 1565: St. Augustine. About 1610: Santa Fe. 1848: the Southwest, until then Mexican, becomes part of the US. 2025: an executive order designates English as the official language.

questions.stem: Build the sentence in Spanish.
questions.prompt: I realized my mistake.
questions.explanation: "Darse cuenta de" is "to realize": me di cuenta (preterite of dar, reflexive). "Realicé" means "I carried out", a false friend.

questions.stem: Marta wants to say "I studied in the library." Which sentence says that?
questions.explanation: A library is "la biblioteca". "La librería" is a bookshop (a false friend), "la carpeta" a folder and "el éxito" success.

questions.stem: Where does the sign word "Empuje" come from?
questions.explanation: Usted commands swap the vowel: empujar → (yo empujo) → empuje, like tomar → tome (lesson 17). The yo present is "empujo" and the preterite "empujé" or "empujó".

questions.stem: "Actualmente vivo en Chicago" means:
choices: I really want to live in Chicago.
I lived in Chicago in the past.
questions.explanation: "Actual" means current, so "actualmente" means currently, nowadays. "Actually" is "en realidad".

questions.stem: How is the "h" in "hola" pronounced?
questions.explanation: Spanish h is always silent: hola is "OH-lah" and hasta luego is "AHS-tah LWEH-go". The breathy "h" sound you may be thinking of is written j (jota) or g before e and i (gente).

questions.stem: Where is the stress in "apellido" (surname)?
questions.explanation: Apellido ends in a vowel, so the stress falls on the second-to-last syllable: a-pe-LLI-do ("ah-peh-YEE-doh"). There is no written accent because the word follows the rule. a-pe-lli-DO would need an accent (apellidó), and a-PE-lli-do or A-pe-lli-do would need one on the stressed vowel.

questions.stem: Which spelling of "goodbye" is correct?
questions.explanation: Adiós ends in s, so the rule says the stress should be on the second-to-last syllable (A-dios). But it is said a-DIÓS, so the stressed vowel needs a written accent. The Spanish written accent always slants up to the right, as in ó.

questions.stem: What does "sí" (with a written accent) mean?
questions.explanation: Sí with an accent means "yes"; si without one means "if". The accent tells the two words apart, like tú (you) and tu (your), él (he) and el (the).

questions.stem: It's 4 p.m. and you walk up to a hotel reception desk. How do you greet the receptionist?
questions.explanation: From about midday until it gets dark, the greeting is buenas tardes. Buenos días is for the morning, buenas noches for after dark (and for goodbye at night), and hasta mañana means "see you tomorrow".

questions.stem: Someone speaks too fast and you don't catch it. What do you say?
questions.explanation: ¿Puede repetir, por favor? asks the person to repeat, and más despacio asks for it more slowly. De nada answers thanks, con permiso asks to get past, and hasta luego is goodbye.

questions.stem: How is the "ll" in "me llamo" pronounced in Mexico?
questions.explanation: In Mexico and most of the Spanish-speaking world, ll and y sound the same, like English "y" in "yes": me llamo is "meh YAH-mo". This is called yeísmo. (In Argentina and Uruguay it sounds like "sh", which you meet in the honors lessons.)

questions.stem: Why does "lápiz" (pencil) have a written accent?
choices: It ends in z, so the stress would normally fall on the last syllable, but it falls on LÁ
Every word with an a in the first syllable needs an accent
It ends in a consonant, and every word ending in a consonant has an accent
The accent shows that the a is long
questions.explanation: Words ending in a consonant other than n or s are normally stressed on the last syllable (fa-VOR, es-pa-ÑOL). Lápiz is stressed on the first, LÁ-piz, so it needs an accent. Spanish vowels have no long and short forms; the accent marks stress only.

questions.stem: Which vowel goes at each numbered point of the vowel chart? Each answer gives an example word.

image.alt: An upside-down triangle showing where the vowels are made. Front of the mouth (lips spread) is on the left and back (lips rounded) on the right; the top is a closed mouth and the bottom an open mouth. Point 1 is top left, 2 top right, 3 middle left, 4 middle right, 5 at the bottom.

questions.explanation: i (1) is high and at the front with spread lips; u (2) is high and at the back with rounded lips. e (3) and o (4) are halfway down, front and back. a (5) is the most open vowel, low in the middle. y and ñ are consonants.

questions.stem: Type the word "perdon" (sorry) with its written accent.
questions.explanation: Perdón ends in n, so the rule puts the stress on the second-to-last syllable (PER-don). It is said per-DÓN, so the o carries a written accent.

questions.stem: Match each phrase to the situation where you'd use it.
choices: You want to get past someone
You'll see a friend again tomorrow
You meet someone in the morning
questions.explanation: Con permiso asks to pass or leave, disculpe politely gets a stranger's attention, hasta mañana means "see you tomorrow", and de nada answers gracias. In the morning you'd say buenos días.

questions.stem: In Latin American Spanish, which of these words start with an "s" sound? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: With seseo, c before e or i, z and s all sound like "s": cinco, zeta and sí. Casa starts with a "k" sound (c before a), and gente with the breathy "h" sound of g before e.

questions.stem: Build the sentence in Spanish.
questions.prompt: Can you repeat, please? (formal)
questions.explanation: ¿Puede repetir, por favor? Puede is the usted form ("can you"), repetir means "to repeat", and por favor goes at the end after a comma. The whole sentence is a question, so it opens with ¿.

questions.stem: Build the question in Spanish.
questions.prompt: How is the surname spelled?
questions.explanation: ¿Cómo se escribe el apellido? Spanish asks "how" (cómo), not "what", and se escribe means "is written". The question word carries an accent and the question opens with ¿.

questions.stem: At a bank you speak to an older woman you don't know. Which question fits?
questions.explanation: With an older stranger, use usted: ¿Cómo está usted? ¿Cómo estás? and ¿Cómo te llamas? are tú forms for friends and people your age, and ¿Qué tal, amiga? (friend) is far too casual.

questions.stem: Complete: "Usted ___ de Monterrey, ¿verdad?"
questions.explanation: Usted takes the same verb form as él and ella: usted es. Eres goes with tú, soy with yo; son is a plural form.

questions.stem: How do you ask a friend "Where are you from?"
questions.explanation: The preposition de goes in front of the question word: ¿De dónde eres? Spanish can't leave de at the end like English "from". Tú takes eres, not es.

questions.stem: Someone asks "¿Cómo te llamas?" Which answer is correct?
questions.explanation: Me llamo Laura = My name is Laura. Soy de Laura would mean "I'm from Laura", te llamas is "you are called", and llamo alone means "I call".

questions.stem: Ana is introduced to Daniel. What does Ana say?
questions.explanation: A woman says encantada and a man encantado ("delighted"). Ana is a woman, so encantada. Encantados is plural. Mucho gusto works for everyone.

questions.stem: A friend asks: "¿Cómo estás?" What is a natural answer?
questions.explanation: ¿Cómo estás? asks how you are, so answer with bien, muy bien, más o menos or mal, and return the question: ¿y tú? The other answers give your name, where you're from or "nice to meet you".

questions.stem: Which greeting is correct?
questions.explanation: When you speak to someone, señor comes without the article: Buenos días, señor López. You use el only when you talk about him: El señor López es de Monterrey.

questions.stem: Read: "Hola, me llamo Sofía. Soy de Guadalajara, pero vivo en Toronto, en Canadá. ¿Y tú? ¿De dónde eres?" Where does Sofía live?
questions.explanation: Vivo en Toronto means "I live in Toronto". Soy de Guadalajara says where she is from, which is a different thing. Pero means "but".

questions.stem: Match each question word to its meaning.
questions.explanation: Quién = who, cómo = how (¿Cómo te llamas? is literally "how do you call yourself?"), dónde = where, de dónde = where from. "When" is cuándo, from Lesson 4.

questions.stem: Complete with the right form of ser: "Yo ___ de Chicago."
questions.explanation: The yo form of ser is soy: Yo soy de Chicago (or just Soy de Chicago). Eres is the tú form and es the usted/él/ella form.

questions.stem: In Mexico, which people would you normally address with usted? Select all that apply.
choices: an older neighbour you've just met
questions.explanation: Usted is for strangers, older people and people in official or professional roles: the police officer, the new older neighbour and the doctor. Family members and children get tú.

questions.stem: Name the numbered lines on this student card.

image.alt: A student ID card from a language school in Monterrey with a photo and four lines; the label of each line is missing. Line 1 says Daniel, line 2 Ruiz Castro, line 3 Monterrey, line 4 México.

questions.explanation: Daniel is his first name (nombre) and Ruiz Castro his surnames (apellidos; most Mexicans have two). Monterrey is a city (ciudad) and México a country (país). The card shows no phone number or age.

questions.stem: Build the question in Spanish.
questions.prompt: Where are you from? (formal)
questions.explanation: ¿De dónde es usted? The question word with its de comes first, then the verb, then usted. Usted takes es; eres is the tú form.

questions.stem: Build the sentence in Spanish.
questions.prompt: My name is Daniel and I'm from Monterrey.
questions.explanation: Me llamo Daniel y soy de Monterrey. Soy is the yo form of ser and de means "from". The two halves can also swap places: Soy de Monterrey y me llamo Daniel.

questions.stem: How do you write 22 in Spanish?
questions.explanation: From 21 to 29 the number is one word with veinti-: veintidós. It ends in s but is stressed on the last syllable, so it needs an accent. Veinte y dos is an old form you will not see today.

questions.stem: How do you say 45 in Spanish?
questions.explanation: From 31 to 99, say the ten, then y, then the unit, as three words: cuarenta y cinco. Cuarenta cinco leaves out the y, cuatro y cinco is "four and five", and cincuenta y cuatro is 54, the digits the other way round.

questions.stem: How do you say "I'm thirty years old"?
questions.explanation: Spanish "has" its years: Tengo treinta años. Soy and estoy (to be) don't work here. And años needs its tilde: anos is a different, rude word.

questions.stem: Which number is "setenta"?
questions.explanation: Setenta is 70: set- like siete (7). Sesenta is 60 (ses- like seis), diecisiete is 17 and siete is 7.

questions.stem: Complete: "Mi hermano tiene ___ años." (21)
questions.explanation: Before a noun, uno shortens to un, and in 21 it becomes veintiún, with an accent: veintiún años. Veintiuno is the counting form, veintiuna is for feminine nouns, and 21 is one word.

questions.stem: A Mexican cell number has the pair 07 in it. How is that pair usually read?
questions.explanation: A pair that starts with 0 is read digit by digit: cero siete. Setenta is 70, and there is no y between digits.

questions.stem: Which question asks someone for their phone number?
questions.explanation: Spanish uses cuál, not qué, when you ask for one piece of information such as a number, a name or an address: ¿Cuál es tu número? ¿Qué es…? asks for a definition.

questions.stem: Read: "Me llamo Pablo. Tengo diecinueve años y mi celular es el 33 45 18 90 62." How old is Pablo?
questions.explanation: Diecinueve is "ten and nine": 19. Nueve alone is 9, noventa is 90 and veintinueve is 29.

questions.stem: Write 16 in Spanish, in words.
questions.explanation: 16 is one word: dieci- + seis = dieciséis. It ends in s but is stressed on the last syllable (dieci-SÉIS), so it needs an accent.

questions.stem: Match each word to its number.
questions.explanation: quince = 15, cincuenta = 50, catorce = 14, cuarenta = 40, sesenta = 60. 70 would be setenta. Watch the pairs that look alike: cuarenta (40) and cuatro (4), cincuenta (50) and cinco (5).

questions.stem: Which of these numbers are written as one word? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: 16 to 19 and 21 to 29 are single words: veintitrés, dieciocho, diecisiete. From 31 on, the parts are separate words joined by y: treinta y dos, noventa y nueve.

questions.stem: Name the numbered fields on this phone contact.

image.alt: A phone screen showing the contact Daniel Ruiz with four boxes whose labels are missing. Box 1 holds 81 23 45 67 90, box 2 daniel_ruiz@correo.mx, box 3 Calle Hidalgo 15, Monterrey, and box 4 the number 24.

questions.explanation: The ten digits are a Mexican cell number (celular). The text with @ (arroba) is an e-mail address (correo electrónico). A street, a number and a city make an address (dirección). 24 on its own is his age (edad).

questions.stem: Build the question in Spanish.
questions.prompt: How old are you? (informal)
questions.explanation: ¿Cuántos años tienes? is literally "how many years do you have?". Age uses tener (tienes), not ser (eres).

questions.stem: Build the question in Spanish.
questions.prompt: What is your phone number? (formal)
questions.explanation: ¿Cuál es su número de teléfono? Ask with cuál, not qué, for a piece of information. Su is the formal "your", and "phone number" is número de teléfono ("number of phone").

questions.stem: Complete: "Nosotros ___ español."
questions.explanation: The nosotros ending of -ar verbs is -amos: hablamos. Hablo is yo, hablas is tú and hablan is ellos/ellas/ustedes.

questions.stem: Which pronoun can replace "Ana y Daniel"?
questions.explanation: A mixed group of a woman and a man takes the masculine ellos. Ellas is only for groups of women. Ustedes means "you all", and nosotros means "we".

questions.stem: Which sentence means "I'm not working today"?
questions.explanation: No goes directly before the verb: No trabajo hoy (or Hoy no trabajo). Putting no after the verb copies English "work not" and is wrong.

questions.stem: In Mexico you ask a group of colleagues: "Do you all work here?" Which question is right?
questions.explanation: In Latin America ustedes is the only plural "you", with the ellos form: ¿Ustedes trabajan aquí? Vosotros is used in Spain. Tú and usted are for one person.

questions.stem: Complete: "—¿Por qué estudias español? —___ necesito hablar con mis clientes."
questions.explanation: The answer "because" is porque: one word, no accent. The question "why?" is por qué: two words, with an accent. Mis clientes means "my clients".

questions.stem: Which sentence is correct?
questions.explanation: Buscar already means "to look for", so there's no word for "for": Busco mi celular. The same goes for escuchar (to listen to) and mirar (to look at).

questions.stem: Complete with trabajar: "Usted ___ mucho."
questions.explanation: Usted takes the él/ella form: usted trabaja. Trabajas is the tú form; trabajan is for ustedes or ellos.

questions.stem: Read the message: "Hola, Kate. Hoy no trabajo. Estudio inglés con Daniel y practicamos mucho. ¿Llegas a las seis? Laura." What is Laura doing today?
questions.explanation: Hoy no trabajo: today she isn't working. Estudio inglés con Daniel: she's studying English with Daniel. ¿Llegas a las seis? asks whether Kate is arriving at six.

questions.stem: Fill in the pronoun chart: pick the pronouns for each numbered cell.

image.alt: A table of subject pronouns with rows for 1st, 2nd and 3rd person and columns for singular and plural. All six cells are empty and numbered: 1 and 2 in the first-person row, 3 and 4 in the second-person row, 5 and 6 in the third-person row; odd numbers are singular, even numbers plural.

questions.explanation: 1st person: yo (I), nosotros/nosotras (we). 2nd person: tú and usted (you, one person), ustedes (you all). 3rd person: él/ella (he/she), ellos/ellas (they). Mi and tu mean "my" and "your"; me and te are the pronouns of me llamo, te llamas.

questions.stem: Complete with the right form of llegar: "¿Cuándo ___ ellos?"
questions.explanation: Ellos takes the -an ending: llegan. Llega is for él, ella or usted, and llegamos for nosotros.

questions.stem: Match each verb to its meaning.
questions.explanation: escuchar = to listen to, mirar = to look at or watch, buscar = to look for, contestar = to answer, necesitar = to need. "To arrive" is llegar.

questions.stem: Which pronouns can be the subject of "hablan"? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: The -an form goes with ellos, ellas and ustedes. Usted (one person) takes habla, and nosotros takes hablamos.

questions.stem: Build the sentence in Spanish.
questions.prompt: We don't speak English.
questions.explanation: No hablamos inglés. No goes right before the verb, and the -amos ending already says "we", so nosotros isn't needed. Hablan would be "they" or "you all".

questions.stem: Build the question in Spanish.
questions.prompt: When is Ana arriving?
questions.explanation: ¿Cuándo llega Ana? After a question word comes the verb, then the subject. Llega is the form for one other person; llegas would mean "you arrive". The present also covers plans: "is arriving".

questions.stem: In much of the Caribbean, "¿Cómo estás?" can sound like…
questions.explanation: In Cuba, Puerto Rico, the Dominican Republic and the Caribbean coasts, an s at the end of a syllable is often aspirated (a breathy h) or dropped: es-tás becomes "eh-TAH". The "th" sound belongs to Spain, and no variety adds an "eh" after estás.

questions.stem: An Argentine friend says "Vos sos de Córdoba, ¿no?" How would you say it with tú?
questions.explanation: Vos sos is the Río de la Plata form of tú eres (you are). Sos only goes with vos, and es goes with usted, él and ella.

questions.stem: How does a speaker from Madrid usually say "cinco"?
questions.explanation: Central and northern Spain use distinción: c before e or i, and z, are said like English "th" in "think". Latin America says "SEEN-ko" (seseo). "KEEN-ko" would only be right for c before a, o or u.

questions.stem: Why is the Spanish "th" in "gracias" ("GRAH-thyahs") not a lisp?
choices: It is only used by older speakers
It only happens before the letter a
It is how the written accent is pronounced
Spaniards keep s as "s"; only z and c before e or i become "th"
questions.explanation: A lisp would turn every s into "th". In distinción the s stays "s" and only z, ce and ci are "th", so casa (house) and caza (hunting) sound different. It is the standard pronunciation of central and northern Spain, used by nearly everyone there.

questions.stem: In Buenos Aires, "me llamo" often sounds like…
questions.explanation: In Argentina and Uruguay, ll and y are said like "sh" (or the older "zh" of measure). "meh YAH-mo" is the Mexican pronunciation, and ll is never a plain l or a "th".

questions.stem: Your phone rings in Mexico City. What do you say when you pick up?
questions.explanation: Mexicans answer the phone with ¿Bueno? ¿Diga? is Spain's answer and ¿Hola? is usual in Argentina and Uruguay. ¿Mande? means "pardon?" when you didn't catch something.

questions.stem: Which statement about Spanish accents is accurate?
choices: Only the Mexican accent is correct Spanish
Caribbean speakers drop the s because they are careless
Spain's accent is the official standard for Latin America
They are regular varieties of Spanish, used by educated speakers
questions.explanation: Each region's pronunciation follows regular patterns and is used by educated speakers there; the academies treat educated speech from every country as correct. This course uses central Mexican Spanish as a model, not as the only correct form.

questions.stem: A caller asks for Laura. You answer: "¿De parte de quién?" What are you asking?
questions.explanation: ¿De parte de quién? (literally "on behalf of whom?") is the standard way to ask who is calling. The caller answers: De parte de Kate.

questions.stem: A speaker says "gracias" as "GRAH-thyahs" and asks friends "¿Vosotros habláis inglés?" Where is the speaker most likely from?
questions.explanation: Two clues point to Spain: the "th" sound for c before i (distinción) and vosotros for "you all" among friends. Argentina, Mexico and Cuba all use seseo and ustedes.

questions.stem: How do people usually answer the phone in each place? Pick a greeting for each number.

image.alt: Four phones with empty speech bubbles numbered 1 to 4. Phone 1 is marked México, phone 2 Perú, Chile and Venezuela, phone 3 España, phone 4 Argentina and Uruguay.

questions.explanation: Mexico: ¿Bueno? Peru, Chile and Venezuela: ¿Aló? Spain: ¿Diga? (or ¿Dígame?). Argentina and Uruguay: ¿Hola? ¿Mande? asks someone to repeat, and ¿Qué tal? asks how things are.

questions.stem: "Vos hablás inglés" is Río de la Plata Spanish. Complete the same sentence with tú: "Tú ___ inglés."
questions.explanation: The vos form hablás is stressed on the end and has an accent; the tú form is hablas, stressed on HA, with no accent.

questions.stem: Match each feature to where it is typical.
left: z and ce, ci said like "th"
s at the end of a syllable fades to a breath
questions.explanation: Distinción ("th") and vosotros are features of Spain. Sheísmo ("sh") belongs to the Río de la Plata. Aspiration of the s is typical of the Caribbean (and also of other coasts, Chile and southern Spain). None of these is a mistake.

questions.stem: Which of these are normal ways to answer the phone somewhere in the Spanish-speaking world? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: ¿Bueno? (Mexico), ¿Aló? (much of South America) and ¿Diga? (Spain) are all phone greetings. Hasta luego is goodbye, and de nada answers thanks.

questions.stem: Build the sentence in Spanish.
questions.prompt: Sorry, wrong number.
questions.explanation: Perdón, número equivocado. Equivocado means wrong or mistaken, and in Spanish the describing word comes after the noun: número equivocado, literally "number wrong".

questions.stem: What is the apellido paterno of "Carlos Mendoza Ruiz"?
questions.explanation: A full name is first name(s), then the father's surname (apellido paterno), then the mother's (apellido materno). Carlos is the first name, Mendoza the apellido paterno and Ruiz the apellido materno.

questions.stem: In everyday life, how would people refer to Carlos Mendoza Ruiz?
questions.explanation: Daily use takes the first surname, the apellido paterno: el señor Mendoza. The second surname appears on documents and forms. Señor goes with a surname, not a first name.

questions.stem: Carlos Mendoza Ruiz and Elena Vargas Soto have a son, Pablo. Following the traditional order, what is his full name?
questions.explanation: Each parent passes on their first surname, the father's first: Mendoza (from Carlos) and Vargas (from Elena). Ruiz and Soto, the parents' second surnames, don't pass on. Vargas Mendoza is possible in Spain, and in Mexico if the parents ask for it, but it isn't the traditional order.

questions.stem: How do you greet an older neighbour, Carmen Ortiz, with respect?
questions.explanation: Doña goes before a woman's first name, with no article when you speak to her: Buenos días, doña Carmen. Don is for men, and doña never goes with a surname.

questions.stem: A business card says "Lic. Andrea Torres Gil". How do you greet her at the office?
questions.explanation: Lic. means licenciada for a woman. Use the title with her first surname, Torres, and usted. Gil is her second surname, ¿qué tal? with her first name is too casual at first, and doña goes with first names.

questions.stem: Your new boss, older than you, says: "¿Nos tuteamos?" What is a natural answer?
questions.explanation: ¿Nos tuteamos? offers to switch to tú. Accept with ¡Claro! (Of course!) and start using tú. De nada answers thanks, mucho gusto is for a first meeting, and con permiso asks to pass.

questions.stem: Which statement about the order of surnames is accurate?
choices: In Spain, since 2017, parents choose the order of their children's surnames.
In Mexico the mother's surname must always come first.
Children take both of their father's surnames.
Married women in Mexico must take their husband's surname.
questions.explanation: Spain's rule giving the father's surname priority ended in 2017; parents now agree on the order. In Mexico the father's surname usually comes first, though courts have let parents choose. Children take one surname from each parent, and Mexican women keep their own surnames when they marry.

questions.stem: A friend from Bogotá always uses usted with you. What does it most likely mean?
choices: Your friend is angry with you.
In parts of Colombia usted can be warm and friendly among friends.
Your friend thinks you are much older.
Your friend doesn't want to be close.
questions.explanation: In parts of Colombia, such as Bogotá and Antioquia, many people use usted with friends, partners and family (ustedeo). It isn't a sign of distance there.

questions.stem: A Mexican form has three boxes: "Apellido paterno / Apellido materno / Nombre(s)". Kate Elizabeth Hughes has one surname. What goes under "Nombre(s)"?
questions.explanation: Nombre(s) holds all first names: Kate Elizabeth. Hughes goes under apellido paterno, and apellido materno stays empty (or she asks the clerk).

questions.stem: Name the numbered parts of María Fernanda López Ortiz's name.

image.alt: A family diagram: the father José López Ramírez and the mother Ana Ortiz Vega, with arrows to their daughter María Fernanda López Ortiz. Under the daughter's name three brackets lead to empty boxes: 1 under María Fernanda, 2 under López, 3 under Ortiz.

questions.explanation: María Fernanda are her first names (1). López comes from her father, José López Ramírez: her apellido paterno (2). Ortiz comes from her mother, Ana Ortiz Vega: her apellido materno (3). Nombre completo is the whole name, and licenciado is a title.

questions.stem: Complete the offer to switch to tú: "¿Nos ___?" (from tutear)
questions.explanation: Tutear is a regular -ar verb, and the nosotros form ends in -amos: ¿Nos tuteamos? (Shall we use tú with each other?)

questions.stem: Match each form of address to the person it is used for.
choices: a teacher (or a woman with a master's)
a respected older woman, with her first name
questions.explanation: Licenciado (Lic.) is for university graduates, ingeniera (Ing.) for a woman engineer, arquitecto (Arq.) for an architect, maestra (Mtra.) for a teacher or a woman with a master's degree, and doña + first name for an older woman you respect. Children are addressed by name with tú.

questions.stem: Which of these are correct, respectful ways to greet someone in Mexico? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Don and doña go with a first name (don Javier, not doña López), and doña is only for women (not doña Javier). Titles work with the surname or alone: ingeniera, licenciado Hernández.

questions.stem: Build the sentence in Spanish.
questions.prompt: My full name is María López Ortiz.
questions.explanation: Mi nombre completo es María López Ortiz: first name, then the father's surname López, then the mother's surname Ortiz.

questions.stem: Which article goes with "foto" (photo)?
questions.explanation: Foto is feminine although it ends in -o, because it is short for la fotografía: la foto, una foto, las fotos. It is one of the few exceptions to the -o/-a rule, like el mapa.

questions.stem: What is the plural of "el lápiz" (pencil)?
questions.explanation: A noun ending in a consonant adds -es, and a final z becomes c before e: lápiz → lápices. The word stays masculine, so the article is los. The accent stays because lápices is stressed three syllables from the end.

questions.stem: Which noun is feminine?
questions.explanation: It is la llave. Nouns ending in -e or a consonant can be either gender, so they must be learned with the article: el papel and el reloj are masculine, and el cuaderno ends in -o.

questions.stem: Complete: "Necesito ___ computadora."
questions.explanation: Computadora is feminine (-a), so "a" is una: Necesito una computadora (I need a computer). Un is masculine, unos is plural, and el is masculine "the".

questions.stem: What is the plural of "la canción" (song)?
questions.explanation: A consonant ending adds -es: canciones. The accent disappears, because canciones ends in s and is stressed on the second-to-last syllable (-cio-), which is what the stress rule expects. Nouns in -ción are always feminine, so the article is las.

questions.stem: A class has 12 girls and 3 boys. How do you say "the children" for the whole class?
questions.explanation: A mixed group takes the masculine plural, however many girls there are: los niños. Las niñas would mean only the girls. The article and the noun must agree, so las niños and los niñas are never possible.

questions.stem: Read: "En el salón de clases hay una mesa, unas sillas y un mapa. Las plumas y los lápices son para los estudiantes." (hay = there is, there are; para = for) What is for the students?
questions.explanation: The second sentence says "Las plumas y los lápices son para los estudiantes": the pens (las plumas) and the pencils (los lápices) are for the students. The table, chairs and map are only in the classroom.

questions.stem: Which sentence contains a mistake?
questions.explanation: Mapa is masculine although it ends in -a, so it must be "Es un mapa." Llave is feminine, reloj is masculine, and foto is feminine (short for fotografía), so the other three are correct.

questions.stem: Write the definite article ("the") for each noun: ___ foto, ___ papel, ___ mujeres, ___ lentes.
questions.explanation: la foto (feminine, short for la fotografía), el papel (masculine), las mujeres (plural of la mujer), los lentes (glasses: masculine and always plural for one pair).

questions.stem: Match each noun to its plural.
questions.explanation: Nouns ending in a consonant add -es (relojes, mujeres), z becomes c (lápices), and the written accent follows the stress rule: it disappears in canciones and appears in jóvenes. Los relojs and las canciónes break those rules.

questions.stem: Which nouns are masculine? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: El mapa, el día and el idioma are masculine although they end in -a. La mano and la foto are feminine although they end in -o. All five are exceptions worth learning by heart.

questions.stem: Name the numbered things in this classroom, with their articles.

image.alt: A classroom with a window, a map and a clock on the wall, a door on the right, a table with a computer, a book, a notebook, a pen and glasses on it, a chair next to the table and a backpack on the floor. Six things are numbered.

questions.explanation: 1 is the window (la ventana), 2 the clock (el reloj), 3 the door (la puerta), 4 the computer (la computadora), 5 the chair (la silla) and 6 the backpack (la mochila). There is no pencil (el lápiz) or key (la llave) in the picture.

questions.stem: Build the sentence in Spanish.
questions.prompt: It's a map of Mexico.
questions.explanation: Spanish has no word for "it" here: the verb es is enough. Mapa is masculine, so "a map" is un mapa, and "of Mexico" is de México.

questions.stem: Build the sentence in Spanish.
questions.prompt: I need some pencils and a notebook.
questions.explanation: Lápices is masculine plural, so "some" is unos; cuaderno is masculine singular, so "a" is un. The two things can be listed in either order.

questions.stem: Complete: "Ana y ___ hermanos viven en Lima." (her)
questions.explanation: "Her" is su, and the ending matches the thing owned: hermanos is plural, so sus hermanos. Su alone would go with one brother; tus means "your" and mis means "my".

questions.stem: Complete: "Nosotros ___ dos gatos."
questions.explanation: The nosotros form of tener is tenemos. The stem change e → ie happens only when the stress falls on the stem (tienes, tiene, tienen), and the stress of tenemos is on the ending, so tienemos is wrong. Tengo is yo and tienen is ellos.

questions.stem: How do you say "I'm thirty years old"?
questions.explanation: Spanish says you have years: tener … años. Soy, estoy and es are forms of "to be", which English uses for age but Spanish doesn't.

questions.stem: Your mother's sister is your…
questions.explanation: Your parent's sister is your aunt, la tía. Her children are your primos (cousins), and your mother's mother is your abuela.

questions.stem: Someone asks Lucía "¿Tienes hermanos?" She has one brother and one sister. What does she answer?
questions.explanation: Hermanos, the masculine plural, covers a mixed group: one brother and one sister are dos hermanos (two siblings). Dos hermanas would mean two sisters.

questions.stem: Which sentence is correct?
choices: La nuestra familia es de Puebla.
questions.explanation: Nuestro agrees with the thing owned: familia is feminine singular, so nuestra familia. A possessive adjective replaces the article, so "la nuestra familia" is wrong, and nuestras would need a plural noun.

questions.stem: Complete: "Mis primos ___ de Monterrey."
questions.explanation: Mis primos (my cousins) is a plural subject, like ellos, so ser takes the form son. Es is singular, somos is "we are" and eres is "you are".

questions.stem: Read: "Me llamo Diego. Tengo veinticinco años. Mis padres son Roberto y Elena. Tengo una hermana, Lucía. Mi tía Patricia tiene dos hijos." Who is Patricia's son to Diego?
questions.explanation: Patricia is Diego's aunt (mi tía), so her children (sus hijos) are Diego's cousins: su primo and su prima.

questions.stem: In "Su perro se llama Toby", whose dog can it be? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Su is the possessive for él, ella, usted, ellos, ellas and ustedes, so it can mean his, her, their or your (formal). "My" is mi. To be clear, Spanish can say el perro de él, el perro de ella and so on.

questions.stem: Write the correct form of tener: "Yo ___ un perro." "¿Tú ___ hermanos?" "Mis abuelos ___ ochenta años."
questions.explanation: Tener: tengo (with g in the yo form), tienes and tienen (e → ie where the stress falls on the stem). Mis abuelos is a plural subject, so the verb takes the ellos form.

questions.stem: This is Lucía's family tree. Name each numbered person from Lucía's point of view.

image.alt: A family tree with first names only. Top row: Jorge and Carmen. Middle row: their son Roberto with his wife Elena, and their daughter Patricia with her husband Andrés. Bottom row: Lucía (marked yo) and Diego, the children of Roberto and Elena; Sofía and Mateo, the children of Patricia and Andrés. Six people are numbered.

questions.explanation: Jorge and Carmen are Lucía's grandparents (el abuelo, la abuela). Roberto is her father (el padre), and his sister Patricia is her aunt (la tía). Diego is her brother (el hermano), and Patricia's daughter Sofía is her cousin (la prima).

questions.stem: Match each owner to the possessive adjective you use before one masculine noun (… perro).
questions.explanation: yo → mi perro, tú → tu perro (no accent on the possessive), él and ustedes → su perro, nosotros → nuestro perro. Nuestra would go with a feminine noun.

questions.stem: Build the question in Spanish.
questions.prompt: How old is your sister?
questions.explanation: Age uses tener: ¿Cuántos años tiene tu hermana? (literally "How many years does your sister have?"). Tu hermana is like ella, so the verb is tiene; tienes is the tú form.

questions.stem: Build the sentence in Spanish.
questions.prompt: We have two dogs and a cat.
questions.explanation: "We have" is tenemos. Gato is masculine, so "a cat" is un gato. The two animals can be listed in either order.

questions.stem: Complete with vivir: "Nosotros ___ en Guadalajara."
questions.explanation: -ir verbs share the -er endings except in the nosotros form, which is -imos: vivimos. Vivemos uses the -er ending, and viven is the ellos form.

questions.stem: Complete with aprender: "Mi hermana ___ inglés en la universidad."
questions.explanation: Mi hermana is like ella, so the -er verb takes -e: aprende. Aprendo is yo and aprenden is ellos. Aprenda uses an -a- ending, which -er verbs don't have in the present.

questions.stem: A woman says "I'm a teacher". Which is correct?
questions.explanation: With ser and a bare job, Spanish uses no article: Soy maestra. A woman uses the feminine form maestra. Es maestra means "she is a teacher", not "I am".

questions.stem: Which sentence is written correctly?
questions.explanation: In Spanish, nationalities and languages are written with a small letter: mexicana, español. Only countries and cities take a capital (México).

questions.stem: Complete: "Mi esposa es de España. Es ___."
questions.explanation: Nationalities ending in a consonant add -a for a woman: español → española. Españoles is the masculine plural, and the ñ is part of the spelling.

questions.stem: Two women from Canada say "We're Canadian." Which is correct?
questions.explanation: Adjectives in -ense are the same for men and women and only add -s in the plural: canadienses. They are lowercase, like all nationalities.

questions.stem: Read: "Hola, soy Paul. Soy estadounidense, pero vivo en México. Soy ingeniero y trabajo en una oficina. Hablo inglés y aprendo español." Which is true?
choices: Paul lives in the United States.
questions.explanation: "Aprendo español" means "I'm learning Spanish". Paul is American (estadounidense), lives in Mexico and works in an office (una oficina).

questions.stem: Which question asks someone what job they do?
questions.explanation: ¿En qué trabajas? (literally "In what do you work?") asks about someone's job. The others ask where someone is from, which languages they speak, and where they live.

questions.stem: Write the present tense: "Yo ___ un libro." (leer) "Ustedes ___ en Lima." (vivir) "¿Tú ___ la pregunta?" (comprender)
questions.explanation: yo leo (stem le- + -o), ustedes viven (the ellos form, -en for -er and -ir verbs), tú comprendes (-es).

questions.stem: Match each country to its nationality adjective (the form for a man).
questions.explanation: mexicano and colombiano end in -o; español ends in a consonant (feminine española); canadiense and estadounidense end in -ense and don't change for gender. There are no words españolo or canadiano.

questions.stem: Which sentences are correct? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: A bare job after ser has no article (es ingeniero, es estudiante), so "Soy un mesero" is wrong: Soy mesero. The nosotros form of vivir is vivimos, not vivemos. Leemos (we read) is correct, with both e's.

questions.stem: Put the present-tense forms of vivir in the usual order: yo, tú, él, nosotros, ellos.
questions.explanation: yo vivo, tú vives, él vive, nosotros vivimos, ellos viven. Only the nosotros form (-imos) differs from an -er verb like aprender (aprendemos).

questions.stem: Build the question in Spanish.
questions.prompt: What languages does your father speak?
questions.explanation: The question phrase comes first, then the verb, then the subject: ¿Qué idiomas habla tu padre? Tu padre is like él, so the verb is habla; hablas is the tú form.

questions.stem: Build the sentence in Spanish.
questions.prompt: My sister is a doctor and lives in Canada.
questions.explanation: A bare job takes no article (es doctora, not es una doctora), and mi hermana is like ella, so the verb is vive. The two halves can come in either order.

questions.stem: Complete: "Las sillas son ___." (white)
questions.explanation: Blanco is an -o adjective with four forms. Las sillas is feminine plural, so the adjective is blancas.

questions.stem: How do you say "a red backpack"?
questions.explanation: Colours follow the noun and agree with it: mochila is feminine, so una mochila roja. Putting the colour first sounds wrong, and rojo or un would be masculine.

questions.stem: Complete: "Mis primos son muy ___." (nice, friendly)
questions.explanation: Mis primos is masculine plural (a group of male cousins, or a mixed group), so the adjective is simpáticos. Muy never changes.

questions.stem: In Mexican Spanish, complete: "Tengo unos zapatos ___." (zapatos = shoes; brown)
questions.explanation: The colour café (brown, literally "coffee") is often left unchanged: unos zapatos café. The plural cafés (zapatos cafés, ojos cafés) is also correct and common in Mexico, but it needs its accent, so cafes is wrong, and cafeses adds a second plural. Spain and some other countries say marrón, whose plural marrones loses the accent.

questions.stem: Which is correct for "a good friend" (a man)?
questions.explanation: Before a masculine singular noun bueno drops its -o: un buen amigo. (Un amigo bueno is also possible, after the noun.) For a woman it stays buena: una buena amiga.

questions.stem: Which phrase means "a great teacher"?
questions.explanation: Grande becomes gran before a singular noun and then means great: un gran maestro. After the noun, un maestro grande means a big teacher. Grande is never shortened after the noun.

questions.stem: Read: "Mi ciudad es pequeña y bastante bonita. Las calles son largas y las casas son blancas. La gente es muy simpática, pero la vida es un poco aburrida." (la calle = street, la gente = people, la vida = life) What is a little boring?
questions.explanation: "La vida es un poco aburrida" means life is a little boring. The streets are long (largas), the houses are white (blancas) and the people are very nice (muy simpática).

questions.stem: Complete: "El libro y la mochila son ___." (new)
questions.explanation: One adjective for a masculine and a feminine noun together takes the masculine plural: nuevos. Nuevas would mean both nouns were feminine.

questions.stem: Write the adjective in the right form: unas plumas ___ (azul), dos preguntas ___ (fácil), unos hombres ___ (joven).
questions.explanation: Consonant adjectives don't change for gender and add -es in the plural: azules, fáciles, jóvenes. Fáciles keeps its accent, and jóvenes gains one because it is stressed three syllables from the end.

questions.stem: Match each adjective to its opposite.
questions.explanation: grande (big) ↔ pequeño (small), nuevo (new) ↔ viejo (old), alto (tall) ↔ bajo (short), largo (long) ↔ corto (short), fácil (easy) ↔ difícil (difficult). Remember that largo means long, not large.

questions.stem: Name the colour of each numbered square.

image.alt: Eight colour squares in two rows. Top row: red, blue, green, yellow. Bottom row: black, white, grey, brown. Six of them are numbered.

questions.explanation: 1 rojo (red), 2 azul (blue), 3 amarillo (yellow), 4 negro (black), 5 gris (grey), 6 café (brown; Spain marrón). The two squares without numbers are verde (green) and blanco (white).

questions.stem: Which sentences are correct? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Adjectives agree in gender and number: difíciles, alta and simpáticos are right. Los gatos needs negros, and las mochilas needs azules (consonant adjectives add -es in the plural).

questions.stem: Build the sentence in Spanish.
questions.prompt: My brother is tall and very nice.
questions.explanation: Ser + adjective describes what someone is like. Mi hermano is masculine singular, so alto and simpático; muy goes right before the adjective it strengthens.

questions.stem: Build the question in Spanish.
questions.prompt: What colour is your backpack?
questions.explanation: The question is ¿De qué color es…? (literally "Of what colour is…?"). Tu mochila is one thing, so the verb is es.

questions.stem: In how many countries is Spanish the official or main national language, in the usual count?
questions.explanation: The usual count is 20: 18 in the Americas, plus Spain and Equatorial Guinea. Puerto Rico also has Spanish as an official language but is a US territory, not a country. 18 is only the Latin American countries; 21 appears on some websites after Antigua and Barbuda's 2026 policy, which was not yet law when this course was written.

questions.stem: In which of these countries is Spanish NOT the main language?
questions.explanation: Brazil (Brasil), the biggest country in South America, speaks Portuguese. Paraguay (Spanish and Guaraní), Uruguay and Panama are Spanish-speaking.

questions.stem: Complete: "Mis amigas son de Costa Rica. Son ___."
questions.explanation: Costarricense ends in -ense, so it doesn't change for gender; the plural adds -s. Nationalities are lowercase. (Informally, Costa Ricans are also called ticos and ticas.)

questions.stem: What is the capital of Peru?
questions.explanation: Lima is the capital of Perú. Quito is the capital of Ecuador, La Paz is the seat of Bolivia's government, and Santiago is the capital of Chile.

questions.stem: Which spelling is correct for "Puerto Rican"?
questions.explanation: Inside a word, the strong r of Rico must be written rr, so puerto + rico gives puertorriqueño, written as one word and lowercase.

questions.stem: Which sentence is correct?
choices: Lima es el capital de Perú.
Lima es la capital de Perú.
Lima es la capital de peruano.
Lima es la Capital de perú.
questions.explanation: A capital city is la capital (feminine); el capital means money invested in a business. The country name, Perú, takes a capital letter, but capital as a common noun doesn't.

questions.stem: Read: "Me llamo Valentina. Soy argentina, pero vivo en Montevideo, la capital de Uruguay. Mi esposo es uruguayo y nuestros hijos hablan español e inglés." Which is true?
choices: Valentina lives in the capital of Uruguay.
questions.explanation: Valentina lives in Montevideo, the capital of Uruguay. She is Argentinian (argentina), her husband is Uruguayan (uruguayo), and their children speak Spanish and English (español e inglés).

questions.stem: Which statement about Spanish in Mexico is accurate?
choices: A 2003 law makes Spanish the only official language.
English and Spanish are both official.
Spanish is official only in Mexico City.
A 2003 law calls Spanish and the Indigenous languages national languages; no law names one official language.
questions.explanation: Spanish is Mexico's official language in practice, used by the government, schools and courts, but no law declares it official. Mexico's 2003 law on linguistic rights calls Spanish and the Indigenous languages lenguas nacionales with equal validity.

questions.stem: Which country has exactly two official languages, Spanish and Guaraní?
questions.explanation: Paraguay's official languages are Spanish and Guaraní. Bolivia also counts Guaraní among its official languages, but its constitution makes all of the country's Indigenous languages official, so it has many more than two.

questions.stem: Put these capital cities in order from north to south.
questions.explanation: Mexico City (about 19° north) is furthest north, then Guatemala City (about 15° N) and Bogotá (about 5° N, just north of the equator). Lima (about 12° south) and Santiago de Chile (about 33° S) are in the southern hemisphere.

questions.stem: Match each country to its capital.
questions.explanation: Bogotá (Colombia), La Habana (Havana, Cuba), Caracas (Venezuela), Santiago (Chile), Quito (Ecuador). Managua is the capital of Nicaragua and Asunción the capital of Paraguay.

questions.stem: Which nationality adjectives have the same form for men and women? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Adjectives in -ense don't change for gender: nicaragüense, costarricense, estadounidense. Chileno and salvadoreño are -o adjectives with feminine forms chilena and salvadoreña.

questions.stem: Write the nationality adjective. Ana is from Guatemala: "Ana es ___." Pedro is from Venezuela: "Pedro es ___."
questions.explanation: Guatemala → guatemalteco, feminine guatemalteca. Venezuela → venezolano. Both are lowercase and agree with the person.

questions.stem: Build the sentence in Spanish.
questions.prompt: My friends are Peruvian and live in Lima.
questions.explanation: Mis amigos is masculine plural, so the adjective is peruanos and the verb forms are son and viven. Peruanos stays lowercase; Lima is a city name, so it has a capital.

questions.stem: Your sister's husband is your…
questions.explanation: Your sibling's husband is your brother-in-law, el cuñado. El suegro is your spouse's father, and el yerno is your daughter's husband.

questions.stem: Your wife's mother is your…
questions.explanation: Your spouse's mother is your mother-in-law, la suegra. La nuera is your son's wife, la cuñada your sister-in-law and la madrina your godmother.

questions.stem: What is the diminutive of "chico"?
questions.explanation: Drop the -o and add -ito, but c before i would sound like s, so it becomes qu to keep the k sound: chiquito.

questions.stem: What is the diminutive of "el mapa"?
questions.explanation: The diminutive keeps the noun's gender and its final -a: el mapa → el mapita, like el problema → el problemita.

questions.stem: Marta is the godmother of Ana and Luis's daughter. What does Ana call Marta?
questions.explanation: The parents and the godparents become compadres and comadres to each other, so Ana calls Marta comadre. The child calls Marta madrina.

questions.stem: Someone in Mexico asks you "¿Quieres un cafecito?" What does the diminutive mostly add?
choices: that the cup will be very small
questions.explanation: Diminutives often show affection or friendliness rather than size. Un cafecito is a warm invitation to a coffee, usually a normal cup.

questions.stem: Which nickname is usual for "Francisco"?
questions.explanation: Francisco → Paco (also Pancho). Pepe is José, Chuy is Jesús and Memo is Guillermo.

questions.stem: Read: "Soy Toño. Mi esposa se llama Lupita. Sus papás viven en Oaxaca. Mi cuñada Rosa es la madrina de nuestro hijo." Who is Rosa?
choices: Toño's sister-in-law and his son's godmother
questions.explanation: Mi cuñada means my sister-in-law, and Rosa is la madrina (godmother) of their son. Toño's mother-in-law is Lupita's mother, who lives in Oaxaca.

questions.stem: What is "mija" short for?
questions.explanation: Mija is mi hija (my daughter) run together; mijo is mi hijo. Parents use them with their children, and older people often use them with younger people as a term of affection.

questions.stem: Write the diminutives: perro → ___, abuela → ___, amigo → ___.
questions.explanation: Words in -o or -a drop the vowel and add -ito or -ita: perrito, abuelita. In amigo, g before i would sound like the j sound, so it becomes gu: amiguito.

questions.stem: Match each family word to its meaning.
questions.explanation: el suegro = father-in-law, la nuera = daughter-in-law, el yerno = son-in-law, el nieto = grandson, el sobrino = nephew. Brother-in-law is el cuñado and godson is el ahijado.

questions.stem: Which of these are affectionate ways to speak to someone you love? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Mija (my daughter, honey), mi amor (my love) and cariño (darling) are terms of endearment. Señor and usted are polite and formal, not affectionate.

questions.stem: Luis is the godfather of Javier's son. Complete: "Luis y Javier son ___." (one word: what they are to each other)
questions.explanation: A child's father and godfather are compadres to each other (two women would be comadres). The son calls Luis padrino.
