questions.explanation: Ser and ir share the preterite fui, fuiste, fue… The sentence decides: "al cine" (to the movies) is a destination, so this is ir, "I went". "Fue increíble" (it was incredible) would be ser.

questions.stem: Complete: "Mis abuelos ___ de Puebla el domingo." (venir)
questions.explanation: "Venir" has the strong stem vin- and the ellos ending -ieron: "vinieron". "Venieron" keeps the infinitive stem; "vinimos" is "we came"; "vinó" adds an accent and ending that strong forms never have (the él form is "vino").

questions.stem: How do you say "three days ago"?
questions.explanation: "Ago" is hace + the length of time, with hace first: "hace tres días". "Tres días hace" copies the English order, and "pasado" is used for "last" (la semana pasada), not with hace.

questions.stem: Which of these preterite forms are written correctly? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: "Tuvo" (strong preterite, no accent), "busqué" (-car → -qué in the yo form) and "comí" (regular -er yo form with an accent) are correct. Strong forms never take an accent, so "hizó" is wrong (hizo), and one-syllable forms like "dio" have no accent either.

questions.stem: Complete with the preterite of "ver": "Anoche nosotros ___ una película muy divertida."
questions.explanation: "Ver" takes the -er/-ir endings without accents: vi, viste, vio, vimos, vieron. For nosotros: "vimos".

questions.stem: Match each verb to its yo form in the preterite.
questions.explanation: The strong preterites take a new stem and the ending -e with no accent: tuv-e, estuv-e, pud-e, hic-e. "Dar" takes the short forms di, diste, dio. "Hací" and "tení" use the infinitive stems, which these verbs don't use in the preterite.

questions.stem: This timeline runs from the past on the left to today on the right. Name the numbered points.

image.alt: A timeline from left (the past) to right (now). Seven points: five numbered points, one labeled la semana pasada between points 2 and 3, and hoy at the right end.

questions.explanation: From the furthest past to now: hace dos años (two years ago), el año pasado (last year), la semana pasada, anteayer (the day before yesterday), ayer (yesterday), anoche (last night), hoy. "Mañana" and "la semana próxima" are in the future.

questions.stem: Build the sentence in Spanish.
questions.prompt: Yesterday I went to the market with my sister.
questions.explanation: "Fui" is the preterite of ir (I went), for one finished trip. Spanish is flexible here: "ayer" can go first, last or right after the verb (or after "al mercado"), and "con mi hermana" can come before or after "al mercado". "Iba" is the imperfect ("I used to go / was going"), not the past of a single finished event.

questions.stem: Build the sentence in Spanish.
questions.prompt: We had a great time at the beach.
questions.explanation: "Pasarla bien" (to have a good time) keeps "la" and conjugates pasar: "la pasamos" for nosotros. "Lo pasé" is the Spain form and the wrong person. The place can also go first: "En la playa la pasamos muy bien."

questions.stem: A friend asks: "¿Cómo fue la excursión?" Which answer fits?
questions.explanation: "¿Cómo fue…?" asks how the trip was, with "fue" from ser. The answer uses the same form: "Fue increíble" (It was incredible). "Fui increíble" means "I was incredible", and the other two talk about the present or future.

questions.stem: Complete: "Nosotros ___ visitado las pirámides dos veces."
questions.explanation: The present perfect uses haber: he, has, ha, hemos, han. For nosotros: "hemos visitado". "Tenemos" is a common English-speaker mistake (have = tener), but the helper is always haber. "Habemos" is not used in standard Spanish for this.

questions.stem: What is the past participle of "escribir" (to write)?
questions.explanation: "Escribir" has an irregular participle: "escrito" (he escrito, I have written). "Escribido" follows the regular -ido rule, which this verb doesn't use. "Escribo" is the present (I write).

questions.stem: Which sentence is correct?
questions.explanation: Nothing goes between haber and the participle, so "nunca" goes before: "Nunca he comido mole." The helper is haber, not tener, and the participle doesn't agree with "mole" or anything else: always "comido".

questions.stem: A friend in Mexico City asks what you had for lunch today. Which answer sounds most natural in Mexico?
questions.explanation: In Mexico a finished event takes the preterite, even when it happened today: "Hoy comí tacos." "Hoy he comido tacos" is what most people in Spain would say; it's correct Spanish, but less usual in Mexico. "Ayer he comido" isn't standard anywhere, because "ayer" is a finished time.

questions.stem: "¿Has probado el pozole?" You haven't, but you want to. What do you answer?
questions.explanation: "Todavía no" means "not yet": it hasn't happened, but it may. "Ya no" means "not any more", which doesn't fit something you've never done. "Alguna vez" (ever) and "hasta ahora" (so far) aren't answers on their own.

questions.stem: Complete: "Mis hermanas ya han ___ de Cancún." (volver)
questions.explanation: "Volver" has the irregular participle "vuelto". After haber the participle never agrees with the subject, so it stays "vuelto" even with "mis hermanas"; "vueltas" and "volvidas" add an agreement that the perfect doesn't have.

questions.stem: Complete: "Mi papá ___ que la comida está lista." (decir, present)
questions.explanation: The present of decir is digo, dices, dice…: for "mi papá" (él), "dice". "Dije" is "I said", "dicho" is the participle (he dicho), and "decí" is not a standard form in Mexico.

questions.stem: Which of these participles are irregular? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: "Hecho" (hacer), "visto" (ver) and "roto" (romper) are irregular. "Comido" and "hablado" follow the regular rule: -er → -ido, -ar → -ado.

questions.stem: Complete with the present perfect of "ver" (tú form): "¿Alguna vez ___ un volcán?"
questions.explanation: Haber for tú is "has", and the participle of ver is irregular: "visto". Together: "¿Alguna vez has visto un volcán?" (Have you ever seen a volcano?)

questions.stem: Put the conversation in order.
questions.explanation: The perfect asks about the experience (¿Has estado alguna vez…? — Sí, una vez). Once the conversation asks when, it switches to the preterite: ¿Cuándo fuiste? — Fui en 2022.

questions.stem: Build the sentence in Spanish.
questions.prompt: I have never ridden a horse.
questions.explanation: "Nunca" goes before the whole perfect, and nothing comes between "he" and "montado": "Nunca he montado a caballo." The helper is haber (he), not tener.

questions.stem: Build the sentence in Spanish.
questions.prompt: We haven't finished the course yet.
questions.explanation: "Todavía no" (not yet) goes before haber: "Todavía no hemos terminado el curso." The participle never takes a plural ending, so "terminados" is wrong.

questions.stem: In Latin American Spanish, which past form goes with each time expression?
questions.explanation: Expressions of a finished time (ayer, hace dos años, en 2019) take the preterite. Experience up to now (alguna vez) and "not yet" (todavía no) take the present perfect, in Latin America as in Spain.

questions.stem: Complete: "padres ___ hijos" (parents and children)
questions.explanation: "Y" becomes "e" before a word that starts with the sound i (i- or hi-): "padres e hijos". "U" is the form of "o" (or) before an o sound.

questions.stem: Complete: "¿Quieres siete ___ ocho tacos?" (or)
questions.explanation: "O" (or) becomes "u" before a word starting with the sound o: "siete u ocho". "Y" and "e" mean "and", which changes the meaning.

questions.stem: Which is the standard way to open a formal e-mail to Mr López?
questions.explanation: Formal messages open with "Estimado/Estimada …" followed by a colon. The comma is copied from English. "Querido" is for people you know well, and "Hola" with double exclamation marks is chat style.

questions.stem: Complete: "Creo ___ el museo está cerrado hoy."
questions.explanation: "Creo que" (I think that) introduces an opinion, and the "que" can't be left out. It has no accent: "qué" with an accent is the question word "what?".

questions.stem: Complete: "___ llegué a casa, llamé a mi mamá."
questions.explanation: "Cuando" without an accent joins two events: "When I got home, I called my mom." "Cuándo" with an accent is only for questions (¿Cuándo llegaste?).

questions.stem:
Read the message.
"Hola, Marta: Gracias por la invitación. Lo siento, pero el sábado no puedo ir a tu fiesta porque tengo que trabajar. Además, el domingo tengo examen. ¡Felicidades por tu nuevo trabajo! Un abrazo, Tomás" Why is Tomás writing?
choices: To invite Marta to his party
To ask Marta for help with an exam
To say he has a new job
To say he can't come to Marta's party
questions.explanation: "Lo siento, pero el sábado no puedo ir a tu fiesta" (I'm sorry, but I can't come to your party on Saturday): he's declining Marta's invitation, because he has to work. The new job is Marta's (tu nuevo trabajo), not his.

questions.stem: On a form, what does "Estado civil" ask for?
questions.explanation: "Estado civil" is marital status: soltero/soltera (single), casado/casada (married). Nationality is "nacionalidad".

questions.stem: Which are suitable closings for a formal e-mail? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: "Atentamente" and "Saludos cordiales" close formal messages. "Un abrazo" (a hug) is for friends, and "Besos" (kisses) only for family and close friends.

questions.stem: Write the connector that means "what's more" or "besides": "El hotel es barato. ___, está cerca de la playa."
questions.explanation: "Además" adds an extra point, often at the start of a new sentence and followed by a comma. It ends in a stressed -ás, so it needs the written accent.

questions.stem: Emily filled in this form. Which field does each numbered answer belong to?

image.alt: A language school registration form. Some field names are missing and numbered: 1 next to 14/02/1990, 2 next to canadiense, 3 next to soltera, 4 next to 06700, 5 next to a signature.

questions.explanation: 14/02/1990 is a date of birth (day/month/year), canadiense a nationality, soltera a marital status (estado civil), 06700 a Mexican postal code (five digits), and the scribble a signature (firma).

questions.stem: Name the numbered parts of this e-mail.

image.alt: An informal e-mail with four numbered parts: 1 "Querida Sofía:", 2 three sentences about a trip to Oaxaca, 3 "Un abrazo,", 4 "Lucía".

questions.explanation: A message has a greeting (el saludo: Querida Sofía:), a body (el cuerpo), a closing phrase (la despedida: Un abrazo,) and the name or signature (la firma: Lucía).

questions.stem: Build the sentence in Spanish.
questions.prompt: I think it's going to rain.
questions.explanation: "Creo que" + the opinion, with "que" (no accent) always written: "Creo que va a llover." "Qué" with an accent is the question word.

questions.stem: Build the sentence in Spanish.
questions.prompt: I'm sorry, I can't go to the party.
questions.explanation: "Lo siento" is the phrase for bad news or saying no: "Lo siento, no puedo ir a la fiesta." "Perdón" is "excuse me" or a quick "sorry" when you bump into someone.

questions.stem: How long is the reading test (Comprensión de lectura) of the DELE A1?
questions.explanation: Reading takes 45 minutes. Listening and writing take 25 minutes each, and speaking 10 minutes after 10 minutes to prepare (official exam guide, version 2020).

questions.stem: A candidate gets 40 of 50 points in group 1 (reading + writing) and 27 of 50 in group 2 (listening + speaking). What is the result?
choices: No apto, because group 2 is under 30
Apto, because the average is over 30
No apto, because the total is under 70
questions.explanation: The DELE A1 has no overall pass mark: you need at least 30 points in each group. Group 2 has only 27, so the result is No apto, even though the total (67) looks good.

questions.stem: Complete: "No hay ___ en la oficina." (There's nobody in the office.)
questions.explanation: "Nadie" is nobody. After the verb it comes with "no" before the verb: "No hay nadie." "Alguien" is somebody, "algo" something, "todo" everything.

questions.stem: Which sentence means "I don't see anything"?
questions.explanation: Spanish uses a double negative: "no" before the verb and "nada" after it. "No veo algo" copies English "anything" with "algo", which is wrong here. If "nada" comes first, there's no "no": "Nada veo" is possible but rare; "Nada no veo" is wrong.

questions.stem: Someone uses the word "cemita" and you don't know it. What do you ask?
questions.explanation: "¿Qué significa…?" asks what a word means. "¿Cómo se dice…?" is the other way round: how do you say an English word in Spanish. "¿Qué es significa" mixes two questions.

questions.stem: An exam instruction says: "Elija la opción correcta." What should you do?
questions.explanation: "Elija" is the usted command of elegir (to choose): "Choose the correct option." "Explique" would be "explain", "Complete" is "complete".

questions.stem: Can you answer the DELE A1 in Latin American Spanish?
choices: No: only Spain's Spanish is accepted.
Yes: any standard variety used consistently is accepted.
Only if you also use vosotros.
questions.explanation: The official guide says any standard variety of Spanish is valid in your answers, as long as you use it consistently. The exam's own texts are mostly based on Spain's Spanish, so recognize vosotros and Spain's words, but you don't need to use them.

questions.stem: Which DELE A1 tests are in group 2? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Group 2 is listening + speaking (50 points); group 1 is reading + writing (50 points). You need at least 30 points in each group.

questions.stem: Match each DELE A1 test to its time.
questions.explanation: Reading 45 minutes, listening 25, writing 25, and speaking 10 minutes, with 10 minutes to prepare beforehand.

questions.stem: Complete with the present of "elegir": "Yo siempre ___ la opción más fácil."
questions.explanation: "Elegir" changes e → i, and g becomes j before o to keep the sound: "elijo". The other forms are eliges, elige, elegimos, eligen.

questions.stem: Build the sentence in Spanish.
questions.prompt: Nobody understood anything.
questions.explanation: "Nadie" comes first, so no "no" is needed before the verb; "nada" after the verb completes the double negative: "Nadie entendió nada." "Algo" would mean "something".

questions.stem: Build the sentence in Spanish.
questions.prompt: I don't understand what this word means.
questions.explanation: "No entiendo qué significa esta palabra." The "qué" keeps its accent because it still asks "what", inside a longer sentence (as in "no sé qué es", lesson 23).

questions.stem: Review (lesson 09): "La fiesta ___ en mi casa."
questions.explanation: Events take ser for where they take place: "La fiesta es en mi casa." Estar gives the location of people and things (La casa está en el centro), so "está" is the classic mistake here.

questions.stem: Complete: "Anoche mis amigos ___ un pastel." (traer)
questions.explanation: "Traer" has the strong stem traj-, and after j the ellos ending is -eron: "trajeron". "Trajieron" adds an i that verbs with j-stems (dijeron, trajeron) drop.

questions.stem: Complete: "Yo ___ la mesa para la cena." (poner)
questions.explanation: "Poner" has the strong stem pus-: puse, pusiste, puso. Strong forms have no accent, so "pusé" is wrong, and "poní" and "ponió" use the infinitive stem.

questions.stem: What does "Ayer supe que Ana está en México" mean?
choices: Yesterday I knew that Ana is in Mexico.
Yesterday I wanted Ana to be in Mexico.
Yesterday I can't believe Ana is in Mexico.
Yesterday I found out that Ana is in Mexico.
questions.explanation: In the preterite, saber points to the moment you came to know something: "supe" = I found out, I learned.

questions.stem: What does "El niño no quiso comer" mean?
questions.explanation: "No quiso" (preterite of querer with no) describes a refusal at a moment: the boy refused to eat. "Couldn't eat" would be "no pudo comer".

questions.stem: In the story "La tormenta", why did the narrator almost cry on the bus?
choices: Paola got lost in the storm.
Her backpack, with her phone, was still by the river.
questions.explanation: "Supe que mi celular estaba en la mochila… y la mochila, en la piedra junto al río. Casi lloré." She realized her phone was in the backpack she had left on a rock by the river.

questions.stem: In the story, who brought the backpack to Cuernavaca?
questions.explanation: "Su hijo encontró la mochila, y el lunes me la trajo a Cuernavaca": the woman's son found it and brought it. The woman (la señora) phoned Paola.

questions.stem: In "Era de noche y hacía frío. De repente, alguien abrió la puerta," which verb tells the event?
questions.explanation: "Abrió" (preterite) is the action that happened. "Era" and "hacía" are imperfect forms that describe the scene: it was night, it was cold. "De repente" is an adverb (suddenly), not a verb.

questions.stem: Complete: "Esperamos el camión durante una hora. ¡___ llegó!"
questions.explanation: "Por fin" (at last) shows relief after waiting. "Al principio" (at first) opens a story, and "anteayer" and "hace" don't fit after an hour of waiting.

questions.stem: Complete with the preterite of "decir": "Ellos nos ___ la verdad."
questions.explanation: "Decir" has the stem dij-, and after j the ellos ending is -eron: "dijeron" (not "dijieron").

questions.stem: Match each verb to its yo form in the preterite.
questions.explanation: All five are strong preterites: new stem + -e, with no accent: quis-e, pus-e, sup-e, dij-e, traj-e.

questions.stem: Put these events from "La tormenta" in the order they happened.
choices: Paola y la narradora llegaron a la cascada.
Una señora abrió la puerta de su casa.
El hijo de la señora encontró la mochila.
questions.explanation: They reached the waterfall, then the storm started, then a woman opened her door to them, and later her son found the backpack by the river.

questions.stem: Which of these verbs from the story are imperfect forms (background)? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: "Hacía" (sol), "era" (bonito) and "estaba" (asustada) describe how things were: imperfect. "Llegamos" and "abrió" are preterite events.

questions.stem: Build the sentence in Spanish.
questions.prompt: At first I didn't understand anything.
questions.explanation: "Al principio no entendí nada." "No … nada" is the double negative from lesson 24, and the time phrase can also go at the end.

questions.stem: In a chat, what does "xq" stand for?
questions.explanation: "Xq" is "porque" (because) or "por qué" (why): x stands for "por" and q for "que". "Por favor" is written "x fa".

questions.stem: Why does "x" stand for "por" in Spanish chat shorthand?
choices: Because the letter x is called "por".
Because the multiplication sign × is read "por".
questions.explanation: In Spanish, "dos × tres" is read "dos por tres", so × (and x) stands for "por": xq = porque, x fa = por favor.

questions.stem: Which request fits a formal e-mail to a landlord?
choices: ¿Me mandas a un técnico x fa?
¿Puede mandar a un técnico esta semana?
questions.explanation: A formal e-mail uses usted (¿Puede…?) and full words. The other three use tú, chat shorthand or a blunt command.

questions.stem: A woman ends a formal e-mail. Which line is correct?
questions.explanation: "Atento" agrees with the writer: a woman writes "atenta". In a formal e-mail "your" is "su" (usted), not "tu".

questions.stem: Complete: "La estufa no ___ desde el lunes."
questions.explanation: Machines "funcionan": "La estufa no funciona" (the stove doesn't work). People "trabajan". "Descompuesta" is an adjective (out of order) and would need "está".

questions.stem: In Mexico, what does "El refri está descompuesto" mean?
choices: The fridge is out of order.
questions.explanation: "Descompuesto" is the Mexican word for a machine that has stopped working (Spain: estropeado). "El refri" is short for el refrigerador.

questions.stem: The task: write to Marcos, greet him, say what you did last weekend, invite him to do something on Saturday, and say goodbye. An answer: "Querido Marcos: ¿Qué tal? El fin de semana pasado fui a Puebla y comí mole. ¡La pasé muy bien! Un abrazo, Ana" Which point is missing?
questions.explanation: The greeting (Querido Marcos: ¿Qué tal?), last weekend (fui, comí, la pasé) and the goodbye (Un abrazo) are there, but there's no invitation for Saturday, such as "¿Quieres ir al cine el sábado?"

questions.stem: On a form, what do you write in "Fecha de nacimiento" if you were born on 9 July 1992?
questions.explanation: Forms in Mexico and Spain write day/month/year: 09/07/1992. "07/09/1992" is the US order and would be read as the 7th of September.

questions.stem: Write the chat shorthand "ntp" in full Spanish.
questions.explanation: "Ntp" = "no te preocupes" (don't worry).

questions.stem: Match each chat abbreviation to its full form.
questions.explanation: q = que, tmb = también, x fa = por favor, bn = bien, tqm = te quiero mucho. Recognize them, but don't use them in formal writing.

questions.stem: Put the parts of this formal e-mail in order.
choices: Le escribo porque la estufa no funciona.
¿Puede mandar a un técnico esta semana?
questions.explanation: Subject line, greeting with a colon, the reason for writing, the request, the closing line, and finally the sign-off with your name.

questions.stem: Which of these should you NOT write in the DELE writing test? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Chat shorthand and chat laughter (xq, x fa, jaja) don't belong in the exam. "Querido Marcos:" and "Un abrazo," are the correct frame for an informal message.

questions.stem: Build the sentence in Spanish (formal, to usted).
questions.prompt: I'm attaching a photo.
questions.explanation: "Le adjunto una foto" (le = to you, for usted). "Adjunto una foto" without "le" is also fine. "Te" would be informal (tú).

cards.front: Official days off in Mexico (LFT art. 74)
cards.back: 1 January; first Monday of February (Constitution); third Monday of March (Juárez); 1 May; 16 September; third Monday of November (Revolution); 25 December. Also election days and 1 October every six years.
Independence Day (1810). The Grito, ¡Viva México!, is on the night of the 15th; the parade and the day off on the 16th.
6 January: the Three Kings bring presents in many families; everyone shares a rosca de reyes. Whoever finds the figure brings tamales on 2 February (la Candelaria).
Nine nights, 16–24 December: guests sing to ask for lodging (pedir posada), then a party with a piñata and ponche.
Christmas Eve (24 December, big late dinner) / Christmas (25 December).
Holidays yes (la Navidad, la Semana Santa), months no: el 25 de diciembre. Day before month.
From the end of October to 2 November. In much of Mexico 1 November is for children, 2 November for adults. UNESCO intangible heritage list, 2008.
velas, flores de cempasúchil, pan de muerto, papel picado, calaveras de azúcar, photos, favourite food and drink, water and salt.
Mexican marigold (Tagetes erecta). From Nahuatl cempohualxochitl, usually explained as "twenty flower". Its petals mark the path home for the souls.
the cemetery (Mexico); everywhere: el cementerio. Families clean and decorate the graves for Día de Muertos.
ayer, el año pasado → preterite; hoy, todos los años → present; mañana, el 2 de noviembre → ir a + infinitive; alguna vez, nunca → perfect.
Pusimos… Find the infinitive after vamos a and give its preterite: vamos a ir → fuimos; va a cocinar → cocinó.
About 9.2 million people in the city (2020 census), more than 20 million in the metropolitan area; about 2,240 m above sea level.
The Mexica (Aztec) capital, traditionally founded in 1325 on an island in a lake; taken by Spanish forces in 1521. Mexico City was built on top of it.
The capital was officially el Distrito Federal until 2016; now la Ciudad de México (CDMX). People: capitalinos, informally chilangos.
North side: la Catedral Metropolitana. East side: el Palacio Nacional (Diego Rivera murals). North-east: el Templo Mayor. West, along calle Madero: la Torre Latinoamericana.
Where is…? (places): Queda al lado de la catedral. Not quedarse (to stay): Me quedo en Coyoacán.
e → ie: recomiendo, recomiendas, recomienda, recomendamos, recomiendan. Te recomiendo el museo.
el siglo veinte, the twentieth century. Centuries use Roman numerals, read as numbers.
Read once for the main idea, then for details. Find the time marker before the verb: hoy, ayer, esta semana, la próxima semana.
Both look the same for -ar and -ir verbs with nosotros. The time marker decides: hoy en la mañana (over), ayer → preterite.
Find the entry and the sentence, look for porque or a colon, answer with Porque… and change the person: estoy → está.
A traditional story, often explaining something real (a mountain, a bird, a city). It changes from telling to telling; no version is the only true one.
"smoking mountain" (active; nicknamed Don Goyo) / "white woman" (la Mujer Dormida). Two volcanoes south-east of Mexico City, both over 5,000 m.

cards.front: The volcano legend in one line
cards.back: A warrior and a princess fall in love; he goes to war; she dies (of a lie or of sadness); he lays her on a mountain and keeps watch; the gods turn them into volcanoes.
The gods, with no clay or corn left, make a tiny jade arrow and blow on it: the hummingbird, which carries people's wishes and thoughts.
The Mexica settled where they saw an eagle on a nopal cactus eating a snake. The scene is on the Mexican flag.
to fall in love with: Se enamoró de un guerrero (de, not con). Se enamoraron = they fell in love.
Once upon a time… (había = there was). Also: Hace muchos siglos… (many centuries ago).
Telling a past story in the present: Los dioses crean el mundo. Common in retellings and summaries.
hicieron / voló / fue. -ar verbs never change their stem in the preterite (volar → voló).
murió, murieron (o → u, like durmió). Participle: muerto.
Census Bureau: 70.1 million Hispanic people (1 July 2025, about 21%); nearly 45 million people aged 5+ speak Spanish at home (2024).
St. Augustine, Florida (1565); Santa Fe, New Mexico (about 1610); much of the Southwest was Mexican until 1848.

cards.front: Spanish place names in the US
cards.back: Florida (flowery), Colorado (red, reddish), Nevada (snowy), Montana (montaña), Los Ángeles, Las Vegas (the meadows), El Paso.
Designated English as the official language of the US; agencies are not required to stop offering material in other languages.
code-switching (moving between the languages: Tengo un meeting mañana) and adapted loanwords (parquear, la troca, el lonche).
pregnant (NOT embarrassed: avergonzado; Mexico: me da pena)
success (exit = la salida) / folder (carpet = la alfombra)
bookshop / library
current / currently (actually = en realidad)
to carry out, make happen / to realize: Me di cuenta de mi error.
Push / Pull: usted commands of empujar and jalar. Spain: Tire (tirar) for pull.
usted command (Empuje, Espere aquí), no + infinitive (No fumar, No estacionarse), a phrase (Salida, Piso mojado, Peligro).
a, e, i, o, u: short, pure, always pronounced the same (no gliding, no "uh"). Only the u in que, qui, gue, gui is silent.
Always silent: hola = "OH-lah", hasta = "AHS-tah".

cards.front: j, and g before e or i
cards.back: A breathy "h" from the throat: jota, gente. Elsewhere g is hard (gracias); gu before e/i is hard g (guitarra), gü = "gw".
s, z and c before e/i all sound like "s" in Latin America: sí, zeta, cinco.
ll and y sound the same, like English "y": me llamo, yo.
Single r inside or at the end of a word = one tap (pero, favor). rr, or r at the start of a word or after l, n, s = rolled (perro, Roberto, Enrique).
Ends in a vowel, n or s → stress the second-to-last syllable (HO-la). Other consonant → last syllable (fa-VOR). Breaks the rule → written accent (adiós, lápiz).

cards.front: sí / si, tú / tu, él / el
cards.back: yes / if, you / your, he / the. The accent changes the word.

cards.front: B and V names in Mexico
cards.back: be grande (b) and ve chica (v); they sound the same. Spain: be and uve.
perdón (sorry), disculpe (to get attention), con permiso (to get past or leave).
¿Puede repetir, por favor? Más despacio. Otra vez. ¿Cómo se escribe? (In Mexico you'll hear ¿Mande?)

cards.front: buenos días / buenas tardes / buenas noches
cards.back: Morning until about midday / afternoon until dark / after dark (also goodbye at night).
tú: friends, family, children, people your age. usted: strangers, older people, work, officials. Not sure? usted.
yo soy, tú eres, usted es, él/ella es.
¿De dónde eres? (tú) / ¿De dónde es usted? — Soy de Denver.
¿Cómo te llamas? (tú) / ¿Cómo se llama usted? — Me llamo Laura.
Mucho gusto. Encantado (man) / Encantada (woman). Reply: Igualmente.
¿Qué tal? ¿Cómo estás? ¿Cómo está usted? — muy bien, bien, más o menos, mal. ¿Y tú? / ¿Y usted?
With the article when you talk about someone (el señor López); without it when you talk to them (Buenos días, señor López).
who, how, where, where from. Question words carry an accent.
One word: dieciséis, diecisiete…, veintiuno, veintidós… Accents on dieciséis, veintidós, veintitrés, veintiséis.
Ten + y + unit, three words: treinta y uno, cuarenta y cinco, noventa y nueve.
60 (ses- like seis) vs 70 (set- like siete).
cien = exactly 100 (cien años); ciento before more numbers (ciento uno).
un (masculine), una (feminine): un año, una letra, veintiún años.
¿Cuántos años tienes? — Tengo treinta años. (Never "soy treinta"; always años with ñ.)
Ten digits, read in pairs: 55 12 34 07 80 = cincuenta y cinco, doce, treinta y cuatro, cero siete, ochenta.
@ = arroba, . = punto, _ = guion bajo, - = guion.
Ask for a number, name or address with cuál, not qué.
yo, tú, usted, él, ella; nosotros/nosotras, ustedes, ellos, ellas. (vosotros: Spain only)
ellas only for all-female groups; any mixed group is ellos.
The only plural "you" in Latin America; takes the ellos form: ustedes hablan.
-o, -as, -a, -amos, (-áis), -an: hablo, hablas, habla, hablamos, hablan.
The ending shows the person: Hablo inglés. Use the pronoun for contrast: Yo estudio, pero él trabaja.
no right before the verb: No hablo francés. ¿Estudias? — No, no estudio.
Same words as a statement, rising voice, ¿…?: ¿Hablas español? No "do" word.
¿Por qué? (two words, accent) = why? Porque (one word) = because.
No preposition: busco la oficina, escucho música, miro el mapa.
An s at the end of a syllable fades to a breath or disappears: ¿Cómo estás? → "KOH-mo eh-TAH".

cards.front: Río de la Plata ll and y
cards.back: Said "sh" (or "zh"): me llamo → "meh SHAH-mo", yo → "sho".
Río de la Plata forms of tú eres, tú hablas. Recognize them; keep using tú.
Argentina, Uruguay, Paraguay and much of Central America, plus parts of Colombia, Venezuela and Chile.
z and ce, ci like English "th"; s stays "s". Not a lisp: casa ≠ caza.
Spain's informal "you all": ¿Vosotros habláis inglés? Latin America says ustedes.
Crisp consonants and a clear s; some areas have a buzzing rr ("zh") and keep ll distinct from y.
Mexico ¿Bueno? · Peru, Chile, Venezuela ¿Aló? · Spain ¿Diga? / ¿Dígame? · Argentina, Uruguay ¿Hola?
Who's calling? — De parte de Kate.
Número equivocado. colgar (cuelgo, cuelgas…): to hang up.
nombre(s) + apellido paterno + apellido materno: María Fernanda López Ortiz.

cards.front: Which surnames does a child get?
cards.back: Usually the first surname of each parent, the father's first: López (father) + Ortiz (mother).

cards.front: Which surname is used every day?
cards.back: The first one: María Fernanda López Ortiz is la señora López.
Spain: parents choose since 2017. Mexico: father's first by tradition; courts let parents choose.
Sorted by the first surname: LÓPEZ ORTIZ, María Fernanda. Forms: Apellido paterno / Apellido materno / Nombre(s).
Respect for older people, before the first name: don Javier, doña Carmen. Not with a surname alone; in careful speech, not without a name.
Lic. (licenciado/a), Ing. (ingeniero/a), Arq. (arquitecto/a), Dr./Dra., Mtro./Mtra. Used with the surname or alone.
Shall we use tú? Usually offered by the older or senior person. Answer: ¡Claro!
Mexican way to say "call me tú".
usted among friends and family in parts of Colombia; warm, not distant.
el (m. sg.), la (f. sg.), los (m. pl. or mixed), las (f. pl.).
a/an (m.), a/an (f.), some (m.), some (f.).
-o usually masculine, -a usually feminine; -ción and -dad always feminine; -e or a consonant: learn it.
el mapa, el día, el problema, el idioma; la mano, la foto (short for la fotografía).
Vowel + s (libros); consonant + es (papeles, relojes); z → ces (lápices).
canción → canciones (accent goes), joven → jóvenes (accent comes), lápiz → lápices (stays).

cards.front: A mixed group of boys and girls
cards.back: Masculine plural: los niños.
Feminine, but el in the singular because of the stressed a-: el agua fría, las aguas.
What is this? — Es un reloj. / Son unos lentes.
tengo, tienes, tiene, tenemos, (tenéis), tienen.
tener … años: Tengo treinta años. ¿Cuántos años tienes?
soy, eres, es, somos, (sois), son.

cards.front: los padres, los hermanos, los abuelos
cards.back: parents; brothers or siblings; grandparents. In Mexico mis papás = my parents.
mi(s), tu(s), su(s), nuestro/a/os/as. The ending matches the thing owned.
His, her, its, their or your (usted, ustedes). For clarity: el perro de él / de ella / de usted.
la hermana de Ana. Spanish has no 's.
-o, -es, -e, -emos, (-éis), -en.
-o, -es, -e, -imos, (-ís), -en. Only nosotros (and vosotros) differ from -er.
Soy maestra. No article with a bare job.
mexicano/mexicana; español/española; canadiense, estadounidense (no change).
Countries yes (México); nationalities and languages no (mexicana, español).
estadounidense: neutral. Americano can mean anyone from the Americas.
Usually after the noun: un libro nuevo, una mochila roja.

cards.front: How many forms does an adjective have?
cards.back: -o: four (nuevo, nueva, nuevos, nuevas). -e or consonant: two (grande, grandes; azul, azules).
un buen amigo, un mal día (masculine singular only); gran before any singular noun = great: una gran ciudad.
very, quite, a bit (un poco with negative qualities: un poco aburrido).
Brown; same for both genders (una silla café); plural café or cafés (los ojos cafés). Spain: marrón.
False friends: largo = long (not large); simpático = nice, friendly.

cards.front: How many countries have Spanish as official or main language?
cards.back: 20 (usual count): 18 in the Americas, Spain and Equatorial Guinea. Plus Puerto Rico, a US territory.
Paraguay (Guaraní), Bolivia (Indigenous languages), Peru (Quechua, Aymara where predominant), Equatorial Guinea (French, Portuguese).
Mexico, Argentina, Chile, Uruguay: no law names an official language.
Same for men and women: nicaragüense, costarricense, canadiense, estadounidense.
hondureño, salvadoreño, panameño, puertorriqueño (rr inside).
From Guatemala (-teco, not -ano).
la capital = capital city; el capital = money invested.
Sucre by the constitution; the government sits in La Paz.
Ciudad de la Paz, by a decree of January 2026 (before: Malabo).
father-in-law, brother-in-law, son-in-law, daughter-in-law.
grandson (grandchild), nephew. Feminine nieta, sobrina.
godfather, godmother, godson.
What a child's parents and godparents call each other; also a close friend in Mexico.
perro → perrito, abuela → abuelita; -cito after -e, -n, -r: cafecito, amorcito.
chico → chiquito, amigo → amiguito, lápiz → lapicito.
No: el mapa → el mapita, el problema → el problemita.
mi hijo, mi hija: affectionate address from parents and older people.
José, Francisco, Guadalupe, Jesús, Guillermo.
estoy, estás, está, estamos, están (Spain: estáis). Write the accents.
¿Dónde está el baño? Location always takes estar, even for cities: Guadalajara está en México.

cards.front: Ser or estar? The A1 rule
cards.back: ser: identity, origin, job, what something is like, where an event takes place. estar: where someone or something is, feelings, conditions right now.

cards.front: The party is at my house.
cards.back: La fiesta es en mi casa. (An event takes ser for its place.)
es aburrido = is boring; está aburrido = is bored.
es listo = is clever; está listo = is ready.
Estoy cansada. The adjective agrees with the speaker.

cards.front: The shop is closed. The coffee is cold.
cards.back: La tienda está cerrada. El café está frío. (conditions right now: estar)
near / far from: Mi casa está cerca de la escuela. Alone: Está cerca. Está lejos.
with / without: café con leche, té sin azúcar (no article after sin).
there is / there are. One form only: Hay un sofá. Hay dos baños. No hay jardín.
hay + un/una, a number or no article (something new); está/están + el/la, mi… or a name (a known thing): Hay un sofá. El sofá está en la sala.
¿Cuántos cuartos hay? — Hay tres.

cards.front: on top of / under / next to
cards.back: encima de / debajo de / al lado de

cards.front: in front of, opposite / behind / between
cards.back: enfrente de / detrás de / entre (no de after entre)
del: al lado del sofá, cerca del centro. No change with la, los, las.
la cocina, la sala, el comedor, el baño, el cuarto (bedroom; also la recámara), la escalera, el jardín
departamento / piso; clóset / armario; refrigerador / nevera; estufa / cocina; renta, rentar / alquiler, alquilar
me gusta + one thing or an infinitive (me gusta el café, me gusta bailar); me gustan + several things (me gustan los tacos).
me, te, le, nos, les. Add a mí, a ti, a él… for emphasis: A mí me gusta, pero a él no.
A mí también (after yes). A mí tampoco (after no). Disagree: A mí no / A mí sí.
to love (a thing): me encanta / me encantan. Usually without mucho (it's already strong).
quiero, quieres, quiere, queremos, quieren (e → ie except nosotros)
Quisiera… (I would like…): Quisiera un café con leche, por favor.
Tengo hambre / Tengo sed. Very hungry: tengo mucha hambre (hambre is feminine).
food, and also the main meal of the day, usually in the early afternoon.
jugo / zumo; papa / patata; frijoles / judías; tortilla (corn flatbread) / tortilla (potato omelette)

cards.front: How much is it? / How much are they?
cards.back: ¿Cuánto cuesta? / ¿Cuánto cuestan? Total at the till: ¿Cuánto es?
cien alone or before a noun (cien pesos); ciento before another number (ciento veinte).
quinientos (500), setecientos (700), novecientos (900)
mil (never un mil; no plural: dos mil). un millón de pesos, dos millones de pesos.
Comma for thousands, point for centavos (like the US). Spain writes 1.250,50.
este, esta, estos, estas / ese, esa, esos, esas; without a noun: esto, eso
más barato que / tan caro como
mejor / peor (for quality, not más bueno, más malo)
otro café (never un otro)
desayuno in the morning; la comida, the main meal, about 2–4 pm; a light cena at night.
"A little craving": a corn-based snack such as a taco, quesadilla, sope or tamal.
Central and southern Mexico: el jitomate = red tomato; el tomate (verde) = green tomatillo. Elsewhere el tomate = red tomato.
un taco de pollo (main thing first, filling after de)

cards.front: Can I have…? / Could you bring me…?
cards.back: ¿Me da…? / ¿Me trae…? — ¿Me trae la cuenta, por favor?
¿Para aquí o para llevar?
A small, simple restaurant; its fixed-price set lunch with soup, rice, a main dish and the agua del día.
Enjoy your meal! Said to people eating, even strangers. Reply: Gracias.
la propina: about 10–15 % is a common guide; voluntary (Profeco).
aguacate, elote, jitomate, tomate, chile

cards.front: de la mañana or por la mañana?
cards.back: de la mañana / tarde / noche after a clock time (a las siete de la mañana); por la mañana (or en la mañana) without one.

cards.front: la mañana / mañana; la tarde / tarde

lunes, martes, miércoles, jueves, viernes, sábado, domingo.
Before the verb (Nunca trabajo) or after it with no before the verb (No trabajo nunca).

cards.back: Before a conjugated verb (Me levanto), or on the end of the infinitive (Voy a levantarme = Me voy a levantar). Never in between.

cards.back: despertarse (ie), levantarse, bañarse, lavarse, vestirse (i), irse, quedarse, acostarse (ue).

+ infinitive: antes de salir, después de bañarme (pronoun attached, matching the subject).

cards.front: el día hábil, la hora pico
cards.back: working day (Monday to Friday, not holidays); rush hour (Spain: la hora punta).
Sorry I'm late (literally "sorry for the delay"). puntual = punctual; en punto = sharp.
la liga, el campeonato, el estadio, el aficionado, el jugador, el gol (los goles), meter un gol.
Ganamos dos a uno. Pierden tres a cero. Empatan uno a uno.

cards.front: jugar al fútbol / jugar fútbol / jugar a fútbol
cards.back: Standard / accepted in Latin America (probably a calque of English) / not considered good usage (Spain, Catalan influence).
Top sport in parts of the Caribbean (Cuba, Dominican Republic, Puerto Rico, Venezuela); big in northern and south-eastern Mexico. el jonrón = home run.

Cumbia: Colombia's Caribbean coast, now huge in Mexico, Peru, Argentina. Salsa: New York, Cuban and Puerto Rican musicians, roots in Cuban son.
a la derecha = to the right; derecho = straight ahead (Spain: todo recto). Siga derecho y doble a la derecha.

cards.front: How do I get to the square? (and to the bank?)
cards.back: ¿Cómo llego a la plaza? ¿Cómo llego al banco? (a + el = al)
A city block, the normal unit for distance in Latin America: Está a dos cuadras. Spain: la manzana.

cards.front: How to make a tú command
cards.back: Use the él form of the present: toma, dobla, sigue, vuelve. Stem changes stay.
decir di, hacer haz, ir ve, poner pon, salir sal, ser sé, tener ten, venir ven.

cards.front: How to make an usted command
cards.back: yo present minus -o, plus -e (-ar verbs) or -a (-er, -ir verbs): tomo → tome, como → coma, sigo → siga, tengo → tenga.
-car → -que, -gar → -gue, -zar → -ce: busque, llegue, cruce.
ser sea, ir vaya, saber sepa, estar esté, dar dé.
Add -n to the usted command: tomen, sigan, crucen, vayan (recognition at A1).
All usted commands used as fixed phrases: excuse me, excuse me / listen, look, come in.

cards.front: by bus, by plane, on foot
cards.back: en autobús, en avión (en + vehicle, no article); a pie.
The everyday Mexican word for a bus (city or long-distance); also a truck. El autobús is understood everywhere.
To wait for the bus: no word for "for" after esperar.
Destination: el camión para Puebla. Purpose + infinitive: para viajar (in order to travel).
conocer (conozco): people and places (Conozco a Ana, Conozco Oaxaca). saber (sé): facts and skills (Sé dónde está, Sé manejar).

cards.front: boleto sencillo / de ida y vuelta
cards.back: One-way ticket / round-trip ticket (Mexico also: viaje redondo).
la habitación = a hotel room; el cuarto = a room in a house.
el + number + de + month: el 5 de mayo, el 16 de septiembre de 2026. Months lowercase; no word for "on".

cards.front: The first of May (Mexico vs Spain)
cards.back: Mexico and most of Latin America: el primero de mayo. Spain: usually el uno de mayo.
dos mil veintiséis; mil novecientos noventa y nueve (whole numbers, never pairs).
Hace calor, frío, sol, viento, buen tiempo, mal tiempo. Very = mucho: Hace mucho calor.

cards.front: It rains. It snows. It's cloudy.
cards.back: Llueve. Nieva. Está nublado. (llover o → ue, nevar e → ie; no subject)

cards.front: Hace frío / Tengo frío / Está frío
cards.back: The weather is cold / I (a person) am cold / it (a thing) is cold.
la temporada de lluvias: in most of the country about May or June to October; the rest of the year is la temporada de secas.

cards.back: Me duele la cabeza. Me duelen los pies. (doler works like gustar)

cards.back: la playera / la camiseta; la chamarra / la chaqueta; los tenis / las zapatillas.
Mexico and Colombia: the flu (and, in Mexico, a bad cold). Most other countries: la gripe.

A taxi from a stand with a base / a taxi hailed in the street.
Mexico City's four long-distance bus stations: east (TAPO), north, south (Taxqueña), west (Observatorio).
Calle + número exterior, Int. (inside number), Col. (colonia), C.P. (5-digit postcode), city or alcaldía, state.
sin número (no number); esquina (corner of); between … and … (the cross streets).
¿Dónde me bajo? (for the museum: ¿Dónde me bajo para el museo?)

cards.back: Tengo tos y me duele la garganta.
Soy alérgico/alérgica a la penicilina. / Tengo alergia a la penicilina.
For two days (answer to ¿Desde cuándo?).
A prescription (also a recipe). In Mexico antibiotics are sold only with a receta (since 2010).
Every 8 hours, i.e. three times a day.

cards.front: No se deje al alcance de los niños

911, nationwide since January 2017. Hospital emergency department: Urgencias.
False friend (Spain): to have a cold. "Constipated" is estreñido.
é, aste, ó, amos, aron: hablé, hablaste, habló, hablamos, hablaron
í, iste, ió, imos, ieron: comí, comiste, comió, comimos, comieron
hablo = I speak (present); habló = he/she/you (usted) spoke. The accent changes the meaning.
-qué, -gué, -cé: busqué, llegué, empecé. Only the yo form changes.
fui, fuiste, fue, fuimos, fueron (the same for both; the sentence tells you which)
tener tuv-, estar estuv-, poder pud-, venir vin-, hacer hic- (hizo); endings -e, -iste, -o, -imos, -ieron, no accents
di, diste, dio, dimos, dieron; vi, viste, vio, vimos, vieron (no accents)
Only él and ellos change, e → i or o → u: pidió, pidieron; durmió, durmieron
hace dos días (hace comes first)
la semana pasada / el año pasado (pasado agrees with the noun)

cards.front: Present perfect: how is it built?

-ar → -ado (hablado); -er, -ir → -ido (comido, vivido); leído, oído, creído with an accent
hecho, dicho, visto, puesto, escrito, abierto, vuelto, roto

cards.front: Hoy comí or hoy he comido?
cards.back: Mexico and most of Latin America: hoy comí (preterite). Spain often: hoy he comido.

cards.back: Experiences up to now (¿Has probado el mole?) and ya / todavía no.
todavía no: Todavía no he terminado.
digo, dices, dice; dije, dijo, dijeron; dicho; tú command di

elijo, eliges, elige…; eligió, eligieron
querer quise, poner puse, saber supe, decir dije, traer traje
After a j-stem the ellos ending is -eron, not -ieron.

traer = bring (toward the speaker); llevar = take (away)

cards.back: Preterite tells the events; imperfect describes the background.

cards.back: Quedo atento / atenta a su respuesta.
